docs.title: GlitchyGames Getting Started
docs.text:
GlitchyGames is a wrapper around Pygame for games that run at 60 FPS on Raspberry Pi and other low powered Linux systems. Requirements shows what each measured machine runs today: at 60 FPS's 16.7 ms frame budget, the Raspberry Pi 5 runs every game measured, and the Raspberry Pi 4 every game but Brave Adventurer, which fits a 30 FPS target there.

The engine is written to provide:

  • Readability as a first principle
  • Scene primitives
  • Advanced event handling
  • Human readable/editable sprite file formats

docs.title: Example Game
docs.text:
Let's make a new game called Bitrot Adventures.

The goal of our game will be to draw a pixel on the screen and handle key events to move the pixel around.

bitrot_adventures.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Bitrot Adventures: a pixel on the screen that the arrow keys move."""

import pygame

from glitchygames.engine import GameEngine
from glitchygames.input import ActionMap
from glitchygames.scenes import Scene
from glitchygames.sprites import Sprite
from glitchygames.world import CoordinateSpace

PIXELS_PER_SECOND = 60.0
# Each direction is a physical key position (a scancode): the same place on every layout
ARROW_KEYS = {
    'left': pygame.KSCAN_LEFT,
    'right': pygame.KSCAN_RIGHT,
    'up': pygame.KSCAN_UP,
    'down': pygame.KSCAN_DOWN,
}


class Pixel(Sprite):
    """One white pixel. A world sprite: the game moves world_x and world_y, the engine draws it."""

    COORDINATE_SPACE = CoordinateSpace.WORLD

    def __init__(self, *, x, y, groups):
        super().__init__(x=x, y=y, width=1, height=1, name='Pixel', groups=groups)
        self.image.fill('white')
        self.world_x = x
        self.world_y = y


class BitrotAdventures(Scene):
    """A pixel on a black screen, moved by the arrow keys."""

    NAME = 'Bitrot Adventures'
    VERSION = '0.0.0'

    def __init__(self, options=None, groups=None):
        super().__init__(options=options, groups=groups)
        self.background_color = (0, 0, 0)
        width, height = self.screen.get_size()
        self.pixel = Pixel(x=width // 2, y=height // 2, groups=self.all_sprites)
        self.actions = ActionMap.from_engine_options(self.options)
        for direction, scancode in ARROW_KEYS.items():
            self.actions.bind(direction, scancode=scancode)

    def dt_tick(self, dt):
        """Game logic: move the pixel while an arrow key is held."""
        super().dt_tick(dt)
        step = PIXELS_PER_SECOND * dt
        if self.actions.is_held('left'):
            self.pixel.world_x -= step
        if self.actions.is_held('right'):
            self.pixel.world_x += step
        if self.actions.is_held('up'):
            self.pixel.world_y -= step
        if self.actions.is_held('down'):
            self.pixel.world_y += step
        # This frame's key events come after dt_tick
        self.actions.begin_frame()

    def on_key_down_event(self, event):
        self.actions.handle_event(event)

    def on_key_up_event(self, event):
        self.actions.handle_event(event)
        # The base scene quits on Escape or Q
        super().on_key_up_event(event)


def main():
    # Pass the Scene class uninitialized; the engine creates it
    GameEngine(game=BitrotAdventures).start()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Galimore (1998–2001): what it is and how its tools work
docs.text:
A survey of the Galimore project (1998–2001), the author's earlier game and its tools, made on 2026-10-18 to inform GlitchyGames' level tools (plans/2026-10-18-level-tools.md).

Conventions: SRC/ = the original files (galimore_files/, kept outside this repository); X/ = where the survey extracted each archive (one directory per archive). [read] = read directly in a file; [inferred] = concluded from sizes, layouts or context. R/ = PNG renders the survey decoded from the original data with a small read-only decoder, used to confirm the binary layouts below (the decoder and renders are not in this repository). Nothing from the archives was executed.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Not a Mac game. Galimore is a top-down tile RPG ("similar to Final Fantasy 3 (English) or Zelda", Galimore Clean Up/Old Galimore Folder/Galimore Archive/public_html copy/index.html) [read] for MS-DOS, developed on an iMac (Photoshop 5.02 for art, Virtual PC for code: "Yeah, I'm using a Mac to write a PC game", public_html copy/development.html) [read]. Hence the resource forks, MacBinary .bin, CR line endings and ƒ folder names.
  • Two engine generations:
  • 1999, Borland C++ 16-bit DOS: BGI SVGA256.BGI, 256 colours, XMS. A playable GALIMORE.EXE plus tools GEDIT, GMAP, GATTRIB, MAKEDAT, GTORAW/RAWTOG (X/CU_galisource072399/) [read].
  • Aug 1999 – Aug 2000, DJGPP (gcc 2.8.1) + Allegro 3.9.32 WIP, 640×480 at 16/15-bit colour. Only the toolchain exists: Galibmap (bitmap/sprite editor), Mapedit (map editor), Galimake (data packer) and a fire-effect demo. The new game was "Not yet started, but should use most of the mapeditor engine" (development.html) [read].
  • Successor: in Aug 2000 the code was relicensed (LGPL) as "RPG Tools" / "Phosphor", a SourceForge map editor (Galimore/Old Galimore Folder/RPG Tools Code/) [read]; only headers and a Makefile exist (no rendering code; graphics were Allegro 2D, with no OpenGL anywhere).
  • Formats: every file is a raw fwrite dump of a C++ object: no header, no version, little-endian, compiler-specific padding. File type is detected purely by size (2332 / 49152 / 3072 / 4608 bytes). All are fully decoded in §2.

docs.title: 1.3 File counts (2,301 originals)
docs.text: Art: 845 .raw, 203 .fg, 192 .bg, 46 .gif, 26 .psp, 19 .psd, 14 .get, 3 .spr, 4 .big. Code: 297 .h, 293 .cpp, 75 .o, 25 .gpr + 25 .gdt (RHIDE), 14 .exe. Other: 34 .zip, 11 .map, 10 .dat, 19 .html, 8 .log, ~21 extension-less Mac sound files. .raw sizes: 675 × 3072 (32×32 RGB), 44 × 4608 (32×48 RGB), 118 × 768 (16×16 RGB), 4 × 6144, 4 × 4170.

docs.title: 1.4 Not extracted / unreadable / skipped
docs.text:
• Zip members inside ƒ folders failed ("Illegal byte sequence"); their unpacked copies were read.
  • 060400.zip member test<non-ASCII> (a 49,152 B sprite).
  • Nested gbe_4_17_00.zip, gme_4_17_00.zip, gali.zip (May 2000 archive).
  • No unar/lsar; no StuffIt/BinHex archives found in scope.
  • Sounds: data forks are 0 bytes; audio is only in resource forks (sfil, System 7 sound).
  • ClarisWorks design docs read via strings only (fragmentary).
  • .psd/.psp/.big identified, not viewed.
  • Skipped as personal: a personal page in public_html copy/ and an e-mail contacts file in RPG Tools Code/.

docs.title: 2. Tools and file formats
docs.text: All written with ofstream::write((char*)&obj, sizeof(obj)), little-endian x86.

docs.title: 2.1 Galibmap: bitmap and sprite editor (2000)
docs.text:
Sources src/galibmap.cpp, src/bmap_gui.cpp, src/gmore_raw.cpp, src/g_object.cpp, src/g_sprite.cpp; binary X/bitmap_Binary/galibmap.exe. - Space toggles object mode (8 frames of 32×32) and sprite mode (16 frames of 32×48). - 6× zoomed canvas: left-drag paints, right-drag eyedropper; drag frames in the strip to copy or reorder. - R/G/B sliders, three colour wells (C cycles, R replaces colour 2 with colour 1); New / Save / Load / Quit; keys 1–8, N, L, S, Esc. - Load branches purely on file_size: 2332 → object, 49152 → sprite, 3072 → raw tile, 4608 → raw sprite frame (the file browser filters by the same sizes).

GALIMORE_OBJECT (tile/object), 2332 bytes (.bg, .fg, .get): | Offset | Size | Field | |---|---|---| | 0 | 2048 | INT16 array[32][32], [x][y] (offset (x·32+y)·2), RGB565; 0xF81F = transparent | | 2048 | 21 | objectName | | 2069 | 1 | objectType | | 2070 | 1 | objectState | | 2071 | 1 | objectSpecial | | 2072 | 2 | objectIsUsableBy (UINT16) | | 2074 | 1 | objectWeight | | 2075 | 256 | objectDescription | | 2331 | 1 | pad |

The attribute block is all zeros in every shipped .dat (never authored).

GALIMORE_SPRITE, 49,152 bytes (.spr): 16 × short array[32][48], [x][y] RGB565. Frame plan (spriteguide.html): front / away / side × still / walk-R / walk-L, side mirrored → 9 used. pockets.spr uses 6 (rest grey).

RAW, 3072 / 4608 bytes (.raw): headerless 8-bit RGB, row-major, 32×32 or 32×48 (Photoshop Raw export). Pipeline: Photoshop → .raw → Galibmap → .bg/.fg/.get/.spr.

docs.title: 2.2 Galimake: data packer
docs.text: .dat = 2332-byte records back to back (58,300 = 25×2332, 67,628 = 29×2332, 4,664 = 2×2332). Stable tile IDs: maps store 1-based indices; on update Galimake loads the existing .dat, zeros (doesn't delete) records whose pixels no longer match a file, refreshes matches, and puts new tiles in the first blank slot, so map indices never shift.

docs.title: 2.3 Mapedit: map editor
docs.text:
Sources src/mapedit.cpp, src/mapeditor_gui.cpp, src/g_map.cpp, include/g_map.h. - 14×14 map view with scroll bars; 4×6 tile palette; layer tabs Fgnd / Bgnd / Obj / Spr / Mask; floor radios 1F / 2F with show-layer checkboxes; "Make a Mask" and "Eraser" (tile 0). - Brush sizes 1–4; s / l save / load; Esc quits. - Mask tab: drag to stamp, right-click to pick up; magenta = no mask, purple = current, black = other. - Mask bits: 0 LAYER_SWITCH, 1 UNPASSABLE_GOOD, 2 UNPASSABLE_BAD, 3 UNPASSABLE_NEUTRAL, 4 DEEP, 5 BRIDGE, 6 CHASM, 7 PUSHABLE, 8 TRANSPARENT. An older plan (g_mask.h, Dec 1999) added exits, burnable/bombable/freezable, hot/cold, anti-magic, death, door, soil, farmed, layer 2; "Mask Cases" planned a replacement tile in the upper 16 bits (e.g. burnt version) — never implemented.

GALIMORE_MAP, 114,692 bytes (arrays [floor][x][y]; verified by decoding house.map): | Offset | Size | Field | |---|---|---| | 0 | 1 | landscape (always 0) | | 1 | 8192 | UINT8 fgLayer[2][64][64] (N → record N-1 of fg.dat; 0 = empty) | | 8193 | 8192 | UINT8 bgLayer → bg.dat | | 16385 | 1 | pad | | 16386 | 16384 | UINT16 objectLayer → get.dat | | 32770 | 16384 | UINT16 spriteLayer (unimplemented) | | 49154 | 2 | pad | | 49156 | 65536 | UINT64 maskLayer |

64×64 cells per floor, 2 floors. Samples: house.map (cottage on grass, 14 fg tiles, 1 object, 40 fully-impassable mask cells), map.map (lattice test), test.map (18 cells of tile 1).

docs.title: 2.4 The 1999 tools
docs.text:
GEDIT (32×32, 256 colours, rotate/mirror/replace/transparent colour, 8-frame sprites); GMAP (15×15 maps, layer toggles, exits); GATTRIB (attributes); GTORAW / RAWTOG (bitmap ↔ RGB raw, palette as a switch). The two DOCs are swapped (GMAP.DOC documents GEDIT).

Bitmap, 1312 B bitmapSize, transparentImage, transparencyColor (default 15); byte array[32][32] palette indices [x][y]; attribs (name[21], 3 type bytes, misc, weight, description[256]). BKG.DAT 19,680 = 15×1312. Sprite, 9262 B 8 frames (DOWN½, UP½, LEFT½, RIGHT½) + speed, dimensions, direction, X, Y + temp array + struct time. Map 1458 B = unsigned char Map[6][15][15] + 6 exits (old: 2808 B with int). Exit = name[13] + pad + int X, Y. Layers: background, wall, object, scenery, door.

docs.title: 4. Code quality and notable points
docs.text:
Good ideas: stable tile IDs (blank instead of delete); size-based type sniffing; Allegro driver trimming; reusable ID-dispatched widget toolkit with a "GUI Shell" starter template; per-function debug gating; Photoshop RAW interop; two-floor maps with a 64-bit per-cell property mask and layer-switch bit; palette-gradient fire for animated tiles; the editor doubles as the renderer.

Bugs spotted (reported, not changed): 1. g_map.cpp saveMap()/loadMap(): char *fileName; strcpy(fileName, …) (uninitialized pointer). 2. g_map.cpp drawATile(): uninitialized theTileVector, no default: case. 3. mapeditor_gui.cpp: visibleLayers bit layouts disagree, and init uses && for &. 4. "Transparent" mask checkbox has no handler. 5. GALIMORE_OBJECT::getBitmap() has no return. 6. convertTo15() is identical to convertTo16(). 7. Sprite-frame copy constructor copies only 32×32 of 32×48; displayFrame() size mismatch. 8. Attribute copy/assignment skip objectWeight. 9. ~GALIMORE_BITMAP_OBJECT destroys bitmaps shared by vector copies. 10. g_mask.h constants are unsigned short but shift up to bit 25 (bits ≥ 16 are zero). 11. loadDataFile dedups by pixels, so identical tiles would collapse [inferred risk]. 12. do{}while(infile) processes the failed final read once more. 13. .dat order depends on directory order; memory-dump formats are compiler/endian-specific.

Unfinished: no 2000-era game runtime; sprite layer; object attributes; mask replacement tiles; Linux port; script editor, character generation, NPC AI, OpenPlay networking.

RPG Tools / Phosphor (Aug 2000): rpg_map.h (map class renamed C_RPGMap), rpg_raw.h (LGPL), gcc Makefile, a CodeWarrior project (the only real classic-Mac toolchain artefact), CVS at cvs.rpgtools.sourceforge.net, naming style in Text Docs/CODING_STYLE.txt (C_ classes, S_ structs, g globals, k/gk constants).

docs.title: 5. Relevance to GlitchyGames
docs.text: Roadmap #11 "Level/room data format (and tilemaps)" is open; each game rolls its own ScreenData/FloorData/LevelManager (plans/engine-audit.md).

docs.title: 5.1 Worth porting
docs.text:
1. Map model for #11: Galimore's ordered layers (bg → fg → objects → actors), per-cell properties kept separate from the art, and named exits with entry points. The GlitchyGames design built from these ideas, adjusted for today's games and constraints (object layers, a typed property vocabulary, exit regions with named spawn points), is plans/2026-10-18-level-tools-a-tilemap-format.md.
  2. Stable tile IDs: explicit IDs or tombstones, never list position.
  3. Collision on the map cell, separate from the art.
  4. Editor features: Mapedit's brush sizes, property-paint mode with pick-up/stamp, layer and floor visibility, tileset palette, eraser = 0; Galibmap's colour wells, frame drag-reorder, and the 9-frame walk-cycle convention.
  5. Animated tiles via animation frames, or a procedural fire buffer.

docs.title: 5.2 Converting Galimore data
docs.text:
The survey's read-only decoder (not in this repository) decodes everything below to PNG; sub-plan E (plans/2026-10-18-level-tools-e-galimore-import.md) plans a reviewed converter.

Tiles <1024H, transpose from [x][y], RGB565 → RGB888, 0xF81F → magenta; write TOML pixels + [colors] (10–60 colours per tile); keep the 1-based .dat index as the tile ID. Sprites 16 × 32×48 frames (<1536H, [x][y]); drop all-grey frames; walk_down (0–2), walk_up (3–5), walk_side (6–8, mirrored). Raw RGB888 row-major → PNG for Bitmappy. Maps Offsets in §2.3; layers per floor; mask bits → named properties. 1999 data 1312 B indexed bitmaps (palette from GTORAW or GALIMORE PALLETE.GIF; honour transparencyColor), 9262 B 8-frame sprites, 1458 / 2808 B maps with exits — the best test case for a room/exit design. Caveats Tiles may be RGB555 if saved in 15-bit mode; attribute blocks are empty; sounds need resource-fork extraction first (e.g. DeRez).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Multi-Controller System enables up to 4 simultaneous controllers to navigate and interact with the bitmappy tool independently. Each controller has its own visual indicator, navigation state, and can operate simultaneously without conflicts.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Multi-Controller Support Up to 4 simultaneous controllers Independent Navigation Each controller navigates film strips and frames independently Visual Distinction A unique color for each controller (Red, Green, Blue, Yellow): triangles on the film strips, squares on the canvas, circles on the sliders Smart Positioning Automatic collision avoidance when multiple controllers select the same spot State Preservation Controllers maintain their selection state when switching between them Hotplug Support Controllers can be connected/disconnected during operation

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
1. MultiControllerManager (src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/controllers/manager.py) - Central singleton managing all controllers
  2. ControllerSelection (src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/controllers/selection.py) - Individual controller state management
  3. VisualCollisionManager (src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/indicators/collision.py) - Smart positioning and collision avoidance
  4. ModeSwitcher (src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/controllers/modes.py) - Each controller's mode (film strip, canvas, A/R/G/B slider), switched with the L2/R2 triggers
  5. Integration with Bitmappy - ControllerEventHandler (src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/controllers/event_handler.py) and the per-mode button strategies (src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/controllers/strategies.py)

The button and trigger bindings are listed in CONTROLLER_CONTROLS_README.md at the repository root.

docs.title: Controller Color Scheme
docs.text:
MultiControllerManager.CONTROLLER_COLORS, indexed by controller ID. In Bitmappy, activating a controller (Start) gives it the next color in activation order (assign_color_to_controller), so the first controller activated is red:

Controller 0 Red (255, 0, 0) Controller 1 Green (0, 255, 0) Controller 2 Blue (0, 0, 255) Controller 3 Yellow (255, 255, 0)

docs.title: Basic Setup
docs.text:
from bitmappy.controllers import ControllerSelection, MultiControllerManager
from bitmappy.indicators import VisualCollisionManager

# Initialize the system (MultiControllerManager is a singleton)
manager = MultiControllerManager()
visual_manager = VisualCollisionManager()
controller_selections = {}

# Find the connected controllers (through the engine's devices door; at most once a second)
connected_instance_ids = manager.scan_for_controllers()

# Set up a controller: only a connected controller can be assigned (None otherwise)
instance_id = connected_instance_ids[0]
controller_id = manager.assign_controller(instance_id)
controller_selections[controller_id] = ControllerSelection(controller_id, instance_id)

docs.title: Controller Activation
docs.text:
# Activate a controller
controller_selections[controller_id].activate()
manager.activate_controller(instance_id)

# Set initial selection
controller_selections[controller_id].set_selection("animation_name", 0)

# Add visual indicator
visual_manager.add_controller_indicator(
    controller_id=controller_id,
    instance_id=instance_id,
    color=manager.CONTROLLER_COLORS[controller_id],
    position=(100, 100)
)

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text:
# Navigate to different animation/frame
controller_selections[controller_id].set_selection("new_animation", 5)

# Get current selection
animation, frame = controller_selections[controller_id].get_selection()
print(f"Controller {controller_id} is at {animation}, frame {frame}")

# Get navigation history (an entry is added when the animation changes)
history = controller_selections[controller_id].get_navigation_history()
for entry in history:
    print(f"Previous: {entry['animation']}, frame {entry['frame']}")

docs.title: Multi-Controller Navigation
docs.text:
# Set up multiple controllers
for i, instance_id in enumerate(manager.scan_for_controllers()):
    controller_id = manager.assign_controller(instance_id)
    controller_selections[controller_id] = ControllerSelection(controller_id, instance_id)
    controller_selections[controller_id].activate()

    # Each controller can navigate independently
    controller_selections[controller_id].set_selection(f"animation_{i}", i)

    # Add visual indicators
    visual_manager.add_controller_indicator(
        controller_id=controller_id,
        instance_id=instance_id,
        color=manager.CONTROLLER_COLORS[controller_id],
        position=(100 + i * 50, 100)
    )

# All controllers can navigate independently
controller_selections[0].set_selection("animation_A", 0)
controller_selections[1].set_selection("animation_B", 1)
controller_selections[2].set_selection("animation_C", 2)
controller_selections[3].set_selection("animation_D", 3)

docs.title: Visual Collision Avoidance
docs.text:
# Multiple controllers at same position
for i in range(3):
    visual_manager.add_controller_indicator(
        controller_id=i,
        instance_id=i,
        color=(255, 0, 0),
        position=(100, 100)  # Same position
    )

# System automatically applies offsets (VisualCollisionManager.POSITION_PATTERNS) to prevent overlap
visual_manager.get_final_position(0)  # (100, 100) - no offset
visual_manager.get_final_position(1)  # (85, 85) - (-15, -15) offset
visual_manager.get_final_position(2)  # (115, 85) - (15, -15) offset

docs.title: Controller State Management
docs.text:
# Check controller status
if manager.is_controller_active(instance_id):
    print(f"Controller {instance_id} is active")

# Get controller information
info = manager.get_controller_info(instance_id)
if info:
    print(f"Controller {info.controller_id}: {info.status.value}")

# Deactivate controller (the manager has no deactivate; cleanup_inactive_controllers()
# unassigns controllers idle for more than ASSIGNMENT_TIMEOUT seconds)
controller_selections[controller_id].deactivate()

docs.title: Hotplug Support
docs.text:
# Handle controller connection
def on_controller_connected(instance_id):
    controller_id = manager.assign_controller(instance_id)
    if controller_id is not None:
        controller_selections[controller_id] = ControllerSelection(controller_id, instance_id)
        print(f"Controller {controller_id} connected")

# Handle controller disconnection
def on_controller_disconnected(instance_id):
    if instance_id in manager.assigned_controllers:
        controller_id = manager.assigned_controllers[instance_id]
        if controller_id in controller_selections:
            del controller_selections[controller_id]
        print(f"Controller {controller_id} disconnected")

docs.title: Event Handling
docs.text:
Bitmappy's ControllerEventHandler.on_controller_button_down_event scans for controllers, assigns the controller on its first button press, and passes the button to its current mode's strategy (FilmStripModeStrategy, CanvasModeStrategy or SliderModeStrategy). A simplified version of the film strip navigation:

def on_controller_button_down_event(event):
    """Handle controller button presses in bitmappy."""
    controller_id = manager.get_controller_id(event.instance_id)
    if controller_id is not None:
        if event.button == pygame.CONTROLLER_BUTTON_START:
            # Start button - activate the controller on the first frame of the first animation
            if controller_id in controller_selections:
                controller_selections[controller_id].activate()
                controller_selections[controller_id].set_selection("first_animation", 0)

        elif event.button == pygame.CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_LEFT:
            # D-pad left - previous frame
            if controller_id in controller_selections:
                current_animation, current_frame = controller_selections[controller_id].get_selection()
                if current_frame > 0:
                    controller_selections[controller_id].set_selection(current_animation, current_frame - 1)

        elif event.button == pygame.CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_RIGHT:
            # D-pad right - next frame
            if controller_id in controller_selections:
                current_animation, current_frame = controller_selections[controller_id].get_selection()
                controller_selections[controller_id].set_selection(current_animation, current_frame + 1)

def update_film_strip_indicators():
    """Update visual indicators on film strips."""
    for controller_id, selection in controller_selections.items():
        if selection.is_active():
            animation, frame = selection.get_selection()

            # Update visual indicator position
            if animation in film_strips:
                # frame_layouts maps (animation, frame) to the frame's rect on the strip
                frame_rect = film_strips[animation].frame_layouts[animation, frame]
                visual_manager.update_controller_position(controller_id, frame_rect.midtop)

docs.title: 1. Controller Lifecycle Management
docs.text:
def setup_controller(instance_id):
    """Properly set up a new controller."""
    controller_id = manager.assign_controller(instance_id)
    if controller_id is not None:
        controller_selections[controller_id] = ControllerSelection(controller_id, instance_id)
        controller_selections[controller_id].activate()
        manager.activate_controller(instance_id)
        return controller_id
    return None

def cleanup_controller(instance_id):
    """Properly clean up a controller."""
    if instance_id in manager.assigned_controllers:
        controller_id = manager.assigned_controllers[instance_id]
        if controller_id in controller_selections:
            controller_selections[controller_id].deactivate()
            del controller_selections[controller_id]

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
A computer meets GlitchyGames' minimum for a game when that game's typical frame takes less than 16.7 ms of work, the budget for the engine's default 60 FPS. Pick a target and a measure below, and a platform from the tabs: every verdict and color follows your choice. Three machines have been measured so far: a Raspberry Pi 4, a Raspberry Pi 5 and an Apple M4 Max.

Provisional

These numbers were measured from November 5 to 9, 2026. They will change once the in-flight work lands: the Arcade's engine-context sub-plans, Lucid Circuit Stage 4b and the Raspberry Pi speedups. Then every machine gets re-measured and this page updated (plans/future-work.md, Performance and pacing).

docs.title: What a machine needs
docs.text:
Requirement Minimum Recommended Each game's frame work in the replay benchmark (its typical p99, unless you pick another measure below) Under the frame budget: 16.7 ms at 60 FPS, 33.3 ms at 30 Under 60% of it (10 ms at 60 FPS), leaving the rest to draw the frame on screen Operating system Ubuntu 26.04 LTS or later, or macOS 27 Same Python and pygame-ce Python 3.14 and pygame-ce 2.5.8 (uv installs both) Same Memory 4 GB, the smallest machine measured Same

The 60% recommended line (10 ms at 60 FPS) is a proposal. The benchmark doesn't time drawing to the screen, so the line leaves room for it. Windows passes the test suite in CI, but no Windows machine has been measured.

docs.title: Measured platforms
docs.text:
Loading the measurements…

The FPS column is the rate a game would run at if every frame took the measure you picked (1000 ÷ ms), colored from red at 15 FPS to green at 60 FPS and above; the line on the scale marks the target. The ranges are the lowest and highest across a machine's runs.

Raspberry Pi 4Raspberry Pi 5Apple M4 Max

The Pi 4 has no added cooling and boots from an SD card. At 60 FPS, Brave Adventurer is too slow on it; it fits a 30 FPS target. A one-off CircleCI job (build 2857) measured a 30.1 ms flip per frame on SDL's wayland driver at 2560x1440: on a screen that size, presenting alone takes more than the 60 FPS budget.

The Pi 5 has active cooling, and its NVMe case is a large heat sink. With only two runs, its ranges are thin. Drawing to a real screen hasn't been measured on it.

The highest p99s (up to 20.2 ms) come from a few runs, most likely ones measured while the Mac was busy with other work. The typical run is ten times faster: pick "Slowest run's p99" to see what those runs alone would say.

docs.title: How this was measured
docs.text:
Source The replay ledger, quality/replay-ledger/ (Replay Performance), summarized in docs/data/requirements.json, which this page reads. Each ledger row is one measured run of one golden replay or bundled demo. The pre-push hook measures both Pis for each new code tree. What a number is Each frame's processing time while the recording replays headless, unpaced, on SDL's dummy driver. It is the game's own work, without drawing to a real screen. Typical The median across a machine's runs. Typical p99, the measure picked first, is the median of each run's 99th-percentile frame. Runs are from November 5 to 9, 2026.

What the numbers leave out

Drawing to a real screen A one-off CircleCI job on the Pi 4 (build 2857) measured a 30.1 ms flip per frame on SDL's wayland driver at 2560x1440. Real-driver timing is planned, not yet measured. Memory Not recorded in the ledger. Thermals The ledger doesn't record temperature on Linux. The Pi 4, with no added cooling, varies about 12% across runs. Other machines No Windows PC, x86 Linux machine or older Mac has been measured.

docs.title: Command-Line Argument System
docs.text: GlitchyGames uses a composable argparse architecture where the engine, event managers, font system, and individual games each contribute argument groups to a single parser. Every game built on the engine automatically inherits all engine-level flags, and can extend the parser with its own game-specific options.

docs.title: How Arguments Are Assembled
docs.text:
GameEngine.initialize_arguments(), called from GameEngine.__init__(), builds one parser from three layers. Here is what happens when you run Bitmappy (uv run bitmappy): the Engine box adds layers 1 and 2, the Bitmappy box layer 3, and argparse's ArgumentParser is outside both.

sequenceDiagram
    participant PARSER as ArgumentParser
    box rgb(232,238,255) Engine
    participant INIT as initialize_arguments
    participant ENGINE as GameEngine.args
    participant MANAGERS as the 12 event managers
    end
    box rgb(255,243,224) Bitmappy
    participant GAME as BitmapEditorScene.args
    end

    INIT->>PARSER: ArgumentParser("Bitmappy version 1.0")
    INIT->>ENGINE: GameEngine.args(parser)
    Note over ENGINE: Layer 1<br/>Graphics Options (15)<br/>Diagnostics Options (15, 2 hidden)
    loop for each of the 12
        ENGINE->>MANAGERS: manager.args(parser)
    end
    Note over MANAGERS: Layer 2, in this order<br/>App, Audio, Controller (1), Drop,<br/>Font (7), Game (3), Joystick, Keyboard,<br/>Midi, Mouse, Touch, Window<br/>(the 9 without a count add empty groups)
    INIT->>PARSER: add_argument_group("Bitmappy v1.0 Options")
    INIT->>GAME: BitmapEditorScene.args(group)
    Note over GAME: Layer 3<br/>-v, -s
    INIT->>PARSER: parse_args()
    PARSER-->>INIT: the parsed options
    Note over INIT: engine.options = the options<br/>target_fps resolved

Every option each layer adds is listed in the Complete Flag Reference.

docs.title: The Argument Group Hierarchy
docs.text:
Each layer adds its own add_argument_group(), so --help shows clearly separated sections, in the order of the layers. The layers mirror the engine's architecture.

%%{init: {"flowchart": {"wrappingWidth": 500}}}%%
flowchart TB
    subgraph ENGINE_ARGUMENT_LAYERS["Engine"]
        L1["<b>Layer 1: the engine</b> (GameEngine.args)<br/>Graphics Options, Diagnostics Options"]
        L2["<b>Layer 2: event managers and fonts</b> (each one's args)<br/>Controller Options, Font Options, Game Options,<br/>and 9 reserved groups with no options yet"]
    end
    subgraph GAME_ARGUMENT_LAYERS["Your game"]
        L3["<b>Layer 3: your game</b> (its scene's args)<br/>GameName vX.Y Options"]
    end
    L1 --> L2 --> L3

In --help (Bitmappy's or Paddle Slap's) the groups hold 15 Graphics, 15 Diagnostics (2 more hidden), 1 Controller, 7 Font and 3 Game options, then the game's own; the nine empty groups are left out. The Complete Flag Reference lists them all.

docs.title: How Games Add Arguments
docs.text:
A game adds arguments by defining a @classmethod called args() on its scene class. The engine discovers this method via getattr(game, 'args', None) and calls it with a dedicated argument group. If the game does not define args(), the engine logs an informational message (INFO, once the command line has set the level, so --log-level info shows it; the default warning does not) and continues.

flowchart TD
    subgraph Engine["Engine: GameEngine.initialize_arguments()"]
        CHECK{"getattr(game, 'args', None)"}
        CHECK -->|"method exists"| GROUP["parser.add_argument_group(\nGameName vX.Y Options)"]
        GROUP --> CALL["game.args(group)"]
        CHECK -->|"None"| LOG["log.info: Game does not\nimplement arguments"]
    end

    subgraph GameCode["Your game: its scene class"]
        ARGS["@classmethod\ndef args(cls, parser):\n    parser.add_argument(...)"]
    end

    CALL --> ARGS

docs.title: Pattern: Minimal Game
docs.text:
class MyGame(Scene):
    NAME = 'My Game'
    VERSION = '1.0'

    @classmethod
    def args(cls, parser):
        parser.add_argument(
            '-v', '--version',
            action='store_true',
            help='print the game version and exit',
        )

docs.title: Pattern: Game with Custom Options
docs.text:
class TimedDemo(Scene):
    NAME = 'Timed Demo'
    VERSION = '1.0'

    @classmethod
    def args(cls, parser):
        parser.add_argument(
            '--time', type=int, default=10,
            help='time in seconds to wait before quitting',
        )
        parser.add_argument(
            '-v', '--version',
            action='store_true',
            help='print the game version and exit',
        )

Note that the game receives an argument group, not the root parser. This means game arguments appear under their own heading in --help output.

docs.title: OPTIONS Dictionary Flow
docs.text:
After parsing, the Namespace is converted to a plain dict and propagated to every component that needs it. Each engine keeps its own (engine.options), and its scene manager its own copy (manager.engine_options), so two games in one process (two engine contexts) never share options; GameEngine.OPTIONS and SceneManager.OPTIONS are read-only views of the current game's (Engine Context). The game's class keeps none: it is shared by every context.

flowchart TD
    PARSE["parser.parse_args()"] --> VARS["vars(args)\nNamespace -> dict"]
    VARS --> OPT["engine.options (the engine's own)"]

    OPT --> FPS["options['target_fps'] resolved\n(--target-fps, else the game's TARGET_FPS, else 60.01)"]
    FPS --> SM_OPT["manager.engine_options = engine.options\n(the game_engine setter)"]
    SM_OPT --> SCENE_INIT["Scene.__init__(options=engine.options)"]
    SCENE_INIT --> SELF_OPT["self.options = options"]

    subgraph Access["Runtime Access"]
        A1["self.options['target_fps']"]
        A2["self.options['font_name']"]
        A3["self.options['log_level']"]
        A4["self.options['debug_events']"]
        A5["engine.options['resolution']"]
    end

    SELF_OPT --> Access

docs.title: Logging level and the startup options block
docs.text:
A game logs at WARNING unless --log-level says otherwise (the owner, 2026-10-28: games default to WARNING, as the replay tools do), so a plain run prints only warnings and worse: the exit code it ended with, whether its seed was rolled or given, and the end-of-run performance reports are INFO, shown with --log-level info. Nothing else sets a level (the logger guards: no level set at import). Each failure a player sees (a crash, exit 70; a failed teardown; a playback that failed) logs one more line after its traceback, exit_codes.BUG_REPORT_HINT: "To report this, run the game again with --log-level info and include the output." The glitchygames command has no --log-level, so its own tool crashes do not say it.

Every engine start (start() or start_async()) logs the run's whole options dictionary once, at CRITICAL, so it shows at every level ("for now": plans/future-work.md):

game.engine - CRITICAL - Options for Paddle Slap (secrets redacted):
    allow_dirty             = False
    ...
    log_level               = 'warning'
    ...
    replay_trace            = 'src/games/paddleslap/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz'

Names are sorted, one name = value per line, aligned, with values as Python writes them; a nested mapping is indented below its name. Path options (the tools' and the engine's, the set a recording's header stores) are shown relative to the project root when inside it and absolute otherwise. An option whose name holds key, token, secret, password or credential, in any case, shows <redacted>. The environment is never read. A replay's options are the recorded run's. random_seed is the seed the run uses, rolled or given (the owner, 2026-10-28: "The seed should definitely be in the options"), never None, so --random-seed with it plays the run again.

docs.title: Complete Flag Reference
docs.text: Every option, by the layer that adds it and grouped as uv run bitmappy --help prints it: each with its type and default, then its help text.

docs.title: Graphics Options
docs.text:
Added by GameEngine.args() in src/glitchygames/engine/game_engine.py.

  • -f, --target-fps TARGET_FPS (float): cap the framerate (default: the game's TARGET_FPS, else 60.01; 0 = uncapped)
  • --fps-log-interval-ms FPS_LOG_INTERVAL_MS (float): how often to log the FPS counter in ms (default: 1000)
  • -w, --windowed, --no-windowed (bool): run in a window; --no-windowed runs fullscreen (default: windowed)
  • -r, --resolution RESOLUTION (str): the resolution to use (default: 800x480)
  • --use-gfxdraw (store_true, default False): not used yet: stored, but nothing draws with pygame.gfxdraw because of it
  • --update-type {update,flip} (choice): update or flip (default: update)
  • --timer-backend {auto,fast,pygame} (choice): timer backend for draw loop pacing (default: auto, the fast backend with this machine's sleep delay measured, so each sleep wakes in time; fast assumes sleeps wake on time; pygame is the legacy backend)
  • --sleep-granularity-ns SLEEP_GRANULARITY_NS (int, default 1000000): how long before each frame deadline the fast backend is to wake from its sleep and spin (ns); 0 spins only
  • --windows-timer-1ms (store_true, default False): on Windows, request 1ms system timer resolution
  • --random-seed RANDOM_SEED (int): master seed for every engine random stream (default: a random 64-bit seed, logged in recordings)
  • --screen-shake-intensity SCREEN_SHAKE_INTENSITY (float): screen shake strength from 0.0 (off) to 1.0 (default: 1.0)
  • --rumble-intensity RUMBLE_INTENSITY (float): controller rumble strength from 0.0 (off) to 1.0 (default: 1.0)
  • --live-voice-pool LIVE_VOICE_POOL (int): mixer channels reserved for real-time synth voices (default: 4)
  • --sound-channels SOUND_CHANNELS (int): mixer channels reserved for the sound library (scene_manager.audio) (default: 32)
  • --sound-cache {none,ram,disk} (choice, default ram): how compiled sounds are kept: none (compiled again at every play), ram (in memory, default) or disk (arrives in M3; refused with OPTIONS_REFUSED until then). Replay-local: a recording replays under any mode
  • --sound-cache-memory MB (int, default 256): megabytes the ram sound cache may hold before the least recently played idle sounds go
  • --crt-power-on-sound {on,off} (choice, default on): play the CRT power-on sequence with its sound
  • --crt-power-on {auto,on,off} (choice, default auto): show the game's canvas switching on like a CRT before the game starts: auto (default: when someone can see it, so not on SDL's dummy driver or before a replay, audit, rebaseline or recording), on (always; refused with a replay or a recording) or off
  • --default-background {test-pattern,channel-3} (choice): the background of a scene that sets none: the TV test pattern or the channel 3 blue screen (default: test-pattern)
  • --video-driver {cocoa,offscreen,dummy} (choice, default None): SDL's video driver for the display (sets SDL_VIDEODRIVER for the run; default: SDL_VIDEODRIVER's own value, then Wayland on a Linux Wayland session, then SDL's choice; --headless overrides it)

--video-driver choices by platform (SDL 2's video driver names, by platform.system(); --help above is macOS's):

Platform Choices macOS (Darwin) cocoa, offscreen, dummy Windows windows, offscreen, dummy Linux x11, wayland, kmsdrm, offscreen, dummy any other offscreen, dummy

docs.title: Diagnostics Options
docs.text:
Added by GameEngine.args() right after the Graphics Options: how any run is watched, recorded, replayed or diagnosed, whatever the game; they change no game settings. Recording and replay are described in Gameplay Recording and Replay. Two more are hidden from --help: the watched replay's restart internals.

  • --log-timer-jitter (store_true, default False): log frame pacing jitter statistics periodically
  • --perf-trim-percent PERF_TRIM_PERCENT (float, default 5.0): percent of frames to trim from top and bottom in the game's global FPS report
  • --fps-histogram {equal-range,target-relative} (choice, default equal-range): FPS histogram buckets in the game's shutdown report: equal-range (10 equal buckets spanning the analyzed min to max, default) or target-relative (10% steps of the target FPS)
  • --debug-overlay, --no-debug-overlay (bool, default False): show the debug overlay at startup (F3 toggles, F4 cycles panels)
  • --sound-diagnostics (store_true, default False): start with the debug overlay on, showing the Audio panel (replay-local)
  • --debug-events (store_true, default False): log a warning the first time each unhandled event type arrives (--no-unhandled-events raises on one instead)
  • --record-trace PATH (PATH): record the session (sprites, frame times, input events, random seed) to a gzip JSON Lines trace for inspection and later replay (default: off)
  • --replay-trace PATH (PATH): replay a --record-trace recording exactly through the engine, comparing every frame with it and reporting the first divergence (default: off)
  • --replay-fps {recorded,real} (choice, default None (read as recorded)): with --replay-trace: post FPS events from the recorded frame times (recorded, the default: exact, and compared with the recording) or from this machine's measured frame times (real: what this machine achieves; FPS events are then not compared, and sprites that draw the FPS value may diverge)
  • --audit, --no-audit (bool, default False): with --replay-trace: instead of replaying, replay the recording twice in fresh headless processes with different hash seeds and compare every frame with the recording and between the runs; exits 0 when both match, 3 otherwise, 70 if a run could not finish
  • --compare-processing (store_true, default False): with --replay-trace --headless: measure each frame's processing time (its work, without presenting or pacing) and report how it compares with the recording's (only meaningful on the machine that recorded)
  • --max-processing-slowdown PERCENT (PERCENT, default None): with --replay-trace --headless (implies --compare-processing): a replay that matched but took more than PERCENT longer than the recording's processing time exits 8; a recording without processing times exits 65
  • --replay-pause-at-frame N (N (non-negative int), default None): with --replay-trace, watched: skip the start screen, run frames 0 to N - 1 without showing them, then pause with frame N next (what step back restarts with; ignored with --headless)
  • --rebaseline NEW (NEW, default None): with --replay-trace OLD and --headless: replay OLD on the current code without stopping at divergences, write the run's recording (OLD's inputs, the current sprites) to NEW, print a summary of the frames and sprites that changed and exit 0
  • --replay-digest PATH (PATH, default None): with --replay-trace: write a SHA-256 of every replayed frame, then the divergence, to PATH as JSON lines (used by --audit)
  • --list-input-devices (store_true, default False): print every joystick and game controller the game would see (index, instance id, name, GUID, whether SDL maps it as a game controller, its axes, buttons, hats and balls; how many SDL counted before its queue was pumped and each device added or removed while listening, with when), then exit 0 without running the game. At a terminal, when none is found it asks you to plug one in and waits for it (Ctrl-C stops). Refused with --replay-trace or --record-trace
  • --headless (store_true, default False): run on SDL's dummy video and audio drivers: no window, no sound. With --replay-trace the replay also runs unpaced and prints its report to stdout (exit 0 when it matches, 1 when it diverges, 65 for a truncated recording)

docs.title: Controller Options
docs.text:
Added by ControllerEventManager.args() in src/glitchygames/events/controller.py (see Event System).

  • --input-mode {auto,joystick,controller} (choice): Which gamepads the game sees (default: auto, every device; a mapped pad sends controller events, any other device joystick events; joystick: every device sends joystick events; controller: mapped pads only)
  • --axis-deadzone (unit_interval): Gamepad axis deadzone from 0.0 to 1.0: an axis position nearer its center reads as centered (default: 0.15). One value for every device and both event layers (a deadzone belongs to the physical stick, which --input-mode can read on either layer). A game's maps follow it when built with ActionMap.from_engine_options(options), as every bundled game's are; a player's deadzone saved with a map (ActionMap.to_dict) wins over it on load unless the game passes deadzone= to from_dict

docs.title: Font Options
docs.text:
Added by FontManager.args() in src/glitchygames/fonts/font_manager.py.

  • --font-name FONT_NAME (str): Font to use (default: the bundled Vera; the bundled variants are Vera, VeraBd, VeraIt and VeraBI; any other name is looked up among the system's fonts)
  • --font-size FONT_SIZE (int): size of the default font, used by text that asks for no font of its own (default: 14)
  • --font-bold (store_true, default False): draw text bold
  • --font-italic (store_true, default False): draw text italic
  • --font-antialias, --no-font-antialias (BooleanOptionalAction): antialias text (default: True). freetype fonts carry it; every pygame.font render call passes FontManager.antialias(), except the channel 3 screen's digit, which stays hard-edged on purpose
  • --font-dpi FONT_DPI (int): the resolution, in dots per inch, font sizes are scaled at (a size is in pixels at 72) (default: 72)

The style options reach every font FontManager loads; a font configuration that gives its own font_bold, font_italic, font_antialias or font_dpi overrides them. All four are in the font cache key. - --font-system {pygame,freetype} (choice, default freetype): Font system to use: freetype (enhanced, default) or pygame (built-in)

docs.title: Game Options
docs.text:
Added by GameEventManager.args() in src/glitchygames/events/game.py.

  • -l, --log-level {debug,info,warning,error,critical} (choice, default warning): set the logging level (default: warning; a bug report asks for info)
  • --no-unhandled-events (store_true, default False): fail on unhandled events
  • -p, --profile (store_true, default False): enable profiling

docs.title: What --help Looks Like
docs.text: uv run bitmappy --help prints a usage line, the options: group (-h, --help), then each group in the order the layers add them: Graphics, Diagnostics, Controller, Font and Game Options, then Bitmappy v1.0 Options. argparse leaves out groups with no arguments (App, Sound Mixer and the other reserved groups). Every option it prints, with its help text, is listed in Complete Flag Reference.

docs.title: How to Add Arguments to a New Event Manager
docs.text:
If you are adding arguments to a currently-empty event manager group, follow the existing pattern:

# In src/glitchygames/events/mouse.py

@classmethod
def args(cls, parser: argparse.ArgumentParser) -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    group = parser.add_argument_group('Mouse Options')

    group.add_argument(
        '--mouse-sensitivity',
        type=float,
        default=1.0,
        help='Mouse sensitivity multiplier (default: 1.0)',
    )

    return parser

The engine already calls your manager's args() method — you just need to add add_argument() calls to the existing group.

docs.title: How to Create a New Game with Arguments
docs.text:
from glitchygames.engine import GameEngine
from glitchygames.scenes import Scene


class MyGame(Scene):
    NAME = 'My Game'
    VERSION = '1.0'

    @classmethod
    def args(cls, parser):
        """Add game-specific arguments.

        Args:
            parser: An argument group (not the root parser).
        """
        parser.add_argument(
            '-v', '--version',
            action='store_true',
            help='print the game version and exit',
        )
        parser.add_argument(
            '--difficulty',
            choices=['easy', 'medium', 'hard'],
            default='medium',
            help='game difficulty level',
        )

    def __init__(self, options):
        super().__init__(options=options)
        # Access your arguments via self.options
        self.difficulty = self.options['difficulty']


def main():
    GameEngine(game=MyGame).start()

Your arguments will automatically appear under "My Game v1.0 Options" in the --help output, separate from all engine-level flags.

docs.title: Bitmappy Architecture
docs.text: Bitmappy is GlitchyGames' pixel art editor. These diagrams show how it is wired up through the engine, from bootstrap to rendering.

docs.title: Its package
docs.text:
Bitmappy is an app, not part of the engine: the first member of the apps layer of the uv workspace, at src/apps/bitmappy/. The distribution, the import package and the console script are all bitmappy (uv run bitmappy), and its scene's logical name, the one a recording holds, is apps.bitmappy.editor:BitmapEditorScene. A recording made when the scene lived in the engine (glitchygames.bitmappy.editor:BitmapEditorScene) is refused by a plain replay, which names the remedy; --replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless converts it (gameplay replay).

  • Its code is src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/. The engine never imports it, and Bitmappy uses the engine's public API (sprite file-format detection, for one, is the engine's src/glitchygames/sprites/file_format.py).
  • Its sprite library is 71 sprites in src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/resources/sprites/, shipped as package data and found through bitmappy.SPRITE_CONFIG_DIR. They are also the AI's training data (load_ai_training_data() below), so they stay in the package.
  • Its other resources (the window icon and bitmappy.cfg) are beside them, in src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/resources/.
  • Its tests are in src/apps/bitmappy/tests/, rootless, every file named test_bitmappy_*.py.
  • The Load and Save dialogs (the engine's glitchygames.ui dialog scenes) treat every file the same: the name is used as given, with surrounding whitespace trimmed, and a sprite in the library is opened by its path. The example: prefix they once understood is gone, and Save applies a per-platform rule to : in a file name (_file_name_problem, the platform passed in and sys.platform by default); nothing is written, the full refusal is shown in the editor's debug text, and the dialog stays open with the name kept and a short reason in its prompt (REFUSED_FILE_NAME_PROMPT), so the name can be corrected in place:
Platform : in a Save name Windows (win32, cygwin) Allowed only in a letter-drive designator (C:\a.toml, C:/a.toml, C:a.toml, \\?\C:\a.toml, \\.\C:\a.toml); anywhere else, including inside a UNC server or share name, it is refused: NTFS would read it as an alternate data stream, so examples:foo.toml would leave an empty file called examples macOS (darwin) Refused everywhere: Finder shows : as / (a Classic Mac OS leftover) Linux and others Allowed Browser (emscripten) Allowed (Save is a download; the browser sanitizes the name)

Load is unchanged (a missing name is reported as "File not found").

docs.title: Bootstrap & Main Loop
docs.text:
How Bitmappy starts up: entry point through main(), GameEngine initialization, scene setup, and the main loop (one frame per pass, ended by _finish_frame). The Bitmappy box is the editor's own code (src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/); the Engine box is what every game gets.

sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    box rgb(255,243,224) Bitmappy
    participant main as main()
    participant BES as BitmapEditorScene
    end
    box rgb(232,238,255) Engine
    participant GE as GameEngine
    participant SM as SceneManager (singleton)
    end

    User->>main: uv run bitmappy
    main->>GE: GameEngine(game=BitmapEditorScene, icon=...)
    GE->>GE: parse CLI args (GameEngine.args() + BitmapEditorScene.args())
    GE->>GE: pygame.init(), create display
    main->>main: load_ai_training_data()
    main->>GE: engine.start()
    GE->>BES: BitmapEditorScene(options=OPTIONS)
    BES->>BES: EditorSetup.init_undo_redo_system()
    BES->>BES: EditorSetup.setup_menu_bar()
    BES->>BES: EditorSetup.setup_canvas(options)
    BES->>BES: SliderManager.setup_sliders_and_color_well()
    BES->>BES: EditorSetup.setup_debug_text_box()
    BES->>BES: FilmStripCoordinator.setup_film_strips()
    GE->>GE: _initialize_event_managers()
    GE->>SM: scene_manager.switch_to_scene(game)
    SM->>BES: setup() (AIManager.setup() starts the AI worker)
    GE->>SM: scene_manager.start()

    loop Main Game Loop (while active_scene is not None)
        Note over SM: dt = the previous frame's start-to-start time
        SM->>SM: camera.begin_frame()
        SM->>BES: _update_scene() (Scene.dt_tick: logic and collision)
        SM->>GE: _process_events()
        GE->>GE: _pump_events() (active_sources().pump_events(): live, pygame.event.get())
        GE->>SM: event_handlers[event.type](event)
        SM->>BES: on_*_event(event)
        SM->>SM: _run_supervisor_slot() (supervisors, e.g. a recording's)
        SM->>SM: _update_frame_services() (shake, rumble)
        SM->>SM: _aim_active_camera() (camera_target / follow)
        SM->>SM: _position_active_world_sprites() (world sprites' rect, culling)
        SM->>SM: _render_scene() (BitmapEditorScene.update: animation, controllers, AI, then draw)
        SM->>SM: _advance_still_camera_shake() (WORLD shake nothing advanced)
        SM->>SM: _present_frame() (overlay, display update)
        SM->>SM: _finish_frame() (pace, then set dt once from perf_counter)
    end

docs.title: Event dispatch chain (how events reach your scene)
docs.text:
Every scene has every on_*_event() handler, but it gets them a different way from the engine. A Scene inherits them: AllEventStubs gives it a default for each one, which reports the event as unhandled, and your scene overrides the ones it uses. GameEngine and SceneManager inherit no handlers at all. They pass on_*_event() calls along at runtime through __getattr__.

  • Solid arrows are inheritance, pointing at the base class.
  • Dotted arrows are the runtime calls, numbered in the order an event takes them.
  • The Engine box is the engine's classes; the Bitmappy box is the editor's scene.
classDiagram
    direction TB
    namespace Engine {
        class EventInterface {
            <<interface, abc.ABC>>
            #95;#95;subclasshook#95;#95; counts any class with every handler
        }
        class EventInterfaces["MouseEvents, KeyboardEvents, ... (13)"] {
            <<interface, abc.ABC>>
            every on#95;#42;#95;event abstract
        }
        class EventStubs["MouseEventStubs, KeyboardEventStubs, ... (13)"] {
            <<mixin>>
            every on#95;#42;#95;event calls unhandled#95;event
        }
        class AllEventStubs {
            <<mixin>>
            all 13 stub mixins
        }
        class GameOptionsProvider {
            <<Protocol>>
            options dict
        }
        class Scene {
            a default for every on#95;#42;#95;event
        }
        class ManagerProxy["MouseEventManager.MouseEventProxy (one per manager)"] {
            implements MouseEvents
            each on#95;#42;#95;event calls game.on#95;#42;#95;event
        }
        class ResourceManager {
            proxies list
            #95;#95;getattr#95;#95; forwards to its proxies
        }
        class EventManager
        class GameEngine {
            process#95;#42;#95;event calls the event manager
            #95;#95;getattr#95;#95; turns on#95;#42;#95;event into missing#95;event
        }
        class SceneManager {
            #95;#95;getattr#95;#95; sends on#95;#42;#95;event to the active scene
        }
    }
    namespace Bitmappy {
        class BitmapEditorScene {
            overrides the handlers it uses
        }
    }

    EventInterface <|-- EventInterfaces
    EventInterface <|-- EventStubs
    EventStubs <|-- AllEventStubs
    AllEventStubs <|-- Scene
    Scene <|-- BitmapEditorScene
    EventInterfaces <|-- ManagerProxy
    ResourceManager <|-- EventManager
    EventManager <|-- GameEngine
    EventManager <|-- SceneManager

    GameEngine ..> ManagerProxy : 1. process#95;mouse#95;event
    ManagerProxy ..> SceneManager : 2. game.on#95;#42;#95;event
    SceneManager ..> Scene : 3. #95;#95;getattr#95;#95; forwards it
    SceneManager ..> GameEngine : 3b. no active scene, missing#95;event
    EventStubs ..> GameOptionsProvider : unhandled#95;event(game)

The interfaces are abstract base classes, not typing.Protocols, but EventInterface's __subclasshook__ makes them structural: any class with every handler of an interface counts as one. GameOptionsProvider is a real Protocol: unhandled_event() needs only the scene's options. Both scene classes also inherit SceneInterface (left out to keep the diagram readable).

Event flow — how an SDL event reaches your handler in Bitmappy (the stub a missing handler falls to is the engine's):

flowchart TD
    SDL["SDL Event"] --> GE
    subgraph ENGINE_BITMAPPY_EVENT_FLOW["Engine"]
        GE["GameEngine\nO#40;1#41; event_handlers lookup"]
        GE --> MGR["Event Manager\ne.g. MouseEventManager"]
        MGR -->|"updates state,\nsynthesizes events"| SM["SceneManager\nforwards to active_scene"]
        STUB["No handler?\nThe stub calls unhandled_event#40;#41;"]
    end
    subgraph APP_BITMAPPY_EVENT_FLOW["Bitmappy"]
        BES["BitmapEditorScene\n#40;the active scene#41;"]
        BES --> HANDLER["Your handler runs\non_left_mouse_drag_event#40;#41;"]
    end
    SM --> BES
    BES --> STUB

The GameEngine receives every SDL event and does an O(1) dict lookup to find the right event manager. The event manager updates its internal state (button tracking, axis values, drag detection) and may synthesize higher-level events (drag, drop, chord). It then forwards to the SceneManager, which passes everything to the active_scene. In Bitmappy, that's BitmapEditorScene, which overrides handlers like on_key_down_event(), on_left_mouse_button_down_event(), on_left_mouse_drag_event(), and on_controller_button_down_event(). Events it doesn't override hit the stubs, which call unhandled_event(): it does nothing by default, logs each event type once when debug_events is on (the --debug-events flag, off by default), and raises UnhandledEventError under --no-unhandled-events (as the tests run).

docs.title: Sprite hierarchy (renderable objects)
docs.text:
DirtySprite is pygame's base for all sprites that support dirty-rect rendering. GlitchyGames extends it through RootSprite → Sprite → BitmappySprite to add mouse events, non-optional image/rect, named parent tracking and TOML load/save. AnimatedSprite derives from DirtySprite directly. DirtySprite is pygame's, outside both boxes; the Bitmappy box holds the editor's own sprites.

flowchart TD
    DS["DirtySprite\ndirty, image, rect"]
    subgraph ENGINE_SPRITE_HIERARCHY["Engine"]
        RS["RootSprite\nmouse event support\nnon-optional image/rect"]
        RS --> SP["Sprite\nx, y, name, parent"]
        SP --> BS["BitmappySprite\nload#40;#41;, save#40;#41;"]
        AS["AnimatedSprite\n_animations, frame_manager\nset_animation#40;#41;, set_frame#40;#41;"]
    end
    subgraph APP_SPRITE_HIERARCHY["Bitmappy"]
        ACS["AnimatedCanvasSprite\npixels_across, pixels_tall\ncanvas_interface.set_pixel_at#40;#41;, show_frame#40;#41;"]
        FSS["FilmStripSprite\nfilm_strip_widget\non_left_mouse_button_down_event#40;#41;"]
    end
    DS --> RS
    DS --> AS
    BS --> ACS
    BS --> FSS

docs.title: Event Flow
docs.text:
How pygame events propagate through the system: from GameEngine._pump_events() (live: pygame.event.get()) through the engine's own event_handlers dispatch table, into specialized event managers, through the scene manager, and finally into Bitmappy's scene and sprite handlers. The top Engine box is the dispatch every game gets, the Bitmappy box is the editor's handlers, and the bottom Engine box is the engine's UI widgets (glitchygames.ui) the editor's clicks reach.

flowchart TD
    subgraph ENGINE_BITMAPPY_DISPATCH["Engine"]
        PG["GameEngine._pump_events()\nactive_sources().pump_events()"] --> GE["GameEngine.process_events()"]
        GE --> EH{"event_handlers[event.type]"}

        EH -->|KEYDOWN| KEM["KeyboardEventManager"]
        EH -->|MOUSEBUTTONDOWN| MEM["MouseEventManager"]
        EH -->|CONTROLLERBUTTONDOWN| CEM["ControllerEventManager"]
        EH -->|DROPFILE| DEM["DropEventManager"]
        EH -->|"WINDOW* events"| WEM["WindowEventManager"]
        EH -->|FPSEVENT| GEM["GameEventManager"]

        KEM --> SM["SceneManager.on_key_down_event()"]
        MEM --> SM2["SceneManager.on_left_mouse_button_down_event()"]
        CEM --> SM3["SceneManager.on_controller_button_down_event()"]
        DEM --> SM4["SceneManager.on_drop_file_event()"]
    end

    subgraph APP_BITMAPPY_DISPATCH["Bitmappy"]
        BES["BitmapEditorScene.on_key_down_event()"]
        BES2["BitmapEditorScene.on_left_mouse_button_down_event()"]
        BES3["BitmapEditorScene.on_controller_button_down_event()"]
        BES4["BitmapEditorScene.on_drop_file_event()\nFileIOManager"]

        BES -->|"Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y, Ctrl+Shift+Z"| UNDO["handle_undo() / handle_redo()"]
        BES -->|"Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V"| COPY["Copy / paste frame"]
        BES -->|"Ctrl+Shift+Arrow"| PAN["Pan the frame's pixels"]
        BES -->|"Arrow keys, 0-9, Space"| CANVAS["AnimatedCanvasSprite.handle_keyboard_event()"]
        BES -->|"O key"| ONION["Toggle Onion Skinning"]

        BES2 -->|"Canvas area"| PIXEL["canvas.canvas_interface.set_pixel_at(x, y, color)"]
        BES2 -->|"Ctrl+click"| FLOOD["canvas._flood_fill(x, y, color)"]
        BES2 -->|"Film strip area"| FRAME["FilmStripSprite: select frame"]

        BES3 --> CEH["ControllerEventHandler"]
        CEH --> MCM["MultiControllerManager\n(assigns the controller)"]
        CEH --> MS["ModeSwitcher strategy"]
        MS -->|"Canvas Mode"| CPAINT["Canvas navigation/paint"]
        MS -->|"Film Strip Mode"| FNAV["Frame navigation/select"]
        MS -->|"Slider Mode"| SADJ["Slider adjustment"]
    end

    subgraph ENGINE_BITMAPPY_WIDGETS["Engine: glitchygames.ui widgets"]
        MENU["MenuItem: dialog scene"]
        SLIDER["SliderSprite: adjust RGBA"]
    end

    SM --> BES
    SM2 --> BES2
    SM3 --> BES3
    SM4 --> BES4
    BES2 -->|"Menu item"| MENU
    BES2 -->|"Slider area"| SLIDER

docs.title: Rendering Pipeline
docs.text:
The steps of each frame, in order (SceneManager._run_scene_frame, then _finish_frame). Bitmappy has no world-space sprites, so steps 5 and 6 leave its widgets alone. Dirty-rect optimization ensures only changed regions are redrawn and pushed to the display. The engine runs every step; the Bitmappy box is the editor's update(), which step 7 calls.

flowchart TD
    subgraph ENGINE_BITMAPPY_FRAME["Engine"]
        BEGIN["1. camera.begin_frame()\nclear the camera's update and shake-advance flags"] --> LOGIC
        LOGIC["2. _update_scene()\nScene.dt_tick(dt): logic, animation, collision\n(dt capped by MAX_FRAME_SECONDS when set)"] --> EVENTS
        EVENTS["3. _process_events(), then _run_supervisor_slot()\nthe engine's event_handlers dict - O(1) lookup\nBitmapEditorScene handlers modify sprites"] --> SERVICES
        SERVICES["4. _update_frame_services()\nshake and rumble"] --> AIM
        AIM["5. _aim_active_camera()\ncamera_target() / follow target\n(skipped when the scene was switched mid-frame)"] --> POSITION
        POSITION["6. _position_active_world_sprites()\nworld sprites' rect from the camera, culling\n(screen-space sprites untouched)"] --> RENDER
        RENDER["7. _render_scene()\nScene.update() (visual only), LayeredDirty.draw"] --> CHECK{"sprite.dirty?"}
        CHECK -->|"dirty=0"| SKIP["Skip - no redraw"]
        CHECK -->|"dirty=1 or 2"| REDRAW["Blit sprite.image at sprite.rect\ncollect changed rects"]
        SKIP --> STILL
        REDRAW --> STILL
        STILL["8. _advance_still_camera_shake()\nadvance a WORLD shake nothing advanced this frame\n(no aim, no game camera.update())"] --> PRESENT
        PRESENT["9. _present_frame()\ndebug overlay, pygame.display.update rects or flip"] --> FINISH
        FINISH["10. _finish_frame()\npace, then one perf_counter reading sets the next dt"]
    end
    subgraph APP_BITMAPPY_FRAME["Bitmappy"]
        FM["BitmapEditorScene.update()\ncanvas.update_animation(dt)\nFilmStripCoordinator.update_film_strip_animation_timing()\nFilmStripSprite.dirty = 1 when a frame advances"]
    end
    RENDER --> FM

docs.title: Undo/Redo & Operations
docs.text:
How user actions flow through operation trackers into the central undo/redo stack. Canvas operations are batched per drag with 0.1s debounce for efficiency.

flowchart LR
    subgraph UserActions["User Actions"]
        PAINT["Paint pixels"]
        FILL["Flood fill"]
        FSEL["Select frame"]
        FDEL["Delete frame"]
        FCOPY["Paste frame"]
        CMOVE["Controller move / mode change"]
    end

    subgraph Trackers["Operation Trackers"]
        COT["CanvasOperationTracker\npixel-level, batched per drag"]
        FOT["FilmStripOperationTracker\nframe-level operations"]
        FOM["FrameOperationManager\nFramePasteCommand"]
        CPOT["ControllerPositionOperationTracker\ncontroller positions and modes"]
    end

    subgraph URM["UndoRedoManager (max_history=50)"]
        STACK_F["Per-frame Undo/Redo Stacks"]
        STACK_U["Global Undo Stack"]
        STACK_R["Global Redo Stack"]
    end

    PAINT --> COT

docs.title: Engine Context
docs.text:
An engine context is the state one running game owns, so several games can run in one process (the Arcade's demo tiles; design: plans/2026-10-25-engine-context.md). Ordinary games never create one: they run in the default context, exactly as before.

What is per game today: the seventeen slots below, and the engine's and the scene manager's own attributes (an engine's options, game, running_game, event_handlers and its event bookkeeping; a scene manager's engine_options), which belong to the object, so two engines never share them. The old class-level names of that state (GameEngine.OPTIONS, SceneManager.OPTIONS, Sprite.SPRITE_COUNT, ...) are now read-only views of the current game's (below). What is still one per process is the audit's shared rows (S1-S20 in plans/2026-10-25-engine-context.md): the display and window services, the mixer and music, SDL's event queue and its blocked types, the joystick subsystem, the process services (signal handlers, the SDL environment, pygame.init()), the player's clipboard and files, and a few recursion guards and registries; later sub-plans keep an inner context off each of them. The engine does not run a game in another context yet; the one switch in src/ is the sound-file loader's scratch context for building a file's waves (src/glitchygames/audio/assets.py).

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. Per-context state is a ContextSlot (src/glitchygames/engine_context.py), declared once at module level with a unique dotted name and a factory. ContextSlot is internal to the engine: only engine modules declare slots, and games keep their state on their scenes. The tests' COUNTER_SLOT exists only to test the class.
  2. Code reads a slot when it needs it, current_context().value(slot=...), never as its module is imported: the test suite scans the engine and every workspace member for such reads.
  3. A context makes each value with the slot's factory the first time it is read there.
  4. current_context() is the context switched to last in this thread or asyncio task, else the default context.
  5. with context.active(): makes a context current and puts the previous one back when the block ends, also by an exception; switches nest. An asyncio task made inside a switch keeps it, a switch held across an await is never seen by another task, and a thread sees it only when started with context=contextvars.copy_context() (or on an interpreter whose sys.flags.thread_inherit_context is set, such as free-threaded 3.14 builds).
  6. A context owns only what its slots hold. The display, the mixer, SDL's event queue and the joystick subsystem are one per process. So are read-only caches of values computed only from their keys, such as the background pattern cache and the engine's own compiled sounds (glitchygames.audio.library.ENGINE_SOUND_CACHE: the CRT power-on's, compiled once per process and shared by every context as read-only samples; each context makes its own Sound over them).
  7. current_engine() (glitchygames.engine) is the engine made last in the current context, until it shuts down; with none running it raises NoRunningEngineError.

docs.title: What belongs to a context today
docs.text:
