the GameEngine views read it) 'glitchygames.recording.internal_posts' src/glitchygames/recording.py post_event, post_input_event, start_tracking_internal_posts, stop_tracking_internal_posts, reset_internal_post_tracking, forget_pending_posts, pending_internal_posts, live_game_posts, pending_code_post_count 'glitchygames.performance.adaptive_clamping.managers' src/glitchygames/performance/adaptive_clamping.py AdaptiveClamping() (the context's performance manager: its FPS statistics and shutdown report) 'glitchygames.events.base.shared_instances' src/glitchygames/events/base.py ResourceManager() subclasses (the shared event managers and the FontManager: one per class per engine context), ResourceManager.release_shared_instances, release_shared_instance 'glitchygames.fonts.font_manager.options' src/glitchygames/fonts/font_manager.py FontManager.OPTIONS (a view of it), FontManager.set_font_system, get_font_system 'glitchygames.sprites.bitmappy_sprite.singletons' src/glitchygames/sprites/bitmappy_sprite.py Singleton(), SingletonBitmappySprite(), FocusableSingletonBitmappySprite() (one per class per engine context) 'glitchygames.events.base.unhandled_event_types' src/glitchygames/events/base.py unhandled_event (the event types already logged under --debug-events) 'glitchygames.sprites.sprite.counters' src/glitchygames/sprites/sprite.py sprite_counters() (the sprite creation counters and breakpoints the teardown report logs), Sprite.break_when

tests/test_engine_context.py proves, for every slot, that two contexts in one process never see each other's values; a slot added without such a check fails the suite.

docs.title: Read-only views
docs.text:
The class attributes that held one game's state are now read-only views. Each is read-only, the current game's, and None (or its empty default) outside a game; engine code reads the instance or the slot's owner function instead, and so does any code that writes.

View What it reads Outside a game Where to write GameEngine.game the current engine's game class (engine.game; the scene it built is engine.running_game.instance) None the engine's own: engine.game GameEngine.OPTIONS the current engine's parsed options None the engine's own: engine.options GameEngine.EVENT_HANDLERS the current engine's dispatch table, event type to bound handler None the engine's own: engine.event_handlers GameEngine.LAST_EVENT_MISS the on_*_event name the current engine last looked up and missed None the engine's own: engine.last_event_miss GameEngine.MISSING_EVENTS the handler names the current engine missed (each logged once) None the engine's own: engine.missing_events GameEngine.UNIMPLEMENTED_EVENTS the event types no handler of the current engine took (each logged once) None the engine's own: engine.unimplemented_events SceneManager.OPTIONS the current context's scene manager's copy of its engine's options (never makes a manager) None the manager's own: manager.engine_options (the game_engine setter sets it) FontManager.OPTIONS the current context's font options an empty dict the current context's font options in place (FontManager.OPTIONS.update(...)) or FontManager.set_font_system(...) Sprite.SPRITE_COUNTERS the current context's sprite counters, by sprite type an empty dict glitchygames.sprites.sprite.sprite_counters().counters Sprite.SPRITE_BREAKPOINTS the current context's sprite breakpoints (Sprite.break_when) None (no breakpoints) a breakpoint with Sprite.break_when(...) Sprite.SPRITE_COUNT how many sprites the current context made 0 glitchygames.sprites.sprite.sprite_counters().count glitchygames.performance.performance_manager AdaptiveClamping(), the current context's performance manager (made on first read) a fresh manager, with no statistics yet nothing: AdaptiveClamping() is the current context's manager; patch its methods

Read on an instance, a class view answers that object's own state (engine.OPTIONS is engine.options). The rules (src/glitchygames/read_only_views.py):

  • A view stores nothing: its functions run on every read.
  • A view is declared in its class body (ReadOnlyView, or ClassOnlyView for a name each instance keeps as its own attribute, engine.game). A module view is a name its module marks in READ_ONLY_MODULE_VIEWS and answers in its __getattr__; a module __getattr__ alone (glitchygames.audio's lazy VoiceAssistant) is not a view.
  • Writing or deleting a view, on its class, an instance or its module, raises ReadOnlyViewError naming where to write instead (the last column).
  • A class-level read costs about 2.3 slot reads (Performance, below), so engine code never reads a view: it reads its own objects (self.options, self.event_handlers), a slot once per function into a local, or the owner function (sprite_counters(), AdaptiveClamping()).

current_engine() answers the engine itself, for code that has none at hand.

docs.title: Guards
docs.text:
• tests/test_engine_context.py: every slot's isolation check, the import-time read scan, and that every test ends in the default context.
  • tests/test_read_only_views.py: every view has a check (two contexts each see their own value, a fresh context reads None or the empty default, and writing it raises naming where to write); the engine never reads a view; this page lists every view and where to write, and the costs below stay within the gate.
  • tests/test_process_state_guard.py: the audit as an allowlist scan of the engine and every member; module- or class-level mutable state that is neither a slot nor listed with its audit row and reason fails the suite.
  • tests/test_shared_font_cache_guard.py: nothing changes a cached font's style in place, so the process-wide font caches (audit row R9) stay safe to share.
  • tests/test_suite_collection.py: no living document writes a read-only view.

Each game's performance report covers that game alone (its context's AdaptiveClamping()); an outer game that steps others (the Arcade's wrapper) reports the aggregate of every game it steps.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
What each kind of read costs (Apple M4 Max, Python 3.14):

Read Cost per read Measured attribute read 30 ns engine.options; Task 17, 2026-11-10, median (0.33 slot reads) instance property 19 ns timeit; the owner, 2026-10-28 slot read 90 ns current_context().value(slot=...); Task 17, 2026-11-10, median (the reference) read-only view 210 ns GameEngine.OPTIONS with an engine running; Task 17, 2026-11-10, median (2.32 slot reads) current_engine() 113 ns Task 17, 2026-11-10, median (1.25 slot reads) context switch 430 ns with context.active(): entered and left; timeit; the owner, 2026-10-28

The four Task 17 rows are the medians of gate ©'s per-read benchmarks (tests/benchmarks/test_engine_context_benchmarks.py, -k reading, pytest-benchmark, one run on 2026-11-10, the machine's one-minute load 5.2). Each benchmarked function makes one read, so each of those four medians includes the same one Python function call (about 18 ns: the attribute read's 30 ns here against 12 ns under timeit): they compare with each other, not with the two timeit rows, which have no call around the read. They replace Task 1's and Task 16's timeit best-of-five figures (slot read 61 ns, view 126 ns or 2.07 slot reads, current_engine() 79 ns or 1.30 slot reads, attribute 12 ns).

What they mean per frame:

  • Engine code reads its own objects (self.options, self.event_handlers: the dispatch runs per event), so those reads cost no more than before. What is new per frame: two slot reads per pump (the internal-post tracker, pending_internal_posts() and forget_pending_posts(), about 50 ns more each than the old global), and one clock.raw_counter_seconds() per unpaced step, which is BUGS.md #268's fix, not the contexts.
  • The slot-backed state a frame reads (the doors, the random streams, the polled input, the frame clock, the sprite counters, the internal-post tracker) costs roughly 1-3 µs a frame by the plan's estimate (not counted read by read). Task 17 (2026-11-10) measured it against main before the plan (cd60bd42), on a bare frame step of about 19-21 µs, in one informational longer pair (~70-85k rounds each, load 5.6-5.7): the frame step about 0.6-1.7 µs more, and dispatching a batch of two events about 0.3-1.2 µs more (minimum to median). That frame-step figure runs paced=False, so it includes #268's clock read. In gate ©'s six short per-call pairs (two sets of three, load 3.6-4.1), pytest-benchmark's 5% median check failed 3 of 6 for the frame step and 2 of 6 for event dispatch, never all three of a set, so not a regression by the gate's rule. In the games' goldens and bundled demos neither p50 nor p99 moved beyond timer noise (gate (a)).
  • The Arcade pays about 0.4 µs per game per tick for switching.
  • Each game's performance report covers that game alone; an outer game's (the Arcade wrapper's) is the aggregate of every game it steps.

The rules that follow:

  • Engine code never reads a view (test_the_engine_never_reads_a_view enforces it).
  • Games, tools and tests may read views for convenience, but read their own object or a local in a hot loop.
  • Task 17's gate keeps the numbers honest and is never relaxed: the recordings A/B against the base with behaviour unchanged, the per-call benchmarks, and each read's ratio to a slot read (READ_RATIO_LIMITS in tests/benchmarks/test_engine_context_benchmarks.py: a view at most 4 slot reads, current_engine() at most 2; tests/test_read_only_views.py checks this table against them).

docs.title: Event System Architecture
docs.text:
GlitchyGames makes it easy to port simple pygame projects into more advanced games with little effort. If you already have a pygame game using pygame.event.get() and if/elif chains, you can bring it into GlitchyGames and immediately benefit from named event handlers, automatic state tracking, and synthesized higher-level events — without rewriting your existing event logic.

Porting can be incremental: a scene that defines process_event(event) receives every raw pygame.event.Event from the engine, in order, instead of the on_*_event() callbacks (GameEngine.process_events), so an existing if/elif loop body moves in as it is. Adopt the GlitchyGames handlers one event at a time as you need their benefits. Don't call pygame.event.get() yourself: the engine reads SDL's queue once per frame, and whatever another reader takes never reaches the engine.

Replay

Code that polls pygame directly cannot be replayed exactly. For sessions that replay (--replay-trace), read polled input from current_input() and take events through the engine; see Gameplay Recording and Replay. Code inside the glitchygames package must always do so (tests/test_engine_doors.py).

What GlitchyGames adds on top of raw pygame:

  • Named handlers — override on_key_down_event() instead of writing if event.type == pygame.KEYDOWN. No if/elif dispatch chains.
  • Automatic state tracking — event managers cache button states, axis values, hat positions, and mouse focus so you can poll the current state very cheaply at any time.
  • Synthesized events — GlitchyGames generates events that pygame doesn't provide: mouse drag and drop (on_mouse_drag_event, on_left_mouse_drag_event, on_mouse_drop_event), keyboard chords (on_key_chord_down_event), and per-button mouse events (on_left_mouse_button_down_event vs raw MOUSEBUTTONDOWN with a button field).
  • Custom event types — three engine-level event types (FPSEVENT, GAMEEVENT, MENUEVENT) allocated by name (named_custom_event_type), plus an extensible GAMEEVENT bus for posting arbitrary game-specific events with per-subtype callbacks.
  • An unhandled event safety net — every on_*_event() has a default stub that reports the event as unhandled (a warning once per type, or an UnhandledEventError under --no-unhandled-events), and the engine counts every unhandled event type and logs the table at teardown.

Events flow from SDL through pygame, into specialized event managers that track state and synthesize higher-level events, through the scene manager, and finally into scenes and sprites.

docs.title: Event Dispatch Overview
docs.text:
The path an event takes from SDL to your scene's handler. Every event family follows the same path; the engine's event_handlers dict picks the family's method in one lookup (the table below says which method each event type gets). The Engine box is the same for every game; the Your game box is where your scene's and sprites' code runs.

%%{init: {"flowchart": {"wrappingWidth": 400}}}%%
flowchart TB
    PATH_SDL["SDL event queue"] --> PATH_PUMP
    subgraph ENGINE_PATH["Engine"]
        PATH_PUMP["active_sources().pump_events()<br/>(live: pygame.event.get())"]
        PATH_PUMP --> PATH_PROCESS["GameEngine.process_events()"]
        PATH_PROCESS --> PATH_WRAP["HashableEvent.from_pygame()"]
        PATH_WRAP --> PATH_LOOKUP{"event_handlers[event.type]"}
        PATH_LOOKUP -->|"no entry, or not handled"| PATH_UNHANDLED["process_unimplemented_event()<br/>counted in unhandled_events"]
        PATH_LOOKUP --> PATH_FAMILY["GameEngine.process_family_event()<br/>(one per event family, table below)"]
        PATH_FAMILY --> PATH_MANAGER["the family's event manager"]
        PATH_MANAGER --> PATH_PROXY["its proxy: keeps state, synthesizes events<br/>(one proxy per device for joysticks and controllers)"]
        PATH_PROXY --> PATH_SCENE_MANAGER["SceneManager on_*_event()"]
    end
    subgraph GAME_PATH["Your game"]

        PATH_SCENE["the active scene's on_*_event()"]
        PATH_SCENE --> PATH_SPRITES["focused or collided sprites' on_*_event()"]
    end

    PATH_SCENE_MANAGER --> PATH_SCENE

docs.title: The proxy layers
docs.text:
Every manager is a ResourceManager that passes calls on to a proxy. The proxy implements the family's interface (MouseEvents for the mouse), keeps the family's state, synthesizes higher-level events (drag, drop and focus for the mouse; chords for the keyboard) and calls the same handler on its game, which is the SceneManager. The SceneManager hands every on_*_event() to the active scene (__getattr__). The mouse, as an example:

%%{init: {"flowchart": {"wrappingWidth": 400}}}%%
flowchart LR
    subgraph ENGINE_MOUSE["Engine"]
        MOUSE_ENGINE["GameEngine<br/>process_mouse_event()"] --> MOUSE_MANAGER["MouseEventManager<br/>proxies: the MouseEventProxy"]
        MOUSE_MANAGER --> MOUSE_PROXY["MouseEventProxy<br/>button states, drag tracking<br/>drag, drop, focus synthesized<br/>proxies: SceneManager, pygame.mouse"]
        MOUSE_PROXY -->|"game.on_mouse_*_event()"| MOUSE_SCENE_MANAGER["SceneManager<br/>__getattr__"]
    end
    subgraph GAME_MOUSE["Your game"]
        MOUSE_SCENE["active scene<br/>on_mouse_*_event()"]
    end
    MOUSE_SCENE_MANAGER --> MOUSE_SCENE

docs.title: Joysticks and controllers
docs.text:
These two add a filter and keep one proxy per device. SDL sees a mapped gamepad as one device on two layers, the raw joystick layer and the controller layer, and sends both layers' events, so the engine lets each device's input through from one layer only (its event_layer: the controller layer when SDL maps the pad, else the joystick layer), and only for devices --input-mode shows the game (src/glitchygames/input/input_devices.py).

%%{init: {"flowchart": {"wrappingWidth": 400}}}%%
flowchart TB
    DEVICE_EVENT["JOY* or CONTROLLER* event"] --> DEVICE_PROCESS
    subgraph ENGINE_DEVICE["Engine"]
        DEVICE_PROCESS["process_joystick_event()<br/>or process_controller_event()"]
        DEVICE_PROCESS --> DEVICE_FILTER{"input_devices.dispatches()<br/>this device shown by the input mode,<br/>and this is its event layer?"}
        DEVICE_FILTER -->|"no: the other layer's copy,<br/>or a hidden device"| DEVICE_DROPPED["dropped (counted as handled)"]
        DEVICE_FILTER -->|"yes"| DEVICE_MANAGER["JoystickEventManager.joysticks<br/>or ControllerEventManager.controllers<br/>[event.instance_id]"]
        DEVICE_MANAGER --> DEVICE_PROXY["that device's proxy<br/>opened through the devices door<br/>proxies: SceneManager, the device"]
        DEVICE_PROXY -->|"game.on_joy_*_event() or<br/>game.on_controller_*_event()"| DEVICE_SCENE_MANAGER["SceneManager"]

        DEVICE_PROCESS -->|"device added or removed:<br/>always passes the filter"| DEVICE_DEVICES["the manager opens or drops<br/>the device's proxy"]
        DEVICE_DEVICES --> DEVICE_SYNCHRONIZE["GameEngine._synchronize_input_devices()<br/>InputDevices follows the managers"]
    end
    subgraph GAME_DEVICE["Your game"]
        DEVICE_SCENE["active scene's handler"]
        DEVICE_NOTIFY["active scene's<br/>on_input_device_added(device=...)<br/>or on_input_device_removed(device=...)"]
    end
    DEVICE_SCENE_MANAGER --> DEVICE_SCENE
    DEVICE_SYNCHRONIZE --> DEVICE_NOTIFY

A mapped pad's device events arrive twice (the joystick layer's, then the controller layer's); InputDevices adds it once, with both layers, and removes it once neither manager holds it.

docs.title: Event performance tiers
docs.text:
Not all events pay the same cost. Events fall into three tiers depending on whether they're blocked, unhandled, or handled (SDL's filter is outside both boxes):

%%{init: {"flowchart": {"wrappingWidth": 400}}}%%
flowchart TD
    EVT["SDL event fires"] --> BLOCKED{"Blocked by\npygame.event.set_blocked?"}
    BLOCKED -->|"Yes"| ZERO["Filtered by SDL\nNever enters pipeline\nCost: zero"]
    BLOCKED -->|"No"| WRAP
    subgraph ENGINE_TIERS["Engine"]
        WRAP["Wrap as HashableEvent\nO#40;1#41; event_handlers lookup"]
        WRAP --> STUB{"Scene overrides\nthe handler?"}

Tier When Cost per occurrence Example Blocked pygame.event.set_blocked(type) Zero — SDL filters it before the engine's pump Disabling MOUSEMOTION in a menu-only scene Unhandled The scene keeps the default stub Dispatch path + unhandled_event(): an options lookup, and a warning only for the type's first occurrence JOYAXISMOTION when no joystick handler exists Handled Scene overrides on_*_event() Full dispatch path + your handler executes on_key_down_event() processing a key press

The event_handlers dict lookup is O(1) for all events that reach the pipeline, but every unblocked event still travels the dispatch path (wrap in HashableEvent, dict lookup, proxy forwarding). To eliminate that cost entirely, block the event at the pygame level with pygame.event.set_blocked().

docs.title: Custom Event Types
docs.text:
GlitchyGames defines three custom event types beyond the standard pygame events, allocated from pygame.event.custom_type() when glitchygames.events is imported, so a game's or library's own custom_type() never gets one of their ids (BUGS.md #197). custom_type() hands out USEREVENT + 1, + 2, + 3, ... in order, and the engine's module is imported before any game code runs, so they are usually USEREVENT + 1, + 2 and + 3. Something that calls custom_type() before glitchygames is imported shifts them, so each is registered by name (NAMED_CUSTOM_EVENT_TYPES): a recording's header names the ids it was made with (custom_event_types), and a replay moves the recorded events to its own process's ids (BUGS.md #211.1).

These constants are defined in src/glitchygames/events/base.py (exported by glitchygames.events):

FPSEVENT = named_custom_event_type('FPSEVENT')  # FPS counter updates (usually USEREVENT + 1)
GAMEEVENT = named_custom_event_type('GAMEEVENT')  # Game-specific events, via subtypes (+ 2)
MENUEVENT = named_custom_event_type('MENUEVENT')  # Menu item selections (+ 3)

A game that needs its own event type should allocate it the same way, at import: LEVEL_UP = named_custom_event_type('MY_GAME_LEVEL_UP'). A name is registered once (a second registration raises CustomEventNameTakenError). A type allocated straight from pygame.event.custom_type() has no name, so a recording cannot say which id it had and a replay in a shifted process cannot move it. It can also collide: pygame.quit() restarts pygame's allocation at USEREVENT + 1, so the first raw custom_type() after a quit returns FPSEVENT's id. named_custom_event_type skips every id a name already holds.

GAMEEVENT is intentionally generic — game code posts events with arbitrary payloads via GameEngine.post_game_event(), and can register per-subtype callbacks via GameEngine.register_game_event() (a scene reaches both through self.scene_manager: register_game_event() and game_engine). This gives games an extensible event bus without consuming additional pygame event IDs.

flowchart LR
    subgraph CustomEvents["Custom Event Types (named_custom_event_type)"]
        FPS["FPSEVENT\npygame.USEREVENT + 1\nFPS counter updates"]
        GAME_E["GAMEEVENT\npygame.USEREVENT + 2\nGame-specific events"]
        MENU["MENUEVENT\npygame.USEREVENT + 3\nMenu item selections"]
    end

    subgraph Producers["Producers"]
        subgraph ENGINE_PRODUCERS["Engine"]
            SM_FPS["SceneManager\nposts every fps_log_interval_ms"]
            MENU_ITEM["MenuItem sprites\npost on click"]
        end
        subgraph GAME_PRODUCERS["Your game"]
            GAME_CODE["Game code\nposts via post_game_event()"]
        end
    end

    subgraph Consumers["Consumers (e.g. Your game.)"]
        FPS_H["on_fps_event()"]
        GAME_H["on_game_event()\n+ registered subtype callbacks"]
        MENU_H["on_menu_item_event()"]
    end

    SM_FPS --> FPS --> FPS_H
    GAME_CODE --> GAME_E --> GAME_H
    MENU_ITEM --> MENU --> MENU_H

docs.title: Extending GAMEEVENT in your game
docs.text:
GAMEEVENT is designed as an extensible event bus. Instead of consuming additional pygame event IDs for each game-specific event, you define integer subtypes and register callbacks for them. All subtypes share the single GAMEEVENT ID.

Here's how a game might define custom events for a scoring system and a power-up system:

# Define your game's event subtypes as constants
SCORE_CHANGED = 1
POWER_UP_COLLECTED = 2
LEVEL_COMPLETE = 3

class MyGame(Scene):
    def setup(self):
        # Register callbacks for each subtype
        self.scene_manager.register_game_event(SCORE_CHANGED, self.on_score_changed)
        self.scene_manager.register_game_event(POWER_UP_COLLECTED, self.on_power_up)
        self.scene_manager.register_game_event(LEVEL_COMPLETE, self.on_level_complete)

    def on_score_changed(self, event: HashableEvent):
        new_score = event.score
        self.hud.update_score(new_score)

    def on_power_up(self, event: HashableEvent):
        power_type = event.power_type
        duration = event.duration
        self.player.apply_power_up(power_type, duration)

    def on_level_complete(self, event: HashableEvent):
        # The SceneManager switches to it after this frame
        self.next_scene = LevelTransitionScene(event.next_level)

Any code in the game can fire these events:

# From a collision handler, enemy class, pickup sprite, etc.
# (SceneManager is a singleton: SceneManager().game_engine works anywhere)
self.scene_manager.game_engine.post_game_event(
    event_subtype=SCORE_CHANGED,
    event_data={'score': self.score},
)

self.scene_manager.game_engine.post_game_event(
    event_subtype=POWER_UP_COLLECTED,
    event_data={'power_type': 'speed_boost', 'duration': 5.0},
)

Under the hood, post_game_event creates a pygame.event.Event with type GAMEEVENT and a subtype field, then posts it with glitchygames.recording.post_event (so recordings mark it internal). SceneManager.on_game_event() looks up game_engine.registered_events[event.subtype] and calls the matching callback. If no callback is registered for that subtype, it logs an error telling you to call register_game_event().

This pattern gives you an unlimited number of game-specific event types while consuming only one pygame event ID.

docs.title: Native window messages (SYSWMEVENT)
docs.text:
SYSWMEVENT carries the window system's raw messages: on x11 every X event the window gets (focus, exposure, property and configure notifications), on Windows each window message (hwnd, msg, wparam, lparam). SDL leaves the type disabled, and so does the engine: GameEngine allows every event type through allow_every_event_type() (src/glitchygames/events/base.py), which keeps SYSWMEVENT blocked. Before, a plain pygame.event.set_allowed(None) turned it on, so on a real X server the queue, every --record-trace recording and every instant-replay journal filled with messages no game read.

A game that wants them opts in on its scene class (the one given to GameEngine), like TARGET_FPS:

class MyGame(Scene):
    NATIVE_WINDOW_MESSAGES = True  # anything but a bool is refused with TypeError

    def on_sys_wm_event(self, event: HashableEvent) -> None:
        # A plain HashableEvent (SYSWMEVENT has no class in EVENT_CLASSES) holding
        # pygame's platform fields: event.event (the raw XEvent bytes) on x11
        ...

The route is GameEngine.process_game_event → GameEventManager.on_sys_wm_event → SceneManager → the active scene's on_sys_wm_event. A game that opts in records them like any other event (an x11 message's bytes are stored as {"__bytes__": "<hex>"}), and a replay serves the recorded ones; a replay's input blocking (src/glitchygames/replay/input_blocking.py) restores the type to blocked when it ends. pygame-ce 2.5.8 reports SYSWMEVENT as allowed until something blocks it through pygame, although SDL ignores it, which is why the engine blocks it explicitly: a snapshot-and-restore of the blocked types would otherwise turn it on.

docs.title: ResourceManager Proxy Pattern
docs.text:
Each event manager is a shared-instance ResourceManager that delegates to inner proxy objects. The proxy chain provides two capabilities:

  1. Event dispatch: When GameEngine calls on_*_event() on an event manager (e.g., MouseEventManager), the event manager forwards to its inner proxy, which updates internal state (tracking pressed keys, button states, drag sequences, etc.) and then forwards the event to self.game — the active scene.

  2. Attribute fallthrough: An attribute the manager doesn't have is looked up on its proxies by ResourceManager.__getattr__ (src/glitchygames/events/base.py), each in turn until one has it: mouse_manager.get_pos() falls through the inner proxy and the scene to pygame.mouse (BUGS.md #198: the lookup used to stop at the first proxy).

Poll input from the snapshot

The pygame modules in the proxy lists below read the device live. Polled input should come from glitchygames.input.state.current_input(): it is the frame's snapshot, which a replay serves exactly.

Why this matters: Scenes and sprites never need a direct reference to the event plumbing. They talk to the event manager, a shared instance accessible from anywhere (MouseEventManager() is the engine's), and the manager handles state tracking (what buttons are held, what sprite has mouse focus, what keys form a chord).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Each manager follows the same two-layer structure:

MouseEventManager (shared-instance ResourceManager)
├── proxies: [MouseEventProxy]
│
└── MouseEventProxy (inner class, also a ResourceManager; SHARES_INSTANCE = False)
    ├── proxies: [self.game, pygame.mouse]
    ├── state: mouse_state, dragging, focus tracking
    └── on_*_event(): update state, synthesize events, forward to self.game

The inner proxy holds the real state and logic. The outer manager is just a shared-instance wrapper that ensures only one proxy chain exists per subsystem.

docs.title: Proxy resolution order
docs.text:
When an attribute is accessed on a manager, ResourceManager.__getattr__ walks the proxy list in order. The first proxy that has the attribute wins:

sequenceDiagram
    box rgb(255,243,224) Your game
    participant CODE as Your game code
    end
    box rgb(232,238,255) Engine
    participant ENGINE as GameEngine
    participant MGR as MouseEventManager
    participant PROXY as MouseEventProxy
    participant GAME as SceneManager (self.game)
    end
    participant PG as pygame.mouse

    Note over ENGINE,PG: Event dispatch path
    ENGINE->>MGR: on_mouse_motion_event(event)
    MGR->>PROXY: on_mouse_motion_event(event)
    Note over PROXY: Track drag state<br/>Check sprite collisions<br/>Synthesize focus/drag events
    PROXY->>GAME: on_mouse_motion_event(event)
    PROXY-->>GAME: on_left_mouse_drag_event(event, trigger)
    Note over GAME: forwards to the active scene's handler<br/>(its stub when the scene has none)

    Note over CODE,PG: Attribute proxy path
    CODE->>MGR: get_pos()
    Note over MGR: __getattr__: not on self<br/>try proxies[0]...
    MGR->>PROXY: get_pos()
    Note over PROXY: __getattr__: not on self<br/>try proxies[0]=game... AttributeError<br/>try proxies[1]=pygame.mouse
    PROXY->>PG: get_pos()

docs.title: Proxy lists by manager
docs.text:
Each inner proxy's list (the outer manager's list holds the inner proxy, or for the joystick and controller managers, the game):

Manager Proxy list pygame API exposed MouseEventManager [self.game, pygame.mouse] get_pos(), set_visible(), etc. KeyboardEventManager [self.game, pygame.key] get_pressed(), get_mods(), etc. AudioEventManager [self.game, pygame.mixer] get_busy(), set_num_channels(), etc. JoystickEventManager [self.game, self.joystick] per JoystickEventProxy Per-joystick: get_axis(), get_button(), etc. ControllerEventManager [self.game, self.controller] per ControllerEventProxy Per-controller: get_axis(), get_button(), etc. WindowEventManager [self.game] No pygame subsystem (events only) TouchEventManager [self.game, pygame._sdl2.touch] ([self.game] when it is unavailable) get_num_devices(), etc. DropEventManager [self.game] No pygame subsystem (events only) GameEventManager [self.game] No pygame subsystem (events only) AppEventManager [self.game] No pygame subsystem (events only) MidiEventManager [self.game, pygame.midi] get_count(), get_device_info(), etc.

Managers without a pygame subsystem in their proxy list (like DropEventManager) only forward events — __getattr__ falls through to the game object.

docs.title: Shared instances
docs.text:
ResourceManager.__new__ keeps the shared instances in the current engine context (SHARED_INSTANCES_SLOT, src/glitchygames/events/base.py), keyed by concrete class type: one per class per engine context. Constructing MouseEventManager(game) a second time returns the original instance as it is: ResourceManager.__init_subclass__ wraps each class's __init__ so a shared instance is initialized once (BUGS.md #198: Python runs __init__ on whatever __new__ returns, so a second construction rebuilt the manager for game=None).

A class with SHARES_INSTANCE = False gets a new instance at every construction: the proxies (a manager owns its own; the controller manager one per controller) and EventManager (GameEngine, made for each run, and SceneManager, whose own __new__ keeps one per engine context). Each engine run calls ResourceManager.release_shared_instances() (the current context's) before it makes its managers, so a second engine in one process (a recording, then its replay) builds its own, opening devices through its own doors.

docs.title: HashableEvent Wrapper
docs.text:
Raw pygame events are converted to HashableEvent (HashableEvent.from_pygame) to enable hashing, immutability and serialization. This is the universal event type throughout the system: every event of a type with a class of its own is an instance of that class (below).

pygame.event.Event is not hashable

Raw pygame.event.Event objects cannot be hashed or used as dictionary keys. HashableEvent is a UserDict subclass holding the event's type and a copy of its fields (the pygame event itself is not kept), and it provides __hash__().

docs.title: The problem with raw pygame event handling
docs.text:
In raw pygame, handling events looks like this:

for event in pygame.event.get():
    if event.type == pygame.KEYDOWN:
        # handle key press
        ...
    elif event.type == pygame.MOUSEMOTION:
        # handle mouse move
        ...
    elif event.type == pygame.JOYAXISMOTION:
        # handle joystick
        ...
    # ... and so on for every event type

This has several problems:

  1. Silent event dropping: Any event type you don't have an elif for is silently ignored. You get no feedback that your game is missing a handler — bugs hide behind silence.

  2. No separation of concerns: The entire event dispatch is one giant if/elif chain in one place. Every subsystem's event handling is tangled together.

  3. No state tracking: Raw pygame events are fire-and-forget. If you want to know "is button 3 currently held?", you have to track that yourself with your own variables.

  4. No higher-level events: Pygame gives you MOUSEBUTTONDOWN and MOUSEMOTION separately. If you want drag, drop, or focus events, you build the state machine yourself.

GlitchyGames solves all of these: events are dispatched through named on_*_event() methods (no if/elif chains), event managers track state (buttons, axes, focus), and synthesized events (drag, drop, chord) are generated automatically.

Raw events and polling

A scene that defines process_event(event) gets every raw pygame.event.Event instead of the on_*_event() handlers. For smooth movement, poll the frame's input snapshot (current_input().key_pressed(...), see Gameplay Recording and Replay) while still receiving on_key_down_event() for discrete key actions; polling pygame directly (pygame.key.get_pressed()) works live but cannot be replayed. Never call pygame.event.get() yourself: the engine is the queue's only reader.

But this architecture creates a new problem: what happens to events that nobody handles?

docs.title: The unhandled event problem
docs.text:
GlitchyGames gives every on_*_event() a default stub (the *EventStubs classes in src/glitchygames/events/input_event_interfaces.py and system_event_interfaces.py; Scene inherits AllEventStubs). If your scene doesn't override on_joy_axis_motion_event, the stub catches the event instead of silently dropping it and calls unhandled_event() (src/glitchygames/events/base.py). This is powerful for debugging — you can see exactly which events your game isn't handling.

But stubs run on every occurrence of their event. A joystick thumbstick drifting slightly generates JOYAXISMOTION events continuously, even when nothing is listening, so unhandled_event() must be cheap and quiet after the first one.

docs.title: Example: one frame at 60 FPS
docs.text:
Imagine a player is moving the mouse while a joystick is connected. In a single frame (~16ms), pygame might deliver these events:

Event Source Has a handler? MOUSEMOTION Mouse moved 3px Yes — scene implements on_mouse_motion_event JOYAXISMOTION Joystick thumbstick drift No — scene doesn't handle joystick JOYAXISMOTION Same thumbstick, new value No — still unhandled JOYAXISMOTION Same thumbstick, new value No — still unhandled

The handled MOUSEMOTION flows through the proxy chain and reaches the scene's real handler.

But the three JOYAXISMOTION events hit the stub, which calls unhandled_event().

docs.title: One warning per type, then silence
docs.text:
unhandled_event() reads the game's options and:

  • with no_unhandled_events (--no-unhandled-events, and every test) raises UnhandledEventError;
  • with debug_events (--debug-events), logs Unhandled Event: <name> <event> at WARNING the first time it sees each event type (a module-level set of seen types), and nothing after;
  • otherwise does nothing.
Frame 1:  WARNING: Unhandled Event: JoyAxisMotion ...   ← first occurrence, logged
Frame 1:  (type already seen, nothing logged)
Frame 1:  (type already seen, nothing logged)
Frame 2:  (nothing logged)
...
(1 log call total, then 0 per frame)

Separately, GameEngine.process_unimplemented_event handles events that no process_*_event method dispatched (types with no event_handlers entry, or a handler that returned False): it counts each type in GameEngine.unhandled_events (count, first-seen time, attribute names) and the engine logs that table at teardown.

docs.title: Why HashableEvent
docs.text:
Raw pygame.event.Event objects are not hashable, so they cannot be dictionary keys, set members or functools.cache arguments, and they are mutable. HashableEvent is hashable by its content and immutable, and its fields (pos, button, key, etc.) read as attributes. Events are also serializable: to_json() / from_json() (below), pickling, structured logging. Raw pygame.event.Event objects support none of these.

The synthesized events — drag, drop, chord, focus — carry their extra context as extra handler arguments, never by changing the event: the mouse drag handler receives both the current MOUSEMOTION event and the MOUSEBUTTONDOWN trigger that started the drag, and the keyboard chord handlers receive the held keys' KEYDOWN events as keys: tuple[KeyEvent, ...].

docs.title: Typed event classes
docs.text:
HashableEvent(type, **fields) builds the class its type maps to in EVENT_CLASSES (src/glitchygames/events/base.py, exported by glitchygames.events), so a MOUSEMOTION is a MouseMotionEvent however it was built (the engine's dispatch, HashableEvent.from_pygame(pygame_event), tests, games). The classes only declare the fields pygame-ce gives their types, for the type checker; they store, hash, compare, pickle and serialize exactly as HashableEvent. Equality is by type and fields, never by Python class. Custom and field-less types (QUIT, MENUEVENT, USEREVENT, the APP_* events) stay HashableEvent, whose undeclared fields read as Any.

Class Types Fields KeyEvent KEYDOWN, KEYUP key, mod, scancode, unicode, window MouseMotionEvent MOUSEMOTION pos, rel, buttons, touch, window MouseButtonEvent MOUSEBUTTONDOWN, MOUSEBUTTONUP pos, button, touch, window MouseWheelEvent MOUSEWHEEL x, y, flipped, precise_x, precise_y, touch, window TextInputEvent, TextEditingEvent TEXTINPUT, TEXTEDITING text (start, length), window JoyAxisEvent, JoyBallEvent, JoyHatEvent, JoyButtonEvent JOY*MOTION, JOYBUTTON* instance_id and axis/value, ball/rel, hat/value, button JoyDeviceAddedEvent, JoyDeviceRemovedEvent JOYDEVICEADDED, JOYDEVICEREMOVED device_index, guid / instance_id ControllerAxisEvent, ControllerButtonEvent CONTROLLERAXISMOTION, CONTROLLERBUTTON* instance_id, axis/value, button ControllerDeviceAddedEvent, ControllerDeviceEvent CONTROLLERDEVICEADDED, CONTROLLERDEVICEREMOVED/REMAPPED device_index, guid / instance_id ControllerTouchpadEvent CONTROLLERTOUCHPAD* instance_id, touch_id, finger_id, x, y, pressure TouchFingerEvent, MultiGestureEvent FINGER*, MULTIGESTURE touch_id, finger_id, x, y, dx, dy, pressure / rotated, pinched, num_fingers WindowEvent, WindowGeometryEvent, WindowDisplayChangedEvent WINDOW* window (x, y for moved/resized/size changed; display_index) DropEvent, DropFileEvent, DropTextEvent DROP* window (file, text) AudioDeviceEvent, MidiEvent AUDIODEVICE*, MIDIIN/MIDIOUT which, iscapture / status, data1-data3, timestamp, vice_id ActiveEvent, VideoResizeEvent ACTIVEEVENT, VIDEORESIZE gain, state / size, w, h FpsEvent, GameEvent FPSEVENT, GAMEEVENT fps / subtype (plus the game's own fields)

Handlers name their class (def on_mouse_motion_event(self, event: MouseMotionEvent)), so event.pos is a tuple[int, int] to the type checker. A game's own subclass of a type's class (or of HashableEvent for a custom type) is kept; a class called with another family's type raises ValueError.

docs.title: Immutability and the cached hash
docs.text: An event never changes after construction. Item and attribute assignment, deletion, update, clear, pop, popitem, setdefault and |= raise TypeError; event.with_fields(**changes) (or event | changes) returns a changed copy of the same class (its type cannot change). event.dict is a read-only view. The hash is computed on the first hash(event) and kept in a slot outside the fields, so it never shows in iteration, len(), dict(event), the pickled state or to_json(); a pickled or with_fields copy computes its own. Field values should be immutable too: a list inside a game event is hashed by its contents once.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
event.to_json() returns {"type": <number>, "attributes": {...}}, the attributes encoded as a recording encodes an event's (glitchygames.recording.json_safe_value: tuples as lists; lists, dicts, bytes and non-finite floats tagged), except that a window is written as None, as a replay serves it. HashableEvent.from_json(record) reverses it, and also reads a recording's event records (a recorded window reference becomes None). Recordings themselves still store the raw pygame events (recording.event_to_record); their format is unchanged.

flowchart LR
    subgraph PygameEvent["pygame.event.Event"]
        TYPE["type: int"]
        DICT["dict: standard pygame fields"]
    end

    subgraph HE["HashableEvent #40;UserDict#41;"]
        H_TYPE["type: int"]
        H_DICT["a copy of the fields"]
        H_HASH["__hash__#40;#41; — by content, cached"]
        H_ATTR["immutable; typed per-type class"]
    end

    PygameEvent -->|"HashableEvent.from_pygame#40;#41;"| HE

docs.title: Mouse Event Synthesis
docs.text:
The MouseEventManager's proxy (src/glitchygames/events/mouse.py) synthesizes button-specific and drag/drop events from primitive pygame mouse events. Button-specific variants are generated for the left, middle and right buttons (and scroll down/up for the old wheel buttons 4 and 5 on button down).

sequenceDiagram
    participant PG as pygame
    participant MM as MouseEventProxy
    participant SCENE as Scene

    Note over MM: mouse_state holds the latest event<br/>per button (and per MOUSEMOTION)

    PG->>MM: MOUSEBUTTONDOWN (button=1)
    MM->>MM: mouse_state[1] = event
    MM->>SCENE: on_mouse_button_down_event()
    MM->>SCENE: on_left_mouse_button_down_event()

    PG->>MM: MOUSEMOTION (while button 1 held)
    MM->>SCENE: on_mouse_motion_event()
    MM->>MM: mouse_state[1] is a MOUSEBUTTONDOWN:<br/>drag, mouse_dragging = True
    MM->>SCENE: on_mouse_drag_event(event, trigger)
    MM->>SCENE: on_left_mouse_drag_event(event, trigger)
    Note over SCENE: trigger = the<br/>MOUSEBUTTONDOWN event

    PG->>MM: MOUSEBUTTONUP (button=1)
    MM->>MM: mouse_state[1] = event
    MM->>SCENE: on_left_mouse_button_up_event()
    MM->>SCENE: on_mouse_button_up_event()
    MM->>MM: Was dragging? Yes: mouse_dragging = False
    MM->>SCENE: on_mouse_drop_event(event, trigger=event)
    MM->>SCENE: on_left_mouse_drop_event(event, trigger=event)
    Note over SCENE: the drop's trigger is the<br/>MOUSEBUTTONUP itself

The proxy also passes MOUSEMOTION to the topmost sprite under the cursor (collided_sprites()), and Scene passes mouse events on to the sprites at the event's position. Focus follows that topmost sprite: when the sprite under the cursor changes, the one left gets on_mouse_unfocus_event(event) and the one entered on_mouse_focus_event(event, current_focus), before it gets the motion (the proxy's current_focus and previous_focus hold them).

docs.title: Keyboard Chord Detection
docs.text:
The KeyboardEventManager tracks all currently pressed keys and emits chord events, enabling multi-key shortcut detection.

sequenceDiagram
    participant PG as pygame
    participant KM as KeyboardEventManager
    participant SCENE as Scene

    Note over KM: keys dict holds each key's<br/>latest event, by key code

    PG->>KM: KEYDOWN (key=LCTRL)
    KM->>KM: keys[LCTRL] = event
    KM->>SCENE: on_key_down_event(event)
    KM->>SCENE: on_key_chord_down_event(event, (LCTRL down,))

    PG->>KM: KEYDOWN (key=Z)
    KM->>KM: keys[Z] = event
    KM->>SCENE: on_key_down_event(event)
    KM->>SCENE: on_key_chord_down_event(event, (LCTRL down, Z down))
    Note over SCENE: Scene detects Ctrl+Z chord

    PG->>KM: KEYUP (key=Z)
    KM->>KM: keys[Z] = event (no longer down)
    KM->>SCENE: on_key_up_event(event)
    KM->>SCENE: on_key_chord_up_event(event, (LCTRL down,))

    PG->>KM: KEYUP (key=LCTRL)
    KM->>KM: keys[LCTRL] = event (no longer down)
    KM->>SCENE: on_key_up_event(event)
    KM->>SCENE: on_key_chord_up_event(event, ())

docs.title: Controller State Machine
docs.text:
The ControllerEventManager maintains per-controller state via inner proxy objects. Each physical controller gets its own proxy identified by instance_id.

flowchart TD
    subgraph ControllerEventManager["ControllerEventManager (singleton)"]
        CONTROLLERS["controllers dict\ninstance_id -> ControllerEventProxy"]
    end

    subgraph Proxy0["ControllerEventProxy 0"]
        AXES0["_axes: list of 6 ints\nleft_x, left_y, right_x,\nright_y, left_trigger, right_trigger"]
        BUTTONS0["_buttons: list of 15+ bools\nA, B, X, Y, DPAD,\nshoulders, sticks, guide"]
        META0["_name, _id, _instance_id\n_mapping, _attached"]
    end

    subgraph Proxy1["ControllerEventProxy 1"]
        AXES1["_axes: list of 6 ints"]
        BUTTONS1["_buttons: list of 15+ bools"]
        META1["_name, _id, _instance_id"]
    end

    CONTROLLERS -->|"instance_id=0"| Proxy0
    CONTROLLERS -->|"instance_id=1"| Proxy1

    subgraph Dispatch["Event Dispatch"]
        EVENT["CONTROLLERBUTTONDOWN\ninstance_id=0"]
        ROUTE{"Route by\ninstance_id"}
    end

    EVENT --> ROUTE
    ROUTE -->|"0"| Proxy0
    ROUTE -->|"1"| Proxy1

docs.title: Complete Event Category Map
docs.text:
All pygame event types organized by category, showing the mapping from SDL event to GlitchyGames handler method. Each diagram shows SDL events on the left and the on_*_event() handlers they produce on the right. Synthesized events (dashed borders) are derived from primitive SDL events by the event managers.

The event parameter in every handler is a HashableEvent wrapping the original SDL event, as its type's class (KeyEvent, MouseMotionEvent, ...; see Typed event classes) — the same fields shown in the left box (e.g., pos, button, key) are accessible as event.pos, event.button, event.key, etc. Synthesized handlers may receive additional arguments beyond the event (noted in their signatures).

docs.title: Joystick vs Controller: Two Input Subsystems
docs.text: GlitchyGames supports two distinct SDL input subsystems for gamepads: Joystick (low-level) and Controller (high-level). They coexist because they serve different needs, and some devices only work with one or the other.

docs.title: Why two subsystems?
docs.text:
Joystick (pygame.joystick) Controller (pygame._sdl2.controller) Abstraction level Raw hardware — axes, buttons, hats, balls are numbered Semantic — A/B/X/Y, D-pad, triggers, thumbsticks by name Device support Everything SDL recognizes as a joystick Only devices with an SDL GameController mapping Button/axis identity Button 0, Axis 2 (meaning varies by device) CONTROLLER_BUTTON_A, CONTROLLER_AXIS_LEFTX (consistent) Mapping None — raw hardware indices SDL's built-in GameController DB maps hardware to semantic names Hotplug ID device_index (unstable) + instance_id (stable) the same: added by device_index, everything after by instance_id Touchpad support No Yes (CONTROLLERTOUCHPAD* events) Remapping events No Yes (CONTROLLERDEVICEREMAPPED)

A mapped gamepad is one SDL device read on both: the joystick layer and the controller layer, with one instance id, and SDL sends every press on both (JOYBUTTONDOWN and CONTROLLERBUTTONDOWN). The engine runs both managers and hands each press to the game once (below).

docs.title: One device, one event layer
docs.text:
InputDevices (src/glitchygames/input/input_devices.py, whose docstring holds the rules) is the engine's list of the devices a game sees, by instance id: GameEngine.input_devices, or self.input_devices in a scene. Each InputDevice has the devices door's descriptor (name, GUID, device index, instance id, counts), a joystick layer (always) and a controller layer (a mapped pad only); both read the frame's input snapshot, so polling either always works and replays exactly. event_layer is the layer whose events reach on_*_event handlers: the controller layer when the device has one, else the joystick layer. The engine drops the other layer's input events (handled, never unhandled), so a mapped pad's press arrives once, as on_controller_button_down_event, and any other device's as on_joy_button_down_event. Device events (added, removed, remapped) always pass; a scene is also told of each device with on_input_device_added(device=...) / on_input_device_removed(device=...) once the registry has it (a mapped pad, which arrives and leaves on both layers, once each way).

--input-mode filters what the game sees: auto (the default) every device as above, joystick every device on its joystick layer only (SDL blocks controller events), controller mapped pads only (other devices are hidden and their events dropped). ActionMap binds the same families: auto binds a controller_button to both. The joystick demo (src/demos/joystick-demo/src/joystick_demo/__init__.py) lists every device with its event layer's live inputs.

for device in self.input_devices:
    layer = device.controller if device.controller is not None else device.joystick
    print(device.name, layer.axes, layer.buttons)

Disabling joystick events disables controller events

SDL's GameController API is built on top of the joystick subsystem. If you call pygame.event.set_blocked() on joystick event types (JOYAXISMOTION, JOYBUTTONDOWN, etc.), SDL will also stop delivering the corresponding controller events (CONTROLLERAXISMOTION, CONTROLLERBUTTONDOWN, etc.). If you need controllers but not raw joysticks, leave the joystick events unblocked: the engine already drops a mapped pad's joystick-layer input events (One device, one event layer, above).

docs.title: JoystickEventManager architecture
docs.text:
Unlike other event managers, JoystickEventManager manages multiple proxy objects — one per connected joystick. The outer manager is still a singleton, but it maintains a self.joysticks dict keyed by instance_id, and routes each event to the correct proxy based on the event's joystick identity.

This is necessary because:

  1. Multiple devices: There can be 1–N joysticks connected simultaneously. Other managers (Mouse, Keyboard) handle a single global device.
  2. Per-device state: Each joystick has its own axis values, button states, hat positions, and trackball deltas. These must be tracked independently.
  3. ID instability: SDL's device_index can change when devices are added/removed. The manager uses instance_id (stable for the lifetime of a connection) as the dict key instead.

docs.title: Cached properties
docs.text:
The proxy reads several joystick properties once, at init (some hardware answers metadata queries slowly):

  • _name — joystick name string
  • _guid — hardware GUID
  • _init — initialization status
  • _power_level — battery level (if supported)
  • _numaxes, _numballs, _numbuttons, _numhats — capability counts

The proxy exposes get_name(), get_numaxes(), etc., matching the pygame.joystick.Joystick API. get_name() asks the joystick first and returns the cached _name only when that fails; the others return the cached values.

docs.title: Event routing
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    EVT["SDL Joystick Event\n(JOYAXISMOTION, etc.)"] --> MGR["JoystickEventManager\n(singleton)"]
    MGR --> RESOLVE{"Resolve joystick\ninstance_id from event"}
    RESOLVE -->|"event.instance_id\nor fallback event.joy"| LOOKUP["self.joysticks[instance_id]"]
    LOOKUP --> PROXY["JoystickEventProxy #N"]
    PROXY --> STATE["Update cached state\n(_axes, _buttons, _hats, _balls)"]
    STATE --> GAME["Forward to self.game\non_joy_*_event()"]

    ADD["JOYDEVICEADDED"] --> MGR2["JoystickEventManager"]
    MGR2 --> CREATE["Create new JoystickEventProxy\n(init joystick, cache properties)"]
    CREATE --> DICT["self.joysticks[instance_id] = proxy"]
    DICT --> NOTIFY["proxy.on_joy_device_added_event()"]

    REM["JOYDEVICEREMOVED"] --> MGR3["JoystickEventManager"]
    MGR3 --> CLEANUP["Notify proxy, then\nself.joysticks.pop(instance_id)"]

docs.title: ControllerEventManager architecture
docs.text:
ControllerEventManager follows the same multi-proxy pattern as Joystick — one ControllerEventProxy per connected controller, keyed by instance id in self.controllers (the id every controller event carries). The key differences:

  1. SDL GameController API: Uses pygame._sdl2.controller instead of pygame.joystick. This provides semantic button/axis names (A, B, X, Y, left trigger, etc.) instead of raw hardware indices.
  2. Fixed axis/button sets: Controller proxies define AXIS and BUTTONS class variables with the standard SDL GameController constants. The proxy still allows dynamic growth for non-standard buttons.
  3. Touchpad events: Controllers support CONTROLLERTOUCHPADDOWN, CONTROLLERTOUCHPADMOTION, and CONTROLLERTOUCHPADUP — events that have no joystick equivalent.
  4. Remapping: CONTROLLERDEVICEREMAPPED fires when SDL updates a controller's button mapping at runtime. No joystick equivalent.
  5. No caching needed: The SDL GameController API doesn't suffer from the slow flash-read problem that raw joysticks have, so controller names and metadata are queried directly.
  6. Hotplug: CONTROLLERDEVICEADDED names a device index; the manager opens the controller there and keys it by the instance id it opens with, so a replugged controller (a new instance id at the same index) is found by its events. CONTROLLERDEVICEREMAPPED and CONTROLLERDEVICEREMOVED carry the instance id.

docs.title: Event routing
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    EVT["SDL Controller Event\n(CONTROLLERBUTTONDOWN, etc.)"] --> MGR["ControllerEventManager\n(singleton)"]
    MGR --> LOOKUP["self.controllers[event.instance_id]"]
    LOOKUP --> PROXY["ControllerEventProxy #N"]
    PROXY --> STATE["Update state\n(_axes, _buttons)"]
    STATE --> GAME["Forward to self.game\non_controller_*_event()"]

    ADD["CONTROLLERDEVICEADDED"] --> MGR2["ControllerEventManager"]
    MGR2 --> CHECK{"is_controller(device_index)?"}
    CHECK -->|"Yes"| CREATE["Create ControllerEventProxy\n(init SDL GameController)"]
    CHECK -->|"No"| SKIP["Log warning, skip"]
    CREATE --> DICT["self.controllers[proxy.instance_id] = proxy"]

    REM["CONTROLLERDEVICEREMOVED"] --> MGR3["ControllerEventManager"]
    MGR3 --> CLEANUP["Notify proxy, then\ndel self.controllers[instance_id]"]

docs.title: Joystick state tracking
docs.text: Each JoystickEventProxy maintains cached arrays for every input on its device. They start from the frame's input snapshot (current_input(), so live play and a replay start alike; a device hot-plugged this frame starts zeroed), never from the hardware, and events update them. To poll a device, prefer InputDevices (above), which reads the snapshot.

docs.title: Button state
docs.text:
Buttons are tracked as a list[bool]. The list grows dynamically if a device reports a button index beyond the initially detected count.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Released : init#58; snapshot.button#40;i#41;
    Released --> Pressed : JOYBUTTONDOWN
    Pressed --> Released : JOYBUTTONUP

    state Released {
        [*] : _buttons[i] = False
    }
    state Pressed {
        [*] : _buttons[i] = True
    }
# Proxy state update on JOYBUTTONDOWN
if event.button >= len(self._buttons):
    self._buttons.extend([False] * (event.button + 1 - len(self._buttons)))
self._buttons[event.button] = True

# Proxy state update on JOYBUTTONUP
self._buttons[event.button] = False

docs.title: Axis state
docs.text:
Axes are tracked as a list[float]. Each axis value ranges from -1.0 to 1.0.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle : init#58; snapshot.axis#40;i#41;
    Idle --> Updated : JOYAXISMOTION
    Updated --> Updated : JOYAXISMOTION

    state Idle {
        [*] : _axes[i] = 0.0
    }
    state Updated {
        [*] : _axes[i] = event.value, range -1.0 to 1.0
    }
# Proxy state update on JOYAXISMOTION
self._axes[event.axis] = event.value

docs.title: Hat state
docs.text:
Hats (D-pads) are tracked as a list[tuple[int, int]]. Each value is an (x, y) pair where x and y are -1, 0, or 1.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Centered : init#58; snapshot.hat#40;i#41;
    Centered --> Pressed : JOYHATMOTION
    Pressed --> Pressed : JOYHATMOTION
    Pressed --> Centered : JOYHATMOTION value 0,0

    state Centered {
        [*] : _hats[i] = 0, 0
    }
    state Pressed {
        [*] : _hats[i] = tuple x,y where each is -1, 0, or 1
    }
# Proxy state update on JOYHATMOTION
self._hats[event.hat] = event.value  # (x, y) tuple

docs.title: Trackball state
docs.text:
Trackballs are tracked as a list[tuple[int, int]] (starting at (0, 0): they are not in the snapshot) storing the relative motion of the last event.

# Proxy state update on JOYBALLMOTION
self._balls[event.ball] = event.rel  # (dx, dy) tuple

docs.title: Controller state tracking
docs.text: Controllers use the same button and axis state tracking as joysticks, but with SDL GameController semantics — buttons and axes have fixed semantic identities rather than raw hardware indices.

docs.title: Controller button state
docs.text:
Identical to joystick buttons, but the indices map to SDL GameController constants (CONTROLLER_BUTTON_A, CONTROLLER_BUTTON_B, etc.). The list grows dynamically for non-standard buttons.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Released : init#58; snapshot.controller_button#40;i#41;
    Released --> Pressed : CONTROLLERBUTTONDOWN
    Pressed --> Released : CONTROLLERBUTTONUP

    state Released {
        [*] : _buttons[i] = False
    }
    state Pressed {
        [*] : _buttons[i] = True
    }
# Standard SDL GameController button constants
BUTTONS = [
    CONTROLLER_BUTTON_A,      CONTROLLER_BUTTON_B,
    CONTROLLER_BUTTON_X,      CONTROLLER_BUTTON_Y,
    CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_UP, CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_DOWN,
    CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_LEFT, CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_RIGHT,
    CONTROLLER_BUTTON_LEFTSHOULDER, CONTROLLER_BUTTON_RIGHTSHOULDER,
    CONTROLLER_BUTTON_LEFTSTICK, CONTROLLER_BUTTON_RIGHTSTICK,
    CONTROLLER_BUTTON_BACK, CONTROLLER_BUTTON_GUIDE, CONTROLLER_BUTTON_START,
]

docs.title: Controller axis state
docs.text:
Six fixed axes with semantic names. Values range from -32768 to 32767 for sticks, 0 to 32767 for triggers.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle : init#58; snapshot.controller_axis#40;i#41;
    Idle --> Updated : CONTROLLERAXISMOTION
    Updated --> Updated : CONTROLLERAXISMOTION

    state Idle {
        [*] : _axes[i] = 0
    }
    state Updated {
        [*] : _axes[i] = event.value
    }
# Standard SDL GameController axis constants
AXIS = [
    CONTROLLER_AXIS_LEFTX,       CONTROLLER_AXIS_LEFTY,
    CONTROLLER_AXIS_RIGHTX,      CONTROLLER_AXIS_RIGHTY,
    CONTROLLER_AXIS_TRIGGERLEFT, CONTROLLER_AXIS_TRIGGERRIGHT,
]

docs.title: Unhandled Event Safety Net
docs.text:
When an event has no handler, the stub system catches it. The behavior is configurable: silent, logged, or error-raising (used in tests).

Both settings come from the command line, through the scene's options (the engine's own engine.options; GameEngine.OPTIONS is the current game's, read-only): no_unhandled_events is the --no-unhandled-events argument (Game Options), and debug_events is the --debug-events flag (Diagnostics Options, off by default: a run opts in to the warnings). A replay keeps its own --debug-events, never the recording's (REPLAY_LOCAL_OPTIONS).

flowchart TD
    EVENT["Event arrives at\non_*_event() stub"] --> UH["unhandled_event()"]
    UH --> CHECK_STRICT{"options#91;'no_unhandled_events'#93;?<br/>#40;the --no-unhandled-events argument#41;"}
    CHECK_STRICT -->|"Yes"| RAISE["Raise UnhandledEventError\n(used in test suite)"]
    CHECK_STRICT -->|"No"| CHECK_DEBUG{"options#91;'debug_events'#93;?<br/>#40;the --debug-events flag, off by default#41;"}
    CHECK_DEBUG -->|"Yes"| LOG_W["Log WARNING\nfirst occurrence of the type only"]
    CHECK_DEBUG -->|"No"| SILENT["Nothing"]

Events no process_*_event method handled go to GameEngine.process_unimplemented_event, which counts them by type in GameEngine.unhandled_events; _shutdown logs the table at teardown (unhandled_event_report(): e.g. JOYDEVICEADDED (1541) x1, first at 0.3 s, attributes: device_index, guid).

docs.title: Scene Manager Event Forwarding
docs.text:
The SceneManager implements every event handler method and forwards to the active_scene. This provides the indirection layer that enables scene switching without rewiring event handlers.

flowchart LR
    subgraph ENGINE_FORWARDING["Engine"]
    subgraph Managers["Event Managers"]
        AM["AudioEventManager"]
        CM["ControllerEventManager"]
        KM["KeyboardEventManager"]
        MM["MouseEventManager"]
        JM["JoystickEventManager"]
        WM["WindowEventManager"]
        GM["GameEventManager"]
        DM["DropEventManager"]
        TM["TouchEventManager"]
    end

    subgraph SM["SceneManager (singleton)"]
        FWD["Forwards all on_*_event()\ncalls to active_scene"]
        AS["active_scene reference"]
    end
    end

    subgraph GAME_FORWARDING["Your game"]
        SCENE["Active Scene\non_*_event()"]
    end

    AM & CM & KM & MM & JM & WM & GM & DM & TM --> FWD
    FWD --> AS
    AS --> SCENE

docs.title: Scene transitions in Bitmappy
docs.text:
The active_scene pointer determines which scene receives all events. A scene asks for a switch by setting self.next_scene; after the frame, the SceneManager calls switch_to_scene(next_scene), which:

  1. Calls cleanup() on the current scene
  2. Calls setup() on the next scene
  3. Updates active_scene to point to the next scene
  4. All subsequent events flow to the new scene

A next_scene of None means no switch is pending; it never ends the game. A scene that names itself is treated the same way and reset to None (a scene referring to itself is a reference cycle, which only the cycle collector frees). A scene ends the run with self.scene_manager.quit(), which posts a QUIT event.

The following diagram shows what user actions trigger each scene transition in the Bitmappy pixel art editor. The editor is Bitmappy's; the dialogs are the engine's:

stateDiagram-v2
    state "Bitmappy" as APP_BITMAPPY_SCENES {
        state "BitmapEditorScene" as BitmapEditorScene
    }
    state "Engine: src/glitchygames/ui/dialogs.py" as ENGINE_DIALOG_SCENES {
        state "LoadDialogScene" as LoadDialogScene
        state "SaveDialogScene" as SaveDialogScene
        state "NewCanvasDialogScene" as NewCanvasDialogScene
        state "DeleteFrameDialogScene" as DeleteFrameDialogScene
        state "DeleteAnimationDialogScene" as DeleteAnimationDialogScene
    }

    [*] --> BitmapEditorScene : GameEngine.start()

    BitmapEditorScene --> LoadDialogScene : User opens File > Load
    BitmapEditorScene --> SaveDialogScene : User opens File > Save
    BitmapEditorScene --> NewCanvasDialogScene : User opens File > New
    BitmapEditorScene --> DeleteFrameDialogScene : User clicks delete frame
    BitmapEditorScene --> DeleteAnimationDialogScene : User clicks delete animation

    LoadDialogScene --> BitmapEditorScene : User confirms or cancels
    SaveDialogScene --> BitmapEditorScene : User confirms or cancels
    NewCanvasDialogScene --> BitmapEditorScene : User confirms or cancels
    DeleteFrameDialogScene --> BitmapEditorScene : User confirms or cancels
    DeleteAnimationDialogScene --> BitmapEditorScene : User confirms or cancels

    BitmapEditorScene --> [*] : User closes window (QUIT), or releases Q/Escape with nothing focused

Every transition goes through SceneManager.switch_to_scene(). Dialog scenes (src/glitchygames/ui/dialogs.py) store a reference to previous_scene so they can return to the editor when the user confirms or cancels. The SceneManager itself is a singleton (one per engine context) — there is only one active_scene at a time, and only that scene receives events.

docs.title: EVENT_HANDLERS Dict Construction
docs.text: Each engine's own event_handlers dict (engine.event_handlers; GameEngine.EVENT_HANDLERS is the current game's, read-only) is built once during GameEngine.__init__() by initialize_event_handlers(), so two engines in one process (two engine contexts) never share one. This pre-computation avoids per-event if/elif chains, giving O(1) dispatch.

docs.title: How it's built
docs.text:
At startup, initialize_event_handlers() iterates over each event category's list of pygame event type constants and maps every one to the corresponding process_*_event method:

Event list pygame types Handler AUDIO_EVENTS AUDIODEVICEADDED, AUDIODEVICEREMOVED process_audio_event CONTROLLER_EVENTS CONTROLLERAXISMOTION, CONTROLLERBUTTONDOWN, ... process_controller_event KEYBOARD_EVENTS KEYDOWN, KEYUP process_keyboard_event MOUSE_EVENTS MOUSEMOTION, MOUSEBUTTONDOWN, MOUSEBUTTONUP, MOUSEWHEEL process_mouse_event JOYSTICK_EVENTS JOYAXISMOTION, JOYBUTTONDOWN, JOYBUTTONUP, ... process_joystick_event WINDOW_EVENTS WINDOWCLOSE, WINDOWRESIZED, WINDOWMOVED, ... process_window_event (WINDOWDISPLAYCHANGED, WINDOWICCPROFCHANGED unhandled) DROP_EVENTS DROPBEGIN, DROPFILE, DROPTEXT, DROPCOMPLETE process_drop_event TOUCH_EVENTS FINGERDOWN, FINGERMOTION, FINGERUP, MULTIGESTURE process_touch_event (MULTIGESTURE unhandled) GAME_EVENTS every other supported type, plus FPSEVENT, GAMEEVENT, MENUEVENT (QUIT, ACTIVEEVENT, USEREVENT, ...) process_game_event APP_EVENTS APP_TERMINATING, APP_LOWMEMORY, ... process_app_event MIDI_EVENTS MIDIIN, MIDIOUT process_midi_event TEXT_EVENTS TEXTEDITING, TEXTINPUT process_text_event (both passed to the scene manager)

The result is a flat dict mapping every pygame event type integer to its category's handler method; each process_*_event then picks the manager method for the type and returns whether it handled it.

docs.title: How it dispatches at runtime
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    EVENT["Incoming event\nevent.type = 768\n#40;KEYDOWN#41;"] --> LOOKUP["self.event_handlers#91;768#93;"]
    LOOKUP --> HANDLER["process_keyboard_event#40;event#41;"]
# What the dict looks like after construction:
self.event_handlers = {
    768: process_keyboard_event,   # KEYDOWN
    769: process_keyboard_event,   # KEYUP
    1024: process_mouse_event,     # MOUSEMOTION
    1025: process_mouse_event,     # MOUSEBUTTONDOWN
    1026: process_mouse_event,     # MOUSEBUTTONUP
    # ... one entry per pygame event type
}

# Runtime dispatch in GameEngine.process_events — O(1) lookup:
event_was_handled = False
if event.type in self.event_handlers:
    event_was_handled = bool(self.event_handlers[event.type](event))
if not event_was_handled:
    self.process_unimplemented_event(event)

docs.title: Games as Their Own Packages
docs.text: A GlitchyGames game, demo or app lives in its own package beside the engine: a uv workspace member under src/, depending on glitchygames like any third-party game would. This page explains what a member is, how to work with one, and how to add one. The why is in the plan, plans/2026-10-24-workspace-packages.md; how the games got here is under "History" below.

docs.title: The layout
docs.text:
Four layers, all under src/:

src/
  glitchygames/        the engine (distribution glitchygames); it has no examples package:
                       every game and demo is a member, and its resources/ holds only what the
                       engine itself ships
  games/<game>/        one member per game: every game (mr-muncher, clockwork-keep,
                       brave-adventurer, paddleslap, drawing-fire)
  demos/<demo>/        one member per demo (dt-demo, joystick-demo, sound-board-demo,
                       text-input-demo): a small
                       program that shows one engine feature (console scripts `dt-demo`,
                       `joystick-demo`, `sound-board-demo`, `text-input-demo`; no browser build)
  apps/<app>/          one member per application (Bitmappy)
tests/                 the engine's own tests
scripts/               tools

Nothing at the repository root is importable as one of our packages. Tests and tools run from the root import the installed engine and members (uv sync installs them editable, nox non-editable), and tests/test_suite_collection.py checks that import glitchygames resolves to the installed package. Coverage maps the installed copies back to src/ ([tool.coverage.paths]), so its report names the files in the repository.

docs.title: Two meanings of "demo"
docs.text:
• A demo (a demos-layer member): a program under src/demos/<demo>/, run with its console script or python -m <package>. It is code.
  • A game's bundled demo recording: <package>/demos/<name>.jsonl.gz, package data inside a game (PaddleSlap's rally.jsonl.gz), replayed by that game's console script. It is data, and glitchygames.bundled_demos finds it (see "Bundled demos" below).

A demos directory inside a package is therefore never a demos-layer member, and a demos-layer member's recordings (it has none today) would still be that member's own package data.

docs.title: What a member is
docs.text:
A member is a directory under its layer, named after its distribution (with hyphens), holding:

src/<layer>/<member>/
  pyproject.toml       its metadata (below)
  README.md            one paragraph: what it is, how to play and test it
  src/<package>/       its import package (underscores: a hyphen cannot be imported), never at
                       the member's root, so nothing in the member directory can be imported by
                       accident in place of the installed package
  tests/               its tests (no __init__.py); a game's golden replay is in
                       tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz

Its pyproject.toml follows Mr. Muncher's (src/games/mr-muncher/pyproject.toml):

[project]
name = "<distribution>"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "<one line>"
requires-python = ">=3.14,<4.0"
# What it imports (decision 10: a member declares every distribution it imports)
dependencies = ["glitchygames>=1.0.0", "pygame-ce"]

[project.scripts]
<console-script> = "<package>:main"

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src/<package>"]

[tool.uv.sources]
glitchygames = { workspace = true }

A member declares every distribution its code imports, and the engine with a version floor (tests/test_workspace_config.py: test_every_member_declares_what_it_imports, test_every_member_depends_on_the_engine_with_a_floor): Mr. Muncher's list is ["glitchygames>=1.0.0", "pydantic", "pygame-ce"]. A member that reuses another member's code depends on it too ("<other>" in dependencies, <other> = { workspace = true }). Files inside the import package (a sprite TOML, a bundled demo) ship as package data: read them through the module's own path (Path(__file__).parent / 'sprites'), never through the repository.

docs.title: Working with a member
docs.text:
From the repository root:

uv sync --all-extras --all-groups --all-packages   # the engine and every member, with the dev tools
uv run <console-script>                            # play it
uv run pytest --no-cov src/<layer>/<member>/tests  # its tests alone (no coverage gate on a subset)
uv run pytest                                      # everything: the engine's and every member's tests

A plain uv sync keeps every member installed (each is in the root's dev dependency group), but drops the dev tools: use the full command above. The 100% coverage gate covers the engine and every member together, so it is met only by the whole run.

Each layer is also an extra of the engine, naming that layer's members, so an installer picks the engine alone or with them:

uv build --all-packages                                    # every wheel, into dist/
                                                           # (nox -s build-wheel does the same)
pip install --find-links dist glitchygames                 # the engine
pip install --find-links dist "glitchygames[games]"        # the engine and every game
pip install --find-links dist "glitchygames[demos,apps]"   # the engine, the demos and the apps

The names are not yet on PyPI (neither glitchygames nor any game's), so install from the built wheels as above: a plain pip install glitchygames would fetch whatever package someone else published under that name.

(uv sync --extra games does the same in the repository.) A layer with no member yet is an empty extra; tests/test_workspace_config.py keeps each extra equal to its layer's members.

  • Recordings name games by logical names: <layer>.<module path inside the package>:<class> (games.mr_muncher.game:MrMuncherScene). A recording therefore does not depend on where the code lives. The layers are data in the engine, src/glitchygames/logical_names.py: MEMBER_LAYERS (kept equal to the workspace by tests/test_workspace_config.py).
  • Golden replays live with the member's tests; the golden plugin collects them from every member, so the engine's uv run pytest replays each one.
  • The browser build ships a member's package as its own archive (<package>.zip) beside the engine's glitchygames.zip (scripts/build_browser_bundle.py, GameSpecification.member_packages).
  • API reference: scripts/gen_ref_pages.py writes a page per member package (<package>/index.md), listed in zensical.yml under "Games API Reference", "Demos API Reference" or "Apps API Reference" by its layer.
  • Wheels: nox -s build-wheel builds the wheel of the engine and of every member (uv build --all-packages).

docs.title: Adding a member
docs.text: A new game, demo or app starts as a member. The Sound Board demo (src/demos/sound-board-demo/, added with the sound engine) is the newest and the smallest to copy; Mr. Muncher is the game to copy. The workspace is the list of members in the root pyproject.toml ([tool.uv.workspace] members): once a member is listed there, tests/test_workspace_config.py finds it and fails, naming the file and key, for every tool's configuration below that leaves it out. The steps say which entries no test checks.

docs.title: 1. Create the member
docs.text:
• src/<layer>/<member>/pyproject.toml (above), README.md, and src/<package>/ whose __init__.py defines or re-exports main (and __main__.py, for python -m <package>).
  • tests/, with no __init__.py, holding test files named for the member: test_<distribution with - as _>.py or test_<distribution with - as _>_<subject>.py (tests/test_suite_collection.py::test_every_members_test_modules_are_named_for_it). Every member has these subjects where they apply:
  • _logical_names.py (every member, required by the same test): its scene classes have the logical names its recordings will hold (demos.sound_board_demo:Game);
  • _install_location.py: the package imports from <member>/src/, or site-packages in a wheel install;
  • _entry_points.py: the console script and python -m <package> resolve to main;
  • _package_data.py and _wheel.py, for a member that ships data (a sprite library, a bundled demo): the data is inside the package, checked without building a wheel, and the wheel holds only the package and its data.
  • pytest imports every test module by its path from the repository root, never by its bare file name (--import-mode=importlib in the root pyproject.toml), so two members may have test files or helpers of the same name (BUGS.md #224 item 31). To patch a test module's own names, use __name__ (mocker.patch(f'{__name__}.LOG')). A helper module beside the tests is imported by that same path (from src.apps.bitmappy.tests.film_strip_support import ...), never by its bare name (tests/test_suite_collection.py::test_no_member_test_imports_a_module_by_a_bare_name). A member directory whose name holds a dash cannot be named in an import statement: give its tests their shared helpers as conftest.py fixtures (the simplest), or load one with importlib.import_module('src.games.mr-muncher.tests.maze_support').
  • A member may have a tests/conftest.py (Drawing Fire's drains the event queue). It is imported by its path too, so nothing may import conftest by name: look a conftest up as pytest registered it, by its path (pytestconfig.pluginmanager.get_plugin(str(pytestconfig.rootpath / 'conftest.py'))).

docs.title: 2. Register it in the root configuration
docs.text:
File What to add pyproject.toml [tool.uv.workspace] members (first: this is what makes it a member), [tool.uv.sources], the dev dependency group, its layer's extra (games, demos or apps in [project.optional-dependencies]), pytest testpaths and addopts (--cov=<package>), coverage source and [tool.coverage.paths], ruff src, include and namespace-packages (its tests), isort known-first-party, ty environment.root and src.include, deptry package_module_name_map (its distribution -> its import packages; not known_first_party, which would hide the extra's use). Not checked by a test: [tool.glitchygames] games (its console script, so glitchygames verify and glitchygames measure with no --game take its recordings; a golden or bundled demo no listed game claims fails tests/test_our_measured_recordings.py, a member with neither fails nothing), and, for a demo, deptry's DEP002 list (nothing at the root imports a demo, so nox -s lint-dependencies reports its extra entry as unused) pyrightconfig.json include; its src/ in the extraPaths of the tests environment and of every member's tests environment (each is a copy of tests's); a tests environment for it (a copy of tests's), before its own environment ("extraPaths": ["src", "<member>/src"]) noxfile.py _CODE_DIRS, _SOURCE_PACKAGE_DIRS, _MEMBER_DISTRIBUTIONS wily.cfg The path list zensical.yml The mkdocstrings paths (its src/; not checked by a test, but without it nox -s lint-docs fails to render its API page), and its API page under its layer's "API Reference" uv.lock Regenerate: uv lock, then read its diff: only the new member

The per-layer entries need nothing: the ruff per-file ignores and ty's src.exclude name each layer's tests by a glob (src/demos/*/tests/**/*.py). A game that is one module adds a per-file ruff ignore (see "Special cases").

docs.title: 3. The tables written by hand
docs.text:
Some tests compare what they find with a list written out on purpose, because an expectation derived from the thing it checks checks nothing. Every member:

  • src/glitchygames/logical_names.py: its package in MEMBER_LAYERS (checked by tests/test_workspace_config.py); and the two tables in tests/test_logical_names.py.
  • tests/workspace_expectations.py: its console script in EXPECTED_ALL_CONSOLE_SCRIPTS.
  • tests/replay/tools/test_settings.py: its console script in OUR_GAMES.

A game also has a golden replay, recorded from a scripted session, and a golden trace:

  • tests/workspace_expectations.py: EXPECTED_GOLDENS and EXPECTED_GAME_CONSOLE_SCRIPTS (and EXPECTED_BUNDLED_DEMOS for a bundled demo).
  • scripts/golden_inputs.py: its golden input script (<package>_script) and controls tail (<package>_controls), each a callable taking no arguments that returns an InputScript, importing what it reads of its game inside the function. Any tool reaches them as MODULE:NAME from the repository root (--input-script scripts.golden_inputs:<package>_script, --controls-tail scripts.golden_inputs:<package>_controls).
  • scripts/record_golden_traces.py: a '<module>:<class>' reference in GAME_SCENES (never a module-level import of a member: the subprocess import test fails on one), GAME_MODULES (whose value is the bare package name) and its input script's builder in SCRIPT_BUILDERS. It records on the engine's golden-trace harness (glitchygames.replay.tools.golden_traces).
  • scripts/record_scripted_session.py records the golden replay on the engine's scripted-session recorder (glitchygames.replay.tools.scripted_sessions, the record-session tool): its controls tail in CONTROLS_TAIL_BUILDERS, and the game in INPUT_ONLY_PLACEMENT_GAMES or POLLED_INPUT_GAMES when its script needs it. It derives its fixture directories from GAME_MODULES and the workspace (REPLAY_FIXTURE_DIRECTORIES), and refuses a game no member holds; add its command to the docstring's list.
