Record with SDL_VIDEODRIVER=dummy SDL_AUDIODRIVER=dummy uv run python -m scripts.record_scripted_session --game <package> --frames N.
  • tests/replay/golden_replay_controls.py: its control tables (GAMEPLAY_ACTION_MAPS, ENGINE_SCENE_CONTROLS, UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS), and tests/replay/test_record_scripted_session.py::test_a_member_games_fixture_is_directly_in_the_members_replay_fixtures.

The recording tools themselves are the engine's, and a member has them without declaring anything (--record-golden-trace, --record-session, --verify, --measure, ..., or glitchygames <tool>: Tools for any game).

Engine tests never borrow a member, by import or by path: tests/test_suite_collection.py (engine_test_imports_of_members) fails on any root test that imports one. A test only the member's code can answer goes in the member's tests; an engine test that needs a game uses a stand-in (tests/stand_in_harness_games.py, tests/stand_in_games.py). The exemptions are listed with their reasons (MEMBER_IMPORT_EXEMPT_MODULES and MEMBER_IMPORT_EXEMPT_NAMES in tests/test_suite_collection.py; a stale one fails): the per-game control tables in tests/replay/golden_replay_controls.py, and the per-game world rules tests/world/test_golden_traces.py imports.

docs.title: 4. The browser build (games and apps)
docs.text: In scripts/build_browser_bundle.py, a GAMES entry: its module and scene_class, its title, and member_packages (a tuple, dependencies first: each ships as its own archive), and a TOUCH_LAYOUTS entry for its touch controls. tests/test_build_browser_bundle.py pins which games ship member packages. Demos have no browser build.

docs.title: 5. The docs
docs.text:
• docs/games/<game>.md (a game) or a section of the page for the feature a demo shows (the Sound Board demo's is in Sound), with an "Its package" line linking here; and its entry in zensical.yml's nav.
  • README.md and CLAUDE.md: where it lives and how to run it.

docs.title: 6. Verify
docs.text:
uv lock                                     # then read its diff: only the new member
uv sync --all-extras --all-groups --all-packages
uv run --extra dev nox -s format-code lint-code lint-dependencies
uv run basedpyright && uv run nox -s static-analysis-ty
uv run pytest --dummy-only --no-cov -q src/<layer>/<member>/tests
# The configuration guards and the hand-written tables
uv run pytest --dummy-only --no-cov -q tests/test_suite_collection.py \
    tests/test_workspace_config.py tests/test_workspace_packages.py tests/test_logical_names.py \
    tests/replay/tools/test_settings.py tests/engine/test_every_game_powers_on.py
uv run pytest                               # the whole suite, both drivers, 100% coverage
uv build --package <distribution>           # the member builds on its own
uv run nox -s lint-docs                     # the docs build strictly

A game also checks its golden and its browser build (no -k <package> on the member's own tests: a golden's id is <console-script>/golden, hyphenated, so it would be deselected):

uv run pytest --dummy-only --no-cov -q \
    tests/replay/test_golden_replays.py tests/world/test_golden_traces.py -k <package>
uv run <console-script> --verify            # its golden replay and bundled demos, replayed headless
uv run glitchygames unmeasured --game <console-script>   # what --measure would measure of it
uv run python -m scripts.build_browser_bundle <console-script> --output <scratch directory>
uv run nox -s browser -- <console-script>   # its browser bundle, served and opened

The bundle built without serving must list <package>.zip in its pyscript.toml.

docs.title: 7. Commit
docs.text: The replay-metrics pre-commit hook (scripts/measure_staged_replays.py, which runs glitchygames unmeasured, then glitchygames measure --code-tree TREE --rows-directory DIR) measures every recording on the new code and stages the rows (about 12 s). It refuses a commit with untracked files under src/ or a partial commit, so stage the whole member and its registration (git add -A src tests scripts docs) before committing.

docs.title: Special cases
docs.text:
• Several games in one project (Brave Adventurer and its Egyptian edition, Papyrus): one member, built and published together, with layered import packages in its own src layout (src/games/brave-adventurer/src/): the primitives both games share (brave_adventurer_core), each game on top of them (brave_adventurer, brave_adventurer_papyrus), and a launcher (brave_adventurer_modes) as the member's one console script. The launcher starts the game a recording's header names, so the golden-replay plugin's one console script per member replays every game's golden; the goldens are named apart (golden-<game>.jsonl.gz). A member that keeps several console scripts instead has each recording replayed through the one whose entry point's module holds the game its header names (src/glitchygames/replay/tools/children.py, recorded_games_console_script). scripts/record_scripted_session.py names each such game's golden (GOLDEN_FIXTURE_NAMES) and keys its console scripts by game (GAME_CONSOLE_SCRIPTS), as tests/replay/test_golden_replays.py keys each golden's controls: one script can replay several games' goldens. Share only by mechanical moves: recordings and golden traces name sprites by class name and creation order, so a class may change module but not name, and nothing may be created in a different order. Its browser bundle lists every archive a game needs, the shared ones first.
  • A game that is one module (PaddleSlap; the Sound Board demo is one too): its recordings name games.paddleslap:Game, so Game stays defined in the package itself (src/games/paddleslap/src/paddleslap/__init__.py), not in a game.py it re-exports: a re-export does not change the class's __module__, and the logical name would become games.paddleslap.game:Game. Ruff's non-empty-init-module (RUF067) is ignored for that __init__.py in the root pyproject.toml, with the reason. A package's __init__ never runs as __main__, so its if __name__ == '__main__' is in __main__.py (python -m paddleslap).
  • Bundled demos ship inside the package as package data, <package>/demos/<name>.jsonl.gz (PaddleSlap's paddleslap/demos/rally.jsonl.gz, read through Path(__file__).parent). The engine finds them in the installed packages: glitchygames.bundled_demos.bundled_demos() (find_spec over the packages its caller names, with no default; bookmarked copies left out) returns BundledDemo records (console script, installed path, install name). It is the one lookup: the replay plugin's bundled_demo_paths (which raises for a demo no console script replays) and glitchygames.replay.tools.recordings.game_recordings (a game's own demos, which --verify and --measure take) both call it. Development installs are editable (uv sync, and the replay-metrics nox session's uv run --all-packages), so the demos are found in the repository and the ledger names them by repository path; under a built install (site-packages, as nox's test sessions install on purpose) a recording outside the repository is named by its install name (glitchygames.replay.tools.measure.recording_ledger_name).
  • Engine-private names: a member uses only the engine's public API. Where a member needs something the engine keeps private, give the engine a public read-only API first: PaddleSlap reads its ball's path through BallSprite.trajectory and record_trajectory_point.
  • A known exemption, member tests: a member's tests may use the engine's test seams (for example SceneManager._reset and FontManager._font_cache, which reset engine state between tests); the member's code may not. A public testing helper for them is a follow-up (plans/future-features.md, item #56).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• A plain uv sync drops the dev tools (pytest among them): use uv sync --all-extras --all-groups --all-packages.
  • A member-only test run fails the coverage gate: add --no-cov, and let the whole run check coverage.
  • A member's console script resolves through its installed distribution: the golden plugin cannot find it unless --all-packages installed the member.
  • A directory left on disk by a removed or renamed package (its git-ignored __pycache__) is importable as a namespace package and can shadow the member: delete it.

docs.title: History: the moves out of the engine
docs.text:
Every game and demo began in the engine's examples package, and Bitmappy in the engine itself; all moved into members by 2026-10-26 (Part 3). The plans record each move step by step (plans/2026-10-24-workspace-packages.md and its parts; Mr. Muncher's, the first, is plans/2026-10-24-workspace-packages-1-foundation.md, Task 9). What still matters:

Logical names A game moved from the examples package kept its logical name, so no recording changed. Bitmappy, which was not in a layer, did not: its scene's logical name was its module path (glitchygames.bitmappy.editor:BitmapEditorScene) and is now apps.bitmappy.editor:BitmapEditorScene. A plain replay refuses a recording made before the move, naming the remedy, and --replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless converts it (a rebaseline compares the game and each scene by qualified name alone and writes the current logical names: gameplay replay). Moved recordings keep their history The root pyproject.toml's [tool.glitchygames.recording-renames] maps each moved recording's old path to its new one, so its run-ledger rows stay connected (each moved member's _recording_history.py test checks its lines). Each lookup is one step: a recording moved twice needs a line from each of its old paths. Old checkouts A checkout from before the moves can hold ignored leftovers (their __pycache__) in the old places, src/glitchygames/examples, src/glitchygames/bitmappy and tests/examples, which resolve as namespace packages in an editable install. The moved members' test_the_old_example_module_is_gone (PaddleSlap's and the demos'), Bitmappy's test_the_old_engine_package_is_gone and the engine's test_the_engines_examples_directory_is_gone fail on them, naming the leftover; the remedy is rm -rf src/glitchygames/examples src/glitchygames/bitmappy tests/examples.

docs.title: Gameplay Recording and Replay
docs.text:
GlitchyGames can record a play session and replay it exactly through the real engine. Same engine version and same recording give bit-identical sprite traces: every frame's sprite rect and visible match the recording. Audio is played during a replay but is not compared.

This page covers recording, exact replay, watching a replay (with step back and bookmarks), headless runs, the determinism audit, golden replays and rebaselining them, the tools any game gets (as its own flags and as the glitchygames command), in-game playback (demos, instant replay, ghosts), and the rules game code follows so its sessions replay. See plans/2026-10-19-gameplay-replay.md for the design and plans/future-work.md for the follow-ups. For how it works (a frame's steps and doors, speeds and timing, the file's fields, stored versus derived, and how playback is tested), see the overview, Gameplay Playback; this page is the command reference.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
# Record a session
uv run paddleslap --record-trace session.jsonl.gz

# Watch it replay exactly, comparing every frame with the recording (press Space to start)
uv run paddleslap --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz

# The same with no window, no sound and no pacing; the report goes to stdout, and the exit
# code says whether it matched (0) or diverged (1)
uv run paddleslap --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz --headless

# Check that it replays the same way twice, in fresh processes with different hash seeds
uv run paddleslap --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz --audit

# After an intentional change: replay the same inputs on the current code, write what it does
# to a new recording and print what changed
uv run paddleslap --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz --rebaseline new-session.jsonl.gz --headless

# Did the code get slower? Compare this machine's processing time per frame with the
# recording's; with a limit, more than 10% slower exits 8
uv run paddleslap --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz --headless --max-processing-slowdown 10

# Onion skin: watch a replay with another recording's items drawn over it, half transparent
uv run paddleslap --replay-trace new-session.jsonl.gz --compare-trace session.jsonl.gz

# Play live against a recording: its items drawn over your game, half transparent
uv run paddleslap --compare-trace session.jsonl.gz

# The same tools as the glitchygames command (the game comes from the recording), and a
# recording's runs, speed changes and behavior changes
uv run glitchygames replay-trace session.jsonl.gz --headless
uv run glitchygames report session.jsonl.gz

Every flag above is one of the engine's tools, which every game has without declaring anything; Tools for any game lists them all.

docs.title: The doors
docs.text:
The engine takes everything from the outside world through a small set of doors, and game code reaches them only through the engine. Live play plugs live providers into the doors; replay plugs in providers that serve the recording. The game cannot tell which one it is talking to, so a replay runs the real engine and the real game code again.

Door Live (LiveSources) Replay (ReplaySources) Event pump pygame's queue recorded batch N for pump call N Frame time the measured start-to-start time the recorded dt Polled input captured from pygame once per frame the recorded snapshot Devices real joysticks and controllers stand-ins built from the recording Saves files on disk (DiskSaveManager) in memory (MemorySaveManager), seeded from the recording Wall clock the real time the recording's start time plus the frame clock Random seed --random-seed or 64 random bits the recorded seed Pacing the target FPS the target FPS; none under --headless

The modules:

  • src/glitchygames/sources.py: the EngineSources protocol and the registry (active_sources(), install_sources(sources=...), reset_sources()) and the frame clock. It is a leaf module with no engine imports, which avoids an import cycle between the engine and the scenes. install_sources is allowed only before the first frame, so a run never mixes live and recorded input.
  • src/glitchygames/live_sources.py: LiveSources.
  • src/glitchygames/recording.py: RecordingSources, which wraps the live doors under --record-trace and records what passes through them.
  • src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py: ReplaySources, the comparison and the divergence report.

tests/test_engine_doors.py scans the package and fails if any file but src/glitchygames/clock.py uses the time module (a read, time.sleep, anything) or reads datetime's now, or if anything outside the doors polls pygame's keyboard or mouse, reads or posts pygame events directly, uses pygame's timers, or enumerates or opens joysticks and controllers. Its ALLOWED_BYPASSES lists the few exceptions, each with its reason. The engine's own pacing, measurement and diagnostics read real time through the clock module's raw functions (raw_counter_ns(), raw_counter_seconds(), raw_sleep(), raw_wall_clock_time()), which are never replayed and are not for game code.

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
Read time from src/glitchygames/clock.py or Scene.game_time, never from time, datetime or pygame.time. Import the module and call through it (from glitchygames import clock, then clock.elapsed_seconds()), never a function by name: it is the one clock, so one patch on glitchygames.clock reaches every reader (the doors guard checks it):

Use For Scene.game_time gameplay timers and cooldowns; stops while the scene is paused frame_clock_seconds(), frame_clock_milliseconds() blinks, animation, "how long since" in UI; never pauses wall_clock_time(), wall_clock_epoch_seconds() timestamps (save metadata, undo history, logs) elapsed_seconds() throttles, debounces, repeat intervals, timeouts (subtract two readings) measured_seconds() real durations for logs and metrics only

elapsed_seconds() is the frame clock, live and in a replay, so a throttle near its threshold decides the same way both times; such timers advance once per frame. In a recorded run (and its replay) wall_clock_time() is the recording's start time (recorded_at) plus the frame clock, so a timestamp the game shows replays exactly; live play without recording reads the real wall clock.

measured_seconds() never changes what is drawn, played or recorded

It is real monotonic time and is never replayed: a value read from it differs in a replay, so anything it decides diverges.

Text-widget cursor blinks use the frame clock, not Scene.game_time. A paused scene's widgets are neither updated nor drawn, so a blink cannot be seen advancing while the game is paused.

docs.title: Polled input
docs.text:
Read held keys, modifiers, the mouse and device positions from the frame's input snapshot, never from pygame:

from glitchygames.input.state import current_input

snapshot = current_input()          # or GameEngine.input
snapshot.key_pressed(pygame.K_LEFT)                # by key code (follows the layout)
snapshot.scancode_pressed(scancode=pygame.KSCAN_W)  # by physical position (every layout)
snapshot.modifiers                  # KMOD bits
snapshot.mouse_position             # (x, y)
snapshot.mouse_buttons              # (left, middle, right)
snapshot.axis(device_id=instance_id, axis=0)                 # joystick layer, -1.0 .. 1.0
snapshot.button(device_id=instance_id, button=3)
snapshot.hat(device_id=instance_id, hat=0)
snapshot.controller_axis(device_id=instance_id, axis=pygame.CONTROLLER_AXIS_LEFTX)  # int scale
snapshot.controller_button(device_id=instance_id, button=pygame.CONTROLLER_BUTTON_A)

The snapshot is immutable and is taken once per frame, right after the frame's first event pump. dt_tick runs before the pump, so there it is the previous frame's snapshot (the same lag as polling pygame had). Devices are keyed by instance id. A game controller is read on two layers: its joystick view (axis, button, hat) and the controller layer (controller_axis, controller_button).

Held keys are physical positions (scancodes), and a key code depends on the keyboard layout (the key in the A position is K_q on AZERTY). A recording therefore also holds the key codes the held keys had on the recording machine, and a replay answers key_pressed(pygame.K_q) as that machine did, whatever the replaying machine's layout. Only pygame's K_* key codes are recorded.

Limitation (BUGS.md #83): keys a layout adds that pygame names no K_* constant for, such as French é, German ß or Spanish ñ (SDL gives them their character's code point as the key code), are not in that list. The recorder can only find the held key codes by trying every K_* constant (pygame lets Python ask a key code's position, not a position's key code), so a game that polls one, say key_pressed(ord('é')), reads it held live but not held in a replay, even on the machine that recorded it. Key events are unaffected (a recorded KEYDOWN or KEYUP keeps its key, whatever its value), and so are positional controls (scancode_pressed, ActionMap.bind(scancode=...)). Handle such keys through events or by position, not by polling their key code.

For positional controls (movement, say), poll scancode_pressed(scancode=pygame.KSCAN_*): no keymap is consulted, so it is the same key on every layout, live or replayed, as ActionMap.bind(scancode=...) is for events.

docs.title: Devices
docs.text: Enumerate and open joysticks and controllers only through active_sources().devices() (src/glitchygames/input/devices.py): joystick_count(), controller_count(), is_controller(device_index=...), name_for_index(device_index=...), open_joystick(device_index=...), open_controller(device_index=...) and joystick_for_instance(instance_id=...). A recording stores every answer (failures included) and a descriptor of every opened device. A replay gives the recorded answers and stand-ins (ReplayJoystick, ReplayController) whose positions come from the snapshot and whose rumble is dropped, so it never needs the recorded hardware and never sees a device that happens to be plugged in.

docs.title: Saves
docs.text: Open a save store with glitchygames.state.open_saves(app_name=...). Live play gets a DiskSaveManager. A replay gets a MemorySaveManager seeded from the recording's snapshot of that namespace: reads see what the original session saw, writes stay in memory, and real saves are never touched. Both are SaveManagers, which hold every rule of the save format. A recording's header holds each store as it was first opened, so a first scene whose setup() writes to its saves (adds one to a play count) replays from the saves it found. Slots saved at the same time are listed by name, so list_slots() gives the same order everywhere.

docs.title: Events and randomness
docs.text:
• Post events with glitchygames.recording.post_event, not pygame.event.post, so a recording can mark them internal. Replay delivers internal events from the code that posts them again; an SDL-type event posted directly would be delivered twice.
  • Code that drives the game from outside its logic, as a player would (a supervisor, a test harness, a tool), posts with glitchygames.recording.post_input_event instead. The event is recorded as external input, whatever its type, so --replay-trace, instant replays and demos serve it whether or not they run the poster again (a copy the replayed code posts is dropped). A supervisor that posts with post_event is taken for the game itself, and a replay that does not run it diverges. While a demo or instant replay plays, its input posts of SDL types (keys, buttons, device and window events) are the player's input: a press ends a demo, a release is held for the live game, exactly as a replay of the session without the supervisor serves them.
  • A supervisor may post any event this way, game events (GAMEEVENT, MENUEVENT, any pygame.event.custom_type()) included. The rule: input of an SDL type posted during a demo or instant replay counts as the player's; everything else reaches the game (after the demo or instant replay, if one is playing), live and replayed alike.

Draw random numbers only from the seeded named streams

Use random_stream('name') or numpy_stream('name') from src/glitchygames/randomness.py, never the global random functions, secrets or an unseeded numpy generator: a replay serves the recorded seed only to the streams.

docs.title: The supervisor hook and control events
docs.text:
A supervisor (src/glitchygames/supervision.py) is called once per frame at a fixed place: after logic and events, before frame services, camera aim and positioning. What it changes is drawn that frame and seen by collision on the next one.

scene_manager.add_supervisor(supervisor=my_supervisor)   # my_supervisor.on_frame(frame_number=..., scene=...)
scene_manager.add_control_event_handler(kind='breakpoint', handler=on_breakpoint)
scene_manager.record_control_event(kind='breakpoint', data={'label': 'ball through paddle'})

A control event is a supervisor action recorded in the frame it happened in. A replay applies the recorded control events again at the same frame's supervisor slot, so sessions with supervisor actions replay exactly. A future cheat device will use this hook and channel.

docs.title: Recording (--record-trace PATH)
docs.text: A recording is a gzip JSON Lines trace (format version 3; versions 2 and 3 can be read): a header line, then exactly one line per main-loop frame. Each frame holds its dt, every event batch the engine read from SDL's queue (each event tagged external or internal) and the sprites. Format 3 adds per-frame input_changes, control_events, devices_opened, saves_opened, device_enumeration and scene_start (each written only when not empty). The header holds the game, scene and versions, every option, the start time, the random seed, and the saves and devices the run took in before recording started. The full format is described in the src/glitchygames/recording.py module docstring.

docs.title: Scene starts
docs.text:
A recording also holds how each scene began, so in-game playback (demos, instant replay) can rebuild a scene from its start: the scene's first logic frame (the first frame whose dt_tick runs on it) carries its scene_start (its class's module and qualified name, so two loaded scenes of the same name are told apart, replay_arguments(), every random stream's state and the frame clock as its __init__ began and again as its first setup() began, the saves as they were before its __init__ ran, and the state its first logic frame began in; src/glitchygames/scene_start.py). A playback starts there. Frame 0 holds the first scene's start when the run was started with --record-trace (or --rebaseline). Starts are captured only while they can be used (recording, playback, or a scene that opts into instant replay), so live play pays nothing. A scene that cannot be rebuilt on its own sets CAPTURES_SCENE_START = False (the pause screen does). A replay never compares starts.

A scene built with arguments besides options (Clockwork Keep's next floor carries the score and lives) returns them from replay_arguments(), as they were when it was built; they must read back from JSON exactly as returned:

class FloorScene(Scene):
    def __init__(self, floor_index=0, player_score=0, options=None, groups=None):
        super().__init__(options=options, groups=groups)  # first: the start capture begins here
        self.floor_index = floor_index
        self.starting_player_score = player_score

    def replay_arguments(self):
        return {'floor_index': self.floor_index, 'player_score': self.starting_player_score}

Draw random numbers only after super().__init__(): the capture begins there.

docs.title: Replay (--replay-trace PATH)
docs.text:
At startup the replay reads the recording, applies its recorded options and seeds the random streams with its seed. It refuses, logging the reason and exiting with one of the exit codes, when:

  • the recording is of another game (the header's game and each scene start's scene name their classes by logical names, src/glitchygames/logical_names.py: the layer, the module path inside the game's package, then : and the qualified name, as in games.mr_muncher.game:MrMuncherScene, which stay the same when the game's code moves; a recording made before logical names is compared by its exact game_module and scene_module, and a --rebaseline of it writes the logical names), cannot be read (not gzip, no permission, a directory) or has an unsupported format version: UNUSABLE_INPUT (65);
  • the recording's game or scene has the same class name as the one loaded but another logical module (any class that moved to another logical module, for instance Bitmappy's scene, which left glitchygames.bitmappy.editor for apps.bitmappy.editor:BitmapEditorScene): a plain replay cannot tell a moved class from a different class of that name, so it refuses with UNUSABLE_INPUT (65) and a message naming the remedy, --replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless (REBASELINE_REMEDY in src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py). A --rebaseline compares such records by qualified name alone (modules_not_compared, used for the game by check_recorded_game and for each scene start by find_scene_class in src/glitchygames/replay/playback.py), and NEW holds the current logical names;
  • the file does not exist: MISSING_INPUT (66);
  • --record-trace is given too: OPTIONS_REFUSED (64). Recording over a replay is what --rebaseline does, and only it;
  • its window does not open at the recorded display size: UNUSABLE_INPUT (65), with one line naming both sizes (Cannot replay PATH: it was recorded on a 800x600 display, but the window opened at 800x480 (the window manager chose another size); refusing to replay it).

Games read the display's size (PaddleSlap places its paddles at half the screen height), so the replay opens its window at the size the recorded display had (the header's screen_size), not at the recorded --resolution: a window manager may have given the recorded window another size than it asked for. A headless replay always gets that size; a watched one gets it unless the window manager refuses, and then the replay is refused as above. A recording whose header holds no screen_size (the engine's recorder always writes one; a hand-made header may not) replays at its recorded --resolution with a warning. A window resized during the recorded run is not recorded, so a game that reads the live size every frame can still diverge.

A recording made by a different engine version replays with one warning. A version-2 recording replays with one warning too: it has no input snapshots, so polled input reads as idle.

Each frame, the replay serves the recorded events, dt, input, devices, saves and clocks. Then it compares the frame with the recording: the active scene's class, then each recorded sprite in draw order (present, rect, visible), along with the frame's internal events, control events and pump count. The first difference stops a headless replay, as does the last recorded frame; a watched replay pauses there instead. Closing the window stops any replay. Then it reports how it went (logged, or printed to stdout under --headless). A sprite divergence lists that sprite in the last 20 frames up to the divergent one, as recorded and as replayed:

Replay diverged at frame 6120: sprite Ball#2 rect expected [412, 300, 16, 16], got [412, 301, 16, 16]
Ball#2, last 20 frames (expected | got):
  6100: [400, 290, 16, 16] visible | [400, 290, 16, 16] visible
  ...
  6120: [412, 300, 16, 16] visible | [412, 301, 16, 16] visible

Other divergences (the scene, an event, the frame or pump count) are reported on their one line. A replay that matched reports Replay matched 9800 frames (end of recording) (or (quit before the end), when the window was closed or a watched replay's viewer pressed Esc), and one that matched up to the cut-off of a truncated recording Replay ended early at frame 4312: the recording is truncated.

Every replay that ends normally, watched or headless, exits with its result: SUCCESS (0) when it matched or was quit before the end, REPLAY_DIVERGED (1) when it diverged, UNUSABLE_INPUT (65) for a truncated recording. A crash, Ctrl-C, a signal or the game's own exit ends the run as for any run, and the report then says only where the replay stopped (Replay stopped at frame 12: the run ended with INTERNAL_ERROR (70)); if the replay had already reached its result, the report gives it, then then the run ended with ... (see exit codes). The game's own successful exit (sys.exit(0)) before the replay reached its result exits REPLAY_DIVERGED (1), never SUCCESS, which would say it matched (a rebaseline takes it as the game ending early instead: below). A recording whose header or first frame cannot be decoded (a malformed device, saves or input field) is refused as unusable (UNUSABLE_INPUT, 65), like an unreadable file.

While a replay runs, real keyboard, mouse, touch, joystick, controller, device and window events are blocked at SDL, so they never reach the game (a watched replay leaves key presses and releases unblocked for its controls, which never pass them on to the game). The block is applied again on every pump (event managers created mid-run allow their types again). Each type's earlier blocked state is restored exactly when the replay ends, normally or after an error. QUIT, the window's close event and custom event types are never blocked, so closing the window still ends the replay. Blocking also refuses posts of those types: game code that fakes input by posting KEYDOWN loses the post, which shows up as a missing internal event divergence. A watched replay leaves KEYDOWN and KEYUP unblocked, so such a post arrives there and matches its recording: a recording of a game that posts keys can match watched and diverge headless (and under --audit). Recorded window references in events are served as None, as live events of the display window carry.

docs.title: Watching a replay
docs.text:
A replay without --headless is watched: a read-only game inside a game (src/glitchygames/replay/viewer.py). The outer loop, the replay viewer, owns the window: it ticks 60 times a second of real time whatever the speed and whether paused, reads the viewer's keys, and presents the recorded game's latest frame with the status bar drawn on it. The inner loop, the recorded game, runs its frames in full (logic, update and render) at their recorded frame times: each tick runs as many as the real time since the last tick, times the speed, pays for, only within an 11 ms real-time budget per tick, so keys and drawing keep their 60 Hz. At every speed the budget is the only per-tick limit (no frame count), so an uncapped recording whose frames cost what they did live may still not keep up on a real machine, and "can't keep up" then means exactly that. Up to 1x a tick runs at most one recorded frame unless the replay is genuinely behind (it owes that frame plus a whole tick): a frame the live game ran long and the short frame its pacing caught up with then get a tick each, so both are presented, and the replay then stays about a tick behind real time (a constant lag, not a drift; a pause resets it). A recording faster than 60 FPS is behind by that measure every tick, so a tick runs several of its frames and presents the last. Above 1x the same limit follows a frame lasting at least a tick of inner time at that speed (17 ms of real time for a 34 ms frame at 2x), so fast-forward still shows it; shorter frames run several a tick and the last is presented. What it owes is capped (32.5 frames, never below a frame plus a 60 Hz tick plus the tick paid for, so a slower display keeps the rate): after a stall it runs one bounded burst and drops the rest, and when the recorded game cannot keep up with the speed the status bar says so and shows the real speed (can't keep up: ×3.2). So 1x shows about one recorded frame per tick, 8x about eight, ¼x one every fourth tick. Which frames run when never changes what they do, so a watched replay is exactly as exact as a headless one.

It first runs frame 0, then holds on a start screen: that frame dimmed, "Press Spacebar to Start Game Replay" centred, and a smaller line naming the debug overlay's keys (F3: debug overlay F4: next panel). Frame 0's sounds play before Space, and a one-frame recording reaches its end at the start screen. The screen is drawn by the pause screen's MessageScreen (src/glitchygames/ui/message_screen.py) with its own message and look, as an overlay on the presented frame: switching to a real pause scene would change the recorded scene sequence. Nothing runs while the replay is held: no frame, no frame clock, no recorded input. The viewer's keys go to the replay's controls (src/glitchygames/replay/controls.py), never to the game. Each key acts once per press (the key repeat games turn on is ignored); . and , held act once, then after 300 ms ten times a second:

Key Action Space Start the replay from the start screen, then pause or resume . While paused, run one frame , While paused, step back one frame (held: one more frame back per repeat, restarting once on release) Home Restart at the beginning, paused after frame 0 D Restart just before the divergence, once the replay has found one ] / [ Double or halve the playback speed (0.25 to 8) B Bookmark the frame shown in the status bar S Save a copy of the recording with the bookmarks as breakpoints Esc Quit the replay F3 / F4 Toggle the debug overlay / show its next panel

A status bar at the bottom centre shows frame 6120 / 9800 · 1:42.0 · ×1 · paused · diverged at 6120 (the parts that apply), drawn on the presented frame after the debug overlay, so it is never in a screenshot or a trace. At a divergence or the end of the recording the replay pauses with the debug overlay on and a banner above the status bar (Diverged at frame 6120: ... or End of recording); stepping past the end does nothing, and Esc ends the run with the replay's result.

docs.title: Step back, Home and D
docs.text: A replay cannot run backwards, and the engine cannot be rebuilt in-process, so these keys restart the replay in a fresh process (src/glitchygames/replay/rebuild.py) with the same command line (every option kept, --replay-fps included) plus --replay-pause-at-frame N, an explicit --debug-overlay or --no-debug-overlay, and the viewer's speed, debug panel and the divergence found so far (--replay-viewer-state, internal; D works at once after a restart). The window closes and a new one opens; the end-of-run performance reports wait for the last replay. The restarted replay skips the start screen and rebuilds: frames 0 to N - 1 run in full, unpresented and unpaced, in silence (each frame's sounds are stopped after it and music is paused until the rebuild ends, unless the game paused it itself), with Rebuilding: frame k / N shown on a cleared window every 0.1 s and printed every second (Esc still quits). It then pauses with frame N next, showing frame N - 1's picture; frame 0 always runs, so Home pauses after it. The first replay process supervises the restarts: each later replay that steps back hands its restart command to it (--replay-restart-handoff, internal) instead of starting a process of its own, so there are never more than two (the supervisor keeps the memory its own replay used). The run exits with the last replay's status, but REPLAY_DIVERGED once any of the runs diverged; SIGTERM or SIGHUP to the supervisor ends the child too (killed with SIGKILL, without its teardown: a replay never records, so nothing is lost). Stepping back from far into a long recording takes as long as rebuilding up to there. --replay-pause-at-frame is ignored with --headless (nothing could unpause the replay).

docs.title: Bookmarks (B and S)
docs.text:
B bookmarks the frame the status bar shows (frame N: paused with frame N next). S writes a copy of the recording next to it, x.bookmarked.jsonl.gz for x.jsonl.gz, with a {"kind": "breakpoint", "label": "bookmark"} control event added to frame N - 1 (the frame whose picture was shown) for each bookmark, and logs where. With no bookmarks it writes nothing and says no bookmarks to save. Saving the same bookmarks again writes nothing (bookmarks already saved to ...), unless that copy was deleted since. A copy an earlier session saved from the same recording keeps its bookmarks: a new save adds to them. A file of that name that is a copy of another recording is never written over.

The copy's header names its source (bookmarked_copy_of), and only a file with that field is ever updated in place. The original recording is never written, even one you named something.bookmarked.jsonl.gz yourself; its copy is something.bookmarked.bookmarked.jsonl.gz. The copy is written aside and then moved into place.

The copy replays exactly like its source, headless included:

  • Breakpoints are applied again on their frame and never compared.
  • A truncated source's copy is marked source_truncated, so it still ends as truncated (UNUSABLE_INPUT headless, the truncated banner when watched).
  • A version-2 source's copy is marked input_capture_format_version: 2, so it keeps the version-2 input warning and does not compare control events.

A watched replay of the copy pauses at each breakpoint, showing frame N again with breakpoint: bookmark. A rebuild after a restart runs past breakpoints to its own pause frame.

Stepping back (or Home, or D) with bookmarks saves the copy first and restarts on the copy, so bookmarks survive restarts. In the restarted replay:

  • The bookmark list starts with the copy's bookmarks, so S keeps them.
  • Playing forward pauses at every earlier bookmark again.
  • If the copy cannot be saved, the restart uses the recording it was replaying and logs a warning naming the bookmarks lost.

docs.title: Onion skin (--compare-trace OLD)
docs.text:
--replay-trace NEW --compare-trace OLD watches NEW as usual, with OLD's items from the frame of the same number drawn over each frame shown, at --compare-alpha PERCENT opacity (default 50; 0 to 100, anything else is refused by the parser). NEW itself stays fully opaque: OLD's background is never drawn. The status bar stays on top.

What counts as one of OLD's items. Each frame is judged on its own. OLD's background colors are the colors that cover at least 5% of OLD's frame: a floor, a wall. One of OLD's items is a pixel where OLD differs from NEW and OLD's color is none of those. It is blended over whatever NEW shows there; every other pixel is NEW's, exactly. So:

Your dot OLD's dot What you see there there there your dot there eaten your dot, solid eaten there OLD's dot, half transparent, over your floor eaten eaten your floor

A frame both runs share draws nothing. Three costs of the rule: a part of OLD's sprite drawn in a background color (the floor's) is not shown; a background made of many small colors (a texture, a gradient) may show some of them as items; and one color covering 5% or more of OLD's frame is background even when it is OLD's item (a large sprite, about 139x139 pixels at 800x480, many pickups of one color, a full-screen overlay), so it vanishes from the ghost. The blend costs about 2.4 ms a frame when the runs match and 4.7 ms with a few sprites apart, for an 800x480 window; a frame whose every pixel has a color of its own (noise) costs about 19 ms, and a textured backdrop falls in between. OLD's items are drawn over NEW's whole finished frame, so an item OLD still has where NEW's character stands (an uneaten dot under NEW's Mr. Muncher) is drawn over that character; painting the two games layer by layer fixes it once OLD can run in the same process (decision 20 of the Part 3 plan). NEW replays, compares and exits exactly as it would alone: only the shown copy is drawn on. The glitchygames command takes the same options (glitchygames replay-trace NEW --compare-trace OLD).

OLD is replayed by a headless child process (OLD's own game, under OLD's own seed), which streams each frame's pixels to the viewer over a loopback socket, proving itself with a token drawn for that run. The viewer reads one frame per frame it shows, so pausing and stepping move both runs together, and only one OLD frame is held in memory. Stepping back (or Home, or D) restarts the child at the same frame as the restarted replay; the child rebuilds alongside the replay's own rebuild.

  • OLD shorter than NEW: OLD's last frame stays, labelled OLD ended at frame N. OLD that diverges on the current code stops at its divergence, so it ends there (the log says why).
  • NEW shorter than OLD: the replay ends as usual, and the child is stopped.
  • OLD stalls (its child sends nothing for a minute): OLD ends there, labelled and logged as above, the child is stopped, and NEW's replay goes on.
  • The same recording under another seed shows what the seed changes: --replay-trace OLD --random-seed 7 --compare-trace OLD draws OLD's own run over its run under seed 7 (a replay under another seed compares and writes nothing).
  • Refused before anything runs: with --headless (an onion skin is watched; headless, a replay under another seed or a --rebaseline reports what changed), --audit or --rebaseline (exit 64), and an OLD recorded at another screen size than NEW, or no readable recording (65; a header without its seed counts, as OLD's child could not replay it), or missing (66).

The child always ends with the replay: when it ends, fails, is interrupted or restarts. The contract is the docstring of src/glitchygames/replay/tools/compare.py.

docs.title: Live play against OLD (<game> --compare-trace OLD)
docs.text:
Without --replay-trace, --compare-trace OLD [--compare-alpha PERCENT] lets you play the game live, with real input, while OLD's frame of the same number is drawn over each frame you see. OLD is replayed by the same headless child as above.

Pausing freezes the ghost Frames are paired by game frames: the frames a game's own logic ran in, not its pause screen's. While you are paused, OLD's frame stays where it was, and it moves on when the game does. OLD's own pauses are skipped the same way, so your game frame N meets OLD's game frame N. A replay pairs frames the same way, so --record-trace NEW --compare-trace OLD, and later --replay-trace NEW --compare-trace OLD, show the same pairs. Recordings themselves still count every frame. The seed The game plays under OLD's recorded seed, so the ghost starts in the same world, unless --random-seed N is given. The log names the seed either way. OLD shorter than your play OLD's last frame stays, labelled OLD ended at frame N, and play goes on. The child is stopped when the game quits, fails or is interrupted. Refused before anything runs With --headless (exit 64), an OLD that is missing (66) or not a readable recording (65; a header without its seed counts), or one recorded at another screen size than the game's window (65). --record-trace NEW may be given too, and records the seed played. There is no step back in live play, and this is a game flag only. Not in a browser OLD's child is a separate process, which a browser page cannot start, so --compare-trace (live or with a replay) is refused there before anything starts (exit 64).

docs.title: --replay-fps {recorded,real}
docs.text: With recorded (the default), FPS events, the performance statistics and the debug overlay's performance panel use the recorded frame times, and FPS events are compared exactly. With real, they use this machine's measured frame times and FPS events are not compared; sprites that draw the FPS value may then diverge. Logic always receives the recorded dt.

docs.title: Headless runs (--headless)
docs.text:
--headless runs any game on SDL's dummy video and audio drivers: no window and no sound. It sets SDL_VIDEODRIVER and SDL_AUDIODRIVER to dummy as soon as the options are read, before pygame starts its display and mixer. If pygame was already started before the engine (by code run at import), a display or mixer on another driver is restarted on the dummy one, with a warning. When the run ends, after the engine has shut pygame down, both variables are put back as they were (one that was not set is removed), so a program that goes on after a headless run starts pygame on its own drivers again.

A live headless run is paced to the target FPS as usual (an unpaced live frame would last about a millisecond of game time) and ends however the game ends. A headless replay is not paced at all, since its frame times come from the recording, never waits (no start screen, no pause at a divergence or the end; its key events stay blocked), prints its report to stdout instead of logging it, and exits with its result as above.

docs.title: The determinism audit (--audit)
docs.text:
--replay-trace PATH --audit does not replay in-process. It runs the same command again, with --headless added, as two child processes, with PYTHONHASHSEED set to 1 and 2, and each child writes a SHA-256 digest of every replayed frame. The audit passes (exit SUCCESS, 0) when both runs match the recording and their digests match each other; otherwise it reports the first differing frame and exits AUDIT_NONDETERMINISTIC (3). A child that cannot start, hangs, crashes (exits with any status but 0, or 1 with a recorded divergence) or writes no digests means the audit could not run: INTERNAL_ERROR (70). Fresh processes and different hash seeds make set and dict ordering bugs show up.

The audit compares only what the replay samples: the scene class and each sprite's rect, visible and draw order. Pixels, audio and game state that never moves, hides or reorders a sprite are not compared. It is refused (OPTIONS_REFUSED, 64) with --replay-fps real, under python -E or -I (which would keep PYTHONHASHSEED from reaching the children) and without --replay-trace. A truncated recording is refused before the children start (UNUSABLE_INPUT, 65): an audit needs the whole recording.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
The exit code alone says who refused the run and why. Every code is a member of glitchygames.exit_codes.ExitCode (also importable from glitchygames.engine); the engine logs the code it exits with as Exiting with OPTIONS_REFUSED (64), at INFO (shown with --log-level info; a game's default is warning).

Code ExitCode member Meaning 0 SUCCESS Success; the replay matched; the audit is deterministic; the rebaseline was written 1 REPLAY_DIVERGED A replay's frames differ from the recording 2 ARGUMENT_PARSER_ERROR A usage error from argparse; the engine never exits with it itself 3 AUDIT_NONDETERMINISTIC --audit's two runs differ from each other or from the recording 4 GENERATION_REJECTED The API server rejected the sprite client's generation request 5 EXTRACTION_REJECTED The API server rejected the sprite client's frame extraction 6 AUDIO_DROPOUT_RISK scripts/audio_glitch_probe.py found a risk of audio dropouts 7 REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST --rebaseline wrote NEW, but the run never received some of OLD's input (it ended early, or did not pump a recorded batch) 8 PROCESSING_SLOWER A replay matched, but its processing time exceeded the recording's by more than --max-processing-slowdown 64 OPTIONS_REFUSED The engine refuses the options given (a combination it will not run) 65 UNUSABLE_INPUT The recording or input data is unusable (another game's recording, an unsupported format version, a corrupt or unreadable file, a bad server response) 66 MISSING_INPUT The input file does not exist 69 SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE A required service (the API server) cannot be reached 70 INTERNAL_ERROR An uncaught exception during a run or its teardown (logged with its traceback, after the teardown), or an audit that could not run 73 CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT An output file or directory cannot be created or written (a rebaseline's new recording could not be moved into place) 129 HANGUP Stopped by SIGHUP (Unix only) 130 INTERRUPTED Stopped by SIGINT (Ctrl-C) 143 TERMINATED Stopped by SIGTERM 149 BREAK Stopped by SIGBREAK (Windows only: Ctrl-Break)

0, 64-70 and 73 have the values of BSD sysexits.h (Python's os.EX_OK, os.EX_USAGE and so on, which exist only on Unix, so the values are defined in the engine). The signal codes are 128 + the signal number. A run stopped by one of those signals exits only after the normal teardown, so a recording is complete: the engine handles SIGTERM, SIGHUP and SIGBREAK for the whole run (unless the game installed its own handler) and turns off SDL's own signal handling (SDL_NO_SIGNAL_HANDLERS), which would otherwise turn SIGINT and SIGTERM into a QUIT event. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, Python ignores SIGPIPE, and SIGQUIT keeps its core-dump convention. An engine started off the main thread cannot install its handlers, so SIGTERM then ends it the system's default way, without the teardown. An exception raised before the run starts (while the engine is being constructed) exits with Python's default status 1.

docs.title: Comparing processing time (--compare-processing)
docs.text:
A recording holds each frame's processing time (processing_seconds): the frame's work (logic, events, frame services, positioning and rendering), without presenting it, without the recorder's own writing and without the pacing sleep. The header's latest measurement run (measurement_runs[0], see "Content hashes and measurement history" below) names the machine it was measured on (system, version and architecture, never the host name). These are diagnostics: a replay never compares them with the recording to decide whether it matched, and never serves them to the game. The comparison uses the newest entry, processing_seconds[0].

--replay-trace PATH --headless --compare-processing measures this machine's processing time for every replayed frame the same way and prints one line after the replay's report:

Replay matched 9800 frames (end of recording)
Processing: the replay took 14.2% longer than the recording (9800 frames: 30.410 s against 26.630 s; median frame 3.100 ms against 2.710 ms); slowest against the recording: frame 812 +6.100 ms, frame 813 +5.920 ms, frame 4400 +3.010 ms

--max-processing-slowdown PERCENT (which implies --compare-processing) makes it a check: a replay that matched but took more than PERCENT longer in total exits PROCESSING_SLOWER (8). A divergence still exits REPLAY_DIVERGED (1), and a recording without processing times (made before they were recorded) cannot be checked: UNUSABLE_INPUT (65), with Processing: nothing to compare after the report.

Why processing time and not wall-clock time: a live run is paced (most of each frame is the sleep before the next) and a headless replay is not paced at all, so their total times measure different things. Processing time measures the same work in both. It only compares on the same machine, so make the baseline on the machine that will check it (a CI runner); the report says so when the recording names another machine.

Pacing still slows the work itself: between paced frames the processor idles and clocks down, so a live recording's frames take longer than the same frames in an unpaced replay (one Clockwork Keep session measured about 65% faster replayed than recorded live). So make the baseline with a rebaseline, which is measured unpaced as every later replay is, and check against it:

# Once, on the CI machine: the baseline (the same inputs, measured unpaced)
uv run clockwork-keep --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz --rebaseline baseline.jsonl.gz --headless

# On every change: fail if the work got more than 10% slower
uv run clockwork-keep --replay-trace baseline.jsonl.gz --headless --max-processing-slowdown 10

Replays of the same session against such a baseline land within about 1% of it. The latest measurement run says whether it paced its frames (processing_paced; a live run with a target FPS, as recording began) and names its frame-pacing timer, paced or not (pacing_timer: the timer backend, its final spin and the sleep model --timer-backend auto measured, null if it never did; src/glitchygames/timing.py), and the report adds a note when the baseline was paced. --compare-processing needs --headless (a watched replay presents, steps and rebuilds frames as its viewer asks) and is refused (OPTIONS_REFUSED, 64) with --audit and with --rebaseline (a rebaseline's NEW records the current code's own processing times anyway). The contract is src/glitchygames/replay/processing.py's docstring.

docs.title: Content hashes and measurement history
docs.text:
Every frame a recorder writes carries two histories, newest first, and the header a third (design: plans/2026-10-20-recording-content-hash-and-history.md; contract: src/glitchygames/recording_history.py):

Where Field Each entry Depth constant (10) frame content_hash the frame's content hash CONTENT_HASH_HISTORY_DEPTH frame processing_seconds its processing time (null when not measured) PROCESSING_SECONDS_HISTORY_DEPTH header measurement_runs the run's provenance: machine, processing_paced, pacing_timer (its frame-pacing timer, paced or not: backend, final spin, and the sleep model --timer-backend auto measured, null if it never did), engine, pygame and Python versions, measured_at, rebaselined_from, hash_scheme, and frame_count (how many frames it wrote; filled in when the next rebaseline stacks onto it, null for the newest run, whose count is the file's) MEASUREMENT_RUNS_HISTORY_DEPTH

A fresh recording writes one entry in each. A rebaseline puts its own in front of the replayed recording's and drops the oldest past the depth, so index i means run i in every list. If the runs' depth is tuned below the hash depth, the deeper hashes have no run, so no hash_scheme: treat their scheme as unknown. A reader takes the fields of a run it knows and ignores fields a newer engine added.

The content hash is the first 64 bits of SHA-256 of the frame's content fields as a JSON reader decodes them (string keys, lists), encoded as compact, key-sorted JSON (hash scheme 1), so the stored hash is the one a reader recomputes from the frame it reads. Content is everything the game did or took in: dt, the event batches, input, control events, devices, saves, scene starts, the scene and its sprites. Measurements (the two history fields) are left out. Every frame field is one or the other, and the hash refuses a field that is neither, so a new field cannot slip in or out unnoticed.

A rebaseline copies the inputs, dt included, so an unchanged game gives the same hash one entry deeper, and a changed one shows exactly which frames changed. Two fresh recordings of the same script differ anyway (each measures its own dt, and the game moves by it). A recording's own hash, for any run, is derived from its frames' hashes: recording_content_hash(frames=..., run_index=i); it is not stored.

Neither history is compared by a replay or served to the game. They are the record the baselines in the repository keep: behaviour (hashes) and speed (processing times) over time.

docs.title: Golden replays
docs.text: Each game's workspace member holds a recorded session of it in <member>/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz (PaddleSlap, Clockwork Keep, Mr. Muncher and Drawing Fire; both Brave Adventurer editions as golden-classic.jsonl.gz and golden-papyrus.jsonl.gz). scripts/record_scripted_session.py recorded them through the real engine loop (on the engine's scripted-session recorder, the record-session tool below, with our games' input scripts and controls tails from scripts/golden_inputs.py), with a supervisor posting each game's golden input script, then the game's controls tail: input that presses the controls the script does not, pauses and resumes, and ends with the game's own quit control, so every golden replay ends on a QUIT the game posted and diverges when a control stops working. tests/replay/test_golden_replays.py enforces it: every control the game binds (its ActionMaps, plus the keys the engine's pause screen hard-codes) must be pressed in its golden replay, or be listed in UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS with the reason (gamepad controls: no scripted session has a gamepad). Each recording is a test item of its own: the pytest plugin src/glitchygames/testing/replays.py (registered by the engine's pytest11 entry point, glitchygames.testing.replays, in every pytest run with glitchygames installed) collects every .../fixtures/replays/<console-script>/<name>.jsonl.gz as <console-script>/<name>, replays it headless in a child process through the console script's entry point (--replay-trace PATH --headless) and fails, with the exit code and the child's output (the divergence report), unless it exits ExitCode.SUCCESS. A directory that is not a console script is a collection error. Another project's games get the plugin the same way, with nothing to configure; loading it by name as well (pytest_plugins = ['glitchygames.testing.replays'] or -p glitchygames.testing.replays) still loads it once, and -p no:glitchygames.testing.replays turns it off. The plugin imports no pygame (and prints no banner) until it finds a recording, so a project that is no game gets no item and no output from it. Re-record a fixture only deliberately, after finding out why it stopped replaying; the commands are in the script's docstring. After an intentional change, rebaseline it instead (below), so it keeps its recorded inputs.

docs.title: Rebaselining (--rebaseline NEW)
docs.text:
--replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless replays OLD's inputs on the current code and writes what that code did to NEW: the same inputs and a new picture. The contract is src/glitchygames/replay/rebaseline.py's docstring.

  • A recording whose game or scene classes moved to another logical module is converted here and only here: the run matches them by qualified name alone, and NEW holds the current logical names (a plain replay refuses it, above).
  • The replay does not stop at a divergence: it runs to OLD's last frame (or until the game ends), counting every frame that differs and naming every sprite that differs in them.
  • NEW holds OLD's inputs as the replay served them: the event batches with their origins (code-posted events stay internal, so replaying NEW delivers nothing twice), dt, input_changes, re-applied control events, and each frame's saves_opened, devices_opened and device_enumeration copied from OLD. Its sprites and markers are the current code's. Its header is OLD's (seed, start time, options, saves, devices) with rebaselined_from naming OLD and this run's engine, pygame and Python versions.
  • A cut-off (truncated) OLD gives NEW source_truncated: NEW ends as truncated too, so its replay exits UNUSABLE_INPUT (65) at the cut-off, --audit refuses it, and it cannot be a golden fixture (the plugin expects SUCCESS). Rebaseline a complete recording for those.
  • A version-2 OLD (no input snapshots) gives an honest format-3 NEW: its polled input is the idle input the replay served, recorded as such, and its markers are compared when NEW is replayed (OLD's were not).
  • Input OLD has that the run never received is not moved anywhere else (that would invent an input sequence OLD does not have); it is reported. That is the external events of batches a frame did not pump (the current code pumped fewer times than recorded), and OLD's frames after the game ended early.
  • NEW is written to NEW.partial and moved into place only when the run ends normally; a run that crashes, is interrupted or fails its own exit (sys.exit(1)) writes nothing; the game's own successful exit (sys.exit(0)) ends it early as quit_game() does (NEW holds the frames that ran, exit REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST). If the move fails (say NEW is a directory), the finished NEW.partial is kept, its path logged and printed, and the run exits CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT (73). NEW is never OLD, and NEW.partial is never OLD either. A NEW.partial that cannot be written at all is refused before the replay starts, with one line and CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT (73), as is an unwritable --record-trace or --replay-digest file. NEW is an original, never a bookmarked copy (OLD's bookmarked_copy_of is dropped), so S on a replay of NEW never rewrites it.
  • It prints one line to stdout and exits SUCCESS (0), however many frames differ:
Rebaselined 9800 frames to NEW: 412 frames differ (first at 6120: sprite Ball#2 rect expected [412, 300, 16, 16], got [412, 301, 16, 16]); sprites affected: Ball#2, Ball#3

or Rebaselined 9800 frames to NEW: no frames differ. Lost input (above) is added to the line and logged as a warning, e.g. ; 3 recorded input events not delivered (first at frame 812); ended at frame 500 of 9800. NEW is still written (it replays clean), but the run exits REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST (7) instead, so a script that replaces fixtures notices that NEW is not a faithful re-run of OLD's session.

It is refused (OPTIONS_REFUSED, 64) without --replay-trace or without --headless (a watched replay holds frames and takes the viewer's keys, so it is refused rather than made headless quietly), when NEW or NEW.partial is OLD's file, and with --record-trace, --audit, --replay-digest (the audit's tools; a rebaseline is not audited) or --replay-fps real (FPS events from this machine's frame times would become the baseline). An unusable OLD is refused like any replay (UNUSABLE_INPUT, MISSING_INPUT).

NEW replays on the current code with no divergence when the rebaseline replayed all of OLD: a truncated OLD gives a truncated NEW, whose replay matches up to its cut-off and exits UNUSABLE_INPUT (65) like any truncated recording. Replacing a golden fixture with it stays a deliberate, reviewed step: read the summary, check the change is the intended one, then move NEW over the fixture yourself.

docs.title: Tools for any game
docs.text:
Every recording, replay and measurement tool belongs to the engine (src/glitchygames/replay/tools/), so a game the engine has never seen can record, replay, verify, rebaseline, measure, report on and graph its recordings with only the glitchygames wheel installed. A game passes itself to the engine (GameEngine(game=Game)) and declares nothing else: its package, package directory, console script and git revision all come from that object (identity.py).

Each tool is reachable two ways, with the same name and the same options:

  • As a flag on the game. GameEngine.args adds every tool to every game's command line (uv run paddleslap --report session.jsonl.gz). A tool that does not run the game, or runs it in a harness of its own, runs in place of the game, before the engine starts pygame: no window opens and no scene is built.
  • As the glitchygames command (also python -m glitchygames), one subcommand per tool (uv run glitchygames report session.jsonl.gz). A subcommand whose tool runs the game starts the game as a child process with the tool's flag. Arguments after a bare -- go to that game unchanged (glitchygames record-trace paddleslap run.jsonl.gz -- --resolution 640x480). --project-root DIR is, for the tools that read the project's settings (verify, measure, unmeasured, clear-published, performance-pages), the project they work on (default: the nearest directory at or above the current one whose pyproject.toml has [tool.glitchygames], else the nearest with a pyproject.toml, else the current directory); for record-trace, replay-trace, record-golden-trace and record-session, the directory the game runs in (default: the current directory); report, sound-render and sound-migrate read only what they are given.

Both front ends are generated from one table, TOOLS in src/glitchygames/replay/tools/registry.py, which is the reference for every flag, option, default and help text (glitchygames --help lists each tool with its options; glitchygames TOOL --help describes them). tests/replay/tools/test_registry.py walks the table and fails if a tool or option differs between the front ends, and tests/replay/tools/test_an_unseen_game.py runs every tool, both ways, on a stand-in game in its own git repository.

Tool Runs the game? On the game As the command record-trace yes --record-trace PATH [--random-seed N] [--headless] glitchygames record-trace GAME PATH with the same options replay-trace yes --replay-trace PATH with --headless, --replay-fps, --replay-pause-at-frame N, --audit, --rebaseline NEW, --compare-processing, --max-processing-slowdown PERCENT, --replay-digest PATH, --random-seed N, --compare-trace OLD, --compare-alpha PERCENT glitchygames replay-trace PATH [the same options] [--game GAME] (the game comes from the recording's header) record-golden-trace in its harness --record-golden-trace PATH --input-script MODULE:NAME --frame-count N [--random-seed N] [--headless] glitchygames record-golden-trace GAME PATH with the same options record-session in its recorder --record-session PATH --input-script MODULE:NAME --frame-count N [--controls-tail MODULE:NAME] [--polled-input] [--input-only-placements] [--random-seed N] [--headless] glitchygames record-session GAME PATH with the same options verify in children --verify [PATH ...] [--only TEXT] (default: the game's own recordings) glitchygames verify [PATH ...] [--only TEXT] [--game GAME ...] (default: [tool.glitchygames] games) measure in children --measure [PATH ...] [--force] [--allow-dirty \| --skip-dirty] [--only TEXT] [--code-tree TREE] [--rows-directory DIRECTORY] [--pending PATH] glitchygames measure [PATH ...] with the same options [--game GAME ...] unmeasured no --unmeasured [--code-tree TREE] [--rows-directory DIRECTORY] [--pending PATH] glitchygames unmeasured with the same options [--game GAME ...] clear-published no --clear-published [--pending PATH] glitchygames clear-published [--pending PATH] report no --report PATH [--threshold PERCENT] [--minimum-ms MS] [--spans N] glitchygames report PATH with the same options performance-pages no --performance-pages DIRECTORY [--published] glitchygames performance-pages DIRECTORY [--published] sound-render no --sound-render SOURCE --sound-output PATH [--sample-format int16\|float32] (SOURCE: sounds/pickups.toml#coin or a WAV file; offline, no audio device) glitchygames sound-render SOURCE with the same options sound-migrate no --sound-migrate FILE [--migrated-output PATH] (a version 0 recipe file to version 1, default <stem>.v1.toml beside it, never over FILE) glitchygames sound-migrate FILE [--migrated-output PATH]
  • An option several tools list is one flag on the game: --random-seed (every tool that runs the game) and --headless (the four that record or replay). --random-seed is never needed: a recording rolls a seed (kept in it) and a replay uses the recording's. verify and measure refuse one (exit 64): they always compare, and measure each recording under its own seed.
  • Rebaseline and audit are options of replay-trace (--rebaseline NEW, --audit), since they take the same recording and find the game the same way; so is the onion skin (--compare-trace OLD, above). --replay-frame-stream PORT:TOKEN is a hidden option the onion skin gives OLD's child; it is in neither front end's help.
  • One tool at a time: a game given two tool flags is refused (exit 64), and so is a tool missing a required option (--input-script, --frame-count).
  • Reserved names. Every tool's flag and option is added to every game's parser, so a game must not define an argument of the same name (--threshold, --spans, --only, --force, ...). A game that does is refused on every run, before anything starts (exit 64), with a message naming the flag and saying the engine reserves it. Our games are checked by a test; the full list is glitchygames --help.

docs.title: GAME
docs.text:
The command's GAME (and --game) takes three forms, read in this order; the command says which one it used (glitchygames replay-trace: running paddleslap (an installed console script)):

GAME looks like Meaning The child it runs contains / or ends in .py a script path python <path> --<tool> ... contains : an entry point MODULE:CALLABLE python -c calling it, with the flags in sys.argv a plain name an installed console script, else an importable module the console script's entry point, else python -m <module>

A plain name matching nothing is refused with all three forms named. Every form ends in the game's own GameEngine(game=Game), which adds the flags, so the game never knows how it was started. replay-trace takes the game from the recording's header and asks for --game when that game's module no longer imports (a script that moved).

docs.title: A game's own recordings
docs.text:
--verify and --measure with no paths take the game's own recordings: the goldens that match [tool.glitchygames] golden-globs and that the game's console script replays, plus its bundled demos (<package>/demos/*.jsonl.gz; recordings.py). A golden in fixtures/replays/<console-script>/ is that script's; one directly in a project's tests/fixtures/replays/ is the project's own distribution's ([project] name in its pyproject.toml, whatever its checkout's directory is called; a directory with no pyproject.toml is read as named after its distribution). The command with no paths runs GAME --verify (or --measure) for each --game, else for each of [tool.glitchygames] games; with paths, each recording is replayed by the game its header names (or by the one --game). With the games from the settings, a golden or demo that none of them replays fails both tools, on a line naming it and why (exit 70): none is skipped without a word.

  • verify replays each recording headless in a child process, prints PASS <name>: <result> or FAIL <name>: <exit code>: <why> per recording and verify: N of M recordings passed, and exits 0 only when every one matched (or none was found, which it says), 1 when the only failures diverged, else the first other failure's code.
  • measure rebaselines each recording headless in a child into the run ledger (see Replay Performance), skipping what this machine already measured for the game's commit. A row's commit is the game's own (its package directory's checkout), not the engine's. A game with uncommitted changes, or no known commit, is refused (exit 64) unless --allow-dirty (a trial row, never published) or --skip-dirty (nothing measured, exit 0). unmeasured lists what measure would measure, without running a game.

docs.title: Input scripts
docs.text: record-golden-trace and record-session drive the game with an input script: --input-script MODULE:NAME names a callable taking no arguments that returns an InputScript (glitchygames.replay.tools.golden_traces: press/release per frame, and placements), its module looked for in the current directory first. --controls-tail MODULE:NAME (record-session) names the keys played after the script's frames, ending with the game's own quit. A golden trace runs the game's scene in a headless harness at 1/60 second per frame and samples every sprite each frame; a session runs the game for real, at its own pace, with --record-trace. Our five games' scripts and controls tails are test data in scripts/golden_inputs.py (--input-script scripts.golden_inputs:paddleslap_script, run from the repository root); scripts/record_golden_traces.py and scripts/record_scripted_session.py keep only our games' tables and call the engine.

docs.title: Project settings ([tool.glitchygames])
docs.text:
A project's settings for the tools live in [tool.glitchygames] in its pyproject.toml (src/glitchygames/replay/tools/settings.py). Every key has a default that fits a standard layout, so a project without the table (a player's own local runs) works as it is. Keys are kebab-case, an unknown key is refused by name, and every path is relative to the project root. A path that does not exist yet (no ledger directory before the first measurement) is created by the tool that writes it, or reported; it is never a traceback.

Key Default Ours (the root pyproject.toml) games the project's [project.scripts] the ten members' console scripts golden-globs ["tests/fixtures/replays/**/*.jsonl.gz"] ["src/*/*/tests/fixtures/replays/golden*.jsonl.gz"] ledger-directory "replay-ledger" "quality/replay-ledger" pending-ledger ".glitchygames/pending-ledger.jsonl" "test-results/replay-metrics/pending.jsonl" published-ledger none (nothing published) "origin/gh-pages:quality/metrics/replay-ledger.jsonl" (REF:PATH) landed-ref "origin/main" "origin/main" measured-paths ["src", "tests/fixtures/replays", "pyproject.toml"] the same, and uv.lock unmeasured-paths [] the members' tests/, but for their tests/fixtures/replays/ recording-renames {} each moved recording, old path to new (one hop: refused if a new path is itself an old one; each new path must exist, tests/test_our_stored_paths.py) game-timeout-seconds 3600 (an hour) the default

game-timeout-seconds bounds each game that glitchygames verify and glitchygames measure start (GAME --verify, GAME --measure, one per game): a game still running after it is stopped (asked first, so it can stop its own replays, then killed), reaped, and failed with a line naming the game and the timeout (exit 70). Each recording's replay inside it has its own timeout too. It guards against a console script that is no game (an editor or a server among [project.scripts], which games defaults to) hanging the run; it has no flag, since only the command starts a game per child (--game names the games instead, or set games).

The project's local directory, .glitchygames/, holds what the tools write and nobody commits; it gets a .gitignore of * when it is made.

Stored paths are relative to the project root. The project root is the anchor of every path above and of every path the tools write into a file: a recording header's path options (--record-trace, --rebaseline, ...), a rebaselined recording's rebaselined_from (in its header and its newest run, which a ledger row copies) and a ledger row's recording. It is the nearest project above the current directory (find_project_root), or --project-root where a subcommand takes it; the tools start each game in it. A path inside the project is stored relative to it, POSIX-style. A path inside another checkout of the same project (a clone or a worktree: the nearest directory above the path whose pyproject.toml has the same [project] name) is stored relative to that checkout's root. Any other path (another project, no project) is stored as its file name only (stored_path), so no user name, home or scratch directory is ever written. tests/test_our_stored_paths.py checks every committed recording header and ledger row.

docs.title: The golden-replay pytest plugin
docs.text:
The pytest plugin glitchygames.testing.replays registers itself through the engine's pytest11 entry point (named after its module), so every pytest run of a project with glitchygames installed collects that project's recordings (Golden replays, above) with no conftest line.

  • A project that is no game gets no item and no output from it, unless it has a fixtures/replays/<directory>/*.jsonl.gz: a directory there that is not a console script is a collection error. pytest -p no:glitchygames.testing.replays turns the plugin off.
  • Under a wheel install, pytest rewrites the asserts of the whole glitchygames package (it rewrites every module of a distribution that has a pytest11 entry point): harmless, but it writes *-pytest-*.pyc files into site-packages.
  • The engine wheel also ships glitchygames.testing.frame_comparison (comparing the frames test runs presented on different SDL drivers, with glitchygames.testing.frame_fingerprints, which records them); scripts/compare_driver_frames.py and scripts/driver_frame_matrix.py are its command lines.

docs.title: In-game playback
docs.text:
A running game can play a recording to a rebuilt scene and then go on: attract-mode demos, instant replays and ghosts. Demos and instant replays run in a playback scope, not a new engine run (src/glitchygames/replay/playback.py's docstring is the contract): the scene is rebuilt from its start (see Scene starts above) on scoped doors that serve the recording, the live scene is stashed untouched, saves are a sandbox, the random streams, clocks and FPS timer are put back afterwards, and the live game's own posts and the player's releases, device and window events are held and handed back when the scope ends. A --record-trace session that plays a scope records it, and replays it exactly. An error inside the scope ends the scope (logged) and the live game goes on. scene_manager.last_playback_outcome says how the last scope ended (its kind, reason and frames played).

What belongs to the scope ends with it: supervisors and control event handlers its scene adds (in setup(), cleanup() or an event handler; a live supervisor's additions stay), and the playback scene's own events still queued when it ends (posted in update() or an event handler after its last pump: the live game never receives them, so a goal posted there cannot start a second instant replay). What the live game's own supervisors and handlers post while it plays stays the live game's: a supervisor that calls end_playback() and then posts an event has it delivered to the live game after the scope. Their post_input_event posts of SDL types are the exception: those stand in for the player, so they reach the scope's exit check as the player's presses do (a scripted key ends a demo) and their releases are held with the player's. Their post_input_event posts of other types (a game event) are held and delivered to the live game after the scope, and a replay of the session without the supervisor delivers them at the same frame. A playback never rumbles the player's controllers, and the live scene's synth voices (and those of the game behind a pause screen the instant replay began from) pause behind it and play on after.
