Inside a scope, a replay of the session still applies the session's breakpoints (a bookmark on a frame a demo played pauses there); the played recording's own breakpoints are never applied again. A --record-trace recording of a session that played a scope replays exactly, but cannot itself be played in-game from a frame inside or after that scope (only an instant-replay journal records what a scene's playback requests got and how it resumed).

docs.title: Demos
docs.text:
scene_manager.play_recording(path=DEMO_PATH, then=self)   # any key or button returns to `then`

A demo plays at the game's speed from the start of the next frame and ends at the recording's end, at the player's first press (consumed: it never reaches then), at the recording's own quit, or at a divergence (logged at WARNING as demo diverged: ..., then back to then). A recording that cannot be played (missing, unreadable, another game's, no scene start) is logged at WARNING and nothing starts. Record a demo with scripts/record_scripted_session.py --script-only --output PATH (it runs --record-trace, so its first frame holds the scene start; --script-only leaves out the controls tail, whose quit would end the demo).

Bundled demos are recordings shipped in a game's package as package data, <package>/demos/<name>.jsonl.gz: PaddleSlap's paddleslap/demos/rally.jsonl.gz, which its game-over screen plays after 10 seconds without a press. The engine finds them, for any tool or installed game, with glitchygames.bundled_demos.bundled_demos(): each BundledDemo (a frozen record) holds the game's console script (None when no installed console script is in the package), the demo's installed path and its install name (paddleslap/demos/rally.jsonl.gz, the same under any install). It searches the installed packages its caller names (required, with no default: a game's own package for --verify, MEMBER_LAYERS' for our tests; importlib.util.find_spec, importing no game), leaves out bookmarked copies and sorts them by path. tests/replay/test_bundled_demos.py replays every one headless (through glitchygames.testing.replays.bundled_demo_paths, which refuses a demo nothing replays), so a change that makes a demo diverge fails in CI before it ships; glitchygames measure measures the same demos (each game's --measure takes its own package's, as --verify does).

docs.title: Instant replay
docs.text:
class Match(Scene):
    INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS = 5.0                       # opt in: show the last 5 seconds
    MAX_INSTANT_REPLAY_FAST_FORWARD_SECONDS = 60.0     # the default budget

    def on_goal(self):
        self.scene_manager.instant_replay()            # False (logged) when it cannot play

A scene class that sets INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS keeps, in memory, the recording of every frame since its first logic frame (src/glitchygames/instant_replay.py), sprites included: about 0.5 MB per minute for one sprite moving every frame, about 1.5 MB per minute for PaddleSlap. The journal ends when another scene is presented, and once it holds more frame time than MAX_INSTANT_REPLAY_FAST_FORWARD_SECONDS (paused frames count: all are re-simulated), after which instant_replay() returns False; longer scenes would need state snapshots.

instant_replay() rebuilds the scene from its start, runs the frames before the last INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS of frame time unseen, unpaced and silent, shows the rest at the game's pace with their sounds, then the live scene goes on exactly where it was. The player's presses do not end it. To let the player skip it, read the player's input in a supervisor and end the playback there (end_playback() is honoured only from a supervisor or between frames):

class SkipReplayOnPress:
    def on_frame(self, *, frame_number, scene):
        player_input = scene_manager.playback_player_input   # None outside a playback
        if player_input is not None and player_input.key_pressed(pygame.K_SPACE):
            scene_manager.end_playback()

Instant replays can follow one another (a replay after every goal): a playback suspends the journal, which resumes afterwards, and a request the scene's own code makes while its journal plays back gets the answer it got live.

docs.title: Ghosts
docs.text:
A ghost is a recorded sprite's path and looks drawn beside live play, a time-trial ghost (src/glitchygames/replay/ghosts.py's docstring is the contract). Ghosts are appearance, not play: they have no hitbox and change nothing the game does.

from glitchygames.replay.ghosts import (
    GhostRecorder, GhostSprite, GhostTrack, images_from_animated_sprite,
)

# Recording: from the scene's start until the lap ends
recorder = GhostRecorder(sprite=self.player, scene=self)
...
track = recorder.finish()
saves.save('best_lap', track.to_json())

# Playing it in the next run of the scene (in setup())
track = GhostTrack.from_json(saves.load('best_lap'))
ghost = GhostSprite(track=track, image_for=images_from_animated_sprite(self.player))
ghost.scene = self                     # the ghost follows this scene's game_time
self.all_sprites.add(ghost)            # never to a collision group
  • GhostRecorder is a supervisor: once per frame, after the frame's logic, it samples the scene's game_time, the sprite's world_x/world_y, its appearance (animation, frame, horizontal flip and draw offset of an AnimatedSprite; pass appearance= for anything else) and whether the game shows it (not hidden). It samples only live frames of the scene it was given, and only when that scene's game time advanced: not behind the pause screen, not in a demo or instant replay. It reads game state only, so recording a ghost changes nothing.
  • Supervisors added while a demo or instant replay plays belong to that playback and are removed when it ends, so a recorder the rebuilt scene's setup() makes never outlives it.
  • Samples are keyed by Scene.game_time, which stops while the scene is paused. The ghost shows the last sample not after the current game_time, so it lines up with the live run from the scene's start at any frame rate, and waits while the game is paused.
  • GhostSprite is a world-space sprite: the engine positions and culls it. Its position is read from the track whenever the engine reads it, so it is drawn in this frame's place, not last frame's. Its image is image_for(sample) drawn translucent (alpha, default 96). Hide it with ghost.hidden = True (the game's own flag, as for every world sprite). With nothing to show (before the track's first sample, or a sample the game had hidden) its image is empty, so the engine culls it.
  • A ghost in all_sprites is in a recording's sprite trace like any sprite. Store tracks in saves: a replay serves the saves the recording saw, so a session with a ghost replays exactly.

docs.title: Sound
docs.text:
The sound engine's first milestone (M1) gives every game one call for sound: scene_manager.audio.sound(...). It takes a short name, a path or an Instrument, compiles the sound the first time it is asked for, and hands back the same compiled sound on every later request. Getting a sound never plays it.

The design is in two specifications:

  • Sound engine feature specification: what the engine does, with the requirement ids (AUD-*) used below.
  • Sound engine implementation specification: how each requirement is met, the decision and risk registers, and the measurements.

M2 adds live instruments (sounds that follow game parameters), moves the five games onto this API and removes the old sound paths (SoundBank, load_sound, live_audio). Until then those keep working beside it on channels of their own.

docs.title: One call
docs.text:
from glitchygames.audio import Instrument
from glitchygames.scenes import Scene


class Game(Scene):
    def setup(self):
        audio = self.scene_manager.audio
        self.coin = audio.sound('coin')                        # a short name
        self.slap = audio.sound('sounds/sfx_slap.wav')         # a path
        self.zap = audio.sound(Instrument(wave='square'), pitch='C5', length=0.1)
        self.jingle = audio.sound('coin', notes='C5:0.1 E5:0.1 G5:0.2')

    def on_key_down_event(self, event):
        self.coin.play(volume=0.8, pan=-0.5)                  # a SoundHandle
  • audio.sound(source, *, pitch=None, notes=None, chord=None, length=None, transpose=0.0, parameters=None) returns a compiled Sound. What it is (the source and those arguments) is its identity: the same identity is compiled once and cached.
  • Sound.play(*, volume, pan, bus, priority, loop, persist, ...) plays it and returns a SoundHandle: stop(fade=...), cancel(), release() (a loop ends after its pass), set_volume(volume, fade=...), set_pan(pan) and is_playing. Every method answers False once the voice has ended, and never touches a later voice on the same channel.
  • audio.play(source, ...) is audio.sound(source, ...).play(...) in one call, and audio.beep(pitch='A4', wave='square', length=0.1) plays a basic wave.
  • Pitches may be note names ('A4', 'C#5'), hertz (Hz(440.0) or a float), MIDI numbers (Midi(69)) or scale steps (Scale('C', 'major').step(2), step 0 being the root in octave 4), mixed freely. A4 is 440 Hz.
  • Waves are named (sine, square, saw, triangle, the pulse widths, ...), and new ones can be mixed, blended, drawn as points or built from harmonics (Wave, Harmonics, WavePoint, with the CYCLE and LEVEL named positions). Each engine context has its own wave registry.

Compile in setup(). That is the convention, not a rule: a sound first asked for during gameplay compiles in that frame, and the engine counts it, logs it and shows it in the Audio panel as a gameplay compile, so you can move it into setup(). A setup whose compiles take more than 50 ms logs one INFO line naming its slowest sounds. A loading screen can spread compiles across frames with audio.sounds.warm(requests, budget_ms=...).

docs.title: Short names and paths
docs.text:
A short name ('coin') is looked up in the active scene's SOUND_DIRECTORY (a class attribute, 'sounds' by default), relative to the scene's package directory. Every sound file there contributes its sounds by name; two files defining the same name are an error naming both. A recorded file is a short name too: sounds/sfx_slap.wav is 'sfx_slap'.

A path ('sounds/pickups.toml#coin', 'sounds/sfx_slap.wav') is relative to the scene's package directory and always works, whatever the short-name index holds.

A sound file is TOML (version 1):

[glitchygames]
kind = "sounds"
version = 1

[instruments.pickup]
profile = "chip"
envelope = { attack = 0.002, decay = 0.04, sustain = 0.0, release = 0.02, curve = "steps(16)" }

[instruments.pickup.sources.tone]
wave = "pulse_25"

[sounds.coin]
instrument = "pickup"
notes = "B5:0.06 E6:0.18"
bus = "effects"
volume = 0.6

Version 0 recipe files ([recipes.*]) still load and sound exactly as before; glitchygames sound-migrate FILE converts one to version 1.

docs.title: Cache modes
docs.text:
--sound-cache chooses how compiled sounds are kept (replay-local: a recording replays under any mode):

Mode What happens ram (default) Compiled sounds stay in memory. Above --sound-cache-memory (256 MB) the least recently played sounds that are not playing are dropped, and compiled again on their next request (counted). none Nothing is kept: every play() compiles in its frame. This is the switch that shows what compiling in gameplay costs. Getting a sound renders nothing, and a sound played 5 times compiles 5 times. What a game reads of a sound never depends on the cache (a replay may run under another mode): a synthesized sound's length is worked out without rendering, exactly as a compile would size it; whatever only a compile can tell (every peak, and a recorded file's length and rate) comes from one compile on its first read, counted like any compile, then kept. A play's compile gives them too, so a read after a play compiles nothing more. disk Arrives in M3; refused now (OPTIONS_REFUSED).

docs.title: Voices, channels and buses
docs.text:
The mixer's channels are partitioned once at startup: the live voice pool (--live-voice-pool, 4), then the sound library's channels (--sound-channels, 32), then pygame's 8 for legacy Sound.play() callers. Neither side can take the other's channels.

A play takes the lowest free library channel its bus may use. When none is free it steals a playing voice of lower or equal priority (releasing voices first, then the lowest priority, the earliest play): the stolen channel fades with Channel.fadeout(10) and the new sound starts on another free channel, or on the stolen one a frame later (a delayed play). A play with nothing to steal is dropped. Steals, delayed plays and drops are counted.

What a game sees never depends on the audio device: is_playing and voice endings follow each voice's played time, which advances by the frame's served dt (the recorded dt in a replay), so a replay sees the same answers. Frames run in silence (a watched replay's step-back rebuild, an instant replay's fast-forward) only quiet the channels: their voices go on by frame time, so is_playing, voice endings and steals are the same as when those frames were heard.

Buses form a tree under master: music, effects, ui, ambience and dialogue always exist (ui and music keep two channels each that a storm of effects cannot take), and audio.buses.add(name, parent=...) adds more. A bus has a volume, mute and solo; changes reach every playing voice of the bus at the next frame. audio.stop_all(fade=..., bus=...) fades a bus and the buses under it, or everything.

Plays belong to the scene that started them. When a scene is switched away from directly, its voices fade over 50 ms unless they were played with persist=True; behind a pause screen they pause and resume.

docs.title: Fades on the device (measured)
docs.text:
SDL_mixer (2.8.2 with pygame-ce 2.5.8) changes a channel's level only between mixer chunks, 512 frames (11.6 ms) at 44.1 kHz. Measured through SDL's disk audio driver (tests/audio/test_channel_fades.py; the steal's ordering, which depends on when the mixer thread runs, in tests/benchmarks/test_channel_fade_relations.py under --benchmark-only):

  • Channel.fadeout(10) (a steal) is one plateau or an immediate halt, and Channel.play straight after it replaces the fading sound at the next chunk, so the engine keeps its one-frame wait.
  • The wait orders the fade before the stealer only if the mixer thread mixes a chunk during that frame. A mixer thread kept off the CPU for longer than a frame mixes the stealer into the fade's first chunk, the same cut as playing at once, so the delayed benchmark needs only MINIMUM_DELAYED_STEAL_TRIALS of its trials to show the wait. Both steal benchmarks report every trial, passing or not (the action chunk, both tones' levels in it, and whether the stealer is absent from it and sounds after it), to test-results/channel-fade-steal-delayed.md and channel-fade-steal-immediate.md, so a flaky run can be diagnosed afterwards.
  • A volume or bus fade stepped once per frame over 50 ms reaches the channel as three gain steps of a third, each at a chunk boundary.
  • The CRT skip's Channel.fadeout(20) is one or two plateaus and then a halt.

None of these is a smooth ramp by the feature spec's discontinuity metric (16.1), so steals, short fades and the CRT skip can click. Whether they are heard is the owner's listening check; the fallback, fades rendered into the sound by the engine, is the owner's decision (impl spec risks R4 and R5).

docs.title: Accounting
docs.text:
Every compile, file decode and cache read is timed. Each frame's audio work goes to the recording doors as audio_seconds (the total) and audio_work ((kind, name, microseconds) entries, at most 32 a frame, the rest summed as other), so a recording holds what audio cost frame by frame; the times are measurements and never change what is drawn or played.

audio.diagnostics() returns the totals: voices playing and the voice limit; compiles and their milliseconds, split into setup and gameplay; the last 32 gameplay compiles with their frames; stolen voices, delayed plays and dropped plays; the device format; and the cache's hits, misses, compiles and bytes held.

docs.title: The Audio panel
docs.text: The debug overlay (--debug-overlay, F3; F4 cycles panels) has an Audio panel after Performance. --sound-diagnostics opens the overlay on it. It shows the cache mode, the mixer's format and the voice counts; an audio-time graph stacked by kind of work (compile red, decode orange, live blue, cache grey) on the same time axis as the frame-time graph; a strip with one cell per channel (idle, playing, fading, paused; a stolen channel flashes); the bus meters (a soloed bus is marked); and the compile log, with gameplay compiles in red. Under the All panel only its header lines are drawn. The panel is built from AudioEngine.snapshot() only while the overlay is visible, and never appears in screenshots.

docs.title: The CRT power-on sound
docs.text:
The CRT power-on sequence (src/glitchygames/crt_power_on.py) plays with a sound (src/glitchygames/crt_power_on_sound.py, feature spec 12.1): a power click and a 60 Hz degauss thump at the switch, the flyback whine from the dot, static as the picture opens, then the bars' 1 kHz tone (or channel 3's hiss). All are Instruments requested through audio.engine_sound(...), the engine's own sounds' audio.sound.

They compile once per process, on the first power-on that plays its sound, and every later power-on reuses them: a second game run in one process (the Arcade, the test harness's repeated engines) and every engine context compiles nothing for the CRT. The compiled samples are kept in the engine's process-wide cache (glitchygames.audio.library.ENGINE_SOUND_CACHE), keyed by each sound's identity key, which holds the mixer's rate and the tuning: a mixer restarted at another rate compiles them anew. Only the samples are shared, read-only; each context gets its own Sound over them (its own player and pygame sound), and game sounds stay in each context's library. The cache is exempt from the memory limit's eviction and from --sound-cache none (the CRT is the engine's, not something a game benchmarks): under none the CRT's plays compile nothing. The first compile is counted and attributed like any compile in the context that triggered it; every reuse is a cache hit. Headless runs, tests that never power on and --crt-power-on-sound off compile nothing.

The cues follow the progress that draws the picture, each starting on the frame nearest its point, so at a steady 60 frames a second or more every onset is within 10 ms of its point (AUD-CRT-001); a hitch can delay a cue by a frame.

A key or button skips the sequence and fades every CRT voice over 20 ms (on the device: a plateau or two and a halt, as measured above). Otherwise the tail loops into the game and fades over 500 ms from frame 0's first audio update. --crt-power-on-sound off plays the picture silently; the sound never plays where the picture does not (--headless, tests, replays, recordings).

docs.title: The instrument catalog
docs.text:
glitchygames.audio.instruments holds 658 ready-made instruments in 23 families. Each is an ordinary Instrument, built from the engine's own parts (waves from overtone series, noise, layers with their own envelopes and pitches, filters and drive), so it compiles, caches, plays and renders offline like any other:

from glitchygames.audio import instruments

violin = instruments.get('violin')                       # built once, then kept
tune = audio.sound(violin, notes='G3:0.5 D4:0.5 A4:1')
instruments.entry('alto saxophone').playing_range        # (Note('Db3'), Note('Ab5'))
instruments.names(family=instruments.Family.BRASS)       # every brass instrument
instruments.names(tag=instruments.Tag.MECHANICAL)        # every entry carrying a tag
instruments.get('slapstick')                             # an alias: the same instrument as 'whip'
Family Entries Examples flutes 30 piccolo to contrabass flute, wooden flutes, sopranino to contrabass recorders, whistles, shakuhachi, ocarinas clarinets 9 E-flat to contrabass clarinet, basset horn, chalumeau saxophones 8 sopranino to contrabass, C melody double reeds 23 oboe family, bassoon and contrabassoon, shawms, crumhorns, suona, duduk bagpipes 8 Highland, uilleann, smallpipes, gaita, gaida, musette (drones built in) free reeds 13 accordions (dry, musette, bass), bandoneon, concertina, harmonicas, melodicas, sheng brass 42 piccolo trumpet to contrabass tuba, alto to contrabass trombone, mutes, historic and folk horns bowed strings 27 violin to double bass, sections, pizzicato, viols, erhu, hurdy-gurdy plucked strings 92 guitars (nylon, steel, twelve-string, electric clean to distortion), basses, ukuleles, banjos, mandolins, lutes (angelique), sitar, koto, qanun, tar, ruan, chapman stick, and 27 sound-alikes harps 7 concert, lever, wire-strung, triple harp, lyre, kora struck strings 5 hammered dulcimer, cimbalom, santur, yangqin, berimbau keyboards 11 pianos, harpsichords, clavichord, celesta, toy piano organs 9 pipe organ stops and plenum, positive, combo and theatre organs, calliope electromechanical 11 electric pianos (tine, reed), Clavinet, Pianet, tonewheel organ registrations and percussion electronic 15 theremin, ondes Martenot, leads, pads, basses, chiptune pulses tuned percussion 23 glockenspiel, xylophone, marimba, vibraphone, bells, steel pans, timpani, gamelan plucked idiophones 4 kalimba, mbira, music box, sansula friction instruments 3 glass harmonica, glass harp, terpodion drums and percussion 237 kits (kicks, snares, toms, hi-hats, cymbals), hand drums (daf, dhol, kendang, mridangam), gongs, shakers, blocks, and 131 sound-alikes noise makers 5 whip crack, diaphone, air horn, vehicle horn, party horn sound effects 8 thunder sheet, rain machine, ocean drum, cannon, crash box, coconut shells, door slam voices 55 soprano, mezzo, alto, treble, countertenor, tenor, baritone, bass and basso profundo on ah, eh, ee, oh, oo and humming; whistling choirs 13 soprano, alto, tenor and bass sections on ah, oh and oo; children's choir
  • Names and families are lowercase words separated by spaces ('tenor saxophone', 'double reeds'). get, entry, names and entries lowercase what they are given, so instruments.get('Tenor Saxophone') is the same instrument.
  • A Tag marks a quality that cuts across families (the set is closed): Tag.MECHANICAL, on the music box so far, stays in the family the instrument sounds like. instruments.names(tag=...) and entries(tag=...) list the entries carrying it, and combine with family=.
  • instruments.ALIASES (read-only, as instruments.CATALOG is) maps another name to its catalog name: slapstick to whip, zanza to mbira, cylinder music box and disc music box to music box, wurlitzer electronic piano to reed electric piano, hohner clavinet to clavinet, rain box to rain machine, horse hooves to coconut shells, tavil to thavil and riq to daf (54 in all, among them kanun to qanun, ud to oud and neapolitan mandolin to mandolin). get and entry resolve an alias, while names and entries list catalog names only.
  • A sound-alike is not an alias: it is a verified instrument that sounds like an existing entry (bamboula and conga, tombak and darbuka doum), so it is an entry of its own, listed by names and entries, whose CatalogEntry.sounds_like names the parent whose build it shares (instruments.get('bamboula') == instruments.get('conga'); the parent may be in another family). A pitched sound-alike (the plucked strings' requinto guitar, liuqin) gives its own sourced range, since it may play another span than its parent; it is pitched exactly when its parent is, and an unpitched one has none. sound_changes (empty so far) holds keyword overrides of the parent's builder, for a sound-alike that a source sets apart by one trait; each needs a cited source. Assembly refuses a sounds_like that names no entry, itself or another sound-alike. The 131 drum ones are in drum_sound_alikes.py, the family's builds in drums.py; the 27 plucked string ones are in plucked_sound_alikes.py, the builds in plucked_strings.py (158 sound-alikes in all).
  • Each entry has a title, a family and its playing range, lowest and highest (sounding pitch; folk instruments' are typical of the common keys). Drums and other unpitched entries have no range: their tones are fixed, so give any pitch (pitch='A4'); it does not change the sound.
  • They are synthesized approximations. The engine has no recorded samples, vibrato or moving filters yet, so sustained tones are steady, and a voice's vowel is truest in the middle of its range (its formants are placed for that pitch and move with the note elsewhere).
  • The ranges and models were audited against published references (orchestration texts, the Vienna Symphonic Library, makers' specifications, Fletcher and Rossing, the Csound formant table) on 2026-11-03 and corrected. An organ's range is its keys at 8' pitch (C2-C7; a 16' stop sounds an octave lower). Paired strings double every note, though a twelve-string guitar's or a bouzouki's octave pairs are only on its lower courses, and a church bell leaves out its weak quint, as an instrument has at most four sources.
  • uv run python -m scripts.make_instrument_demos [DIRECTORY] [--only TEXT] renders every instrument climbing its range (or four hits) to build/instruments/<family>/<name>.wav.
  • uv run python scripts/make_pipes.py [DIRECTORY] renders a Highland bagpipe and uilleann pipes (chanter, drones and regulators) and Sí Bheag, Sí Mhór to build/pipes/; uv run python -m scripts.pipe_tunes scripts/pipe_tunes_abc [DIRECTORY] plays the 20 public-domain tunes in scripts/pipe_tunes_abc/ (ABC notation, sources in its index.json) on them, to build/pipes/tunes/.

docs.title: The Sound Board
docs.text: uv run sound-board-demo (src/demos/sound-board-demo/) plays every built-in wave and noise: one row per wave, the eight notes of C major on keys 1-8, Up and Down to pick a row, L to switch the labels between note names, hertz and scale steps (the same pitches play), and C for a C major chord. It starts with the Audio panel open; every sound is requested in setup(), so playing a key never compiles anything.

docs.title: Offline rendering
docs.text: glitchygames.audio.render_to_file(sound, path, ...) writes a sound to a WAV file with no audio device; glitchygames sound-render SOURCE --sound-output PATH does the same from the command line. A sound rendered alone is its compiled buffer, bit for bit.

docs.title: Gameplay Playback
docs.text:
Playback is how GlitchyGames records a play session and runs it again, through the real engine, frame for frame. It is what makes a bug report reproducible, a golden replay a regression test, a demo or an instant replay possible, and a performance measurement repeatable: the same recording, replayed on the same engine, draws the same sprites in every frame (src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py, whose docstring is the replay's contract).

These pages explain how it works. For every flag, option and exit code, the command reference is Gameplay Recording and Replay; these pages link into it rather than repeat it.

docs.title: The idea in one picture
docs.text:
Everything the engine takes in from the outside world (events, frame time, polled input, devices, saves, the clocks and the random seed) passes through one set of doors (src/glitchygames/sources.py, EngineSources). Live play installs the live doors; a recording wraps them and writes down what passes through; a replay installs doors that serve the recording instead. Everything downstream of the doors, the game included, runs unchanged.

flowchart LR
    world["Outside world<br/>(SDL queue, keyboard, pads,<br/>save files, clocks)"]
    live["LiveSources<br/>src/glitchygames/live_sources.py"]
    recording["RecordingSources<br/>src/glitchygames/recording.py"]
    file[("recording<br/>.jsonl.gz")]
    replay["ReplaySources<br/>src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py"]
    engine["SceneManager + the game<br/>(unchanged in every mode)"]

    world --> live
    live --> engine
    live -. "--record-trace wraps" .-> recording
    recording --> engine
    recording --> file
    file --> replay
    replay --> engine

docs.title: The modes at a glance
docs.text:
Mode How it starts Doors Paced? Compares? Writes? Live play <game> LiveSources yes, to the target FPS no nothing Record <game> --record-trace PATH RecordingSources around LiveSources yes no the recording Headless replay --replay-trace PATH --headless ReplaySources no (paced_frame_seconds is 0.0) every frame, stops at the first difference nothing Watched replay --replay-trace PATH ReplaySources, driven by the viewer by the viewer's 60 Hz outer tick every frame, pauses at a difference a bookmarked copy, if asked Live play against OLD <game> --compare-trace OLD the live host's doors, plus a headless child replaying OLD yes no (the onion skin only draws) nothing (or --record-trace) Rebaseline --replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless ReplaySources, with a recorder over them no counts every differing frame, never stops NEW Measure glitchygames measure a rebaseline per recording, in a child no as a rebaseline ledger rows Verify glitchygames verify a headless replay per recording, in a child no as a headless replay nothing Audit --replay-trace PATH --audit two headless replays, in fresh processes no the two runs' frame digests nothing

Sources: the pacing column is paced_frame_seconds in src/glitchygames/sources.py and rule 13 of src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py; the watched replay's tick is CONTROL_TICKS_PER_SECOND in src/glitchygames/replay/controls.py; live play against OLD is rule 9 of src/glitchygames/replay/tools/compare.py; the rebaseline is src/glitchygames/replay/rebaseline.py; measure and verify are src/glitchygames/replay/tools/measure.py and verify.py; the audit is src/glitchygames/replay/audit.py.

docs.title: Which page answers what
docs.text:
1. How a frame runs: the steps of one frame in SceneManager's order, where each door is read, and where a replay's sources take over from the live ones.
  2. Speeds and timing: live pacing, headless and watched replays, the catch-up rule, --replay-fps real, live play against OLD and step back. A frame's logic is the same at every speed; only the waiting differs.
  3. The recording file: the .jsonl.gz layout, every field and why it is kept, what is deliberately not kept, and what is stored versus derived.
  4. How we test playback: golden replays, golden traces, the replay-tool tests on stand-in games, verify, measure and rebaseline, the determinism audit, the doors guard and the memory guard.

Related: Replay Performance (the graphs built from measured runs) and Event System.

docs.title: How a Frame Runs
docs.text: One frame of SceneManager, in the order the code runs it, and where each input comes from. Everything here is in src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py unless another file is named; the doors' interface is EngineSources in src/glitchygames/sources.py.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
SceneManager.start is the blocking loop: begin_frames, then run_frame_step while should_run_frames, then end_frames. A browser host runs the same steps itself, one per tick, unpaced (GameHost.run_async, src/glitchygames/host.py).

  • begin_frames takes the first time.perf_counter() reading. The first frame has no previous frame, so its dt is the short time since that reading (a replay's frame-time door returns the recorded first dt instead).
  • should_run_frames goes on while a scene is active, no quit was requested and the doors do not ask to stop (stop_requested: a replay reached its end).

docs.title: One frame step
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    hold{"hold_frame()?<br/>door"}
    held["present the last frame again<br/>(_present_held_frame)"]
    pace_q["paced_frame_seconds()<br/>door, asked once"]
    period["the frame period: timer.start_frame(target_fps)<br/>when the doors answered None, else theirs<br/>src/glitchygames/timing.py"]
    steps["_run_frame_steps<br/>(the frame's work, below)"]
    proc["processing time =<br/>work, less presenting"]
    finish["_finish_frame:<br/>pace, one perf_counter() reading,<br/>dt through frame_seconds() door,<br/>advance frame clock, FPS sample"]
    next(["next frame starts at<br/>that same reading"])

    hold -- "yes (a paused watched replay)" --> held --> next
    hold -- no --> pace_q --> period --> steps --> proc --> finish --> next

run_frame_step first asks the doors whether to hold (hold_frame): a paused watched replay holds, and the last frame is presented again with the doors' overlay; nothing runs and the frame clock stands still. Otherwise it asks paced_frame_seconds once (None: the target FPS; 0.0: no pacing; a positive number: that period), runs the frame, measures its processing time and ends it in _finish_frame.

docs.title: Inside the frame: _run_frame_steps
docs.text:
1. Start the processing-time clock (measured_seconds(), src/glitchygames/clock.py).
  2. Enter a requested in-game playback scope, if any (_enter_requested_playback; src/glitchygames/replay/playback.py), and apply a recorded resume (_apply_resume_bridge).
  3. Complete the active scene's start on its first logic frame (_begin_scene_logic_frame; src/glitchygames/scene_start.py) and begin the instant-replay journal's frame (_begin_journal_frame; src/glitchygames/instant_replay.py).
  4. Begin the game-frame clock (src/glitchygames/game_frames.py), which pairs onion-skin frames.
  5. Run the frame's contents: a transition frame, or a scene frame (_run_scene_frame, below).
  6. The processing time is the work since step 1, less the time spent presenting (_frame_present_seconds).
  7. End the frame at the doors (_end_frame_at_doors -> end_frame): a recorder samples the sprites and writes the frame here; a replay compares the frame here. Then the journal takes the frame (_journal_frame).

docs.title: A scene frame: _run_scene_frame
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    cam["camera.begin_frame()"]
    tick["_update_scene:<br/>advance_game_time, Scene.dt_tick(scene_dt)<br/>(dt capped at MAX_FRAME_SECONDS)"]
    events["_process_events -> GameEngine.process_events:<br/>pump_events() door (the only read of SDL's queue),<br/>then input_snapshot() door,<br/>then dispatch each event"]
    sup["_run_supervisor_slot:<br/>control_events_for_frame() door"]
    services["_update_frame_services<br/>(shake, rumble)"]
    aim["aim the camera,<br/>position world sprites"]
    render["_render_scene:<br/>Scene.update(), Scene.render(screen)"]
    shake["advance a still camera's shake"]
    present["_present_frame:<br/>presents_frames door"]
    switch["start a pending transition,<br/>or the requested scene switch"]

    cam --> tick --> events --> sup --> services --> aim --> render --> shake --> present --> switch

Points that matter for replay:

  • Logic (dt_tick) runs before the event pump, so dt_tick reads the previous frame's polled-input snapshot. GameEngine.process_events (src/glitchygames/engine/game_engine.py) sets the snapshot right after the pump, so it agrees with this frame's events and stays fixed until the next pump.
  • scene_dt is self.dt capped at the scene's MAX_FRAME_SECONDS when it sets one (_scene_frame_seconds); self.dt keeps the whole frame time for pacing, statistics and services.
  • The supervisor slot runs after logic and events, before positioning, so what a supervisor changes is drawn this frame (src/glitchygames/supervision.py).
  • Presenting asks the doors (presents_frames): a watched replay's inner frames are not presented; the viewer's outer tick presents the latest one.

docs.title: The end of the frame: _finish_frame
docs.text:
In this order: pace (the timer backend's deadline, else the pygame clock; a target of 0 or a frame the doors leave unpaced never waits; _handle_frame_pacing); take one perf_counter() reading, which ends this frame and starts the next; set self.dt from that start-to-start time through the frame_seconds door (_set_frame_time, the one writer of self.dt); add it to the frame clock (advance_frame_clock, src/glitchygames/sources.py); record the FPS sample and post the FPS event when its interval of frame-clock time has passed.

So the dt that frame N's logic receives is the time frame N - 1 took, start to start.

docs.title: The doors read in a frame
docs.text:
Door Read in Module that owns the read hold_frame, paced_frame_seconds run_frame_step src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py pump_events GameEngine._pump_events src/glitchygames/engine/game_engine.py input_snapshot GameEngine.process_events src/glitchygames/input/state.py holds it devices controller and joystick handling src/glitchygames/input/devices.py saves a game opening its save store src/glitchygames/state/manager.py wall_clock_time, frame clock clock.wall_clock_time(), clock.elapsed_seconds() src/glitchygames/clock.py random seed the named streams src/glitchygames/randomness.py control_events_for_frame _run_supervisor_slot src/glitchygames/supervision.py presents_frames _present_frame src/glitchygames/scenes/scene.py end_frame _end_frame_at_doors the doors frame_seconds _set_frame_time the doors

Events a game posts go through post_event (src/glitchygames/recording.py), so a recording can tell code-posted (internal) events from SDL's (external). Only the files the doors guard allows read the raw clock or pygame directly (tests/test_engine_doors.py; How we test playback).

docs.title: The same frame, live and replayed
docs.text:
The frame's steps are identical; only what each door returns differs. A replay installs ReplaySources (src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py) before the first frame.

flowchart LR
    subgraph live ["Live (LiveSources)"]
        direction TB
        l1["hold_frame: never"]
        l2["paced_frame_seconds: None<br/>(the target FPS)"]
        l3["pump_events: SDL's queue"]
        l4["input_snapshot: pygame's polled state"]
        l5["devices: real pads"]
        l6["saves: files on disk"]
        l7["wall clock: the real one"]
        l8["end_frame: discards unclaimed<br/>device answers"]
        l9["frame_seconds: the measurement"]
    end
    subgraph replayed ["Replayed (ReplaySources)"]
        direction TB
        r1["hold_frame: the viewer's tick<br/>(watched); never (headless)"]
        r2["paced_frame_seconds: 0.0"]
        r3["pump_events: recorded batch N<br/>(external rebuilt, internal matched<br/>to the replayed code's posts)"]
        r4["input_snapshot: rebuilt from<br/>each frame's input_changes"]
        r5["devices: ReplayDeviceRegistry<br/>from the header"]
        r6["saves: MemorySaveManager<br/>seeded from the recording"]
        r7["wall clock: recorded_at<br/>+ frame clock"]
        r8["end_frame: compare scene<br/>and sprites with the recording"]
        r9["frame_seconds: the recorded dt"]
    end
    l1 ~~~ r1

Each replayed door is a rule of src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py's docstring: the pump is rule 2, frame time rule 4, input rule 5, devices rule 6, saves rule 7, the end-of-frame comparison rule 8, the clocks rule 9, pacing rule 13 and watching rule 14. The random streams are seeded with the recorded seed at startup (rule 1). A recording made with --record-trace sits between the live doors and the engine (RecordingSources, src/glitchygames/recording.py): it passes every answer through and writes it down.

In-game playback (demos, instant replay, ghosts) uses the same mechanism inside a live game: a scope pushes PlaybackSources on top of the live doors for its frames (src/glitchygames/replay/playback.py; In-game playback).

docs.title: The Recording File
docs.text: A recording (--record-trace PATH, or a rebaseline's NEW) is a sprite trace in the format of src/glitchygames/tracing.py, plus what an exact replay needs (src/glitchygames/recording.py, whose docstring lists every field). The field-by-field command reference is Recording and Content hashes and measurement history. This page explains the layout, and why each part is kept.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
gzip-compressed JSON Lines (tracing.py): line 1 is the header, then exactly one line per main-loop frame, numbered 0, 1, 2, ... Transition frames, paused frames, frames where nothing changed, and a final frame with no active scene are all included (recording.py). The gzip header has mtime 0 and no file name, so identical traces give identical bytes (tracing.py).

flowchart TD
    file[("PATH.jsonl.gz")]
    header["Line 1: header<br/>format_version, source, game (logical name), game_class, game_module,<br/>scene_class, options, screen_size, random_seed, recorded_at,<br/>custom_event_types, engine/pygame/Python versions, saves, devices, device_enumeration,<br/>measurement_runs, rebaselined_from"]
    key["Frame line: keyframe<br/>(frame 0, a new scene object, or forced)<br/>frame, scene, sprites (full list)"]
    delta["Frame line: delta<br/>changed / added / removed / order<br/>against the previous frame"]
    always["On every frame line:<br/>dt, event_batches,<br/>content_hash [history], processing_seconds [history]"]
    sometimes["Only where not empty:<br/>input_changes, control_events, devices_opened,<br/>saves_opened, device_enumeration, scene_start,<br/>redelivered_events"]

    file --> header
    file --> key
    file --> delta
    key --- always
    delta --- always
    key --- sometimes
    delta --- sometimes

A frame's sprite record is {"id": "<ClassName>#<n>", "rect": [x, y, width, height], "visible": bool} for every sprite in the scene's all_sprites, in draw order (sample_scene_frame, tracing.py). Delta frames carry only what changed, and an integer rect change is written as rect_delta (tracing.py).

docs.title: What each part is for
docs.text: Field Why it is kept Read by random_seed every random stream derives from it, so the replay draws the same numbers (src/glitchygames/randomness.py) replay startup (driver rule 1) options, screen_size the replay applies the recorded options (all but the replay's own) and opens the recorded display size (driver rule 1) replay startup game, scene_start.scene (logical names) the game and scenes are found by logical name, not by where their code lives (src/glitchygames/logical_names.py) check_recorded_game, find_scene_class recorded_at the wall clock of the recording, and of its replay, is this stamp plus the frame clock (driver rule 9) clock.wall_clock_time() custom_event_types every named custom event type the run allocated (the engine's FPSEVENT, GAMEEVENT and MENUEVENT, and any a game registered with glitchygames.events.named_custom_event_type): code that calls pygame.event.custom_type() first, or registers in another order, shifts the ids, so a replay moves the recorded event types to its own. Without it, a recording was made with pygame's first three custom ids. An id allocated straight from pygame.event.custom_type() has no name, so it is not moved decoded_replay_sources (custom_event_type_remap) saves, saves_opened save stores as they were first opened, so a replay never touches real saves (driver rule 7) MemorySaveManager devices, devices_opened, device_enumeration the pads the run saw, and every enumeration answer (driver rule 6) ReplayDeviceRegistry dt the frame time logic received; a replay serves it, so timers and physics replay exactly (driver rule 4) frame_seconds door event_batches every read of SDL's queue in the frame, empty ones too, in order, with each event's origin (driver rule 2) pump_events door input_changes the polled input (keys held, mouse, pads) as changes since the previous frame (driver rule 5) input_snapshot door control_events the supervisor's actions in the frame (src/glitchygames/supervision.py), compared at the end of the frame (driver rule 8) end_frame scene_start how a scene began (its arguments, random states and frame clock), so in-game playback can rebuild it (src/glitchygames/scene_start.py) playback scopes scene, sprites what the frame drew, sampled: the comparison's fingerprint of the frame (driver rule 8) end_frame measurement_runs each run's provenance (machine, paced or not, versions, commit, machine state) and its summary (src/glitchygames/recording_history.py) glitchygames report, measure content_hash, processing_seconds per frame, newest run first: what the frame did and how long its work took, per run report, the ledger

docs.title: What is deliberately not kept
docs.text:
• Pixels and audio. A frame is compared by its scene class and each sprite's rect, visible and draw order. Pixels, audio, and game state that is not sampled are not compared, so they are not recorded (src/glitchygames/replay/audit.py; sample_scene_frame). Audio plays during a replay but is not compared (the reference).
  • Wall-clock time per frame. Only recorded_at is stored. Every later wall-clock reading is recorded_at plus the frame clock, and the frame clock is the sum of the recorded dts (src/glitchygames/clock.py).
  • Measured durations as inputs. measured_seconds() is real time for logs and metrics. It is never replayed, so it may never decide anything that is drawn, played or recorded (clock.py). Processing times are recorded as diagnostics, never compared and never served to the game (src/glitchygames/replay/processing.py).
  • The host name. The machine is platform.platform(), with no host name, because recordings are shared and bundled demos ship in the wheel (machine_description, processing.py).
  • Pumps after the last frame. Pumps while the engine shuts down belong to no frame (recording.py).
  • Anything the replay can recompute, such as which events were delivered, discarded or unhandled. That follows from the batch and the game state, so the replay re-derives it (recording.py).

docs.title: Stored, and derived
docs.text: The rule: store what cannot be recomputed; derive the rest, and store a derived value only where history would otherwise be lost.

docs.title: Stored, because it cannot be recomputed
docs.text:
• The inputs: event batches with their origins, the input snapshots (input_changes), device answers, save snapshots and supervisor control events.
  • Frame times (dt) and the seed and options. These are the run's conditions.
  • Logical names (game, scene_start.scene). They name the code, not where it lived.
  • The sampled sprites per frame: the comparison's fingerprint of what each frame drew.
  • Per run, processing times (processing_seconds[i]) and provenance (measurement_runs[i]). They describe that run on that machine, and are gone once it ends.

docs.title: Derived: where each derived value lives, and why
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    frames["Frame content<br/>(stored)"] --> hash["content_hash per frame<br/>stored per run, newest first"]
    hash --> rechash["recording content hash<br/>(recording_content_hash: derived on demand, not stored)"]
    times["processing_seconds and dt<br/>(stored)"] --> summary["RunSummary<br/>p50/p95/p99/max, total, worst frame,<br/>frames over budget, live frame times,<br/>mean and 5% low/high slice means"]
    summary --> header["header: measurement_runs[i].summary<br/>(filled in when the next run stacks)"]
    summary --> row["ledger row (quality/replay-ledger/)<br/>one per recording per run"]
    row --> pages["performance pages<br/>(built from rows on every docs build)"]
    summary -. "display only" .-> fps["FPS = 1 / seconds<br/>(fps_from_seconds, never stored)"]
  • Content hash (frame_content_hash, recording_history.py): 64 bits of SHA-256 of a frame's content fields. It is stored per frame and per run, because a later rebaseline compares runs frame by frame (behavior changes, same-work speed comparisons: src/glitchygames/recording_metrics.py). The recording's own hash for a run is derived from those on demand and never stored (recording_content_hash).
  • Run summaries (RunSummary, recording_history.py): processing p50/p95/p99/max, total, the worst frame and its scene, frames over budget, a live run's frame times (p50/p99/max, late frames), and the mean and the "5% low/high" slice means (slice_frame_count is the one definition of a slice). A summary could be recomputed from the frames, but each recording keeps only MEASUREMENT_RUNS_HISTORY_DEPTH = 10 runs, so the summary is stored twice to outlive them:
  • in the header, written when the next run stacks (stacked_measurement_runs; the newest run's summary is computed on read, recording_run_summaries);
  • in a ledger row, one per recording per run (LedgerRow, recording_metrics.py), each with a per-frame profile (FrameProfile).
  • FPS is never stored. Summaries keep seconds, which average correctly, and FPS is one division away, done for display only (fps_from_seconds, recording_metrics.py).
  • The ledger and the performance pages are built from rows: every docs build merges the row files, the published ledger and pending rows, and graphs them (src/glitchygames/replay/tools/performance_pages.py; Replay Performance).

docs.title: Adding a derived field
docs.text:
The mean and the 5% slices (2026-10-28) are the worked example:

  1. Readers accept its absence. The new field defaults to None (FrameTimeSummary and RunSummary in recording_history.py), so every older header and ledger row still reads, and tools show nothing for it rather than failing. The measure and report lines, and the performance pages' FPS charts, leave such rows out.
  2. No format version. Header and frame fields added later need none: readers pass through fields they do not use (tracing.py), and measurement_runs is read leniently and written strictly (measurement_run_from).
  3. Older recordings get it at their next rebaseline or stacked run. When a run stacks, each earlier run without a summary gets one from the frames. A stored summary that lacks a newer field is completed from the frames too, keeping every value it already holds (summary_lacks_fields, completed_summary). Ledger rows already written are never rewritten, so they keep their absence.
  4. One definition, tested by hand. A derived figure is defined in one function and tested with hand-computed vectors (tests/test_recording_history.py).

docs.title: Speeds and Timing
docs.text:
A frame's logic is identical at every speed; only the waiting differs. Every mode runs the same _run_frame_steps (How a frame runs). What changes is whether _finish_frame waits after the work, whether the doors hold the loop between frames, and which dt the logic receives: the measured one live, the recorded one in a replay (frame_seconds, rule 4 of src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py). A replay at 8x runs exactly the frames a replay at 1x runs. It just runs more of them per real second.

In the timing charts below, the constants come from the code and are named. Bars labelled work stand for however long a frame's work takes. Their lengths are illustrative, not measurements. The charts' positions are whole milliseconds (Mermaid's time axis), so 16.667 ms is drawn at 17.

docs.title: A paced live frame
docs.text:
Live play paces each frame to the target FPS (the default is 60.01 FPS, DEFAULT_TARGET_FPS in src/glitchygames/timing.py). With the fast backend, FastTimer.start_frame turns the target into a period in nanoseconds: 16,666,667 ns at 60 FPS, or about 16,664 µs at 60.01. After the frame's work, SceneManager._handle_frame_pacing asks the timer for the next deadline (compute_deadline) and sleeps until it (sleep_until_next):

Sleep The timer sleeps so that it is predicted to wake DEFAULT_SLEEP_GRANULARITY_NS (1 ms) before the deadline. Under --timer-backend auto, the engine's default, the sleep is shortened by this machine's measured SleepModel (how late its sleeps wake: a constant plus a fraction of the length). Spin It spins the rest.

Then _finish_frame takes one perf_counter() reading, which ends this frame and starts the next.

gantt
    title One paced live frame at 60 FPS (period 16.667 ms, FastTimer.start_frame)
    dateFormat x
    axisFormat %L ms
    section Frame N
    work (_run_frame_steps, illustrative)        :w, 0, 6
    sleep (sized by the SleepModel)              :s, 6, 16
    spin (DEFAULT_SLEEP_GRANULARITY_NS = 1 ms)   :p, 16, 17
    section Frame N+1
    work (illustrative)                          :w2, 17, 22

The frame's processing time is the work alone, without presenting and without the pacing (_run_frame_steps; src/glitchygames/replay/processing.py). Its frame time (dt) is the whole period, start to start. Paced frames process more slowly than unpaced ones, because the processor idles between them; processing.py explains this, and it is why paced and unpaced timings are never compared.

docs.title: A headless replay
docs.text:
A replay never paces: ReplaySources.paced_frame_seconds returns 0.0, so _handle_frame_pacing returns at once (no deadline, no clock tick), and a headless replay never holds. Frames run back to back. Each frame's logic still receives the recorded dt, so the game "sees" the recorded timing however fast the machine runs it (rules 4 and 13 of src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py).

gantt
    title Headless replay: no waits (paced_frame_seconds = 0.0)
    dateFormat x
    axisFormat %L ms
    section Frames
    frame 0 work (logic gets recorded dt 0)   :a, 0, 3
    frame 1 work (recorded dt 1)              :b, 3, 5
    frame 2 work (recorded dt 2)              :c, 5, 9
    frame 3 work (recorded dt 3)              :d, 9, 11

This is the mode every measurement uses: a rebaseline (and so measure) is headless, and its per-frame processing times are pure work.

docs.title: A watched replay
docs.text:
A watched replay has two loops (src/glitchygames/replay/viewer.py, whose docstring is the contract):

Outer The viewer ticks at a fixed real-time rate: CONTROL_TICKS_PER_SECOND = 60 (src/glitchygames/replay/controls.py), on measured_seconds(), never replayed. Each tick reads the viewer's keys, refreshes the status line and presents one frame. Inner The recorded game steps at its recorded frame times. Its frames run whole, but are not presented (presents_frames is False).

Before each inner frame the scene manager asks hold_frame:

  1. No tick open. Sleep until the next tick (with FastTimer while frames run), then add the real time since the last tick, times the speed, to an accumulator.
  2. Tick open. Run another inner frame while the accumulator holds that frame's recorded duration, and consume it, only within INNER_FRAME_BUDGET_SECONDS = 0.011 s of real time per tick, so keys and presenting stay at 60 Hz. At every speed the budget is the only per-tick limit (no frame count), so an uncapped recording whose frames cost what they did live may still not keep up on a real machine, and "can't keep up" then means exactly that. Up to 1x a tick runs at most one inner frame unless the replay is genuinely behind: a second frame in the same tick runs only when the accumulator holds its duration plus a whole tick of inner time (the speed times the tick period); otherwise it runs next tick, the owed time carried. So a frame the live game ran long and the short frame its pacing caught up with are each presented, and the replay then stays about a tick behind real time (a constant lag, not a drift; a pause resets it). A recording faster than 60 FPS still runs several frames a tick and presents the last. Above 1x the same limit follows a frame lasting at least a tick of inner time at that speed (a 60 Hz refresh or more of real time); after shorter frames a tick runs several and presents the last (fast-forward). What the accumulator owes is capped at MAX_OWED_INNER_FRAMES = 32 and a half frames, and never less than a frame plus a 60 Hz tick plus the tick paid for (the real time since the last tick, at least a 60 Hz tick; a stall over STALL_TICK_SECONDS counts as one), in inner time, so very short frames and a slower display's ticks keep their rate: the excess is dropped, and the status bar shows the real speed while the viewer is behind (BEHIND_SPEED_FRACTION = 0.95).
  3. Otherwise the tick closes and the frame is presented.

So at 1x a 60 FPS recording runs one inner frame per tick, at 8x eight, and at ¼x one every fourth tick (the viewer's docstring). The speed keys double or halve the speed (SPEED_STEP_FACTOR = 2.0), within MIN_SPEED = 0.25 and MAX_SPEED = 8.0 (ReplayControls, src/glitchygames/replay/controls.py). The owed limit (32.5 frames, never less than its floor) is what lets the viewer catch up after a stall, in one bounded burst.

gantt
    title Watched replay at 8x: one outer tick (1/60 s) runs several inner frames
    dateFormat x
    axisFormat %L ms
    section Outer tick 1
    keys + accumulator (hold_frame)         :k1, 0, 1
    inner frames, within the 11 ms budget   :i1, 1, 7
    present the latest frame                :p1, 7, 8
    sleep until the next tick               :s1, 8, 17
    section Outer tick 2
    keys + accumulator                      :k2, 17, 18
    inner frames (within the 11 ms budget)  :i2, 18, 24
    present                                 :p2, 24, 25

The accumulator only decides when inner frames run, never what they do, so a watched replay is as exact as a headless one (viewer.py).

docs.title: --replay-fps real
docs.text: --replay-fps changes only which frame time the FPS statistics read, never the logic and never the pacing. Under recorded (the default), the FPS events and performance statistics use the recorded dt, so the FPS events are compared exactly. Under real, they use this machine's measured frame time, and FPS events are not compared. Logic still receives the recorded dt (rule 4 of src/glitchygames/replay/driver.py; SceneManager._performance_frame_seconds). The timing chart is therefore the same as the headless or watched replay above. A rebaseline and an audit refuse real (src/glitchygames/replay/rebaseline.py rule 1; src/glitchygames/replay/audit.py). Flags: --replay-fps.

docs.title: Live play against OLD (the onion skin)
docs.text:
<game> --compare-trace OLD plays live, paced as usual, and draws OLD's items over each presented frame. OLD is replayed headless by a child process that streams its frames back over a loopback socket (src/glitchygames/replay/tools/compare.py, rules 2-5 and 9):

sequenceDiagram
    participant Game as Live game (parent, paced)
    participant Sock as Socket on 127.0.0.1 (FRAME_STREAM_HOST)
    participant Child as OLD's child: --replay-trace OLD --headless

    Game->>Sock: listen on a port
    Game->>Child: start with --replay-frame-stream PORT:TOKEN (on the first presented frame)
    Child->>Sock: connect, send the token first (32 hex characters)
    Note over Game,Sock: a connection without the token is closed and logged
    loop each frame OLD replays
        Child->>Sock: FRAME_HEADER (frame, width, height: 3 x uint32 LE), then RGB pixels
    end
    loop each frame the game presents
        Game->>Sock: read (and drop) until the frame paired by the game-frame clock
        Game->>Game: blend OLD's items over the frame at --compare-alpha
    end
    Note over Game,Child: the parent reads only when it draws: the child blocks on a full socket, so both move together
    Game->>Child: teardown stops it and waits (OnionSkin.stop)

The token is FRAME_STREAM_TOKEN_BYTES = 16 random bytes from secrets, sent as FRAME_STREAM_TOKEN_LENGTH = 32 hex characters. The child has CHILD_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 60 s to connect; a child that stalls for CHILD_READ_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 60 s ends OLD's ghost there, while the game goes on. Frames are paired by the game-frame clock (src/glitchygames/game_frames.py), so a pause on either side freezes the ghost rather than drifting (rule 11). The child is headless, so it runs unpaced, as any headless replay does. The parent's reads keep it in lockstep. Flags: Live play against OLD.

docs.title: Step back: rebuild
docs.text:
A replay cannot run backwards, so step back (,), Home and D restart the replay in a fresh process, paused at frame N (src/glitchygames/replay/rebuild.py, whose docstring is the contract):

sequenceDiagram
    participant First as First replay process (becomes the supervisor)
    participant Child as Restarted replay (--replay-pause-at-frame N)

    First->>First: viewer presses step back: end the run (restart_frame = N), tear down
    First->>Child: run the restart command (run_command), with --replay-restart-handoff PATH
    Note over Child: rebuild: frames 0..N-1 run whole, unpresented, unpaced, silenced
    loop every REBUILD_PROGRESS_INTERVAL_SECONDS (0.1 s) of real time
        Child->>Child: present "Rebuilding: frame k / N"
    end
    Child->>Child: pause at frame N, showing frame N-1's picture
    opt the viewer steps back again
        Child->>First: write a RestartHandoff to PATH and end
        First->>Child: run the next restart (never more than two processes)
    end

The rebuild is a headless-speed run of the same frames, with the same logic: only presenting, pacing and sound are left out (Rebuild.silence_frame; src/glitchygames/replay/silence.py). With an onion skin, the restarted process's child skips straight to the paired game frame (compare.py rule 8). Keys: Step back, Home and D.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Mode Waits after a frame Holds between frames Logic's dt FPS statistics read Live to the deadline (sleep, then spin) never measured measured Headless replay never never recorded recorded (--replay-fps real: measured) Watched replay never until the viewer's tick pays for the frame recorded as headless Rebuild never only to show progress recorded as headless Live vs OLD to the deadline never measured measured OLD's child never never (blocks on a full socket) recorded recorded

docs.title: How We Test Playback
docs.text:
Each tier checks something the others cannot see. The cheapest checks run on every test run; the real games' replays run as test items too, in child processes, so the engine is exercised the way a player's run exercises it.

flowchart TD
    subgraph suite ["Every test run (pytest / nox -s test)"]
        goldens["Golden replays<br/>each fixture is a test item"]
        traces["Golden traces<br/>tests/world/test_golden_traces.py"]
        standins["Replay-tool tests<br/>on stand-in games"]
        doors["Doors guard<br/>tests/test_engine_doors.py"]
        memory["Memory guard<br/>(CI Linux only)"]
    end
    subgraph tools ["On demand, and in the commit hook"]
        verify["glitchygames verify"]
        measure["glitchygames measure<br/>(pre-commit replay-metrics)"]
        rebaseline["--rebaseline<br/>(after an intended change)"]
        audit["--audit<br/>(determinism)"]
    end
    goldens -. "same replay as" .-> verify
    measure -. "is a rebaseline per recording" .-> rebaseline

docs.title: Golden replays
docs.text:
Intent: every game still plays its scripted session exactly as recorded, and every control it binds still works.

  • Each src/<layer>/<member>/tests/fixtures/replays/golden*.jsonl.gz (the golden-globs setting in pyproject.toml) is collected as one test item by the replay plugin (src/glitchygames/testing/replays.py, registered through the engine's pytest11 entry point).
  • The item replays the recording headless in a child process, through the game's console script entry point (--replay-trace PATH --headless --log-level warning).
  • It passes only if the child exits SUCCESS; otherwise it fails with the divergence report.
  • tests/replay/test_golden_replays.py checks the fixtures themselves. Its controls rule is that every golden pauses and resumes, exercises every keyboard control the game binds, and ends with the game's own quit control (test_every_golden_replay_exercises_every_control), so a control that stops working makes its golden diverge.
  • The goldens are recorded through the real engine by scripts/record_scripted_session.py, with scripts/golden_inputs.py.
flowchart LR
    item["pytest collects<br/>golden.jsonl.gz"] --> child["child process:<br/>console script entry point<br/>--replay-trace --headless"]
    child --> replay["ReplaySources: serve inputs,<br/>compare every frame"]
    replay -- "every frame matches" --> pass["exit SUCCESS: pass"]
    replay -- "a frame differs" --> fail["exit REPLAY_DIVERGED:<br/>fail with the report"]

docs.title: Golden traces
docs.text:
Intent: the games that existed before the world-space change still draw exactly what they drew then (tests/world/test_golden_traces.py).

  • The baselines in tests/world/golden/ were recorded by scripts/record_golden_traces.py before the engine's world-space changes.
  • Each test replays the same scripted run in-process, through the golden-trace harness (src/glitchygames/replay/tools/golden_traces.py), and compares every sprite's rect and visibility, frame by frame.
  • A difference fails unless an EXPECTED_DIFFERENCES entry explains it, and an entry that explains nothing fails too, so the list cannot go stale.
  • Later games are covered by their golden replays instead.

docs.title: Replay-tool tests on stand-in games
docs.text:
Intent: the engine's replay machinery works for any game, not just ours. Every tool, every refusal, every exit code.

  • Engine tests never import a workspace member (tests/test_workspace_config.py, tests/test_suite_collection.py), so they record and replay small stand-in games (tests/stand_in_games.py, tests/stand_in_harness_games.py).
  • The end-to-end proof is tests/replay/tools/test_an_unseen_game.py: a stand-in game in its own git repository, run through every tool on both front ends.
  • Uncapped recordings, unless pacing is the point. Stand-in live recordings (record_stand_in_game, in a headless child) are uncapped by default (UNPACED_TARGET_FPS = '0'): their frames never wait, and the engine skips measuring the machine's sleep model, so a 20-frame recording costs its child's start-up and no more. The same frames and sprites are recorded either way. A test that reads the recorded frame times (a watched replay presents frames by them) or the run's pacing (processing_paced, its live frame times) asks for paced=True, which paces at STAND_IN_GAME_TARGET_FPS = '60' as a player's run is; each such call says why. Replays of either are unpaced, as every replay is (tests/stand_in_games.py).
  • Shared recordings. A recording that tests only read is made once per test module (record_stand_in_game_once), and each test is handed its own copy of the file.
  • Unpaced engine runs. Engine tests that need no pacing run uncapped (--target-fps 0, for example tests/engine/test_engine_event_system.py), so they never wait for a frame deadline.

docs.title: Verify, measure and rebaseline
docs.text:
• glitchygames verify replays every golden and bundled demo headless, each in a child (the same replay as the plugin's), one line each, then a summary. A replay still running after REPLAY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 300 s is stopped (src/glitchygames/replay/tools/verify.py, children.py). It always uses each recording's own seed and refuses --random-seed.
  • --rebaseline NEW replays OLD's inputs on the current code, runs on past differences, and writes NEW with a summary of what changed (src/glitchygames/replay/rebaseline.py). It is how a golden follows an intended change. NEW replaces OLD only as a deliberate, reviewed step.
  • glitchygames measure rebaselines each recording headless into a temporary file, in a child, and turns the result into ledger rows (src/glitchygames/replay/tools/measure.py).
  • The replay-metrics pre-commit hook (scripts/measure_staged_replays.py) runs it whenever this machine has not measured the staged code tree, so every commit carries its measurements.
flowchart LR
    change["intended change<br/>to a game"] --> rb["--rebaseline OLD NEW<br/>(review the summary)"]
    rb --> replace["replace OLD with NEW<br/>(deliberate step)"]
    replace --> commit["git commit"]
    commit --> hook["replay-metrics hook:<br/>measure = rebaseline each recording<br/>into a temp file"]
    hook --> rows["ledger rows<br/>staged into the commit"]
    commit --> suite["test run: golden replays<br/>must match"]

Flags and exits: Rebaselining and Tools for any game.

docs.title: The determinism audit
docs.text:
Intent: catch nondeterminism that slipped past the doors (src/glitchygames/replay/audit.py).

  • --replay-trace PATH --audit runs the replay as two fresh child processes, headless, each with a different PYTHONHASHSEED (AUDIT_HASH_SEEDS = '1', '2') and a --replay-digest file: one SHA-256 per replayed frame.
  • Fresh processes give fresh engine state, and different hash seeds expose set and dict ordering bugs.
  • The audit fails if either run diverged from the recording, or if the two digest streams differ.
  • It compares the sampled frame only (scene class, each sprite's rect, visibility and draw order), so nondeterminism that never moves, hides or reorders a sprite goes unnoticed.
  • A child running longer than AUDIT_REPLAY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 3600 s is an AuditRunError.
flowchart LR
    audit["--audit"] --> a["child 1<br/>PYTHONHASHSEED=1<br/>--headless --replay-digest A"]
    audit --> b["child 2<br/>PYTHONHASHSEED=2<br/>--headless --replay-digest B"]
    a --> cmp{"both matched the recording<br/>and digests A == B?"}
    b --> cmp
    cmp -- yes --> ok["SUCCESS"]
    cmp -- no --> bad["AUDIT_NONDETERMINISTIC<br/>(first differing frame)"]

Flags: The determinism audit.

docs.title: The doors guard
docs.text:
Intent: nothing in the engine reads input or time from outside the doors, so a replay reaches all of it (tests/test_engine_doors.py).

  • The test parses every engine source file and follows imports and aliases of the watched modules (time, datetime, pygame and its event, key, mouse, time and joystick modules, ...; WATCHED_DOOR_MODULES).
  • It fails on any direct read outside ALLOWED_BYPASSES and ALLOWED_FUNCTION_BYPASSES, each of which names its reason.
  • The allowed paths are those src/glitchygames/clock.py names: measured_seconds(), pacing, the performance statistics, the audio-glitch probe and the recording's own start stamp.

docs.title: The memory guard
docs.text:
Intent: a test that runs CI's 2 GB Linux container out of memory stops the run and names the test, instead of the kernel killing the job silently (tests/memory_guard.py; tests/test_memory_guard.py).

  • It is on only when GLITCHYGAMES_TEST_RSS_LIMIT_MB is set; CircleCI's Linux job sets 1600.
  • A background thread samples memory every SAMPLE_INTERVAL_SECONDS, and each test's start and end are checked too.
  • It reads the container's memory (cgroup v2) where there is one, else this process's resident memory, and does nothing on macOS or Windows.
  • It matters for playback because the golden replays and the tools' tests start child processes, and the container's figure counts them.

docs.title: bitmappy
docs.text:
Glitchy Games Bitmappy pixel art editor.

Re-exports all public names from submodules for backwards compatibility.
