Delta Time Demo: a square crossing the screen at a speed independent of the frame rate.

Run it with the dt-demo console script or python -m dt_demo; Space starts the square.

docs.title: Brave Adventurer Architecture
docs.text:
Brave Adventurer is a Pitfall-style side-scrolling platformer set in ancient Egypt: the adventurer runs right across 20 screens of desert, jumps stone walls and pits, avoids cobras, scarab beetles and scorpions, and picks up gold scarabs. Every picture is drawn from pygame primitives and every sound is synthesized at startup, so the game ships no asset files.

The Papyrus Edition is the same game with hand-drawn TOML pixel art for the player, the enemies and the collectibles (see The Papyrus Edition below). One command plays both: its title screen offers Classic and Papyrus (see The launcher and its title screen).

This page is for a developer who wants to understand the game or build one like it. It shows which engine features the game uses and where its code puts each of them: world-space sprites, camera follow and parallax layers, the pose rule, hitbox-based terrain collision, ActionMap input, synthesized sounds, saves, recording and replay.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
uv run brave-adventurer                  # the title screen: choose Classic or Papyrus
uv run brave-adventurer --game classic   # Classic at once: every sprite drawn in code
uv run brave-adventurer --game papyrus   # Papyrus at once: the Egyptian edition, sprite-sheet art

brave-adventurer is the project's one console script (src/games/brave-adventurer/, see Its package): the launcher, brave_adventurer_modes.main(). With --game it runs that game's own main(), which runs GameEngine(game=BraveAdventurerScene).start() (or PapyrusBraveAdventurerScene); without it, the title screen. The window is 800 x 480 (SCREEN_WIDTH, SCREEN_HEIGHT in brave_adventurer_core/constants.py). The browser build (/play/brave-adventurer/) starts the title screen.

docs.title: The launcher and its title screen
docs.text:
brave_adventurer_modes.main() (launcher.py) chooses what to start, in this order:

  1. --game classic|papyrus: it reads the flag (parse_known_args), removes it from sys.argv, and runs that game's own main() unchanged. The game's arguments, scene flow, recording header and recordings are its own, exactly as when it had its own command. With a recording as well, the flag still decides, and that game's replay refuses another game's recording.
  2. A recording to replay (--replay-trace PATH): the recording's header names the scene it was made in by logical name, and the launcher starts that game's own main() without the title screen (game_for_recording). The golden-replay plugin, the replay-metrics ledger's rebaselines, watched replays and their restarts all start games this way, so each reaches its own game through the one command. A recording made from the title screen names the title screen (games.brave_adventurer_modes.title:TitleScene) and is replayed from there. Another game's recording is refused with ExitCode.UNUSABLE_INPUT, and so is one made before logical names (name its game with --game). One whose header cannot be read goes to the engine, which refuses it as it refuses any missing or unusable recording.
  3. Otherwise the title screen, TitleScene (title.py), runs.

The title screen draws the games' own sky and pyramids (brave_adventurer_core.drawing), the title, a card for each game with a line on how it differs, and a line of help. It reads its controls through its own ActionMap (TitleScene._create_action_map), keyboard by scancode, as the games do:

Action Keyboard (by position) Gamepad When choose the other game (wraps round) Up or Left, Down or Right D-pad press start the chosen game Space or Return A or Start release, after a press on this screen (as the pause and game-over screens go on), so the game never gets that release quit Q B or Back press (Esc does nothing here, on press or release: the browser's touch Pause button sends it)

Starting a game sets next_scene to a new scene of that game, built with the run's options, in the same engine: the game then runs as it does from its own main(). Its game-over screen restarts that game, not the title screen. A recording made from the title screen holds the title screen's frames first, then the game's.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
The gameplay scene binds every control through one ActionMap (BraveAdventurerSceneBase._create_action_map; the classic edition's adds the mic button). Keyboard controls are bound by scancode, a physical key position, so they sit in the same place on every keyboard layout.

Action Keyboard (by position) Gamepad Read how move_right Right arrow D-pad right held: is_held() in dt_tick move_left Left arrow D-pad left held: is_held() in dt_tick jump Space or Up arrow A press: get_action() in the handler pause Esc none press quit Q none press: scene_manager.quit() posts QUIT mic_toggle (primitives edition only) none DualSense mic button (controller button 15, joystick button 16) press starts listening, release answers

The built-in screens the game switches to have their own keys, by key code:

Screen Keys Pause (PauseScene) Space or a gamepad's Start or A (on release, after a press there) resumes; Esc or a gamepad's B or Back (on the press) quits, Q (on release) quits; regaining window focus more than 0.5 s after pausing resumes too Game over (GameOverScene) Space or a gamepad's Start or A (on release, after a press there) starts a new game; Esc or a gamepad's B or Back (on the press) quits, Q (on release) quits

The analog sticks move nothing: no axis is bound (TestButtonsAndAxesHoldMovement pins it).

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The launcher reads --game; each scene's args() adds -v; everything else is the engine's (see Argument System).

Option Where Effect in this game --game {classic,papyrus} the launcher (launcher.py; listed in -h by TitleScene.args()) Starts that game at once, without the title screen -v, --version TitleScene.args(), BraveAdventurerScene.args(), PapyrusBraveAdventurerScene.args() Prints the name and version and exits before anything starts (argparse's version action): Brave Adventurer 1.0 (the title screen's, and Classic's with --game classic); with --game papyrus, Brave Adventurer: Papyrus Edition 1.0 --input-mode {auto,joystick,controller} engine Passed to the ActionMap: which gamepad event family the D-pad, A and mic bindings answer --axis-deadzone engine Passed to the ActionMap (ActionMap.from_engine_options); the game binds no axes, so it changes nothing yet --screen-shake-intensity engine Passed to Camera2D(shake_intensity=...); the game itself starts no shakes --rumble-intensity engine Scales the death and game-over rumble pulses --target-fps engine The scene sets no TARGET_FPS, so the default 60.01 applies --debug-overlay (or F3, F4) engine Hitboxes by collision layer, physics, camera and performance panels --record-trace, --replay-trace, --headless engine Record and replay a session (see Recording, replay and golden tests)

docs.title: Scenes and how they switch
docs.text:
The game is one gameplay scene plus the engine's built-in pause and game-over screens. Every switch is a plain next_scene assignment or switch_to_scene; the game uses no transitions.

In the diagrams on this page, the Engine box is what every game gets from glitchygames; the Brave Adventurer box (or the PapyrusEdition box) is what this game adds. Here the game's own code is its main() (which starts the engine's GameEngine) and the gameplay scene; the pause and game-over screens are the engine's, which the game constructs and hands to next_scene, and the engine ends the run on QUIT.

Before the game, the launcher (brave_adventurer_modes) either runs a game's own main() or starts the engine on its title screen, which switches to the chosen game's scene:

flowchart TB
    subgraph LAUNCHER["The launcher: brave-adventurer"]
        direction TB
        launch(["brave_adventurer_modes.main#40;#41;"])
        title["TitleScene<br/>both games, a line each"]
    end
    subgraph GAMES["The games"]
        direction TB
        classic_main(["brave_adventurer.main#40;#41;"])
        papyrus_main(["brave_adventurer_papyrus.main#40;#41;"])
        classic["BraveAdventurerScene"]
        papyrus["PapyrusBraveAdventurerScene"]
    end
    quit_title(["QUIT: the run ends"])

    launch -->|"--game classic, or a Classic recording"| classic_main
    launch -->|"--game papyrus, or a Papyrus recording"| papyrus_main
    launch -->|"neither, or a title-screen recording:<br/>GameEngine#40;game=TitleScene#41;.start#40;#41;"| title
    classic_main --> classic
    papyrus_main --> papyrus
    title -->|"Classic chosen: next_scene"| classic
    title -->|"Papyrus chosen: next_scene"| papyrus
    title -->|"Q, B or Back"| quit_title

From there each game runs its own scenes:

flowchart TB
    subgraph GAME_SCENES["Brave Adventurer"]
        direction TB
        start(["main#40;#41;: GameEngine#40;game=BraveAdventurerScene#41;.start#40;#41;"])
        play["BraveAdventurerScene<br/>the gameplay scene"]
        fresh["a new BraveAdventurerScene<br/>type#40;previous_scene#41;#40;options=...#41;"]
    end
    subgraph ENGINE_SCENES["Engine"]
        direction TB
        pause["PauseScene<br/>the frozen game under a translucent overlay"]
        over["GameOverScene<br/>final score and the top 5 high scores"]
        quit(["QUIT: the run ends"])
    end

    start --> play
    play -->|"Esc: _pause_game#40;#41; sets next_scene"| pause
    pause -->|"Space, Start or A released, or focus regained:<br/>resume#40;#41; switches back to the same scene"| play
    play -->|"last life lost: _player_die#40;#41;<br/>saves the high score, sets next_scene"| over
    over -->|"Space, Start or A released: resume#40;#41;"| fresh
    play -->|"Q"| quit
    pause -->|"Esc, B or Back, or Q released"| quit
    over -->|"Esc, B or Back, or Q released"| quit

Resuming from the pause screen switches back to the same scene object, so the game picks up where it stopped; its setup() runs again (it only rebuilds the HUD font and re-follows the player; the sounds are generated once). The pause screen's debug_subject is the paused game, so the debug overlay keeps showing the game's hitboxes over the frozen picture.

The game-over screen does not resume the old scene: GameOverScene.resume() builds a new instance of the previous scene's class with the same options, so a restart is a clean game (and the Papyrus Edition restarts as the Papyrus Edition).

docs.title: World-space sprites and the camera
docs.text:
Every game object is a world-space sprite: it declares COORDINATE_SPACE = CoordinateSpace.WORLD and keeps float world_x / world_y. The game never writes a sprite's rect; the engine places each world sprite from the camera every frame, snapping with the scene's default PIXEL_SNAP_MODE (NEAREST_HALF_UP), and culls the ones off screen. Only the HUD is drawn in screen space, straight onto the display in render().

The camera is a Camera2D built in __init__:

Setting Value Effect lead_x CAMERA_LEAD = 250 The camera aims 250 px left of the player, so the player runs at about x = 250 on screen with the view ahead of it set_bounds(min_x=0.0) left bound only The camera never shows the world left of x = 0; there is no right or vertical bound follow(target=self.player, axes=FollowAxes.X) in setup() The engine aims the camera at the player on x only: the camera stays at the top of the world smoothing the default smooth_factor 0.1 The camera eases toward its goal; with no snap_to() in setup() it eases in from the origin follow(target=None) at game over The world and the camera stand still behind the game-over switch

The scene never calls camera.update(): the engine aims the camera after logic and events, and then positions the sprites (frame steps 5 and 6 in the next section).

docs.title: Parallax layers
docs.text:
Four background layers are added with camera.add_background_layer(...), drawn by the functions in brave_adventurer_core/drawing.py (both editions draw the same backgrounds). Each draw function depends only on its arguments (the layer's offset), so the engine redraws a layer only when its offset changes; none needs animated=True.

Depth Layer scroll_factor Draw function What it draws 0 sky PARALLAX_SKY = 0.0 draw_sky A blue-to-haze vertical gradient (built once per surface size) 1 far PARALLAX_FAR = 0.1 draw_pyramids A sand plane from y = 300 and three pyramids repeating every 2400 px 2 mid PARALLAX_MID = 0.3 draw_dunes_and_oasis Dunes from three summed sine waves, oases repeating every 3000 px 3 near PARALLAX_NEAR = 0.7 draw_near_ground_details Rocks and grass tufts every 60 px, placed by a hash of the world x (no randomness)

The sprites sit above them on layers 4 to 7: terrain, collectibles, enemies, then the player (LAYER_* in brave_adventurer_core/constants.py).

docs.title: Levels and screens
docs.text:
A level is a list of ScreenData, one per 800 px screen. Each screen lists its content in screen-local x (and y for collectibles):

ScreenData field Entries Becomes ground_segments (local_x, width) GroundSegment at GROUND_Y = 400, 80 px tall walls (local_x, height) StoneWall, 32 px wide, standing on the ground enemies (type_name, local_x, kwargs) Cobra, Scarab(speed=...) or Scorpion(patrol_range=...) collectibles (local_x, local_y) GoldScarab

LEVEL_1 ("The Path of the Pharaoh") has 20 screens of rising difficulty: flat ground with scarabs to collect, a first short wall (screen 2), a first pit (screen 4), the first cobra (5), scarab (7) and scorpion (10), then combinations, a triple pit (16), a gauntlet (18) and a collectible run (19). The scene's level manager (ClassicLevelManager, PapyrusLevelManager) builds it once, in the scene's __init__: the shared LevelManager._build() (in brave_adventurer_core/levels.py) makes each screen's ground segments, walls, enemies and collectibles in that order, and each game gives its enemy classes (_get_enemy_class_map()) and its gold scarab (_get_collectible_class()). The level data, the builder and the terrain code are the game's; the sprite group and the collision layers they feed are the engine's Scene services:

flowchart TB
    subgraph GAME_LEVEL["Brave Adventurer"]
        direction TB
        level["LEVEL_1<br/>20 ScreenData, one per 800 px screen"]
        map["_get_enemy_class_map#40;#41;<br/>'cobra', 'scarab', 'scorpion' to classes<br/>#40;an unknown name is skipped#41;"]
        build["LevelManager._build#40;#41;<br/>world x = screen index × 800 + local x"]
        lists["ground_sprites, wall_sprites,<br/>enemy_sprites, collectible_sprites"]
        terrain["terrain collision code in the scene<br/>#40;ground and wall lists#41;"]
    end
    subgraph ENGINE_LEVEL["Engine"]
        direction TB
        group["Scene.all_sprites<br/>#40;a LayeredDirty the engine draws by layer#41;"]
        layers["Scene.collisions, a CollisionManager<br/>layers 'player', 'enemies', 'collectibles'"]
    end

    level --> build
    map --> build
    build -->|"every sprite joins"| group
    build -->|"and one list per kind"| lists
    lists -->|"the scene adds enemies, collectibles"| layers
    lists -->|"ground, walls"| terrain

The scene adds the player to the 'player' layer and every enemy and collectible to theirs; sprite-against-sprite contact goes through self.collisions.check_overlap(...). Ground and walls are not in collision layers: the scene resolves terrain itself (below).

There is no goal at the end of the level: past screen 19 there is no ground.

docs.title: Pits and walls
docs.text:
Pits are the gaps between consecutive ground segments. Nothing in the world represents a pit; render() draws each one (_draw_pits) after the sprites, between the drawn rects of the two segments either side, so the pit edges always meet the ground even at a half-pixel camera position. Every visible enemy that overlaps a pit (a scarab that rolled in) and then the player are blitted once more, so they show in front of the pit fill. Inside a pit the edges of the neighbouring segments act as walls, so the player cannot walk out; falling more than PIT_DEATH_THRESHOLD (100 px) below the screen costs a life.

Walls (StoneWall) are both platform and obstacle: a player whose feet land within 16 px of a wall's top stands on it; otherwise a player overlapping the wall's body is pushed out to the side it came from (see Collision).

docs.title: Enemies and collectibles
docs.text:
Sprite Behaviour (in dt_tick) Cobra Stationary; strikes for 0.3 s every 2 s (STRIKE_INTERVAL, STRIKE_DURATION) Scarab Rolls at roll_speed (negative is left) under gravity; the scene lands it on ground segments or on a pit floor and reverses it at walls Scorpion Walks at 60 px/s between its origin and origin + patrol_range, turning at each end GoldScarab Bobs 4 px up and down (sin(time × 3)); worth COLLECTIBLE_SCORE_BONUS

Touching any enemy costs a life. The primitives edition's enemies follow the pose rule (below) too: each draws its first pose as it is made and redraws it at the end of its dt_tick, so its visible-pixel hitbox is this frame's when the scene checks collision.

docs.title: Movement and physics
docs.text:
Player composes a PhysicsBody (glitchygames.physics) instead of moving itself. Its world_x, world_y, velocity_x, velocity_y, on_ground and facing_right are properties that read and write the body.

Part Setting Effect GravityBehavior GRAVITY = 1200 px/s², MAX_FALL_SPEED = 800 px/s Falls, with a terminal speed AccelerationBehavior PLAYER_ACCELERATION = 1600, PLAYER_DECELERATION = 1200 px/s² Ramps toward a target speed: move_right() / move_left() set ±PLAYER_RUN_SPEED (200 px/s), stop_horizontal() sets 0 BoundsConstraint(min_x=...) the world's left edge Refitted to the hitbox every tick (_fit_world_edge_to_hitbox), so the hitbox, not the image's transparent margin, stops at x = 0 jump() JUMP_VELOCITY = -500 px/s Only when on_ground

There is no ground constraint in the body: the scene decides whether the player stands on something. An AnimationStateMachine (rules written in code in the primitives edition) picks the pose from the body's animation context: idle, running, jumping or falling. Running off a ledge turns to falling (running to falling when velocity_y > 10 and not on the ground), as idle and jumping do.

docs.title: The pose rule
docs.text: The player draws its pose, and so its hitbox, in dt_tick, after physics and the state machine and before the scene's collision runs. Its hitbox is the image's visible pixels (the engine trims transparent margins), so drawing the pose in update() would make collision use the previous frame's pose: a player turning toward a wall would sit inside it for a frame (BUGS.md, the pose fix). After drawing, the world-edge bound is refitted to the new hitbox and applied again. update() does visual work only: the respawn fade (image.set_alpha(...)).

docs.title: Collision
docs.text:
The scene resolves terrain in dt_tick, from the player's collision rect (get_sprite_collision_rect) and offset (collision_rect_offset), never from its rect or its drawn size:

Check Rule Standing support The player's support span is common_hitbox_x_range(): the columns every pose covers for the current facing, measured once by drawing every pose over two seconds of animation. A wider pose (falling is wider than idle) cannot catch a ledge the idle pose has left, so a player at an edge never falls, lands and falls again Ground The trailing foot (the back edge of the support span; the middle when still) must be over a segment, the hitbox bottom at or below GROUND_Y, and the player not rising. Then it is set so the hitbox bottom (the visible feet) rests on the ground Pit edges While below ground and not supported, moving into a segment's side puts the hitbox flush against it Wall top Feet within 16 px of the top, head above it, not rising, and the support span over the wall Wall side Pushed out on the side the hitbox was on before this frame's move (velocity_x × dt back), so a dt hitch cannot carry a fast player through; if it already overlapped (a wider pose), the side of the wall's centre decides (_entered_wall_from_left) Snapping Terrain edges are taken where the engine draws them (snapped_world_position), so collision agrees with the picture Enemies check_overlap('player', 'enemies'): one death per pass even when touching two enemies; none while respawning Collectibles check_overlap('player', 'collectibles'): bonus_points (kept in the score), sound, the scarab removed from the group, its list and its layer

docs.title: Death and respawn
docs.text:
The game decides what a death does; the engine's scene tweens run the fades, its rumble controller sends the pulses, and its GameOverScene is the screen the game switches to:

flowchart TB
    subgraph GAME_DEATH["Brave Adventurer"]
        direction TB
        hit["an enemy hitbox overlaps,<br/>or the player fell 100 px below the screen"]
        die["_player_die#40;#41;: lives -= 1"]
        respawn["death sound<br/>_respawn_player#40;#41;: is_respawning = True,<br/>velocities 0, stop_horizontal#40;#41;"]
        place["back 200 px #40;RESPAWN_OFFSET#41;, on the ground,<br/>is_respawning = False"]
        over["game_over_triggered = True, camera stops following<br/>game-over sound, _save_high_score#40;#41;<br/>next_scene = GameOverScene#40;...#41;"]
    end
    subgraph ENGINE_DEATH["Engine"]
        direction TB
        rumble["scene_manager.rumble.pulse#40;...#41;<br/>the death or game-over pulse"]
        fadeout["Scene.tweens: alpha to 0 over 0.2 s"]
        fadein["Scene.tweens: alpha to 255 over 0.3 s"]
        gameover["GameOverScene<br/>at the end of the frame"]
    end

    hit --> die
    die -->|"lives left"| respawn
    respawn -.->|"pulse"| rumble
    respawn -->|"tween"| fadeout
    fadeout -->|"on_complete"| place
    place -->|"tween"| fadein
    die -->|"no lives left"| over
    over -.->|"pulse"| rumble
    over -->|"next_scene"| gameover

While is_respawning is set, movement input, enemy contact and the pit-death check are skipped. Both editions also clear the walk target (stop_horizontal()), so the player stands still while it fades instead of walking on toward its last direction. The fades are scene tweens (self.tweens), which Scene.dt_tick advances by the frame's dt. Once game_over_triggered is set, dt_tick returns at once, so nothing moves on the last frame before the switch.

docs.title: One frame
docs.text:
The engine runs the frame (CLAUDE.md, SceneManager); the scene's dt_tick does all the game logic in a fixed order, and its render() draws. The Engine box is the SceneManager's frame; the Brave Adventurer box is the scene's code it calls:

sequenceDiagram
    box rgb(232,238,255) Engine
        participant SM as SceneManager
    end
    box rgb(255,243,224) Brave Adventurer
        participant Scene as BraveAdventurerScene
    end

    Note over SM: 1. begin the frame
    SM->>Scene: 2. dt_tick(dt)
    Note over Scene: movement input<br/>every sprite's dt_tick<br/>terrain collision<br/>deaths and pickups<br/>distance score
    Note over SM: 3. pump and dispatch the events
    SM->>Scene: 3. on_*_event handlers
    Note over SM: 5. camera aim<br/>6. position and cull<br/>7. Scene.update(): every<br/>dirty sprite's update()
    SM->>Scene: 7. render()
    Note over SM: 9-10. present and pace
Step Who What happens in Brave Adventurer 2, movement input the scene Scene.dt_tick (dt, tweens; the scene returns here once game over is set), then actions.begin_frame() and is_held('move_right' / 'move_left') set the player's target speed (skipped while respawning); the primitives edition also collects voice assistant responses 2, every sprite's dt_tick the sprites Player physics, state machine and pose; enemy movement; collectible bobbing 2, terrain collision the scene Ground (then the landing sound), walls, then scarabs against ground and walls 2, deaths and pickups the scene The pit-death check and enemy contact (both skipped while respawning), then collectibles 2, score the scene max_distance, then score = round(max_distance / 10) + bonus_points 3 the handlers Jump, pause, quit and the mic button (on_*_event) 5, 6 the engine Aims the camera at the player (x only), then positions and culls every world sprite 7 Scene.update(), render() The player's fade; then sky fill, sprites, pits, any enemy in a pit and the player again, the HUD 9, 10 the engine Present the frame, pace it

(Steps 4 and 8, shake and rumble and the still-camera shake, do nothing visible here: the game starts no shakes, and its rumble pulses run on their own.)

Two things follow from this order:

  • dt_tick runs before the frame's events, so movement uses the ActionMap state from the previous frame's events, and a jump pressed this frame takes effect in this frame's handler (its physics in the next dt_tick).
  • Collision runs before the engine positions the sprites, so this frame's picture already shows the resolved positions. Game logic never reads a world sprite's rect (it holds where the sprite was last drawn); only _draw_pits, in the render phase, does.

render() replaces Scene.render: it fills the sky colour, draws the LayeredDirty group, draws the pits, then any enemy that overlaps a pit and the player on top, then the HUD (score top left, lives top right, each with a 1 px shadow), and sets self.rects = None so the whole screen is presented.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
The engine delivers the events and keeps the ActionMap's held state; the game's scene reads the map and drives its player. SDL, outside both boxes, is where the events come from:

sequenceDiagram
    participant SDL as SDL queue
    box rgb(232,238,255) Engine
        participant Engine as GameEngine and<br/>SceneManager
        participant Actions as ActionMap
    end
    box rgb(255,243,224) Brave Adventurer
        participant Scene as BraveAdventurerScene
        participant Player
    end

    Note over Scene,Player: dt_tick, before this frame's events
    Scene->>Actions: begin_frame()
    Scene->>Actions: is_held('move_right')
    Actions-->>Scene: True (held since a KEYDOWN)
    Scene->>Player: move_right() sets the target speed
    Note over SDL,Engine: event processing
    SDL->>Engine: KEYDOWN (scancode of Space)
    Engine->>Scene: on_key_down_event(event)
    Scene->>Actions: handle_event(event) updates held state
    Scene->>Actions: get_action(event)
    Actions-->>Scene: 'jump'
    Scene->>Player: jump() (sound first if on the ground)

Held actions (move_right, move_left) are read once per frame in dt_tick with is_held(); one-shot actions (jump, pause, quit, mic_toggle) are read from the event in the handlers with get_action(). Every handler first calls actions.handle_event(event), key-up and button-up handlers included, so the held state follows the device. The handlers are on_key_down/up_event, on_controller_button_down/up_event, on_joy_button_down/up_event and on_joy_axis_motion_event (which only feeds the map). A key that maps to no action falls through to Scene.on_key_down_event.

Gamepads. The D-pad and A are bound as controller_button=...; the ActionMap built with the scene's input_mode turns that into controller events, joystick events or both. The scene builds it with ActionMap.from_engine_options(self.options) (the engine's --input-mode, default auto, and --axis-deadzone), so a normal run binds both families and the engine delivers each press once.

Microphone (primitives edition). VoiceAssistant.discover() (in __init__) looks for a controller with both a microphone and a speaker (a DualSense) and returns None when there is none. It runs only when the engine's doors serve the real devices (live play, or a recording): in a replay (or a rebaseline or playback) the voice assistant stays None, so a replay never enumerates audio devices and a recorded mic press neither listens nor calls the AI service (_discover_voice_assistant). Pressing the mic button starts listening; releasing it sends the recording through speech-to-text, an AI model and text-to-speech back to the controller's speaker, and dt_tick collects finished responses (voice_assistant.update()). The DualSense reports its mic button as 15 on the controller API and 16 on the raw joystick API, so each layer binds its own: controller_layer_button=MIC_BUTTON_CONTROLLER (the controller layer only, so raw button 15 is not the mic) and joystick_button=MIC_BUTTON_JOYSTICK. The Papyrus Edition has no voice assistant.

docs.title: Sound
docs.text:
brave_adventurer_core/sounds.py generates five effects once, in setup() (GameSounds.initialize()), with the engine's synthesizer toolkit (glitchygames.audio.synth: oscillator, frequency_curve, apply_envelope, concatenate, to_sound), at the mixer's sample rate:

Sound Made of Played when jump a 0.12 s sine sweep, 220 to 660 Hz jump pressed while on the ground land a 0.06 s 80 Hz thud airborne before this frame's physics, on the ground after collision collect C5, E5, G5, 0.06 s each a gold scarab is picked up death a 0.3 s sweep, 500 to 80 Hz a life is lost game over E4, C4, then a longer A3 the last life is lost

If audio is unavailable (AudioUnavailableError), no sound is set and the game plays silent rather than with some of its sounds; every play_*() checks for None. The game uses plain one-shot pygame.mixer.Sounds: no SoundRecipe files and no live voices.

docs.title: State, score and saves
docs.text:
State Where Rule Lives player.lives, from STARTING_LIVES = 3 One per death; game over at 0 Score player.score The distance score plus the bonus points, set at the end of every dt_tick: round(max_distance / DISTANCE_SCORE_DIVISOR) (the furthest world x reached, over 10) + player.bonus_points, where each collected gold scarab adds COLLECTIBLE_SCORE_BONUS (100) to bonus_points High scores open_saves(app_name='brave-adventurer') (Papyrus: 'brave-adventurer-papyrus'), save 'high_scores' {'scores': [{'score': n}, ...]}, the ten best, descending; written at game over and shown (top 5) on the game-over screen

open_saves returns the door's SaveManager: a DiskSaveManager live, an in-memory one in a replay, so a replayed game over never touches real saves.

docs.title: Engine features it uses
docs.text: Feature How Brave Adventurer uses it World space and culling Every game sprite is CoordinateSpace.WORLD; the engine positions and culls them Camera follow and parallax follow(target=player, axes=FollowAxes.X), a left bound, four parallax layers Physics PhysicsBody with GravityBehavior, AccelerationBehavior, BoundsConstraint Collision layers and hitboxes 'player', 'enemies', 'collectibles' with check_overlap; visible-pixel hitboxes Tweens The respawn fade (self.tweens.tween(target=player, property_name='alpha', ...)) Rumble scene_manager.rumble.pulse(...) on death (0.7 / 0.4, 0.35 s) and game over (1.0 / 0.6, 0.8 s); the game-over pulse is finite, so it outlives the switch Screen shake Only the camera's shake_intensity setting; the game calls no shake() Random streams Not needed: nothing in the game is random (the near-ground details are a hash of the world x) Saves High scores through open_saves Built-in scenes PauseScene, GameOverScene Debug overlay F3 / F4: the collision layers' hitboxes, the player's velocities and ground state, the camera; no debug_draw of its own Recording and replay Every input comes through the engine's doors (ActionMap events, saves), so --record-trace and --replay-trace reproduce a session exactly Transitions, instant replay, demos Not used

docs.title: Recording, replay and golden tests
docs.text:
Because the game takes input only from engine events, and has no randomness and no clock reads of its own, a recording replays it exactly:

uv run brave-adventurer --record-trace /tmp/session.jsonl.gz
uv run brave-adventurer --replay-trace /tmp/session.jsonl.gz            # watch it
uv run brave-adventurer --replay-trace /tmp/session.jsonl.gz --headless # check it

Two kinds of golden test pin the game's behaviour frame by frame:

Golden File Made by What it checks Golden replay src/games/brave-adventurer/tests/fixtures/replays/golden-classic.jsonl.gz (and golden-papyrus.jsonl.gz), both replayed through the launcher, brave-adventurer, which starts the game each header names scripts/record_scripted_session.py --game brave_adventurer --frames 400 through the real engine loop: the golden input script, then a controls tail (walk left, jump with Space, quit with Q): 472 frames Replayed in a child process with --replay-trace PATH --headless by the replay pytest plugin; any divergence fails. tests/replay/test_golden_replays.py also checks that every bound control is exercised, or listed with the reason it is not (no gamepad on the dummy driver) Golden trace tests/world/golden/brave_adventurer.jsonl.gz (and brave_adventurer_papyrus.jsonl.gz) scripts/record_golden_traces.py, before the world-space change tests/world/test_golden_traces.py replays the script and compares every sprite's rect and visibility with that baseline; every difference must be explained by exactly one ExpectedDifference rule (engine culling, separate snapping, the pose fix, scarabs resting on their drawn underside, and the player falling into the screen-4 pit in its falling pose instead of its running pose)

The golden script (brave_adventurer_script() in scripts/golden_inputs.py) runs right over screens 0 and 1 jumping for the higher scarabs, pauses and resumes, then places the player at x = 2400 (a 900-frame run cannot reach the first pit from the start) and jumps the two screen-3 walls and the screen-4 pit before walking back. Re-record either golden only deliberately, after finding out why it changed (the scripts' docstrings give the commands).

timings, hitboxes, pixels, metadata and [[transition]] sections survive a save round trip), and their state machines reload in order

docs.title: The Papyrus Edition
docs.text:
brave_adventurer_papyrus keeps the game and changes its characters. It shares the level data, terrain, background drawing, sounds and constants with the classic edition (brave_adventurer_core, below both games), and replaces the sprites that have pixel art.

Shared with the classic edition (brave_adventurer_core, unchanged) Changed in Papyrus LEVEL_1 and ScreenData (re-exported by its levels.py) The player, the three enemies and the gold scarab are AnimatedSprites loaded from TOML files in sprites/ GroundSegment and StoneWall (variable-width primitives, which do not suit fixed pixel art) Sprites are scaled 2x (SPRITE_SCALE); TOML hitboxes are in native pixels, so scale is set to 2 The four parallax draw functions and the pits The player stands on a fixed foot line, PAPYRUS_PLAYER_HEIGHT = 27 × 2 px below its snapped world y, instead of its hitbox bottom GameSounds and every sound Animation state machines come from the TOML [[transition]] sections (the player's, the cobra's timed strike) Physics, camera, layer, parallax, scoring and colour constants (re-exported by its constants.py) Its own save namespace (brave-adventurer-papyrus) and scene NAME The controls (move, jump, pause, quit) No voice assistant and no mic binding

docs.title: How it is structured
docs.text: The level manager and the scene are both shared by subclassing. The Engine box is what both editions get from glitchygames, the Core box is what both share (brave_adventurer_core), the BraveAdventurer box is the classic edition and the PapyrusEdition box is what the Papyrus Edition adds. Solid arrows are inheritance, pointing at the base class; dotted arrows are runtime use (one class building or calling another). Both scenes also import the core's drawing.py, sounds.py and constants (left out to keep the diagrams readable).

    PrimitiveSprites <.. SpritesLevelManager : builds
    TerrainSprites <.. SpritesPapyrusLevelManager : builds
    PapyrusSprites <.. SpritesPapyrusLevelManager : builds
  • PapyrusLevelManager gives _get_enemy_class_map() (the Papyrus enemy classes) and _get_collectible_class() (PapyrusGoldScarab); the shared LevelManager._build() builds them, as ClassicLevelManager's give Cobra, Scarab, Scorpion and GoldScarab.
  • BraveAdventurerSceneBase (brave_adventurer_core/scene.py) is the gameplay both scenes play by: the camera and parallax, the level and player built in that order (recordings number sprites by creation order), the controls, the dt_tick order, terrain, wall and enemy collision, death, respawn and high scores, the input handlers, render(), the pits and the HUD. Each game's scene stays in its own game.py under its own name (recordings name a scene by its module and class) and gives only what differs: NAME; LEVEL_MANAGER_CLASS, PLAYER_CLASS and PLAYER_START_WORLD_Y; SAVE_APP_NAME (brave-adventurer, brave-adventurer-papyrus); _scarab_class() (the enemy that follows the terrain); and the foot line, _player_top_and_foot_line() and _player_world_y_standing_on(): the classic edition's hitbox bottom (a float world y), Papyrus's _snapped_player_top() + PAPYRUS_PLAYER_HEIGHT (an int). The classic edition adds the voice assistant: it is discovered after the shared __init__, its mic button is bound after the shared controls, and it fills the base's voice hooks, which Papyrus leaves empty.
  • PapyrusPlayer has the same PhysicsBody and move methods as Player. Each dt_tick ticks physics, evaluates the TOML state machine, advances the TOML animation (AnimatedSprite.update(self, dt)), starts image from a fresh copy of the drawn frame (refresh_drawn_image), and mirrors image and hitbox when facing left (hitbox_flip_x), then refits the world-edge bound. That keeps the pose rule: the frame collision uses is the one drawn this frame. frame_anchor = FrameAnchor.BOTTOM draws each frame lower by its draw_offset, so frames whose feet end on rows 24 to 27 all stand on the 27-row foot line. Its standing support uses the engine's AnimatedSprite.common_hitbox_x_range() (the x-span every frame's hitbox shares) where the original measures its procedurally drawn poses.
  • The Papyrus enemies and gold scarab do the same, animating in dt_tick, and make update() a no-op (Scene.update() would call it without a dt: BUGS.md #115).
  • sprite_utils.py: prepare_papyrus_sprite() converts every loaded frame from the magenta colour key to per-pixel alpha and sets the engine's AnimatedSprite.scale to SPRITE_SCALE, which draws every frame, rect, hitbox and draw_offset at 2x (BUGS.md #144); refresh_drawn_image() copies the engine's drawn frame each tick, so the facing flip and the respawn fade never stack or reach the engine's cached surface.
Papyrus TOML sprite Animations Hitbox State machine player.toml (20 x 28) idle, running, jumping, falling per frame 8 [[transition]]s on velocity and on_ground (falling last, mirroring FALLING_VELOCITY_THRESHOLD) cobra.toml idle (looping), strike (once) per frame idle to strike after 2 s, back after 0.3 s scarab.toml roll sprite none scorpion.toml walk sprite none gold_scarab.toml shimmer sprite none

scripts/audit_hitboxes.py audits the Papyrus sprites' hitboxes against their pixels.

docs.title: Its package
docs.text:
Both editions are one package beside the engine, src/games/brave-adventurer/ (distribution brave-adventurer), in a src layout of layered import packages: brave_adventurer_core (the constants, terrain, level data and level manager, background drawing, sounds and the gameplay scene's base both games share; it imports neither game), brave_adventurer (the classic edition), brave_adventurer_papyrus (the Papyrus Edition) and brave_adventurer_modes (the launcher and its title screen, the project's one console script). How such a package is laid out, installed, tested and built, and how a game is moved into one, is in Games as Their Own Packages.

Its recordings name the scenes games.brave_adventurer.game:BraveAdventurerScene and games.brave_adventurer_papyrus.game:PapyrusBraveAdventurerScene, as before the move (the title screen is games.brave_adventurer_modes.title:TitleScene); its golden replays are src/games/brave-adventurer/tests/fixtures/replays/golden-classic.jsonl.gz and golden-papyrus.jsonl.gz, both replayed by the launcher, which starts the game each header names; and its one browser page, the title screen, ships all four archives, the core first.

docs.title: Clockwork Keep Architecture
docs.text:
Clockwork Keep is a steampunk tower climb, one of GlitchyGames' example games. You play the Tinker, a goggled mechanic, climbing three floors of a clockwork tower: jump from platform to platform, collect cogs for points, and ride the elevator at the top of a floor to the next one. The last floor has no elevator: standing on its top platform, under the victory cog, wins the game.

Everything is drawn from pygame primitives (no image files), every sound is synthesized, and the game is small enough to read in one sitting (about 2,700 lines in src/games/clockwork-keep/src/clockwork_keep/). It is also one of the engine's reference games: its golden trace and golden replay pin world space, transitions, pausing and replay, so the page below shows both how the game works and which engine features it leans on.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
uv run clockwork-keep                 # start on the Boiler Room (floor 0)
uv run clockwork-keep --floor 2       # start on the Clock Face
uv run clockwork-keep --debug-overlay # F3 toggles the overlay, F4 cycles its panels

The game adds one option of its own (ClockworkKeepScene.args):

Option Values Effect --floor 0, 1, 2 (default 0) The first floor: 0 = Boiler Room, 1 = Gear Works, 2 = Clock Face. Anything else is refused by argparse (choices=range(len(ALL_FLOORS)))

Every engine option applies too. The ones the game reads or depends on:

Option Used for --input-mode {auto,joystick,controller} The gamepad event family its ActionMap binds (engine default auto) --axis-deadzone Passed to its ActionMap (ActionMap.from_engine_options); the game binds no axes, so it changes nothing yet --screen-shake-intensity Passed to the floor's Camera2D (shake_intensity) --rumble-intensity Scales the elevator's rumble (the scene manager's RumbleController) --random-seed Seeds the engine's shake stream, the only randomness in a session (the rattle shake) --record-trace PATH / --replay-trace PATH Record a session / replay it exactly (see Engine features it uses) --target-fps The game sets no TARGET_FPS, so the engine default (60.01) applies

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Every keyboard control binds a physical key position (a scancode), so it is in the same place on every keyboard layout. The names below are the US QWERTY keys at those positions.

Action Keyboard Gamepad Read how move_left / move_right Left / Right arrow D-pad left / right Held, each dt_tick jump Space or Up arrow A On the press, in the event handler run Left Shift X Held: run speed, and a higher jump interact W Y Pressed this frame, at the top of dt_tick (rides the elevator) pause Esc none On the press: switches to the pause screen quit Q none On the press: scene_manager.quit() ends the run

No stick axis is bound (test_joystick_axis_motion_moves_nothing). On the pause screen Space or a gamepad's Start or A (on its release, after a press there) resumes, and Esc or a gamepad's B or Back (on the press) quits; on the game-over and victory screens the same buttons restart and quit. The engine's screens answer both gamepad event layers (controller and joystick). Losing window focus pauses the game too.

docs.title: Scenes and how they switch
docs.text:
Each floor is its own ClockworkKeepScene instance. The engine builds the first one from options alone (floor_index=None, which takes --floor); the elevator builds the next one with the floor, score and lives it carries. Pausing and game over use the engine's built-in PauseScene and GameOverScene. In the diagram, the Clockwork Keep box is the game's own scene; the Engine box holds the engine's built-in scenes it switches to.

flowchart TB

    subgraph GAME_SCENES["Clockwork Keep"]
        direction TB
        first["ClockworkKeepScene(options)<br/>floor = --floor (default 0)"]
        first --> floors
        subgraph floors["one ClockworkKeepScene per floor"]
            direction TB
            floor0["Floor 0: Boiler Room<br/>960 px tall"]
            floor1["Floor 1: Gear Works<br/>1440 px tall"]
            floor2["Floor 2: Clock Face<br/>1920 px tall, no elevator"]
            floor0 -->|"interact on the elevator<br/>ElevatorTransition, 4 s"| floor1
            floor1 -->|"interact on the elevator<br/>ElevatorTransition, 4 s"| floor2
        end
        victory["ClockworkKeepVictoryScene<br/>a GameOverScene titled VICTORY!"]
    end
    subgraph ENGINE_SCENES["Engine"]
        direction TB
        pause["PauseScene<br/>frozen screenshot of the floor"]
        gameOver["GameOverScene<br/>final score, high scores"]
    end
    floors -->|"Esc, or window focus lost<br/>next_scene = PauseScene"| pause
    pause -->|"Space, Start or A released, or focus<br/>regained after 0.5 s"| floors
    floors -->|"last life lost<br/>FadeTransition, 1 s"| gameOver
    floors -->|"on the Clock Face's top platform<br/>FadeTransition, 1 s"| victory
    gameOver -->|"Space, Start or A released: a new<br/>ClockworkKeepScene(options)"| first
    victory -->|"Space, Start or A released: a new<br/>ClockworkKeepScene(options)"| first
    floors -->|"Q"| quitRun(["run ends"])
    pause -->|"Esc, B or Back"| quitRun
    gameOver -->|"Esc, B or Back"| quitRun
    victory -->|"Esc, B or Back"| quitRun
Switch Code How Next floor _check_elevator → _go_to_next_floor transition_to(next_scene, ElevatorTransition(...)); the engine starts the transition after the frame is presented Pause on_key_down_event (pause), on_window_focus_lost_event self.next_scene = PauseScene(options=...); focus loss after game over does not pause Resume PauseScene.resume() Switches back to the paused floor, which keeps all its state Game over _player_die on the last life transition_to(GameOverScene(final_score=..., high_scores=...), FadeTransition(duration=1.0)) Victory _win, when the Tinker stands on victory_platform (the Clock Face's highest platform) Saves the high score, then transition_to(ClockworkKeepVictoryScene(final_score=..., high_scores=...), FadeTransition(duration=1.0)): the engine's GameOverScene with its title replaced by VICTORY! Restart GameOverScene.resume() (also the victory screen's) type(previous_scene)(options=...): a fresh first floor (the --floor one), score 0, 3 lives Quit scene_manager.quit() Posts QUIT; the run ends after teardown (BUGS.md #202)

The floor never sets next_scene = None to quit: the scene manager reads that as "no switch pending", so quit goes through scene_manager.quit().

docs.title: replay_arguments: rebuilding a floor
docs.text:
replay_arguments() returns the constructor arguments the floor was built with, besides options:

{'floor_index': self.floor_index,
 'player_score': self.starting_player_score,
 'player_lives': self.starting_player_lives}

The engine's default is {}, which rebuilds a scene from options alone. That works for the first floor but not for the others: a floor the elevator built would be rebuilt as the --floor floor with score 0 and 3 lives. A scene start (src/glitchygames/scene_start.py) keeps these arguments, and rebuild_scene(start=..., scene_class=..., options=...) passes them back to the constructor, so a playback scope (a demo, an instant replay) that starts on floor 2 rebuilds floor 2 with the score and lives it began with. The values are the ones the floor began with (starting_player_score, starting_player_lives), not the current ones: cogs collected and lives lost on the floor are what the playback replays, so they must not be in the starting state (test_floor_replay_arguments_rebuild_the_floor). They are plain ints, so they round-trip through JSON exactly, as scene starts require.

docs.title: Its package
docs.text:
Clockwork Keep is a package of its own beside the engine, src/games/clockwork-keep/ (distribution clockwork-keep, import package clockwork_keep). How such a package is laid out, installed, tested and built, and how a game is moved into one, is in Games as Their Own Packages.

Its recordings name it games.clockwork_keep.game:ClockworkKeepScene, its golden replay is src/games/clockwork-keep/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz, its golden trace stays with the engine's trace tests (tests/world/golden/clockwork_keep.jsonl.gz), and its browser bundle ships clockwork_keep.zip.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
Clockwork Keep's own code is the scene, five sprite classes and the floor data, all in src/games/clockwork-keep/src/clockwork_keep/. The rest comes from the engine: Scene and the built-in PauseScene and GameOverScene (glitchygames.scenes), Sprite (glitchygames.sprites) and PhysicsBody (glitchygames.physics). In the diagram, the Engine box is what every game gets; the Clockwork Keep box is what this game adds. Solid arrows are inheritance, pointing at the base class; dotted arrows are how the game uses an engine class; plain arrows are what a game class holds. The scene owns everything on a floor. The five sprite classes all declare COORDINATE_SPACE = CoordinateSpace.WORLD, and the scene keeps each kind in a list of its own (platform_sprites, ...) besides all_sprites.

classDiagram
    direction TB
    namespace Engine {
        class Scene {
            camera, collisions, tweens
            replay_arguments()
        }
        class PauseScene {
            the frozen floor, dimmed
            SPACE or Start/A resumes it, ESC or B/Back quits
        }
        class GameOverScene {
            score and high scores
            SPACE or Start/A restarts, ESC or B/Back quits
        }
        class Sprite
        class PhysicsBody {
            GravityBehavior
            AccelerationBehavior
            BoundsConstraint
        }
    }
    namespace ClockworkKeep {
        class ClockworkKeepScene {
            MAX_FRAME_SECONDS = 0.05
            floor_index, floor_data
            floor_elapsed_time
            platform_sprites, elevator_sprites
            moving_gear_sprites, collectible_sprites
            actions: ActionMap
            sounds: SoundBank
            camera: Camera2D
            saves: SaveManager
            victory_platform
            dt_tick(dt)
            render(screen)
        }
        class ClockworkKeepVictoryScene {
            the GameOverScene layout
            titled VICTORY!
        }
        class Tinker {
            lives, score, floor
            state#95;machine: AnimationStateMachine
            dt_tick(dt)
            update()
        }
        class Platform
        class Elevator
        class MovingGear {
            moved_x, moved_y
            dt_tick(dt)
        }
        class CogCollectible {
            points
            dt_tick(dt)
        }
        class FloorData {
            <<dataclass>>
            platforms, elevators
            collectibles, moving_gears
        }
    }

    Scene <|-- PauseScene
    Scene <|-- GameOverScene
    Scene <|-- ClockworkKeepScene
    GameOverScene <|-- ClockworkKeepVictoryScene
    Sprite <|-- Tinker
    Sprite <|-- Platform
    Sprite <|-- Elevator
    Sprite <|-- MovingGear
    Sprite <|-- CogCollectible
    PauseScene <.. ClockworkKeepScene : next_scene on Esc or focus lost
    GameOverScene <.. ClockworkKeepScene : after the last life
    ClockworkKeepVictoryScene <.. ClockworkKeepScene : on the top platform
    PhysicsBody <.. Tinker : physics
    ClockworkKeepScene --> FloorData : builds its sprites from
    ClockworkKeepScene --> Tinker : player

Tinker's world_x, world_y, velocity_x, velocity_y, on_ground and facing_right are properties that delegate to its PhysicsBody, so the scene and the engine read the body through the sprite. The debug overlay's physics panel finds the body as sprite.physics.

docs.title: Floors
docs.text:
A floor is a FloorData (levels.py): one screen wide (800 px), several screens tall, with walls 100 px wide on each side, leaving a 600 px playfield (x 100 to 700). World coordinates start at the floor's top-left; y grows downward, so climbing means a falling world_y. The Tinker spawns at x 400, 60 px above the floor's bottom.

Floor Height Platforms Cogs (bronze / silver / gold) Points Way up 0 Boiler Room 960 (2 screens) 14 4 / 1 / 1 190 Elevator at the top 1 Gear Works 1440 (3 screens) 19 5 / 3 / 1 300 Elevator at the top 2 Clock Face 1920 (4 screens) 21 5 / 7 / 2 600 The moving gear, then the victory platform

Cogs are worth 10 (bronze), 50 (silver) and 100 (gold) points. There are no enemies.

Victory. The Clock Face (the last floor) has no elevator; its highest platform is the floor's victory_platform (_find_victory_platform; None on the floors below). When ground collision stands the Tinker on it (supporting_platform), dt_tick calls _win() after the cog pickups (so the victory cog above it counts): the floor stops, the camera stops following, the victory chime plays, the high score is saved and the floor fades to ClockworkKeepVictoryScene, the engine's GameOverScene (final score and high scores, Space or a gamepad's Start or A restarts, Esc or B or Back quits) with a gold VICTORY! title.

The floor builds its sprites in __init__, in this order: the parallax background, platforms, elevators, moving gears, cogs, then the player. Sprites of one layer draw in the order they are added, so the order is part of the picture. Each class sets _layer before Sprite.__init__ (LAYER_TERRAIN 4, LAYER_COLLECTIBLES 5, LAYER_PLAYER 7, the background LAYER_FAR_BACKGROUND 0) for the LayeredDirty group.

docs.title: World-space sprites
docs.text:
Every gameplay sprite (Tinker, Platform, Elevator, MovingGear, CogCollectible) declares COORDINATE_SPACE = CoordinateSpace.WORLD and keeps float world_x / world_y. The game never writes their rect: each frame the engine sets it from the camera, culls sprites more than 32 px off screen, and marks moved sprites dirty. The game reads positions from world_x / world_y and from collision rects, never from rect (except rect.width, which does not move). A cog bobs by moving its world_y, not by shifting pixels in its image.

The HUD is not a sprite: render() draws the score (top left), lives (top right) and floor name (top centre) straight onto the screen after the sprites, with a 1 px shadow. Its font is loaded in setup(), so a floor rendered before setup draws no HUD.

docs.title: Camera
docs.text:
Setting Value Effect camera.follow(target=player, axes=FollowAxes.BOTH) in setup() The engine aims the camera at the Tinker every frame set_bounds(min_x=0, max_x=0, ...) in __init__ No horizontal scroll: the tower is one screen wide set_bounds(min_y=0, max_y=height - 480) in __init__ The camera stops at the floor's top and bottom lead_y=200 (CAMERA_LEAD_Y) in __init__ The camera's top edge sits 200 px above the Tinker's top: a little less view above it than below it on the 480 px screen camera.follow(target=None) at game over The floor stands still during the fade

The game never calls camera.update() and has no camera loop (test_scene_has_no_camera_loop). setup() does not snap_to the player, so on a fresh start the camera eases down from the floor's top to the spawn; a floor arriving by elevator is snapped to its target by the transition's arrival capture.

docs.title: The parallax background and the animated clock
docs.text:
Each floor has one parallax layer (camera.add_background_layer, scroll_factor=PARALLAX_FAR = 0.1): the tower walls with brick and windows, plus the floor's machinery (the Boiler Room's furnace glow and pipes, the Gear Works' gears and chain). The engine calls a layer's draw function again only when its offset changes, so these draw functions depend only on the camera position they are given.

The Clock Face's layer is different: a working clock whose hands show CLOCK_START_SECONDS (11:58, two minutes to midnight) plus floor_elapsed_time, the floor's game time. Its picture changes while the camera stands still, so that layer is added with animated=True and redraws every frame (test_only_the_clock_background_is_animated, test_clock_hands_move_on_a_still_camera). The scene passes a bound method (_draw_timed_clock_background) that reads floor_elapsed_time. floor_elapsed_time adds the capped dt in dt_tick, so it stops while paused and after game over.

docs.title: Platforms, elevators, moving gear and cogs
docs.text:
Sprite Image Behaviour Platform 12 px tall metal bar in the floor's theme colours, drawn once One-way support: the Tinker jumps up through it and lands on top of it Elevator 60 x 8 px car with caution stripes and an up arrow Supports like a platform; interact while standing on it rides to the next floor MovingGear size x size/4 bar with teeth along its top, dirty = 2 Moves on centre + range * sin(timer * speed) each dt_tick and records moved_x / moved_y CogCollectible 16 px cog, redrawn each tick with spinning teeth Bobs 3 px; picked up when its collision rect overlaps the Tinker's

The Clock Face's one moving gear (MovingGearData: 64 px wide, ±150 px horizontally, speed 1.2, a 5.2 s round trip) is the only way up its final approach: the centre step is 180 px below the last step, beyond a running jump's ~140 px, so the climber hops onto the gear (90 px up), rides it right, and hops off at the end of its sweep, where it pauses. test_the_route_is_within_a_walking_jump and test_climbing_the_final_approach_on_the_gear pin the route.

docs.title: The player: movement, physics and collision
Physics
docs.text:
Tinker builds a PhysicsBody with:

Piece Values GravityBehavior 1200 px/s², terminal fall speed 800 px/s AccelerationBehavior 1600 px/s² toward the target speed, 1200 px/s² to slow down BoundsConstraint The side walls, refitted to the hitbox every tick Speeds Walk 160 px/s, run 280 px/s Jumps -480 px/s (~96 px high), running -580 px/s (~140 px high)

move_left / move_right / stop_horizontal only set the acceleration behaviour's target velocity; the body accelerates toward it. jump() sets velocity_y only when on_ground, so an airborne Tinker never jumps again.

An AnimationStateMachine picks the pose from the body's animation context: idle, running (abs(velocity_x) > 0.1), jumping (velocity_y < -10) and falling (velocity_y > 50 and not on the ground).

docs.title: The pose rule and hitboxes
docs.text:
The Tinker's hitbox is its image's visible pixels (the engine's default: transparent pixels trimmed, measured on every query). The figure's transparent margin moves with its pose and facing, so the pose must be drawn before anything collides with it. Tinker.dt_tick does, in order:

  1. Fit the wall bounds to the current hitbox, then physics.tick(dt).
  2. Evaluate the state machine.
  3. Draw the pose (_draw_pose: clear the image, draw_tinker(...)).
  4. Refit the wall bounds to the new hitbox and apply them again, so turning toward a wall never puts the hitbox inside it (BUGS.md #64, TestPoseBeforeCollision).

Tinker.update(), which runs in the render phase, only applies the respawn fade (image.set_alpha). Drawing the pose there would make the floor's ground and cog checks use the previous frame's pose.

All support and pickups use collision rects (get_sprite_collision_rect) and collision_rect_offset, not the drawn image: the feet are the hitbox's bottom, and only a hitbox pixel over a platform supports (TestPlatformSupportUsesHitbox, TestHitboxLooseEnds). The scene registers two collision layers, player and cogs; cog pickup is collisions.check_overlap('player', 'cogs', ...), and the debug overlay's hitbox panel draws the same layers.

docs.title: Ground collision
docs.text:
_resolve_ground_collision clears on_ground, then stands the Tinker on the support it finds, falling or at rest (velocity_y >= 0), whose top its feet reached this tick and its hitbox overlapping it horizontally. The fall is swept (_feet_reach_surface): the feet must end the tick at or below the support's top, and have started it (before this tick's movement; a gear's ride is not part of the fall) no more than GROUND_SNAP_TOLERANCE (20 px) below it. So a long tick at the 800 px/s terminal speed, which moves the feet up to 40 px at the 50 ms cap, still lands on the platform it crossed instead of passing through it:

  1. Platforms (their world_y is their top).
  2. Elevators (checked after the platforms, so an elevator standing on its shelf platform wins).
  3. Only if neither held it: moving gears, by the gear's collision rect top (_land_on_moving_gear), which also sets riding_gear.

A gear carries its rider in _ride_moving_gear, which runs after every sprite's dt_tick (the gear has moved) and before ground collision: the rider moves by the gear's moved_x / moved_y, so the collision that follows finds it on the gear again. A jump clears on_ground, so a player leaving the gear is not carried.

docs.title: MAX_FRAME_SECONDS
docs.text: ClockworkKeepScene.MAX_FRAME_SECONDS = 0.05: after a hitch (Cmd-Tab, a slow frame) the engine hands dt_tick and the camera aim at most 50 ms, so the game advances as at 20 FPS at worst instead of jumping. The cap alone does not keep a fast fall out of a platform (40 px in a 50 ms tick); the swept ground check does. The scene manager's own dt (pacing, FPS statistics, shake) stays the raw frame time, and recordings keep the raw dt.

docs.title: One frame
docs.text:
The engine runs the frame; the floor's code runs in two places: dt_tick (logic, physics, collision) and the render phase (update(), then render()). The Engine box is the engine's frame loop; the Clockwork Keep box is the game's scene and sprites.

sequenceDiagram
    box rgb(232,238,255) Engine
        participant SM as SceneManager
        participant GE as GameEngine
    end
    box rgb(255,243,224) Clockwork Keep
        participant CKS as ClockworkKeepScene
        participant T as Tinker and the other sprites
    end

    SM->>SM: camera.begin_frame()
    SM->>CKS: dt_tick(min(dt, 0.05))
    CKS->>T: sprite.dt_tick(dt) for all_sprites
    Note over CKS: elevator check, movement input,<br/>gear ride, ground, pit, cogs
    SM->>GE: process events
    GE->>CKS: on_key_down_event / on_joy_button_down_event ...
    Note over CKS: ActionMap.handle_event(event)<br/>jump right away, pause, quit
    SM->>SM: supervisor slot, then shake and rumble
    SM->>SM: aim the camera at the player
    SM->>SM: position world sprites from the camera, cull
    SM->>CKS: update() (Scene: sprite.update(), the Tinker's fade)
    SM->>CKS: render(screen): fill, draw sprites, HUD
    SM->>SM: present, then start a pending transition or switch
    SM->>SM: finish frame (pace, measure dt)

Input crosses the frame boundary in two ways. A jump happens in the event handler (_try_jump), so its velocity moves the Tinker in the next dt_tick. Interact is read at the top of the next dt_tick with actions.just_pressed('interact'), which is why _check_elevator runs before _process_movement_input calls actions.begin_frame() (which clears the frame's presses).

Everything in it is the game's code (the Clockwork Keep box) except its first step, super().dt_tick(dt), which runs the engine's Scene.dt_tick (the Engine box).

flowchart TB
    tick(["ClockworkKeepScene.dt_tick(dt)"])
    subgraph GAME_TICK["Clockwork Keep"]
        direction TB
        over{"game_over_triggered?"}
        done(["return: the floor stands still"])
        elapsed["floor_elapsed_time += dt"]
        elevator["_check_elevator<br/>interact just pressed, standing on an elevator?"]
        movement["_process_movement_input<br/>actions.begin_frame(), held move and run"]
        sprites["sprite.dt_tick(dt) for every sprite<br/>Tinker: physics, state, pose, walls<br/>gear moves, cogs bob"]
        ride["_ride_moving_gear<br/>carry the rider by moved_x, moved_y"]
        ground["_resolve_ground_collision<br/>platforms, elevators, then gears"]
        land["_play_land_on_touchdown<br/>'land' on the frame the feet touch"]
        pit{"world_y below the floor<br/>by more than 100 px?"}
        die["_player_die"]
        cogs["_check_collectibles"]
    end
    subgraph ENGINE_TICK["Engine"]
        direction TB
        base["Scene.dt_tick: dt, tweens<br/>(the respawn fade runs here)"]
    end
    tick -->|"first: super().dt_tick(dt)"| base
    base -->|"returns"| over
    over -->|yes| done
    over -->|no| elapsed
    elapsed --> elevator
    elevator --> movement
    movement --> sprites
    sprites --> ride
    ride --> ground
    ground --> land
    land --> pit
    pit -->|yes| die
    pit -->|no| cogs
    die --> cogs

_play_land_on_touchdown compares this frame's on_ground with the last frame's. The first result only initializes it, so the arriving floor's off-screen tick during the elevator ride plays nothing, and respawning resets it (test_first_tick_never_plays_land, test_respawn_does_not_play_land).

docs.title: Riding the elevator
docs.text:
The ride itself is the engine's (ElevatorTransition, Engine box); the floors and their callbacks are the game's (Clockwork Keep box).

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Player
    box rgb(255,243,224) Clockwork Keep
        participant New as Floor N+1
        participant Old as Floor N (ClockworkKeepScene)
    end
    box rgb(232,238,255) Engine
        participant SM as SceneManager
        participant ET as ElevatorTransition
    end

    P->>Old: W / Y (interact)
    Old->>Old: _check_elevator (next dt_tick):<br/>on an elevator, not the last floor
    Old->>New: ClockworkKeepScene(floor_index=N+1,<br/>player_score, player_lives, options)
    Old->>ET: ElevatorTransition(duration=4.0,<br/>easing='ease_in_sine', player_surface=...)
    Old->>SM: create_voice(owner=transition), motor.start()
    Old->>SM: transition_to(New, ET)<br/>with a cue at progress 1.0
    loop every frame of the ride
        ET->>Old: on_update: _update_elevator_motor(transition)
        Old->>SM: rumble.set_sustained(low, high)<br/>scaled by car speed
        Note over Old: motor pitch 45 to 110 Hz, volume 0.15 to 0.6
    end
    ET->>Old: cue 1.0: _elevator_arrived()
    Old->>SM: motor.stop_now(), rumble.clear_sustained()
    Old->>SM: play 'elevator_clank',<br/>SCREEN shakes: bounce + rattle
    SM->>New: the ride ends, Floor N+1 is active

The ride is src/glitchygames/transitions/elevator.py: a tall composite of the old floor, a shaft and the new floor scrolls up while the car and the Tinker (a copy of its image) stay pinned at the screen's centre. ease_in_sine arrives at full speed, so the stop reads as a slam. The car's speed is the easing's slope (transition.eased_velocity_at(progress)), divided by its peak (sampled over 101 points when the ride starts), so motor pitch, motor volume and rumble all follow the car.

The callbacks run after the old floor's cleanup(), so they touch only SceneManager services: the live voice, the rumble and SCREEN shakes (a WORLD shake would need the old floor's sprites). A ride with no free live voice, or without audio, rides silently but still rumbles (test_ride_without_free_voice_still_rumbles). _update_elevator_motor ignores the completing frame (progress 1.0): the arrival cue runs first and clears the rumble, and updating again would restart it.

Input pressed during the ride is not delivered to the new floor: a jump pressed and released mid-ride does not jump on arrival (tests/world/test_transition_input.py).

docs.title: Death, respawn and game over
docs.text:
The game decides a death and what follows (Clockwork Keep box); the fade and the game-over screen are the engine's (Engine box).

flowchart TB
    subgraph GAME_DEATH["Clockwork Keep"]
        direction TB
        fall["world_y more than 100 px<br/>below the floor's bottom"] --> lose["lives -= 1"]
        lose --> left{"lives left?"}
        left -->|yes| deathSound["play 'death'"]
        deathSound --> fadeOut["_respawn_player: is_respawning,<br/>velocity 0, fade alpha to 0 (0.2 s)"]
        fadeOut --> respawn["at the spawn point, on the ground,<br/>riding no gear, fade in (0.3 s)"]
        left -->|no| over["game_over_triggered = True<br/>camera.follow(target=None)"]
        over --> sounds["play 'game_over'<br/>_save_high_score()"]
        sounds --> clear["screen_shake.clear()"]
        clear --> fade["transition_to(game over,<br/>FadeTransition(duration=1.0))"]
    end
    subgraph ENGINE_DEATH["Engine"]
        direction TB
        deathFadeTransition["FadeTransition<br/>1 s fade"]
        deathGameOver["GameOverScene(final_score, high_scores)<br/>final score, high scores"]
        deathFadeTransition --> deathGameOver
    end
    fade -.->|uses| deathFadeTransition

While is_respawning, movement input is ignored and the pit check is skipped. After game over dt_tick returns early, so dying again changes nothing (test_dying_after_game_over_changes_nothing).

Every floor's ground spans the playfield wall to wall and the walls stop the hitbox, so a fall lands on the ground: the pit check is a safety net, not a hazard the levels use. Since the ground check sweeps the fall, even a slow frame at terminal speed lands on the ground rather than dropping through it.

docs.title: Sound
docs.text:
sounds.py defines seven SoundRecipes (synthesized tones: oscillators, envelopes, filters, tremolo), played through one SoundBank(ALL_RECIPES) per floor. setup() calls sounds.prerender(), so no sound renders mid-frame (the clank would otherwise render on the slam frame).

Sound When jump _try_jump, when the jump happens land The frame the feet touch down cog_pickup A cog is collected death A life is lost and lives remain game_over The last life is lost elevator_clank The elevator arrives (cue at progress 1.0) victory The Clock Face is won (_win): the clock tower's chime, struck bells (each a fundamental, its octave and a 2.76x overtone) climbing C5, E5, G5, then C6 ringing over a deep C3

The elevator's motor is not a recipe but a live voice: a low-passed sawtooth with tremolo, made with scene_manager.live_audio.create_voice(owner=transition) and retuned every frame of the ride (ELEVATOR_MOTOR_* constants). SoundBank.play is a no-op when audio is unavailable.

docs.title: State, score, lives and saves
docs.text:
State Where Lifetime player.score, player.lives Tinker Carried to the next floor through the constructor starting_player_score, starting_player_lives ClockworkKeepScene As the floor began (for replay_arguments) floor_elapsed_time ClockworkKeepScene The floor's capped game time (the clock) game_over_triggered, riding_gear, supporting_platform ClockworkKeepScene Per floor (game_over_triggered is also set by victory) High scores open_saves(app_name='clockwork-keep'), save high_scores On disk, across runs

The game starts with 3 lives (STARTING_LIVES). At game over and at victory _save_high_score appends {'score': ..., 'floor': ...} to the saved scores list, keeps the 10 best (best first) and saves it; GameOverScene shows the list. A missing save loads as an empty list. In a replay the saves are a MemorySaveManager seeded from the recording, so a replayed game over never touches real high scores.

docs.title: Engine features it uses
docs.text:
Feature How Clockwork Keep uses it World space and camera Every gameplay sprite is a WORLD sprite; the engine follows the player and positions everything Parallax layers One layer per floor; the clock layer is animated=True Physics PhysicsBody with gravity, acceleration and a bounds constraint Collision layers player and cogs, with trimmed (visible-pixel) hitboxes ActionMap Scancode bindings for every key, controller buttons for the gamepad Tweens The respawn fade out and in (self.tweens.tween(...)) Transitions ElevatorTransition (with on_update and add_cue), FadeTransition to game over Shake and rumble Two SCREEN shakes on arrival, ELEVATOR_STOP_BOUNCE (BOUNCE, vertical) and ELEVATOR_STOP_RATTLE (NOISE), each with RumbleSettings(scale_with_strength=False); sustained rumble during the ride Sound synthesis Six recipes and one live voice Saves open_saves, SaveManager.load / save Built-in scenes PauseScene and GameOverScene Debug overlay No debug_draw of its own: the hitbox panel shows the player and cogs layers (platforms, unlayered, as full rects), the physics panel the Tinker's body, the camera panel the bounds Random streams The game draws no randomness itself; the NOISE rattle shake draws from the engine's shake stream, which --random-seed fixes Recording and replay --record-trace / --replay-trace work unchanged: the game reads input only through events and its ActionMap, time only from the dt it is given, and saves only through open_saves, so the doors serve all of it Scene starts replay_arguments() lets any floor be rebuilt for a playback scope

The game does not set INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS, ships no bundled demo, and sets no PIXEL_SNAP_MODE (the default, NEAREST_HALF_UP).

docs.title: Golden trace and golden replay
docs.text:
Clockwork Keep has both of the engine's golden checks:

  • Golden trace (tests/world/golden/clockwork_keep.jsonl.gz, checked by tests/world/test_golden_traces.py): a 900-frame scripted run (clockwork_keep_script in scripts/golden_inputs.py, fixed dt 1/60) recorded before the world-space change. It jumps for a cog, walks both ways, is placed on the first elevator at frame 330 (reaching it takes more platforming than the script holds), presses W at frame 350, rides frames 352-592, then walks and pauses (frames 740-790) on Gear Works. Each sprite's rect and visibility must match the baseline frame by frame; six ExpectedDifference entries explain every difference (engine culling, separate snapping of sprite and camera, and the pose fix's 2 px on frame 0 and during the ride).
  • Golden replay (src/games/clockwork-keep/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz, 532 frames): the same script's first 330 frames plus a controls tail (run right with Left Shift, jump with Space, interact away from an elevator, pause and resume with Esc / Space, quit with Q), recorded through the real engine loop by scripts/record_scripted_session.py --game clockwork_keep --frames 330. The replay plugin replays it in a child process (clockwork-keep --replay-trace ... --headless) and fails unless it exits SUCCESS. tests/replay/test_golden_replays.py also checks that the golden replays exercise every control the game binds (ClockworkKeepScene._create_action_map); the gamepad bindings are listed as unexercised, because the dummy driver has no gamepad.

Both harnesses drop the focus-lost event SDL's dummy driver posts at startup, which would otherwise auto-pause the game. Never re-record either baseline to make a change pass.

docs.title: Drawing Fire Architecture
docs.text:
Drawing Fire is a stick-figure battle drawn in pencil on paper, the way a child draws a war, written as one of the engine's example games. Two armies face each other across a hilly field: the Pencil Platoon in pencil yellow on the left and the Graphite Brigade in graphite grey on the right, both straight off a school pencil. The computer plays every soldier. When one army is wiped out the winner is announced on the paper (when both fall at once, nobody wins), and a new battle starts on its own. At any moment one or two local players can join: press START (Enter on the keyboard), choose a side and a soldier, and fight as him. A player whose soldier dies takes over another soldier of his side, and a player who has had enough holds Back (Escape) to leave.

Every new GlitchyGames game proves a new mechanic for the engine. Drawing Fire proves swatches: recolouring a sprite by palette swap, so one soldier sprite wears both armies' liveries (see Swatches).

This page explains how the game is built, for a developer who wants to understand it or write a game like it. Everything here comes from src/games/drawing-fire/src/drawing_fire/, and the module docstrings there are the detailed reference. The design, with the full vision and the MVP's decisions, is plans/2026-10-25-drawing-fire-design.md. What comes after the MVP is entry 54 in plans/future-features.md.

docs.title: The game as it is
docs.text:
These are screenshots of the MVP.

A battle the computer plays by itself. Each army's name, colour chip and soldier count are at the top. The ground is pencilled with hatching under it, and the sandbags are grey-washed bags:

The winner, announced on the paper before the next battle starts:

Joining. While a device has no seat, a sticky note invites it to press START (Enter on the keyboard). A player who presses it gets a card where he chooses a side (Random, Platoon or Brigade), then a soldier:

Choosing a soldier: a pencil ring highlights one of the side's computer soldiers, LEFT and RIGHT move it, and START takes him:

The debug seats view (F3): a tag over every soldier names his driver, and a panel lists each army's drivers and the latest joins, takeovers and leaves. Its last line, held:, names the keys and mouse buttons the game sees held this frame (from current_input()), so a key the browser keeps from the game shows up missing while you hold it:

docs.title: Where it is going: concept art
docs.text: These pictures are concept art from the brainstorm, not the game. They show the full vision: a battlefield wider than the screen, tunnels, planes and air drops, and bigger guns. None of this is in the MVP (see plans/future-features.md, entry 54).

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
uv run drawing-fire                      # the console script (its member's pyproject.toml)
uv run drawing-fire --debug-overlay      # start with the debug seats view (F3 toggles it)
uv run drawing-fire --random-seed 7      # another battlefield and other battles
uv run drawing-fire --record-trace run.jsonl.gz   # record the session
uv run drawing-fire --replay-trace run.jsonl.gz   # watch it again, exactly
uv run python -m scripts.simulate_drawing_fire --seeds 20   # headless battles: lengths and winners
nox -s browser -- drawing-fire           # the browser build

main() (game.py) is GameEngine(game=DrawingFireScene).start(). The scene adds no options of its own; all its options are the engine's. The battlefield fits the window (800x480 by default), and --random-seed decides the terrain, the sandbags and every soldier's choices.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
The keyboard and mouse count as one device, and each game controller as another. Nothing is bound in an ActionMap: players.py reads every control from the frame's polled input (current_input()), the keys by scancode, so a key is its physical position on every layout.

Input Keyboard and mouse Controller Join (a device with no seat) Enter or keypad Enter Start Choose a side, choose a soldier LEFT/RIGHT: A or the left arrow, D or the right arrow; Enter takes D-pad left/right or the left stick; Start takes Move A or the left arrow, D or the right arrow Left stick Aim The mouse: the soldier aims from his chest at the pointer Right stick, at any angle (the aim stays put while the stick rests) Fire Left mouse button (held: he fires whenever his pistol is ready) Right trigger, or the right shoulder button Leave Hold Escape for a second (LEAVE_HOLD_SECONDS, timed by the frames' dt, so at 30 fps too) Hold Back for a second, or unplug the controller Quit the game Q (on its release) Debug seats view F3 (the engine's debug overlay)

W and S do nothing in the MVP (there is no jump or crouch). Escape never quits: the base Scene quits on the release of Q or Escape, and DrawingFireScene.on_key_up_event ignores Escape's release, because Escape is the keyboard's Back. There is no pause. Battles never stop for anyone: players drop into and out of them, and the next one starts on its own.
