docs.title: Mr. Muncher Architecture
docs.text:
Mr. Muncher is a maze chase set in a cinema, written as one of the engine's example games. You are Mr. Muncher, a red-and-white popcorn bucket. You eat the sprockets (small dots drawn like the holes along a film strip) to finish the reel, while four munchers (spiky fuzzballs) hunt you. A snack (a wrapped candy) gives you a sugar rush: for a few seconds the munchers turn dull blue and run away, and you can eat them. Each life is a take, a cleared maze is a CUT!, and the last life ends with THE END.

This page explains how the game is built, for a developer who wants to understand it or write a game like it. Everything here comes from src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/. The module docstrings there are the detailed reference.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
uv run mr-muncher                      # the console script (pyproject.toml [project.scripts])
uv run mr-muncher --debug-overlay      # start with the debug overlay (F3 toggles it, F4 cycles panels)
uv run mr-muncher --record-trace run.jsonl.gz   # record the session
uv run mr-muncher --replay-trace run.jsonl.gz   # watch it again, exactly

main() (game.py) is just GameEngine(game=MrMuncherScene).start(). The scene does not define an args() class method, so the game adds no options of its own (the engine logs Game does not implement arguments at INFO, shown with --log-level info). All its options are the engine's. These are the ones that matter here:

Option Effect on Mr. Muncher --resolution WxH (default 800x480) The maze is scaled to fit (see Layout). At 800x480 the tiles are 20 px and the maze starts at x = 130 --target-fps The scene sets no TARGET_FPS, so the default is 60.01. Movement uses dt, so the frame rate does not change the game's speed --input-mode {auto,joystick,controller} Which gamepad events reach the ActionMap (both families in auto) --axis-deadzone The left stick's deadzone (ActionMap.from_engine_options; default 0.15) --debug-overlay Shows each muncher's target tile (see Debug overlay) --random-seed INT Seeds the frightened munchers' random turns --screen-shake-intensity, --rumble-intensity Scale the shake and rumble when a muncher catches you --live-voice-pool The projector sound needs one free live voice --record-trace, --replay-trace, --headless Recording and replay (see Engine features)

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Every keyboard control is bound by scancode (ActionMap.bind(scancode=...)), so it is tied to a key's physical position and works the same on every keyboard layout.

Input Action Where it is handled Arrow keys, or W A S D Steer. A direction pressed early is remembered and taken at the next junction ActionMap (move_up, move_left, move_down, move_right) Gamepad D-pad buttons Steer ActionMap (CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_*) Gamepad left stick, pushed past 0.5 Steer ActionMap (CONTROLLER_AXIS_LEFTX/LEFTY, STICK_THRESHOLD) Joystick hat (a pad whose D-pad is a hat) Steer, in the direction pushed on_joy_hat_motion_event (no ActionMap) ESC, P, or gamepad Start Pause (not after the game is over) ActionMap (pause) Window loses focus Pause on_window_focus_lost_event Q Quit (on the press) ActionMap (quit), then scene_manager.quit() On the pause screen: SPACE or gamepad Start or A / ESC or gamepad B or Back / Q Resume (on release, after a press there) / quit (on the press) / quit (on release) The engine's PauseScene (both gamepad event layers) On the game-over screen: SPACE (release), gamepad A or Start / ESC or gamepad B or Back New game / quit MrMuncherGameOverScene and GameOverScene

Note that ESC pauses the game, but ESC on the pause screen quits. The pause and game-over screens are engine scenes and check key codes (event.key), not scancodes.

docs.title: Its package
docs.text:
Mr. Muncher is a package of its own beside the engine, src/games/mr-muncher/ (distribution mr-muncher, import package mr_muncher), the first game moved out of the engine. How such a package is laid out, installed, tested and built, and how a game is moved into one, is in Games as Their Own Packages.

Its recordings name it games.mr_muncher.game:MrMuncherScene, its golden replay is src/games/mr-muncher/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz, and its browser bundle ships mr_muncher.zip.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: File What it holds src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/__init__.py Re-exports main (the mr-muncher console script's entry point) src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/maze.py MAZE_LAYOUT (the maze as text), tile characters, Direction, DIRECTION_PREFERENCE, Maze (a frozen pydantic model: tile questions, wrapping, distances) src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/levels.py LevelSettings and settings_for_level (the difficulty ramp), the scatter/chase schedule helpers, the frightened flash src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/actors.py MazeGeometry (tiles to pixels), MazeActor (tile-to-tile movement), Player, Muncher, MuncherProfile, Personality, MuncherState, ChaseSituation, chase_target src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/game.py MrMuncherScene (one reel: phases, scoring, input, saves, sound, drawing), Phase, GameProgress, MrMuncherGameOverScene, main src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/drawing.py Every picture, drawn with pygame primitives and cached with functools.cache: maze, bucket, munchers, eyes, sprockets, snacks, bonus reel, film-strip panels src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/scenery.py The sprites that never move (Sprocket, Picture, SidePanel) and the text helpers (bundled_font, fitted_font, render_text) src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/sounds.py The sound effects and jingles as synth SoundRecipes src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/autopilot.py Autopilot, a bot that plays the game. The golden replay's script and the tests use it src/games/mr-muncher/tests/test_mr_muncher.py The scene: game flow, scoring, input, saves, screens, whole games src/games/mr-muncher/tests/test_mr_muncher_maze_and_actors.py The parts: maze, levels, actors, pictures, scenery, sounds, autopilot src/games/mr-muncher/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz The golden replay (2,072 frames) scripts/golden_inputs.py mr_muncher_script and MuncherSteering (the autopilot pressing arrow keys) scripts/record_scripted_session.py, scripts/golden_inputs.py The command that records the fixture (on the engine's scripted-session recorder, src/glitchygames/replay/tools/scripted_sessions.py); mr_muncher_controls (the golden replay's controls tail)

docs.title: Scenes and how they switch
docs.text:
A game is a chain of scenes. Each reel is a new MrMuncherScene, built from a GameProgress (a frozen pydantic model holding the reel number, score, lives left and whether the extra life has been given). The scene keeps the progress it started with as starting_progress.

In the diagram, the Engine box holds the engine's built-in PauseScene; the Mr. Muncher box holds the game's own scenes (MrMuncherGameOverScene extends the engine's GameOverScene, see Scene classes).

stateDiagram-v2
    direction TB
    [*] --> Reel : GameEngine(game=MrMuncherScene)
    state "Mr. Muncher" as MrMuncherScenes {
        Reel : MrMuncherScene (reel n)
        NextReel : MrMuncherScene (reel n + 1)<br/>same score and lives
        GameOver : MrMuncherGameOverScene<br/>(extends the engine's GameOverScene)
        NewGame : MrMuncherScene (reel 1)
    }
    state "Engine" as EngineScenes {
        Pause : PauseScene
    }
    Reel --> Pause : ESC, P, Start or focus lost<br/>next_scene = PauseScene
    Pause --> Reel : SPACE, Start or A released<br/>(setup() runs again)
    Reel --> NextReel : CUT! then flash<br/>next_scene = new scene
    NextReel --> Reel : the same flow
    Reel --> GameOver : THE END shown for 2.5 s<br/>transition_to(..., FadeTransition(1 s))
    GameOver --> NewGame : SPACE released, or A or Start<br/>switch_to_scene
    Reel --> [*] : Q (scene_manager.quit())
    Pause --> [*] : ESC, B, Back or Q
    GameOver --> [*] : ESC, B or Back
Next reel _go_to_next_level sets next_scene to a new MrMuncherScene with GameProgress(level + 1, score, lives, extra_life_awarded). It does this only once (it checks that next_scene is still None). Game over _show_game_over_screen fades (1 s FadeTransition) to MrMuncherGameOverScene. This screen shows the engine's GAME OVER layout (score and high score table) plus a headline, either NEW HIGH SCORE! Reel N or You reached reel N. resume() always starts a new game with switch_to_scene(MrMuncherScene(...)), because the previous scene depends on how the screen was reached. Pause The engine's PauseScene shows a frozen screenshot of the game. When play resumes, the scene's setup() runs again. That is why setup() shows the ready message only while the phase is still READY.

docs.title: Scene classes
docs.text:
Mr. Muncher's scenes are two classes in src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/game.py: MrMuncherScene and MrMuncherGameOverScene. Scene and the built-in PauseScene and GameOverScene come from the engine (glitchygames.scenes). In the diagram, the Engine box is what every game gets; the Mr. Muncher box is what this game adds. Solid arrows are inheritance, pointing at the base class; dotted arrows are how the game uses an engine class.

classDiagram
    direction TB
    namespace Engine {
        class Scene {
            next_scene
            transition_to(scene, transition)
            replay_arguments()
        }
        class PauseScene {
            the frozen game, dimmed
            SPACE or Start/A resumes it, ESC, B/Back or Q quits
        }
        class GameOverScene {
            score and high scores
            final_score, high_scores
        }
    }
    namespace MrMuncher {
        class MrMuncherScene {
            NAME = 'Mr. Muncher'
            VERSION = '2.0'
            MAX_FRAME_SECONDS = 0.05
            starting_progress : GameProgress
            phase : Phase
            actions : ActionMap
            saves : SaveManager
            dt_tick(dt)
            render(screen)
        }
        class MrMuncherGameOverScene {
            level_reached : int
            setup()
            replay_arguments()
            resume()
        }
    }

    Scene <|-- PauseScene
    Scene <|-- GameOverScene
    Scene <|-- MrMuncherScene
    GameOverScene <|-- MrMuncherGameOverScene

    PauseScene <.. MrMuncherScene : _pause sets next_scene = PauseScene
    MrMuncherScene ..> MrMuncherGameOverScene : transition_to after THE END
    MrMuncherGameOverScene ..> MrMuncherScene : resume starts a new game

Unlike PaddleSlap, MrMuncherScene names PauseScene itself: _pause sets next_scene = PauseScene(options=self.options), except once the game is over.

docs.title: Phases inside a reel
docs.text:
Inside one scene, Phase decides what each frame does. _run_phase runs the current phase; each waiting phase moves on once phase_seconds (game time since the phase began) is up. Because the phase clocks run on game time, a paused game also pauses its countdowns.

stateDiagram-v2
    direction TB
    [*] --> READY
    READY : READY<br/>3, 2, 1 (new game, 3.6 s)<br/>or TAKE n / REEL n (2.0 s)<br/>ACTION! for the last 0.8 s
    PLAYING : PLAYING
    MUNCHER_EATEN : MUNCHER_EATEN<br/>points shown, all still (0.75 s)
    DYING : DYING<br/>freeze 0.8 s, shrivel 1.5 s, empty 0.7 s
    LEVEL_CLEAR : LEVEL_CLEAR<br/>CUT!, hold 1 s, flash 2 s
    GAME_OVER : GAME_OVER<br/>THE END (2.5 s)
    READY --> PLAYING : time up (_start_playing)
    PLAYING --> MUNCHER_EATEN : touched a frightened muncher
    MUNCHER_EATEN --> PLAYING : time up (_resume_after_eating)
    PLAYING --> DYING : touched by a dangerous muncher
    DYING --> READY : lives left (take + 1)
    DYING --> GAME_OVER : last life (high score saved)
    PLAYING --> LEVEL_CLEAR : last sprocket eaten
    LEVEL_CLEAR --> [*] : next reel (next_scene)
    GAME_OVER --> [*] : fade to game-over screen

The ready message (_ready_message_text) depends on the moment:

Situation ready_seconds Message Cue sound New game (reel 1, score 0) 3.6 (INTRO_READY_SECONDS) 3, 2, 1 (2.8 s split three ways), then ACTION! countdown_beep for each number, then action A later life 2.0 (READY_SECONDS) TAKE n, then ACTION! action A later reel 2.0 REEL n, then ACTION! action

The message is drawn again only when its text or colour changes (message_shown), and each cue plays once, when its text first appears.

docs.title: Layout as text
docs.text:
MAZE_LAYOUT is a tuple of strings, one per row of tiles: 27 columns by 24 rows. It is symmetric from left to right, every corridor is one tile wide, there are no dead ends, and every open tile can be reached from every other. The tests check all four properties.

###########################
#o...........#...........o#
#.####.#####.#.#####.####.#
#.####.#####.#.#####.####.#
T.........................T
#.####.##.#######.##.####.#
#......##....#....##......#
#.####.#####.#.#####.####.#
#.#....##         ##....#.#
#.#.##.## ###-### ##.##.#.#
#...##.   #HHHHH#   .##...#
###.##.## #HHHHH# ##.##.###
#......## #HHHHH# ##......#
#.####.## ####### ##.####.#
#.#....##         ##....#.#
#.#.##.#####.#.#####.##.#.#
#...##.......#.......##...#
#.####.#####.#.#####.####.#
#o..##.......P.......##..o#
###.##.##.#######.##.##.###
#......##....#....##......#
#.##########.#.##########.#
T.........................T
###########################
Character Meaning Player may stand on it # Wall No . Sprocket (252 of them) Yes o Snack (4 of them) Yes space Empty corridor Yes T Tunnel mouth: munchers slow down here Yes H Inside the munchers' house No - The house door: munchers pass through it, the player never does No P Player start (an empty corridor tile) Yes

Maze is a frozen pydantic model. Its validator rejects a layout that is not a rectangle or that does not have exactly one P. It knows nothing about pixels. Positions are in tile units: the centre of the tile in column c, row r is (c, r), so an actor standing on a tile centre has whole-number coordinates.

Tunnels Maze.tile wraps columns, and treats rows outside the maze as wall. Only rows 4 and 22 are open at both edges, so they are the two wrapping tunnels. wrap_x moves an x that has gone more than half a tile past an edge to the other side. tile_distance measures the short way round, so two positions at opposite ends of a tunnel count as close. The house The door is at (13, 9). house_entrance is the corridor tile above it (13, 8), where munchers leave and come back. house_centre is two tiles below the door (13, 11). Geometry MazeGeometry (actors.py) holds tile_size, left and top, and converts a position in tiles to pixels (pixel_centre). maze_geometry (game.py) chooses the tile size.

docs.title: Grid movement and turn buffering
docs.text:
Both the player and the munchers are MazeActors. They move only along corridors, and they choose a direction only when they stand exactly on a tile centre (is_at_tile_centre: both coordinates are whole numbers).

MazeActor.advance(distance=..., choose_direction=...) walks a distance from one tile centre to the next. Each time it reaches a centre, or starts on one, it calls choose_direction to decide the way on (None means stop). When a step reaches a centre, the coordinate is rounded so it lands exactly on it. Because the walk goes centre to centre, a long frame cannot skip past a turn.

The player's turn buffering (Player.travel and _choose_direction):

  1. wanted_direction is the way the player last asked for.
  2. Reversing happens at once, even between centres. If the wanted direction is the opposite of the current one, the player turns round on the spot.
  3. On each tile centre the player takes the wanted direction if it is open. Otherwise it goes straight on if it can, and stops against a wall if it cannot. The wanted direction stays remembered until a junction opens that way.
  4. A new life starts heading left with left wanted, as in the arcade game.

How input sets wanted_direction (_read_direction_input, at the start of each dt_tick): a direction just pressed wins (if two are pressed in one frame, the first of up, left, down, right wins). If no direction was just pressed and the wanted direction's key was just released while another direction is still held, the held one becomes wanted, as with a held joystick. Releasing the last key keeps the wanted direction. Then actions.begin_frame() clears the frame's presses and releases.

docs.title: The munchers
docs.text:
There are four munchers (muncher_profiles). The chaser comes first in the list, because the flanker aims relative to it.

Name Colour Personality Chase target Scatter corner Starts Chomper purple CHASER The player's tile (24, -3), top right Outside, above the door, roaming left Snapper green AMBUSHER 4 tiles ahead of where the player faces (2, -3), top left House centre Gnasher orange FLANKER The pivot 2 tiles ahead of the player, mirrored away from Chomper: 2 * pivot - chaser (26, 24), bottom right House, left seat Nibbles magenta SHY The player's tile while farther than 8 tiles from it, else its own corner (0, 24), bottom left House, right seat

The scatter corners lie outside the maze, so a scattering muncher circles the block of walls nearest its corner.

docs.title: Choosing a turn
docs.text:
At each tile centre, a roaming muncher (Muncher._choose_direction):

  1. Never turns back by itself. The way it came is removed from the options; it is used only at a dead end, and this maze has none.
  2. Considers only open corridor tiles (the same test as the player's, so roaming munchers never walk back into the house).
  3. If frightened, picks one of the options at random from the seeded stream random_stream('mr_muncher.munchers'), so a replay makes the same choices.
  4. Otherwise it takes the option whose next tile is closest in a straight line (tile_distance, tunnel-aware) to its target. On a tie the order is up, left, down, right (DIRECTION_PREFERENCE, the arcade game's order).

The target (_target): the house entrance for eyes, the scatter corner while scattering, chase_target(...) while chasing. The target is stored on muncher.target for the debug overlay. The munchers learn about the game through a ChaseSituation that the scene builds for each step: the player's tile and facing, Chomper's tile, and whether the munchers are chasing.

docs.title: Muncher state machine
docs.text:
MuncherState is where a muncher is in its life. Being frightened is a separate flag (frightened), because a muncher waiting in the house or walking out can be frightened too.

stateDiagram-v2
    direction TB
    [*] --> WAITING : reset() (house seat)
    [*] --> ROAMING : reset() (Chomper starts outside)
    WAITING : WAITING<br/>bobs on its seat
    LEAVING : LEAVING<br/>across, then up through the door
    EATEN : EATEN<br/>only eyes, through the corridors to the entrance
    ENTERING : ENTERING<br/>eyes go down to the house centre
    WAITING --> LEAVING : life_seconds reaches its release time
    LEAVING --> ROAMING : reaches the house entrance
    state ROAMING {
        direction TB
        Scatter : Scatter<br/>target = corner
        Chase : Chase<br/>target = chase_target()
        Frightened : Frightened<br/>random turns (seeded stream)
        Scatter --> Chase : schedule phase ends (turns round)
        Chase --> Scatter : schedule phase ends (turns round)
        Scatter --> Frightened : snack eaten (turns round)
        Chase --> Frightened : snack eaten (turns round)
        Frightened --> Scatter : fright over (scatter phase)
        Frightened --> Chase : fright over (chase phase)
    }
    ROAMING --> EATEN : player touches it while frightened
    EATEN --> ENTERING : eyes reach the house entrance
    ENTERING --> LEAVING : reaches the house centre<br/>(no longer frightened)
State Movement Speed Can touch the player WAITING _bob: up and down 0.35 tiles around its seat house_speed No LEAVING _walk_out: across to the door's column, then up to the entrance house_speed Yes ROAMING advance through the corridors, turning as above tunnel_speed on a T tile, else frightened_speed if frightened, else hurry_speed (Chomper only, with few sprockets left), else muncher_speed Yes EATEN advance towards the house entrance eyes_speed No ENTERING _walk_in: down to the house centre eyes_speed No

A change of mode turns every roaming muncher round. When the schedule's phase changes, or a snack starts a fright, the scene sets reverse_soon, and the muncher reverses on its next step, even between tile centres. This is the only time a muncher reverses.

docs.title: Scatter, chase and fright timing
docs.text:
The scene keeps three clocks per life, all in game time and all reset when a life starts (_reset_actors). _advance_timers advances them on every step:

  • life_seconds decides when each muncher waiting in the house is released (release_seconds, in house order: Snapper, Gnasher, Nibbles).
  • mode_seconds drives the scatter/chase schedule. It stops while the munchers are frightened, so a fright does not use up a scatter phase. munchers_chase(schedule=..., elapsed_seconds=...) gives the mode: phases alternate scatter, chase, scatter, ..., starting with scatter, and after the last phase the munchers chase for good. mode_phase_index detects the change of phase that turns them round.
  • frightened_seconds_left counts down a fright. When it reaches zero, _end_fright clears every muncher's frightened flag.

A snack (_start_fright) frightens every muncher that is not eyes, resets the count of munchers eaten during this fright (which sets their points), and turns the roaming munchers round. Frightened munchers flash white and blue for the last 2 s of the fright (or all of it, if the fright is shorter), switching every quarter second (frightened_is_flashing).

docs.title: Levels and the difficulty ramp
docs.text:
settings_for_level(level) returns a frozen LevelSettings. Each reel is a little faster and meaner than the one before, up to reel 8 (LAST_RAMP_LEVEL); after that, every reel plays like reel 8. Speeds are in tiles per second.

Setting Reel 1 Each reel adds From reel 8 on Player speed 7.5 +0.15 8.55 Muncher speed (fraction of the player's speed) 0.82 +0.018 (at most 0.95) 0.946 (8.09 tiles/s) Fright length 8.0 s -0.9 s (never below 2.0 s) 2.0 s Chomper hurries when this few sprockets are left 20 +5 55 Bonus reel points 100, 300, 500, 700, 1000, 2000, 3000, 5000 (reels 1 to 8) 5000 Scatter/chase schedule (s) 9, 15, 9, 15, 7, 20, 5, then chase 5, 20, 5, 20, 3, 30, 1, then chase (from reel 2) House release times (s) 0.5, 4.0, 8.0 0.5, 2.5, 5.0 (from reel 2)

Other speeds are fixed fractions of the player's speed: frightened munchers 0.55, munchers on a tunnel tile 0.50, munchers moving in or out of the house 0.45, eyes 2.0. During a sugar rush the player is 1.1 times faster, and a hurrying Chomper is 1.08 times faster than the other munchers.

docs.title: Scoring, the bonus reel and lives
docs.text:
Event Points Also Sprocket 10 One of two crunch sounds, alternating Snack 50 Starts a fright (sugar_rush sound) Frightened muncher 200, 400, 800, 1600 (doubling for each one eaten in the same fright) Everything stops for 0.75 s while the points show (camera_flash sound). Mr. Muncher and the eaten muncher are hidden meanwhile Bonus film reel The reel's bonus_points Shown for 2 s (eat_bonus sound)
  • The bonus reel appears on the tile three rows below the house centre (message_cell, where the messages show too) after the 70th and the 170th sprocket of a reel (BONUS_SPROCKET_COUNTS), and stays 9.5 s unless eaten.
  • Extra life: one, the first time the score reaches 10,000 (extra_life sound). The game starts with 3 lives, counting the one in play.
  • Contact: a muncher touches the player when their centres are closer than 0.6 tiles (CONTACT_DISTANCE_TILES, tunnel-aware). Only munchers that are roaming or leaving the house count. The first muncher found touching settles the step: it is eaten if frightened, otherwise the player is caught.
  • High scores use the engine's saves: open_saves(app_name='mr-muncher'), save name high_scores, stored as {'scores': [{'score': ..., 'level': ...}, ...]}, best first, the best 10 kept. The game is added to the table when the last life is lost. The panel's HIGH SCORE is the larger of the best saved score and the current score. In a replay the saves are an in-memory sandbox seeded from the recording, so a replay never touches real saves.

docs.title: One frame
docs.text:
The engine runs dt_tick (logic) before it processes the frame's events, and update() (render phase) after positioning. Mr. Muncher does all its work in dt_tick and does not override update(). MAX_FRAME_SECONDS = 0.05: after a hitch, such as dragging the window, logic advances at most 50 ms in one frame.

In the diagram, the Engine box is the scene manager calling the scene; everything in the Mr. Muncher box is the game's own dt_tick.

flowchart TB
    subgraph ENGINE_FRAME["Engine"]
        direction TB
        A["SceneManager: logic phase<br/>scene.dt_tick(dt), dt capped at<br/>MAX_FRAME_SECONDS (0.05 s)"]
    end
    subgraph GAME_FRAME["Mr. Muncher"]
        direction TB
        B["_read_direction_input()<br/>set wanted_direction from the ActionMap,<br/>then actions.begin_frame()"]
        B --> C["phase_seconds += dt<br/>_run_phase(dt)"]
        C -->|PLAYING| P["_play(dt): split into steps of at most 1/120 s"]
        C -->|DYING| D["_die_a_little()"]
        C -->|other phases| W["wait, then move on when the phase's time is up"]
        P --> S1["_advance_timers(step)<br/>releases, mode schedule, fright, bonus"]
        S1 --> S2["player.travel(speed x step)<br/>_eat_at_player()"]
        S2 --> S3{"phase changed, or<br/>contact?"}
        S3 -->|yes| E["end of play for this frame"]
        S3 -->|no| S4["each muncher.travel(its speed x step,<br/>ChaseSituation)"]
        S4 --> S5{"contact?"}
        S5 -->|yes| E
        S5 -->|"no: next step"| S1
        D --> F
        W --> F
        E --> F["_count_down_bonus_points(dt)<br/>_update_projector()"]
        S5 -->|no steps left| F
        F --> G["_pose_sprites()<br/>every picture for this moment, side panels"]
    end
    A --> B
Sub-steps _play splits the frame into ceil(dt / (1/120)) equal steps (two at 60 FPS, at most six after a capped hitch), so no actor moves far enough in one step to pass through another. In each step the player moves and eats first, and contact is checked both after the player moves and after the munchers move. The pose rule Every sprite's picture is chosen in dt_tick, after its state is decided (_pose_sprites): the bucket's chomp (four mouth steps per tile travelled), the dying animation (24 steps), each muncher's body, frightened or flashing picture or eyes, the skirt's wave (every 0.15 s of game time), and the snacks' twinkle. The side panels are redrawn only when what they show changes. Input timing Key events are handled after dt_tick, so a key pressed in frame N changes wanted_direction in the dt_tick of frame N + 1. The autopilot allows for this delay (see below).

docs.title: Sprites and background
docs.text:
The maze is not made of sprites. When a scene is built, _draw_maze_backgrounds blits drawing.maze_picture(...) onto the scene's background, and onto a copy for the level-clear flash (white trim on lighter velvet). Everything that changes is a sprite in the scene's LayeredDirty group, drawn in layer order:

Layer Sprites Space 0 SPROCKET_LAYER Sprocket (sprockets and snacks; an eaten one is made invisible) Screen 1 BONUS_LAYER Picture named Bonus (the film reel) Screen 2 MUNCHER_LAYER Muncher x 4 World 3 PLAYER_LAYER Player World 4 POPUP_LAYER Pictures MuncherPoints, BonusPoints Screen 5 MESSAGE_LAYER Picture Message (3, 2, 1, ACTION!, TAKE n, CUT!, THE END) Screen 6 PANEL_LAYER SidePanel x 2 (film-strip edges with the score, lives, bonus, control hints) Screen

In the diagram, the Engine box is the engine's Sprite (glitchygames.sprites); the Mr. Muncher box holds the game's sprite classes (actors.py and scenery.py). Solid arrows are inheritance, pointing at the base class.

classDiagram
    direction TB
    namespace Engine {
        class Sprite {
            glitchygames.sprites
        }
    }
    namespace MrMuncher {
        class MazeActor {
            COORDINATE_SPACE = WORLD
            tile_x, tile_y, direction
            world_x, world_y
            advance(distance, choose_direction)
        }
        class Player {
            wanted_direction, facing
            travel(distance)
            pose()
        }
        class Muncher {
            profile, state, frightened
            reverse_soon, target
            travel(distance, situation)
            pose(game_time, flashing)
        }
        class Sprocket {
            cell, is_snack
            eat()
        }
        class Picture {
            centre
            change_image(image)
            move_to(centre)
        }
        class SidePanel {
            contents
            draw(contents, items)
        }
    }
    Sprite <|-- MazeActor
    MazeActor <|-- Player
    MazeActor <|-- Muncher
    Sprite <|-- Sprocket
    Sprite <|-- Picture
    Sprite <|-- SidePanel

The actors are world-space sprites (COORDINATE_SPACE = CoordinateSpace.WORLD). They keep their positions in tiles, report world_x/world_y in pixels (the picture's top-left corner), and the engine places their rects every frame. Hiding one uses hidden = True, never visible, which the engine owns for world sprites. The camera never moves (the scene sets no follow target), so world pixels are screen pixels. The still sprites are screen space and place their own rects.

render() is overridden: it blits the whole background (the flash copy on alternate quarter seconds during the level-clear flash), clears the group with that same background, draws every sprite, and sets self.rects = None so the whole screen is presented.

docs.title: Pictures
docs.text:
drawing.py draws every picture with pygame primitives. Shapes are drawn four times larger (SUPERSAMPLE) and smooth-scaled down, which smooths their edges. The maze is drawn twice as large (MAZE_SUPERSAMPLE) because its blur is the costly part. Every function is cached with functools.cache, because the game asks for the same few pictures every frame, so callers must not draw on the surfaces they get back.

The maze picture: each open tile is drawn as a black square widened by 0.2 of a tile on each side, the wall shape is blurred, and it is cut at two thresholds. The first gives the gold trim with rounded corners, the second the velvet inside it. The door is a bar across its tile.

docs.title: make_opaque on the backgrounds
docs.text: After the maze is blitted onto each background, _draw_maze_backgrounds calls make_opaque(surface=background) (src/glitchygames/opacity.py). The reason is BUGS.md #142. On a display with per-pixel alpha (macOS cocoa), a plain pygame.Surface takes the display's format, including its alpha channel. Alpha-blending a per-pixel-alpha picture such as the smooth-scaled maze onto it leaves alpha 0 in those pixels. Every sprite later blended over such a pixel would be copied unblended, and the window shows alpha 0 as black. Making the backgrounds opaque once, when the scene is built, keeps the sprites' blending correct. The engine also makes every presented frame opaque (SceneManager._show_frame), but that happens too late to fix blending inside the frame.

docs.title: Layout and the side panels
docs.text: maze_geometry makes the tiles as large as the screen's height allows (height // 24), unless the side panels would then be narrower than 100 px ((width - 200) // 27). Tiles are never smaller than 8 px. The maze is centred. The two SidePanels fill the space to its left and right, drawn as film-strip edges with sprocket holes. The left panel shows the title, SCORE, HIGH SCORE and REEL; the right one the spare lives (up to four bucket icons), this reel's BONUS, and the control hints. fitted_font chooses the largest bundled Bitstream Vera size (from the wanted size down to 8) at which each panel's longest text fits.

docs.title: Sound
docs.text:
sounds.py defines every sound as a synth SoundRecipe (src/glitchygames/audio/recipes.py). shared_sound_bank() builds one SoundBank(ALL_RECIPES) for the whole process (functools.cache), and setup() calls sounds.prerender(), so no sound is rendered in the middle of a frame.

Recipe When it plays crunch_one, crunch_two A sprocket or snack is eaten (alternating, so a run of them never repeats exactly) sugar_rush A snack starts a fright (two clapperboard clacks and a rising shimmer) camera_flash A frightened muncher is eaten eat_bonus The bonus reel is eaten film_snap The dying animation starts (the film snaps, then a sad trombone) level_clear The last sprocket is eaten extra_life The score reaches 10,000 countdown_beep Each number of a new game's 3, 2, 1 (a 1 kHz film-leader beep) action ACTION! (a clack and a major chord) the_end THE END

Behind play runs the projector, a live voice (scene_manager.live_audio.create_voice(...)) of low-pass filtered noise with a tremolo, so it flutters like a projector's shutter. _update_projector changes its cutoff and flutter rate only when they change: brighter and faster as the sprockets run out (500 to 1200 Hz, 20 to 30 Hz), slow and low while the munchers are frightened (300 Hz, 8 Hz), and racing while eyes are going home (2000 Hz, 40 Hz). It starts at ACTION!, stops when the player is caught, when the reel is cleared, and in cleanup(). If no live voice or no audio is available, the game logs a warning and plays without it.

docs.title: The autopilot
docs.text:
autopilot.py is a simple bot that plays Mr. Muncher. It reads the scene the way a person reads the screen, and never changes it. Autopilot.choose_direction(scene=...) returns the direction to ask for in each frame. It has two uses:

Steering the golden replay scripts/golden_inputs.py: mr_muncher_script wraps it in MuncherSteering, which holds the arrow key for the direction the autopilot wants (pressing it again if the player still wants another way after 4 frames). With seek_capture_after_seconds=22.0 it walks into a muncher once, so the recording includes a death and the next take. Bot playtests in the tests src/games/mr-muncher/tests/test_mr_muncher.py::TestWholeGames lets it play a last life until game over (setting wanted_direction directly), and TestAutopilot in src/games/mr-muncher/tests/test_mr_muncher_maze_and_actors.py checks its choices.

How it decides:

flowchart TB
    A["decision_point()<br/>the next tile centre the player reaches<br/>(or the one after, if a key pressed now<br/>would arrive too late)"] --> B["danger = corridor distances<br/>from every dangerous muncher"]
    B --> C["for each way on: way_on()<br/>territory = tiles the player reaches<br/>at least 2 tiles before any muncher"]
    C --> D{"seeking capture?"}
    D -->|yes| X["shortest way to a dangerous muncher"]
    D -->|no| E{"any way with a territory<br/>of 16 tiles or more?"}
    E -->|no| T["all are traps: the roomiest way<br/>(turning back counts half)"]
    E -->|yes| G["try ways onward first, then all roomy ways,<br/>shortest safe path to the first goal reachable"]
    G --> H["goals in order: catchable frightened muncher,<br/>bonus, snack (if a muncher is within 7 tiles),<br/>sprocket, any uneaten"]
    H --> R["no goal reachable: the roomiest way"]

INPUT_DELAY_SECONDS (2/60 s) is the delay described under One frame: a key pressed now changes the player's direction about two frames later, so the autopilot decides that far ahead. A frightened muncher is prey only if the player can reach it with at least 0.75 s of the fright left.

The game has no bundled attract-mode demo. The arcade showcase in plans/2026-10-23-arcade-showcase.md is a design draft. Because the golden script is steered by the autopilot, a demo could be recorded with scripts/record_scripted_session.py --game mr_muncher --script-only --output PATH.

docs.title: How it uses the engine
docs.text: Engine feature How Mr. Muncher uses it Game time and dt All movement and timers use the scene's (capped) dt. Phase clocks, the skirt's wave and the snacks' twinkle use game_time, so they stop while the game is paused Random streams The only randomness is the frightened munchers' turns, drawn from random_stream('mr_muncher.munchers') (seeded from --random-seed, kept in recordings) Scene starts replay_arguments() returns {'progress': starting_progress.model_dump()} and the scene accepts a mapping as progress, so a recording can rebuild any reel as it began. MrMuncherGameOverScene.replay_arguments() returns the final score, the table and the reel reached Saves High scores through open_saves (a sandbox in a replay) ActionMap Scancode bindings for the keyboard, D-pad and stick bindings for gamepads, built by MrMuncherScene._create_action_map(options=...). The golden replay test reads the bindings from the same function Pause screen The engine's PauseScene, which also shows the paused game in the debug overlay (debug_subject) Transitions FadeTransition to the game-over screen Screen shake and rumble CAUGHT_SHAKE: a 0.4 s NOISE shake of strength 6 on ShakeTarget.SCREEN, with gamepad rumble (low 0.8, high 0.4), when a muncher catches the player Live audio and synth The projector voice and the recipe bank (see Sound) World space The actors are world sprites, and the engine positions their rects Opacity make_opaque on the maze backgrounds (see above)

docs.title: Debug overlay
docs.text: MrMuncherScene.debug_draw(surface, camera) adds the game's own annotation to the engine's debug overlay (--debug-overlay or F3). For every muncher that is roaming or leaving the house and has a target, it draws a cross in the muncher's colour on the target tile and a thin line from the muncher to it. This shows each personality's aim live: for example, Snapper's cross four tiles in front of the bucket, or Nibbles' cross jumping to its corner when it gets close.

docs.title: Recording, replay and the golden replay
docs.text:
Everything that decides what happens runs on game time and the seeded stream, so a --record-trace recording replays exactly with --replay-trace.

The golden replay src/games/mr-muncher/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz was recorded through the real engine loop by scripts/record_scripted_session.py --game mr_muncher --frames 1950. Its 1,950 scripted frames cover the countdown, a pause with ESC at frame 600 and a resume with SPACE at frame 660, a snack, munchers and the bonus eaten, and a death at about frame 1650 followed by the next take's READY. The script is cut at 1,950 frames to keep the fixture under 100 KB.

Then comes the controls tail (mr_muncher_controls), which presses the controls the script does not use: it taps W, A, S and D (the autopilot steers with the arrows), pauses with P and resumes, and ends with the game's own Q. The recording's last frame holds the QUIT event that the game itself posted, so a replay in which Q no longer quits diverges. With the tail, the fixture holds 2,072 frames. tests/replay/test_golden_replays.py checks that every bound control is exercised. The gamepad controls (D-pad, stick, Start and the hat, listed as steer) are excused in UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS, because the scripted session runs on the dummy driver, which has no gamepad.

The pytest plugin src/glitchygames/testing/replays.py replays the fixture in a child process (mr-muncher --replay-trace ... --headless), and the test fails unless it exits SUCCESS. Re-record the fixture only deliberately (the commands are in the script's docstring), never just to make a failing replay pass.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Both test files below (in the member, src/games/mr-muncher/tests/) use real pygame, the real 800x480 display and real files (saves go to tmp_path). What is drawn is checked by its pixels. The tests patch only sound playback, where a test is about which sound plays.

src/games/mr-muncher/tests/test_mr_muncher_maze_and_actors.py covers the parts:

Class What it pins TestMazeLayout Symmetry, at least two ways on from every corridor tile, everything reachable, one-tile corridors, the sprocket, snack and house counts TestMazeQuestions Wrapping columns, wall outside the rows, the player kept out of the house and door, tunnels, short-way distance, layout validation TestLevels Reel 1 values, the ramp, its end at reel 8 and the shortest fright, no reel 0, scatter then chase, the flash TestPlayerMovement Exact landing on tile centres, walls, buffered turns, immediate reversing, the tunnel, next_cell_ahead, reset TestChaseTargets Each personality's target, the four profiles TestMuncherStates Waiting, bobbing, walking out, eyes going home and back out, scatter and chase targets, never turning back, mode reversal, seeded frightened turns, dead ends TestMuncherSpeeds Every speed, only Chomper hurrying TestPlayerPictures, TestMuncherPictures, TestPictures, TestScenery The pictures by their pixels, fitted fonts, sprockets, pictures and panels TestSounds Every recipe renders, two crunches TestAutopilot Corridor distances, the decision point, each goal, avoiding danger, traps, seeking capture once

src/games/mr-muncher/tests/test_mr_muncher.py covers the scene: layout (TestLayout), the countdown and messages (TestStartingALevel), input including joystick and controller modes, the hat, pause and Q (TestInput), eating, the bonus, the extra life and clearing a reel (TestEating), releases, mode reversal, doubling points, catches with their shake and the game's end (TestMunchers), the projector (TestProjector), the target crosses (TestDebugOverlay), the game-over screen (TestGameOverScreen), whole games through the frame loop (TestWholeGames: a cleared reel leads to REEL 2 with the score kept, and a game over leads to a new game), and main() replaying the golden fixture headless.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text: The mr_muncher package's API reference is its own page, mr_muncher, generated for every workspace member's package (scripts/gen_ref_pages.py).

docs.title: PaddleSlap Architecture
docs.text:
PaddleSlap is the smallest example game in GlitchyGames: two paddles, one or more balls, and no title screen. It is a two-player Pong in which the players share one score, the rally count (every paddle hit by any ball adds one), and the game ends when the last ball has left the court. Paddle hits can spawn more balls, so a long rally fills the court.

It is the reference for a game built from the engine's ready-made parts: BallSprite and VerticalPaddle from glitchygames.game_objects, the collision manager's layers, ActionMap input, the save store, and the built-in pause and game-over scenes. It is also the engine's oldest regression subject: it has a golden trace, a golden replay and a bundled attract-mode demo. This page shows how it is put together, from its scenes down to one frame.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
uv run paddleslap                          # one ball, extra balls spawned by paddle hits
uv run paddleslap --balls 3                # start with three balls
uv run paddleslap --ball-spawn-mode none   # never spawn: a classic one-ball rally
uv run paddleslap --random-seed 42         # the same serves, spawns and colours every run

The game adds these options to the engine's own (Game.args(); the engine's options, such as --target-fps, --resolution and --input-mode, are in Argument System):

Option Default Meaning -b, --balls N 1 Balls on the court when the game starts --ball-spawn-mode MODE paddle_only When extra balls appear: paddle_only, wall_only, ball_only, frequent, rare, none (see Ball spawning) -v, --version off Prints Paddle Slap 1.1 and exits before the game starts (argparse's version action)

The game sets no TARGET_FPS and no MAX_FRAME_SECONDS, so it runs at the engine's default 60.01 FPS and its logic gets the raw frame time.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Action Player 1 (left) Player 2 (right) Paddle up W position, D-pad up, left stick up Up arrow, D-pad up, left stick up Paddle down S position, D-pad down, left stick down Down arrow, D-pad down, left stick down Gamepad the pad with instance id 0 the pad with instance id 1 Scene Key Effect Game Space position (on release) Pause Game Q or Esc (on release) Quit (the base Scene posts QUIT) Pause Space, or a gamepad's Start or A (press, then release) Resume Pause Esc or a gamepad's B or Back (on press), Q (on release) Quit Pause window focus regained (after 0.5 s paused) Resume Game over Space, or a gamepad's Start or A (press, then release) New game Game over Esc or a gamepad's B or Back (on press), Q (on release) Quit Game over nothing for 10 s of game time Play the attract-mode demo; any key or button ends it

The paddle and pause keys are bound by scancode (a physical key position, the same place on every layout: AZERTY players press Z/S). The quit keys and the pause and game-over screens' Space and Esc are the engine's built-in scenes' key codes. Gamepads only move paddles: the pause and game-over screens answer the keyboard only (a button press on the game-over screen just restarts its idle wait).

docs.title: Scenes
docs.text:
PaddleSlap has two scenes of its own and one built in.

Scene Module Role Game src/games/paddleslap/src/paddleslap/__init__.py The court: paddles, balls, collisions, rally count, high scores PauseScene src/glitchygames/scenes/builtin_scenes/pause_scene.py The engine's pause screen: the game's last frame dimmed with PAUSED over it PaddleSlapGameOverScene src/games/paddleslap/src/paddleslap/__init__.py GameOverScene (score, top 5 high scores) plus the attract-mode demo, and a resume that always starts a new Game

In the diagram, the Engine box holds what the engine provides (its pause screen and the playback scope the demo runs in); the PaddleSlap box holds the game's own scenes.

stateDiagram-v2
    direction TB
    state "PaddleSlap" as GAME_SCENES {
        state "Game" as Game
        state "PaddleSlapGameOverScene<br/>(extends the engine's GameOverScene)" as GameOver
        state "switch_to_scene(Game(options))" as NewGame
    }
    state "Engine" as ENGINE_SCENES {
        state "PauseScene" as PauseScene
        state "Demo (playback scope)" as Demo
    }

    [*] --> Game : GameEngine(game=Game).start()
    Game --> PauseScene : Space released<br/>Scene.pause() sets next_scene
    PauseScene --> Game : Space, Start or A, or focus regained<br/>resume() switches back to the same Game
    Game --> GameOver : last ball gone<br/>_show_game_over() sets next_scene
    GameOver --> Demo : 10 s of game time idle<br/>play_recording(then=self)
    Demo --> GameOver : any key or button,<br/>or the demo's end
    GameOver --> NewGame : Space, Start or A<br/>resume()
    NewGame --> Game
    Game --> [*] : Q or Esc
    PauseScene --> [*] : Q or Esc
    GameOver --> [*] : Q, Esc, B or Back
Pause and game over switch at the end of the frame Both set next_scene instead of switching at once, so the scene manager switches after the frame renders. Pausing during event processing would otherwise freeze the previous frame's picture (the comment on Scene.pause()). PauseScene shows previous_scene.screenshot; resume() switches back to the same Game object, so the rally goes on where it was. A new game is always a Game GameOverScene.resume() restarts the type of the scene manager's previous_scene, which a playback scope can change (BUGS.md #81), so PaddleSlapGameOverScene.resume() names Game explicitly. Rebuilding the game-over screen PaddleSlapGameOverScene.replay_arguments() returns final_score and a copy of high_scores, so a recording that starts on this screen can rebuild it (scene starts, in Gameplay Recording and Replay).

docs.title: The attract-mode demo
docs.text:
PaddleSlap has no title screen (a game starts serving at once), so its idle screen is the game-over screen. PaddleSlapGameOverScene.dt_tick compares its game_time with idle_since_game_time; after GAME_OVER_IDLE_SECONDS (10.0) it plays the bundled recording PADDLESLAP_DEMO_PATH (src/games/paddleslap/src/paddleslap/demos/rally.jsonl.gz, package data) with SceneManager.play_recording(path=..., then=self). In the diagram, the PaddleSlap box is the game's own screen and the Engine box is what plays the demo; the player is outside both.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Player
    box rgb(255,243,224) PaddleSlap
        participant GO as PaddleSlapGameOverScene
    end
    box rgb(232,238,255) Engine
        participant SM as SceneManager
        participant PB as Playback scope
    end

    loop each frame
        SM->>GO: dt_tick(dt)
        GO->>GO: idle for 10 s of game_time?
    end
    Note over Player,GO: a key or button down restarts the idle wait
    GO->>SM: play_recording(then=self)
    Note over GO: the idle wait restarts
    SM->>PB: start at the next frame (exit_on_input)
    PB->>PB: rebuild Game, play 450 frames
    Player->>PB: any press ends it (consumed)
    PB->>SM: back to the game-over screen
    Note over GO: its game_time stood still meanwhile
  • The demo is an ordinary recording played in a playback scope: real input reaches only its exit check, saves are a sandbox, and the live game-over screen is stashed, not cleaned up.
  • The press that ends a demo never reaches the game-over screen, so starting a new game after a demo takes a second press (the class docstring).
  • A demo that cannot play is logged at WARNING ("No demo: ...") and nothing starts. A divergence ends it with a WARNING demo diverged: ....

docs.title: Its package
docs.text:
PaddleSlap is a package of its own beside the engine, src/games/paddleslap/ (distribution paddleslap, import package paddleslap). How such a package is laid out, installed, tested and built, and how a game is moved into one, is in Games as Their Own Packages.

PaddleSlap is one module, so Game is defined in the package itself (paddleslap/__init__.py): its recordings name it games.paddleslap:Game, which a Game defined in a submodule would change. Its golden replay is src/games/paddleslap/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz, its bundled demo ships inside the package (src/games/paddleslap/src/paddleslap/demos/rally.jsonl.gz, package data), its golden trace stays with the engine's trace tests (tests/world/golden/paddleslap.jsonl.gz), and its browser bundle ships paddleslap.zip.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text: PaddleSlap's own code is two classes in src/games/paddleslap/src/paddleslap/__init__.py: Game and PaddleSlapGameOverScene. Everything else it uses comes from the engine: Scene and the built-in PauseScene and GameOverScene (glitchygames.scenes), Sprite (glitchygames.sprites), and the paddles and balls of the engine's game-object library (glitchygames.game_objects). In the diagrams, the Engine box is what every game gets; the PaddleSlap box is what this game adds. Solid arrows are inheritance, pointing at the base class; dotted arrows are how the game uses an engine class.

docs.title: Scenes
docs.text:
classDiagram
    direction TB
    namespace Engine {
        class Scene {
            next_scene
            pause requests a PauseScene
        }
        class PauseScene {
            the frozen game, dimmed
            SPACE or Start/A resumes it, ESC or B/Back quits
        }
        class GameOverScene {
            score and high scores
            SPACE or Start/A restarts, ESC or B/Back quits
        }
    }
    namespace PaddleSlap {
        class Game {
            NAME = 'Paddle Slap'
            VERSION = '1.1'
            player1, player2 : VerticalPaddle
            balls : list of BallSprite
            rally_count : int
            p1_actions, p2_actions, pause_actions : ActionMap
            saves : SaveManager
            ball_spawn_mode : BallSpawnMode flags
            dt_tick(dt)
            args(parser)
        }
        class PaddleSlapGameOverScene {
            idle_since_game_time : float
            dt_tick(dt)
            replay_arguments()
            resume()
        }
    }

    Scene <|-- PauseScene
    Scene <|-- GameOverScene
    Scene <|-- Game
    GameOverScene <|-- PaddleSlapGameOverScene

    Game ..> PauseScene : SPACE calls the inherited pause
    Game ..> PaddleSlapGameOverScene : next_scene when the last ball is gone
    PaddleSlapGameOverScene ..> Game : resume starts a new Game

Game never names PauseScene: its pause action calls Scene.pause(), which it inherits, and that requests the engine's PauseScene for the end of the frame. PaddleSlap's game-over screen extends the engine's, adding the attract-mode demo after an idle wait and always restarting a new Game (the engine's resume() restarts whatever scene came before, BUGS.md #81).

docs.title: Sprites
docs.text:
classDiagram
    direction TB
    namespace Engine {
        class Sprite
        class BasePaddle {
            _move : Vertical or Horizontal
            _sub_pixel_x, _sub_pixel_y
        }
        class VerticalPaddle {
            up() down() stop()
            dt_tick(dt): move, then clamp
        }
        class HorizontalPaddle
        class BallSprite {
            COORDINATE_SPACE = WORLD
            world_x, world_y : float
            speed : Speed
            serve_settings, speed_up_settings
            on_paddle_collision, on_wall_bounce
            dt_tick(dt)
            handle_paddle_collision(paddle)
        }
    }
    namespace PaddleSlap {
        class GameSprites["Game"] {
            creates the paddles and balls
            sets the balls' callbacks
            resolves collisions in dt_tick
        }
    }

    Sprite <|-- BasePaddle
    BasePaddle <|-- VerticalPaddle
    BasePaddle <|-- HorizontalPaddle
    Sprite <|-- BallSprite

    VerticalPaddle <.. GameSprites : player1, player2
    BallSprite <.. GameSprites : balls

PaddleSlap defines no sprite classes: both paddles are the engine's VerticalPaddle (src/glitchygames/game_objects/paddle.py) and every ball is its BallSprite (src/glitchygames/game_objects/ball.py). The game creates them, wires the balls' callbacks (on_paddle_collision, on_wall_bounce) to its rally count and sounds, and resolves collisions in Game.dt_tick. HorizontalPaddle is not used by PaddleSlap; it is shown because it shares BasePaddle.

docs.title: Sprites and how they are drawn
docs.text: Sprite Space Size and image Who writes rect VerticalPaddle ×2 Screen (no COORDINATE_SPACE) 20×100 white rectangle; left at x = 0, right at x = screen width − 20, vertically centred The paddle itself: dt_tick rounds its float _sub_pixel_y into rect.y, then clamps it to the screen (stopping it at an edge) BallSprite World (CoordinateSpace.WORLD) 20×20 image with colour key 0 and a filled circle of radius 5 in the middle; colour set through the color property, which redraws the circle The engine: each frame position_world_sprites writes rect from the snapped world_x/world_y The camera never moves Game sets no follow target and no camera_target(), so the camera stays at the origin: world and screen coordinates are the same and the balls are drawn exactly where their logic left them (TestWorldBallsInTheFrame in tests/world/test_frame_integration.py). The balls are world sprites anyway, so the engine is the only writer of their rect: game logic reads world_x/world_y, drawn_center() or the collision rect, never rect (which holds where the ball was last drawn). Pixel snapping The ball's own pixel_snap_mode (default NEAREST_HALF_UP, the scene's default too) rounds its sub-pixel position for drawing and for collision alike. Background The court is BLACK, named on purpose: a scene that sets no background shows the engine's test pattern. Dirty rendering All sprites live in one pygame.sprite.LayeredDirty (all_sprites). The ball sets dirty = 2 (always redrawn); paddles set dirty = 1 every tick. Pose Neither sprite changes its image with its state (a ball's image changes only when its colour is set), so the pose rule has nothing to order here. Collision resolution, the other half of that rule, runs in dt_tick (below).

docs.title: Hitboxes
docs.text:
The collision manager has two layers, balls and paddles (the debug overlay's hitbox panel draws them). Hitboxes are the default visible-pixel trim (src/glitchygames/collision/bounds.py):

  • A ball's hitbox is its visible circle's 10×10 box, offset (5, 5) from the drawn position, not its 20×20 image. BallSprite._visible_rect() returns that box with its offset, and every ball test uses it: walls, paddles and other balls meet the circle the players see.
  • A paddle's hitbox is its whole 20×100 rectangle.

docs.title: One frame
docs.text:
The engine's frame order is in the Bitmappy page and CLAUDE.md. What PaddleSlap does inside it (the PaddleSlap box is the game's one scene class; the Engine box is the engine's scene manager, game objects and collision manager):

sequenceDiagram
    box rgb(255,243,224) PaddleSlap
        participant G as Game
    end
    box rgb(232,238,255) Engine
        participant SM as SceneManager
        participant P as VerticalPaddle x2
        participant B as BallSprite (each)
        participant CM as CollisionManager
    end

    SM->>G: dt_tick(dt)
    G->>G: _process_paddle_input()
    G->>P: up() / down() / stop()
    G->>P: dt_tick(dt): move, write rect.y, clamp to the screen
    G->>B: dt_tick(dt)
    B->>B: move, wall bounce, kill() past an edge
    G->>G: _resolve_collisions()
    G->>CM: check_overlap('balls', 'paddles')
    CM->>G: _on_ball_paddle_collision(ball, paddle)
    G->>B: handle_paddle_collision(paddle)
    B->>G: on_paddle_collision(ball): rally, spawn
    G->>CM: check_overlap('balls', 'balls')
    CM->>G: _on_ball_ball_collision(ball1, ball2)
    G->>G: playable rule, spawns
    G->>G: drop dead balls, game over?
    SM->>G: event handlers feed the ActionMaps
    SM->>SM: position the balls
    SM->>G: update() (render phase)
    SM->>SM: draw, present, pace
  • Logic before events. dt_tick runs before the frame's events are pumped, so it reads the held state the ActionMaps reached at the end of the previous frame; a press shows up in the next frame's dt_tick.
  • Collisions in dt_tick, after every sprite moved. The engine positions the balls after dt_tick and before update() renders, so a bounce, or a ball spawned this frame, is drawn this frame (the comment in Game.dt_tick). update() resolves nothing (test_update_resolves_no_collisions).
  • A dead ball stays in the balls layer until _resolve_collisions removes it, so _on_ball_paddle_collision skips balls that are no longer alive().
  • The paddle's screen clamp runs in its dt_tick. A paddle moved past the top or bottom edge is clamped (and stopped) in the same dt_tick, so this frame's collisions see it on screen (the pose rule keeps update() for visual work; HorizontalPaddle clamps the same way).

docs.title: Ball versus wall
docs.text:
BallSprite._handle_boundary_collisions bounces the ball off the top and bottom walls only (PaddleSlap constructs every ball with bounce_top_bottom=True, bounce_left_right=False). A wall counts as hit when the visible box touches it while the ball moves toward it, so a ball still touching a wall the frame after a bounce does not bounce again. A hit flips the vertical speed, plays the bounce sound, applies a WALL_BOUNCE speed-up if configured (PaddleSlap's is not) and calls on_wall_bounce. _keep_inside_playfield then mirrors any overshoot back inside.

A ball whose visible box is entirely past the left or right edge calls kill(): that is a score.

docs.title: Ball versus paddle
docs.text:
The collision manager pairs overlapping collision rects (an AABB broad phase), and BallSprite.handle_paddle_collision(paddle) does the exact test and the response:

  1. Circle against rectangle. The ball is the circle inscribed in its visible box; the nearest point of the paddle rectangle to its centre must be within the radius (touching counts). Otherwise nothing happens.
  2. Which face. _entered_paddle_from_left looks at where the visible box was before this frame's move (speed.x × the last tick's dt back). If it was clear of the paddle on one side, the ball came in from that side, even when a long frame carried its centre past the paddle's centre; if it already overlapped, the side of the paddle's centre the ball's centre is on decides.
  3. Response. The ball is placed with its visible edge flush against that face, its horizontal speed points away from the paddle, the paddle's slap sound plays, a PADDLE_BOUNCE speed-up is applied, the speed is clamped to max_speed, and on_paddle_collision(ball) is called. PaddleSlap's callback counts the rally hit and may spawn a ball.

docs.title: Ball versus ball
docs.text:
_handle_ball_collisions ticks the per-pair cooldowns, then asks the collision manager for overlapping balls/balls pairs. _on_ball_ball_collision handles each pair:

Step Method What it does 1 cooldown check A pair that collided in the last 10 frames (either order) is skipped 2 _calculate_ball_distance Centre distance of the two collision rects; they collide within the sum of the half widths 3 separating check Skipped if the balls are moving apart and no longer overlap 4 _apply_elastic_collision Equal-mass elastic exchange: swap the velocity components along the collision normal, keep the tangential ones (momentum and kinetic energy conserved) 5 _cap_ball_speeds Each ball's speed capped at 500 px/s 6 _separate_overlapping_balls Move both balls apart along the normal (by at least 3 px in total, at least 1 px on each significant axis), in world_x/world_y 7 record Cooldown of 10 frames for the pair; the pair is kept for the two steps below

After the pass, two game rules apply to every pair that collided this frame:

_keep_collided_balls_playable Exact physics can leave a ball almost stopped, almost vertical (it bounces between the walls and never reaches a paddle) or flat (it slides along a wall). The ball's angle from horizontal is moved into its ServeSettings band (15° to 60°) and its speed raised to at least the serve speed, keeping each component's sign (a zero component points away from the partner). This is deliberately not physics and not part of _apply_elastic_collision, whose physics the collision tests check. _spawn_new_balls_for_ball_collisions One spawn attempt per pair, if ball-ball hits are a spawn trigger; the speed check uses the pair's faster ball. It runs outside the collision manager's pass, so spawned balls never join it.

docs.title: Serves and speed-ups
docs.text:
Setting Value Used by PADDLESLAP_SERVE ServeSettings(): 250 px/s, 15° to 60° from horizontal, either side, either vertical direction, 50 px margin Opening balls (reset() in the constructor picks a random position and serve) PADDLESLAP_SPAWN_SERVE ServeSettings(speed=150.0) Spawned balls in a mode with RANDOM_SPEED (serve() keeps the position the game chose) fixed spawn speed Speed(250.0, 125.0) Spawned balls in a mode without RANDOM_SPEED (no listed mode) PADDLESLAP_SPEED_UP PADDLE_BOUNCE trigger, LOGARITHMIC curve, BOTH axes, multiplier 1.15, max_speed 500 px/s Every ball

The logarithmic curve gives big early boosts that taper off, s0 × (1 + 0.15 × ln(1 + n)) after n paddle hits, and scaling both axes keeps the angle the paddle set. Paddles move at 400 px/s.

docs.title: Ball spawning
docs.text:
BallSpawnMode (src/glitchygames/game_objects/ball.py) is a set of bit flags: triggers (which events may spawn), conditions (cooldown, speed check, random position, speed and colour) and frequency (the cooldown length). --ball-spawn-mode picks one combination:

Option Triggers Cooldown Other flags paddle_only (default) paddle hit 2.0 s speed check, random position, speed and colour wall_only wall bounce 2.0 s as above ball_only ball-ball hit 2.0 s as above frequent all four (paddle, wall, ball, score) 0.5 s as above rare paddle hit 5.0 s as above none none the rally is still counted

Every trigger goes through _spawn_new_ball_on_trigger, so all triggers share one cooldown and one speed check. In the diagram, the Engine box is the engine's BallSprite reporting paddle hits and wall bounces through its callbacks; the PaddleSlap box is the game's spawn rule in Game (which serves each new ball with the engine's BallSprite.serve()):

flowchart TB
    subgraph ENGINE_SPAWN["Engine"]
        direction TB
        ballcallback["BallSprite calls on_paddle_collision<br/>or on_wall_bounce"]
    end
    subgraph GAME_SPAWN["PaddleSlap"]
        direction TB
        gametrigger["Game._resolve_collisions:<br/>ball-ball hit or score"]
        trigger["_spawn_new_ball_on_trigger(trigger, ball)"]
        named{"Is it one of the<br/>mode's triggers?"}
        skip1["No spawn"]
        cooldown{"COOLDOWN_ENABLED and<br/>game_time - last spawn<br/>under the cooldown?"}
        skip2["No spawn"]
        speed{"SPEED_CHECK_ENABLED and<br/>the triggering ball faster<br/>than 1000 px/s?"}
        skip3["No spawn"]
        spawn["_spawn_new_ball()"]
        place["Position: 10 tries for a spot<br/>at least 100 px from every ball<br/>(the last try if none is clear)"]
        serve["Speed: the engine's serve() at 150 px/s<br/>Colour: from the colour stream"]
        join["Added to balls, all_sprites<br/>and the 'balls' layer"]
    end
    ballcallback --> trigger
    gametrigger --> trigger
    trigger --> named
    named -- no --> skip1
    named -- yes --> cooldown
    cooldown -- yes --> skip2
    cooldown -- no --> speed
    speed -- yes --> skip3
    speed -- no --> spawn
    spawn --> place
    place --> serve
    serve --> join
  • The cooldown counts Scene.game_time, so it stops while the game is paused or behind the game-over screen (test_spawn_cooldown_counts_game_time_only).
  • A score spawns before the game-over check, so in frequent mode the last ball scoring brings a replacement (when the cooldown and speed check allow it) instead of ending the game.
  • Each new ball is connected to the same paddle-hit and wall-bounce callbacks, so spawned balls spawn too.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
Each player has an ActionMap (src/glitchygames/input/action_map.py) with up and down; a third holds pause. _create_action_maps binds, per player, a scancode, a D-pad button and the left stick's vertical axis at a ±0.3 threshold, filtered to the gamepad with instance id 0 (player 1) or 1 (player 2). The keyboard bindings have no instance filter. In the diagram, the Engine boxes are the engine's event dispatch (top) and its ActionMap, VerticalPaddle and base Scene (bottom); the PaddleSlap box is what Game's handlers and dt_tick add between them:

flowchart TB
    subgraph ENGINE_INPUT_DISPATCH["Engine"]
        direction TB
        events["Event dispatch: on_key_down/up_event,<br/>on_controller_button/axis_*_event,<br/>on_joy_button/axis_*_event"]
    end
    subgraph GAME_INPUT["PaddleSlap"]
        direction TB
        feed["Game feeds each event to the ActionMaps<br/>(keys: all three, gamepad: the two players')"]
        pause{"Game.on_key_up_event:<br/>pause just released?"}
        tick["Next frame, Game.dt_tick:<br/>begin_frame(), then reads the held state"]
    end
    subgraph ENGINE_INPUT_PARTS["Engine"]
        direction TB
        state["ActionMap held state<br/>(held, just pressed, just released)"]
        paddle["VerticalPaddle: up(), down() or stop()"]
        pausecall["Scene.pause()"]
        base["Scene.on_key_up_event<br/>(Q or Esc quits)"]
    end
    events --> feed
    feed --> pause
    feed -- handle_event --> state
    tick -- "is_held('up') / is_held('down')" --> state
    tick --> paddle
    pause -- yes --> pausecall
    pause -- "not a pause key" --> base
Movement is frame-driven Handlers only update the ActionMaps; the paddles are moved by _process_paddle_input at the top of dt_tick, from the held state. Input mode The ActionMaps take the engine's --input-mode (default auto: a mapped pad's controller events and any other device's joystick events, each press once) and its --axis-deadzone (ActionMap.from_engine_options). PaddleSlap handles both families, so a pad works in every mode. Instance ids, not player slots SDL numbers devices in the order they appear, so the first pad connected drives the left paddle; a pad that is unplugged and plugged back in gets a new instance id and no longer matches its binding. Key repeat PaddleSlap leaves SDL's key repeat off: movement reads held state and pause acts on the release, so nothing needs repeated key-downs (they would only fill event batches and recordings). Polling PaddleSlap never polls pygame: everything it knows about input comes through events, which recordings hold, so a replay serves the same input.

docs.title: Sound
docs.text:
Two sound effects, loaded with glitchygames.game_objects.load_sound from src/glitchygames/game_objects/snd_files/ at volume 0.25 (pygame.mixer.Sound, not the synthesiser):

Sound File Played when SFX.BOUNCE sfx_bounce.wav A ball bounces off a wall (the ball's own sound), or two balls collide (the first ball's sound) SFX.SLAP sfx_slap.wav A ball hits a paddle (the paddle's sound, played by handle_paddle_collision)

docs.title: Score and saves
docs.text:
• rally_count counts paddle hits by any ball; it is the game's only score, shared by both players. _spawn_new_ball_with_speed_check counts the hit whatever the spawn mode.
  • At game over, _save_high_score loads the high_scores slot of the paddleslap save store (open_saves(app_name='paddleslap')), appends the rally, keeps the ten best (best first) and saves it. Live, that is high_scores.json in the platform's save directory (~/Library/Application Support/paddleslap/ on macOS, ~/.local/share/paddleslap/ on Linux, %APPDATA%\paddleslap\ on Windows). The game-over screen shows the final score and the top five.
  • In a replay or a demo the store is a MemorySaveManager seeded from the recording, so the real high scores are never touched (the recordings start from an empty paddleslap store).

docs.title: Engine features it uses
docs.text: Feature How PaddleSlap uses it Random streams Serves draw from 'ball.serve' (SERVE_RANDOM_STREAM), spawn positions from 'paddleslap.spawn' (SPAWN_RANDOM_STREAM), ball colors from 'paddleslap.colors' (COLOR_RANDOM_STREAM): separate streams, so a color draw never moves where the next ball spawns. --random-seed fixes them all Scene.game_time The spawn cooldown and the game-over idle wait Collision layers balls and paddles, check_overlap for the broad phase World space The balls (identity camera); the paddles stay screen space Save store High scores (open_saves) Built-in scenes PauseScene, GameOverScene Playback scope The attract-mode demo (play_recording) Debug overlay F3 and F4 work as in every game; the hitbox panel shows the two layers. The ball keeps speed, not a physics body, so the physics panel has nothing to draw Not used Screen shake, rumble, live synth voices, instant replay, ghosts, camera follow

docs.title: Recordings that pin it
docs.text:
Recording What it is Checked by tests/world/golden/paddleslap.jsonl.gz Golden trace: the scripted run recorded before the world-space change, by scripts/record_golden_traces.py tests/world/test_golden_traces.py compares every sprite's rect and visibility frame by frame; each difference must be explained by one ExpectedDifference src/games/paddleslap/tests/fixtures/replays/golden.jsonl.gz Golden replay: 622 frames at 800×480, seed 20261018, recorded through the real engine loop by scripts/record_scripted_session.py --game paddleslap --frames 600 The replay plugin (src/glitchygames/testing/replays.py) replays it with paddleslap --replay-trace ... --headless and fails unless it exits SUCCESS; tests/replay/test_golden_replays.py checks the fixture set and the controls rule src/games/paddleslap/src/paddleslap/demos/rally.jsonl.gz Bundled demo: 450 frames of Game, recorded with --frames 450 --script-only (before the script's pause, no quit) tests/replay/test_bundled_demos.py replays it headless and plays it through play_recording inside a running game

The golden script (paddleslap_script in scripts/golden_inputs.py) steers both paddles with a PaddleTracker: each paddle holds its up or down key to follow the nearest ball moving toward it, with a 12 px dead zone. It pauses with Space at frame 450 and resumes at frame 510. The golden replay then adds the controls tail (paddleslap_controls): Q and Esc pressed and released, so the recording ends on the game's own QUIT and a replay in which either key no longer quits diverges.

Re-record only deliberately, after finding out why a replay diverged (the commands are in the docstring of scripts/record_scripted_session.py). Replay performance for both recordings is in Replay Performance.
