docs.title: __subclasshook__(subclass) classmethod
docs.text:
Override the default subclasshook to create an interface.

A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the abc contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it).

Returns:

Name Type Description bool bool

True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object.subclasshook as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides.

Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 
@classmethod
@override
def __subclasshook__(cls, subclass: type[Any]) -> bool:
    """Override the default __subclasshook__ to create an interface.

    A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass
    even without inheriting from it. Per the `abc` contract, anything else returns
    NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and
    hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods,
    so the structural check never passes for it).

    Returns:
        bool: True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented
            (typeshed annotates object.__subclasshook__ as bool and types NotImplemented
            as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides.

    """
    # Note: This accounts for under/dunder methods in addition to regular methods.
    interface_attributes = set(cls.__abstractmethods__)
    abstract_methods = getattr(subclass, '__abstractmethods__', frozenset[str]())
    subclass_attributes: set[str] = set(abstract_methods)

    interface_is_implemented = False
    methods: list[bool] = []
    for attribute in sorted(interface_attributes):
        if hasattr(subclass, attribute) and attribute not in subclass_attributes:
            if callable(getattr(subclass, attribute)):
                cls.log.debug('%s.%s -> implemented (callable)', subclass.__name__, attribute)
            else:
                cls.log.debug('%s.%s -> implemented (attribute)', subclass.__name__, attribute)
            methods.append(True)
        else:
            cls.log.debug('%s.%s -> unimplemented', subclass.__name__, attribute)
            methods.append(False)

    # all([]) returns True, so mask it
    #
    # This protects against an empty attribute list
    # which would be a misconfiguration of the interface
    if len(methods) > 0 and all(methods):
        interface_is_implemented = all(methods)

    if interface_is_implemented:
        return True
    return NotImplemented

@classmethod
def break_when(cls: type[Sprite], sprite_type: object | None = None) -> None:
    """Register a breakpoint for a sprite type.

    Args:
        sprite_type (object | None): The sprite type to break on.
            None means break on any sprite.

    """
    # The current context's breakpoints: None means disabled, [] means any
    counters = sprite_counters()
    if counters.breakpoints is None:
        counters.breakpoints = []

    # If none, break always.
    if sprite_type is not None:
        # Register the type asked for (not cls): __init__ compares str(type(self)) with it
        LOG.info('Register break when sprite_type==%s', sprite_type)
        counters.breakpoints.append(str(sprite_type))
    else:
        LOG.info('Register break when sprite_type==<any>')

docs.text:
Bases: Sprite

A sprocket or snack (screen space: it never moves); hidden once eaten.

Source code in src/games/mr-muncher/src/mr_muncher/scenery.py 
class Sprocket(Sprite):
    """A sprocket or snack (screen space: it never moves); hidden once eaten."""

    def __init__(
        self: Self,
        *,
        cell: tuple[int, int],
        is_snack: bool,
        geometry: MazeGeometry,
        layer: int,
        groups: pygame.sprite.LayeredDirty[Any],
    ) -> None:
        """Draw the sprocket centred on its tile.

        Args:
            cell: Its tile.
            is_snack: True for a snack.
            geometry: Where the maze is on screen.
            layer: The sprite layer.
            groups: The sprite group to add it to.

        """
        self._layer = layer
        self.cell = cell
        self.is_snack = is_snack
        self.tile_size = geometry.tile_size
        image = (
            drawing.snack_picture(tile_size=geometry.tile_size, lit=True)
            if is_snack
            else drawing.sprocket_picture(tile_size=geometry.tile_size)
        )
        centre_x, centre_y = geometry.pixel_centre(tile_x=cell[0], tile_y=cell[1])
        side = image.get_width()
        super().__init__(
            x=round(centre_x - side / 2),
            y=round(centre_y - side / 2),
            width=side,
            height=side,
            name='Snack' if is_snack else 'Sprocket',
            groups=groups,
        )
        self.image = image
        self.dirty = 2

    @property
    def eaten(self: Self) -> bool:
        """Whether the player has eaten it (it is then not drawn)."""
        return not self.visible

    def eat(self: Self) -> None:
        """Eat it: it is no longer drawn."""
        self.visible = 0

    def pose(self: Self, *, game_time: float) -> None:
        """Blink a snack (a plain sprocket never changes).

        Args:
            game_time: The scene's game time.

        """
        if self.is_snack:
            lit = math.floor(game_time / SNACK_TWINKLE_SECONDS) % 2 == 0
            self.image = drawing.snack_picture(tile_size=self.tile_size, lit=lit)

Override the default subclasshook to create an interface.

A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass even without inheriting from it. Per the abc contract, anything else returns NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods, so the structural check never passes for it).

Returns:

Name Type Description bool bool

True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented (typeshed annotates object.subclasshook as bool and types NotImplemented as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides.

Source code in src/glitchygames/events/base.py 
@classmethod
@override
def __subclasshook__(cls, subclass: type[Any]) -> bool:
    """Override the default __subclasshook__ to create an interface.

    A class that implements every abstract method of the interface counts as a subclass
    even without inheriting from it. Per the `abc` contract, anything else returns
    NotImplemented rather than False: False would mean "definitely not a subclass" and
    hide real subclasses (every concrete class such as Scene has no abstract methods,
    so the structural check never passes for it).

    Returns:
        bool: True if the subclass implements the interface; otherwise NotImplemented
            (typeshed annotates object.__subclasshook__ as bool and types NotImplemented
            as compatible with it), so the normal inheritance check decides.

    """
    # Note: This accounts for under/dunder methods in addition to regular methods.
    interface_attributes = set(cls.__abstractmethods__)
    abstract_methods = getattr(subclass, '__abstractmethods__', frozenset[str]())
    subclass_attributes: set[str] = set(abstract_methods)

    interface_is_implemented = False
    methods: list[bool] = []
    for attribute in sorted(interface_attributes):
        if hasattr(subclass, attribute) and attribute not in subclass_attributes:
            if callable(getattr(subclass, attribute)):
                cls.log.debug('%s.%s -> implemented (callable)', subclass.__name__, attribute)
            else:
                cls.log.debug('%s.%s -> implemented (attribute)', subclass.__name__, attribute)
            methods.append(True)
        else:
            cls.log.debug('%s.%s -> unimplemented', subclass.__name__, attribute)
            methods.append(False)

    # all([]) returns True, so mask it
    #
    # This protects against an empty attribute list
    # which would be a misconfiguration of the interface
    if len(methods) > 0 and all(methods):
        interface_is_implemented = all(methods)

    if interface_is_implemented:
        return True
    return NotImplemented

@classmethod
def break_when(cls: type[Sprite], sprite_type: object | None = None) -> None:
    """Register a breakpoint for a sprite type.

    Args:
        sprite_type (object | None): The sprite type to break on.
            None means break on any sprite.

    """
    # The current context's breakpoints: None means disabled, [] means any
    counters = sprite_counters()
    if counters.breakpoints is None:
        counters.breakpoints = []

    # If none, break always.
    if sprite_type is not None:
        # Register the type asked for (not cls): __init__ compares str(type(self)) with it
        LOG.info('Register break when sprite_type==%s', sprite_type)
        counters.breakpoints.append(str(sprite_type))
    else:
        LOG.info('Register break when sprite_type==<any>')

def on_quit_event(self: Self, event: HashableEvent) -> None:
    """Handle a quit event.

    Args:
        event (pygame.event.Event): The event to handle.

    """
    # QUIT             none
    self.log.debug('%s: %s', type(self), event)
    # terminate() exists on scenes (SceneInterface), not on Sprite: a sprite that also
    # mixes in a scene's interface ends it here. Cast to Any to allow dynamic dispatch.
    game: Any = self
    game.terminate()

def fitted_font(
    *, bold: bool, texts: tuple[str, ...], width: int, largest: int
) -> pygame.font.Font:
    """Return the largest bundled font, up to a size, in which every text fits a width.

    Args:
        bold: Vera Bold rather than Vera.
        texts: The texts that must fit.
        width: The width they must fit, in pixels.
        largest: The largest size wanted.

    Returns:
        The font (SMALLEST_FONT_SIZE when even that is too wide).

    """
    for size in range(largest, SMALLEST_FONT_SIZE, -1):
        font = bundled_font(bold=bold, size=size)
        if all(font.size(text)[0] <= width for text in texts):
            return font
    return bundled_font(bold=bold, size=SMALLEST_FONT_SIZE)

docs.title: Code Complexity Metrics
docs.text:
How the modules and packages in src/glitchygames/ changed over the project's git history, measured by wily. The explorer below draws one metric at a time (maintainability index, cyclomatic complexity, lines of code, Halstead effort) for modules or packages. Modules come in rank order: the highest total cyclomatic complexity (the sum over their functions and methods) at the published commit first, the top 15 to begin with; type part of a path to narrow them (scenes/, replay), or show 30 or all. Each line has a point at each commit that changed its value, and holds as a step until the next one (click a line in the legend to hide it). wily follows files by path; the engine moved from the repository root into src/glitchygames/ (2026-10-25), so each module's and package's measurements under its former path are joined to its current one (MOVED_PATH_PREFIXES in scripts/generate_complexity_graphs.py), and its line runs through its whole history.

The measurements are generated, not kept in git: every docs build generates them when HEAD changed (nox -s docs-deploy before it builds the published site). To generate them by hand, run uv run python scripts/generate_complexity_graphs.py (or nox -s code-complexity -- --graphs), which measures the committed history (HEAD) in a temporary worktree and writes docs/quality/graphs/complexity-explorer.json; until then this page has only this text.

Generated at commit a7cfb44 (2026-11-11) from all 299 commits: 210 modules and 42 packages of src/glitchygames.

docs.title: Driver Comparison
docs.text: The test suite draws in software on SDL's dummy video driver, which has no window. The platform's own driver (macOS cocoa, Windows windows, Linux wayland or x11) draws through the same code, and the engine presents opaque frames, so every test should show the same pixels on both. When they differ, the engine depends on the driver: on macOS a display with per-pixel alpha once showed black frames (BUGS.md #142) and a black box around the player during Clockwork Keep's elevator ride (BUGS.md #189), neither visible on dummy.

docs.title: Every local run compares
docs.text:
Outside CI, uv run pytest (and nox -s test) runs the suite twice at once:

  1. on dummy, in the pytest process and its xdist workers, with coverage and the 99% gate as always;
  2. on the native driver, as a child pytest run with the same arguments. The usual workers are split between the two runs (the native run gets two thirds: it is slower per test), so the machine is no busier than for one run.

The native run's windows are hidden (tests/hidden_test_windows.py): a shown window under the pointer, or holding the keyboard, receives the machine's mouse and keys as events, which reached tests (BUGS.md #225). A hidden window draws and presents the same pixels and receives no input. GLITCHYGAMES_SHOW_TEST_WINDOWS=1 shows them again, to watch a run; the same holds for any run on a real driver (SDL_VIDEODRIVER=cocoa uv run pytest ..., nox -s compare-drivers).

Both runs record a fingerprint (size and SHA-256 of the RGB bytes, as the window shows them) of every frame each test presents (src/glitchygames/testing/frame_fingerprints.py). When both have finished, the frames are compared (src/glitchygames/testing/frame_comparison.py; its command line is scripts/compare_driver_frames.py). Any difference, or a failure in the native run, fails the run; the differing tests are re-run on both drivers to save the differing frames as PNG files with a difference image (the baseline dimmed to grey, differing pixels magenta) under test-results/driver-comparison/pytest/. The terminal summary names every file and the native run's log.

The comparison is off, and the summary says why, in CI (CI=true), with --dummy-only (fast iteration), when SDL_VIDEODRIVER or SDL_AUDIODRIVER is set (that driver runs alone), and on a Linux machine without a display.

docs.title: Tests whose frames vary
docs.text: A test whose frames are not expected to match between runs or drivers is marked @pytest.mark.frames_vary(reason=...): it is listed with its reason and not compared. Today these are a session recorded through the real frame loop (each frame moves by its measured frame time), watched replays of a live session (the overlay shows the live window's mouse focus, which dummy always reports and a background window does not have) and a test that switches the display back to the run's driver part way through.

docs.title: On demand: nox -s compare-drivers
docs.text:
The session compares every driver configuration available on this machine with every other, an N-way matrix (scripts/driver_configurations.py lists them and finds which run here):

Configuration What runs Needs dummy SDL's windowless driver, run twice (a test whose frames differ between those runs is nondeterministic: it should be marked) nothing; always the baseline cocoa (windows, wayland, x11) the platform's own driver its platform (Linux: WAYLAND_DISPLAY or DISPLAY) x11-macos x11 on this Mac, drawing on XQuartz, through SDL built with x11 macOS, XQuartz, a C compiler and make x11-linux x11 in the Linux container of nox -s test-linux-x11, forwarded to XQuartz over TCP macOS, XQuartz (TCP enabled), Docker

The runs go one after another with four workers each (the container's too), so the machine stays usable. nox -s compare-drivers -- --drivers dummy,cocoa,x11-macos chooses configurations (dummy is always added: it is the baseline; one that cannot run here is refused with the reason), and other arguments select tests (-- tests/scenes). The tests that differ anywhere are re-run on every configuration saving their differing frames, and every differing pair gets both PNG files and a difference image under test-results/driver-comparison/nox/differences/<first>-vs-<second>/.

The report, test-results/driver-comparison/nox/matrix.md (and matrix.json), holds each run's time, a summary row per pair (tests compared, how many differ, by kind: pixels, size, present count, display, outcome), the patterns of agreement ("cocoa differs from all others", "x11-macos and x11-linux differ from dummy and cocoa"), a table per test file and, folded per file, a row per test with a cell per pair: agree, n/a (not recorded by both) or the first differing frame's index and kind with the differing pixel count linked to the difference image. The session prints the pair summary and the patterns at the end. It reports; it never fails on a difference.

It fails when a run recorded no test, naming the run: arguments that make pytest run nothing and exit 0 (-- --help, -- --collect-only) reach every run, and a report of empty runs would say every configuration agrees. It fails too when a pytest run cannot run at all. A comparison that fails or is interrupted never replaces the last complete one: while a comparison runs, the last complete one waits in test-results/driver-comparison/nox-previous/, and it goes back to test-results/driver-comparison/nox/ when the comparison fails; the failed comparison's runs are kept in test-results/driver-comparison/nox-failed/.

docs.title: x11 on macOS: SDL built with x11
docs.text: pygame-ce's macOS wheel bundles an SDL without x11. SDL's dynamic API loads another SDL at run time instead: with SDL_DYNAMIC_API=/path/libSDL2-2.0.0.dylib the wheel's SDL fills its jump table from that library, and every SDL call (pygame's, SDL_image's, SDL_mixer's, SDL_ttf's) runs it. nox -s build-sdl-x11 (run by compare-drivers when needed) builds the very version the wheel reports (pygame.get_sdl_version()) from its GitHub release tarball, its SHA-256 pinned per version in scripts/build_sdl_x11.py, with SDL's autotools build (SDL 2's CMake build never enables x11 on Apple platforms) and x11 against XQuartz's /opt/X11. Cocoa, Metal, Vulkan, MFi, OpenGL and OpenGL ES are left out: the wheel's SDL is loaded too, and two copies of SDL's Objective-C classes in one process make the runtime warn and risk crashes; OpenGL crashed workers on XQuartz (see the caveats below). The build lives in ~/Library/Caches/glitchygames/sdl-x11/<version>/ (never a system path) and is reused while its build.json matches; the session then checks that a child pygame opens and fills a window on XQuartz through it. The runs use SDL_VIDEODRIVER=x11, dummy audio and XQuartz's DISPLAY.

docs.title: x11 caveats
docs.text:
Both x11 configurations draw on XQuartz, a real X server with a window manager, so some tests see what a real desktop does and the dummy driver never shows (measured 2026-10-23, SDL 2.32.10, XQuartz 2.8):

Slow windows Creating a window on XQuartz takes about 0.75 s, so x11-macos ran the suite in 872 s (dummy 46 s, cocoa 110 s) and x11-linux, over TCP, in 552 s. Smallest window XQuartz's window manager widens a window narrower than 72 pixels (a 64x48 window becomes 72x48), so pygame warns "Requested window was forcibly resized by the OS" (an error in this suite). Tests open windows at least 96 pixels wide. Late resizes Resizing an existing window is asynchronous on x11. SDL waits 100 ms for the window manager, then keeps the old size (pygame warns as above) and the new size arrives on a later pump. On a loaded machine every resize came late (over TCP from the container, 8 processes resizing at once: 0.8-3.4 s), so a window changed from 800x600 to 800x480 reported the old size. The engine and the tests set the display mode through glitchygames.display_mode.set_display_mode, which pumps until the size changes and warns only if the window ends at another size than the requested one. Real window events The X server sends focus, exposure and move events for the real window; a recording made on x11 holds them, and tests that assume only the dummy driver's window events see them. Its raw messages (pygame's SYSWMEVENT) stay blocked unless a game opts in (NATIVE_WINDOW_MESSAGES); before 2026-10-23 the engine's allow-all enabled them, filling queues, recordings and instant-replay journals. No OpenGL (x11-macos) With OpenGL, SDL on macOS marks every window OpenGL, loading XQuartz's libGL and Apple's Xplugin into the process, and draws window surfaces through an OpenGL texture. Under load that ended pytest workers without a traceback (GLXBadContext in X_GLXMakeCurrent through Xlib's default error handler; a crash in SkyLight on Xplugin's event thread). The build leaves OpenGL out (--disable-video-opengl), so window surfaces are drawn in software, as in the container, which has no libGL. Root in the container (x11-linux) The container runs as root, who can read a file without read permission, so tests/templates/test_template_errors.py's permission test is skipped there (an outcome difference, not a failure). It runs with an init process (docker run --init) that reaps orphaned processes, as on a real system. Pixels No passing test drew different pixels on x11 than on dummy or cocoa; every x11 difference was a window size or a test's outcome (the two x11 configurations' pixels differed only in the final frames of tests that had already failed on the widened window).

docs.title: Linux in Docker: nox -s test-linux-x11
docs.text: The suite runs on Linux in a container (scripts/linux_x11/Dockerfile) with real X11 windows on the Mac's XQuartz (TCP enabled: defaults write org.xquartz.X11 nolisten_tcp -bool false, then restart XQuartz) and its sound on the Mac's PulseAudio (brew install pulseaudio; the project's .envrc installs it). The session starts XQuartz and, when it is not running, the PulseAudio server with TCP on port 4713, accepting connections without a cookie only from loopback and Docker's private ranges (127.0.0.1;192.168.0.0/16;172.16.0.0/12); both are left running afterwards (pulseaudio --kill stops PulseAudio). The container plays through it with SDL_AUDIODRIVER=pulseaudio and PULSE_SERVER=tcp:host.docker.internal:4713. Without PulseAudio, or when it will not start, one line says so and the container uses dummy audio. compare-drivers' x11-linux runs use dummy audio (frames do not depend on sound); --sound plays theirs through PulseAudio too.

docs.title: Linux as CI runs it: nox -s test-linux-ci
docs.text: nox -s test-linux-x11 runs the suite on Linux for its drivers; nox -s test-linux-ci runs it the way CircleCI's Linux job does, to reproduce that job's failures here. It reads the job (build-and-test-linux) from .circleci/config.yml: its image (cimg/python at PYTHON_LATEST_VERSION), its resource class's memory and CPUs (small: 2 GB, no swap, and one CPU, given to docker run as --memory, --memory-swap and --cpus) and its environment (PYTEST_WORKERS=0: one serial process; GLITCHYGAMES_TEST_RSS_LIMIT_MB=1600: tests/memory_guard.py stops the run past it, naming the test), with CI=true and CIRCLECI=true. The container gets what git would commit from this checkout: tracked files and untracked ones that are not ignored, uncommitted changes included, never an ignored file (the host's caches, Hypothesis's database) and no submodule's contents (CircleCI's checkout has none). Its .git is cloned from the repository's git directory, mounted read-only at its own path, so the session runs from a worktree too; HEAD is this checkout's, on its branch, and the remote branches are this checkout's, as fresh as its last fetch. It installs fontconfig, uv and Python at the job's versions, then nox as a uv tool, and runs nox -s test as the job does. Its test-results/ (junit.xml) come back to test-results/linux-ci/. The memory guard's summary line names the peak it saw (the container's memory less its page cache, what the kernel's 2 GB kill counts), and the last line the container's raw peak (the page cache included, so near 2 GB even on a healthy run). It takes as long as the job (a serial run) or longer: the image is amd64, as CircleCI's machines are (the same wheels: taplo has no arm64 Linux wheel, and building it ran out of the 2 GB), emulated on Apple silicon. Made on macOS; on a Linux host the results are made writable for any user.

docs.title: Replay Performance
docs.text:
How long the engine takes to process each frame of the recorded sessions (the golden replays in each game's tests/fixtures/replays/ and the demos bundled with the games), commit by commit. Every measurement replays a recording headless and unpaced on one machine (--rebaseline, which times each frame's work without the pacing sleep), so a line moves only when the code got faster or slower, or the machine changed. Times compare only on one machine: each machine (its CPU model) and kind of run is its own line. Requirements turns these measurements into a verdict per game for each measured machine.

These measurements replay one game alone in its process. When several games share a process (the Arcade), each keeps its own FPS statistics and shutdown report, the outer game's covering the whole tick; the engine context page's "Performance" section says what contexts cost and how each game's report stays its own.

Until a build generates them, this page has only this text.

docs.title: What the graphs show
docs.text:
The explorer above draws one chart at a time: pick the recording (grouped by game), the chart, the statistics (p50, p99, max) and the machines to compare. Each recording's own page, linked under it, shows every chart at once with the slowest-frame heatmaps.

Processing time per frame The median (p50), the 99th percentile (p99) and the slowest frame (max) of one replay, in milliseconds, by commit (oldest on the left, labelled with the short hash). A frame's budget at 60 FPS is 16.7 ms. Frames over budget Frames whose processing alone took longer than the budget. Live frame time For the runs that recorded a session live (paced, in a window), how long each frame really took, start to start: how steady pacing was. Replays have none. FPS by commit The same runs as frames per second. A live run's line (solid) is the FPS it achieved (1 / its frame time); it is paced, so it never passes the target (the dotted line, 1 / the frame budget). A replay's line (dashed) is its headroom (1 / its processing time): how fast the work alone could run. Each point is the average, with a bar from the "5% low" to the "5% high": the mean of the slowest and of the fastest 5% of frames (at least one frame; pause frames count; a live run's first frame, timed from the clock's start, does not). The axis is logarithmic, as headroom runs to thousands. Paced and unpaced numbers do not compare: the processor slows down between paced frames. Machines Each machine's latest replay, as a bar of its average headroom FPS with the same 5% low and high, so platforms compare at a glance for the same recording. Replays only; machines marked (CI) measured on continuous integration's virtual runners, which are noisy.

The figures are stored in seconds and turned into FPS only for display. Measurements from before them (2026-10-28) have no FPS point. glitchygames measure and glitchygames report print the same FPS beside the milliseconds.

  • Slowest frame across the recording, by commit: a heatmap per machine. Each column is a stretch of the recording (about 1% of it, start to end) and each row a commit; the color is the slowest frame of that stretch. Hover a cell for its frames, its scene and the time. It shows time only: whether the work itself changed (frames whose content hash differs) is what glitchygames report shows. Measurements from before per-frame profiles have no row.

Hover a point for the commit's date and when it was measured.

The game of the recording picked goes in the page's address (?game=mr-muncher), so a view can be linked: the link opens on that game's first recording.

Measurements made on a checkout with uncommitted changes (a trial: nox -s replay-metrics -- --allow-dirty) are never published: the published site leaves them out, while a local build (mkdocs build, mkdocs serve, nox -s docs-serve) shows them, labelled "uncommitted changes". They stay in the pending file after a deploy, so they remain visible locally only.

docs.title: Where the numbers come from
docs.text:
1. Every commit carries the measurements of its code. A pre-commit hook (scripts/measure_staged_replays.py, installed by .envrc) works out the code tree of what is being committed (src/glitchygames/code_tree.py: only what can change how the replays run, the engine, games, demos, apps, recordings, uv.lock and pyproject.toml). When this machine has not measured that code yet, it measures every golden replay and bundled demo on it and adds one small file per recording to the commit, under quality/replay-ledger/. A docs commit after a measured one is instant; code that arrived by a merge from main or a rebase is measured by the next commit (or by hand: nox -s measure-staged, then commit, which also adds a machine without the hook). SKIP=replay-metrics git commit ... skips it. A pre-push hook (scripts/measure_on_raspberry_pi.py) measures the same way on the Raspberry Pis (a Pi 4 and a Pi 5, ansible/inventory.yml's raspberry_pis), both at once, and copies their row files here, staged. A push that brings rows stops so they can be committed, and the next one goes through; a Pi that cannot be reached stops the push before any Pi measures (by hand: nox -s measure-on-raspberry-pi; SKIP=raspberry-pi-replay-metrics git push ... skips it).
  2. The site shows what landed on main. Every docs build reads the repository's row files and keeps each row whose code tree is the code tree of the commit that added its file: on main, the squash merge, so each is shown under the commit its code landed in (code that returns to an earlier tree is shown under the commit that brought it back). Rows of a branch's intermediate commits name another tree and are left out. Each commit's tree is taken with the measured paths its own pyproject.toml names, so changing them later never drops earlier rows. A local build shows a branch's rows before it merges, each as its own point labelled <commit> unlanded (the commit it was measured on top of); only main is ever published (nox -s docs-deploy refuses anything else). This needs squash merges: a merge commit brings its branch's commits into main's history, and each that added rows would land its own (intermediate) code tree, so pull requests are squash-merged only. After each merge to main, CircleCI deploys the site with them; CI never measures (its machines vary).
  3. The history measured before this (rows naming their commit) was moved into the repository too (scripts/import_published_ledger.py). nox -s replay-metrics still measures by hand (glitchygames measure) into the local pending file (test-results/replay-metrics/pending.jsonl), which a local build shows.

The measuring and the pages are the engine's tools, so any game can keep its own ledger the same way (Tools for any game), with the paths in its [tool.glitchygames] (ours: ledger-directory, pending-ledger, published-ledger, measured-paths):

uv run glitchygames unmeasured --game <game>   # what is not measured yet on this machine
uv run glitchygames measure --game <game>      # measure it into the pending ledger
uv run glitchygames performance-pages <directory>   # the ledger and one graph page per recording

(<game> --measure, --unmeasured and --performance-pages <directory> are the same tools as the game's own flags.) Our docs build makes these pages through scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py and scripts/generate_performance_graphs.py, which only add our docs paths and the snippet above.

A recording holds its own last ten runs too; uv run glitchygames report PATH (or <game> --report PATH) prints them, which frames got slower or faster between runs (only frames that did the same work, by their content hash), and where behavior changed (the frames whose content hash differs, with both runs' commits). Design: plans/2026-10-23-recording-metrics.md (Parts 1 and 2).

docs.title: What logging costs
docs.text:
A benchmark rebaselines every golden replay and bundled demo headless three times, through the same child command glitchygames measure runs: at --log-level warning (the replay tools' level and a game's default: logging off), at --log-level info (what a bug report asks a player to run with) and at --log-level debug (everything on). It is not part of the test run (nox -s test; it takes under a minute), but CI runs it with the other benchmarks in the macOS job's nox -s performance-test, where a failed rebaseline fails the job. Run it alone with

uv run pytest tests/benchmarks/test_logging_cost.py -o addopts= -p no:xdist --benchmark-only --dummy-only

or with every other benchmark in nox -s performance-test. It prints two tables and writes them to test-results/logging-cost.md:

  1. Top loggers by volume at debug, per recording: each recording's five chattiest loggers, with their records per frame, record count and share of all the records. A logger far ahead of the others (tens of records a frame) is where logging needs cleaning up: a log.debug inside a per-frame or per-sprite loop.
  2. Logging cost: per recording, the mean processing time per frame at each level and the change of info and of debug against warning, the medians, each run's peak resident memory, the records per frame at each level and how much output info and debug wrote. The processing times are the engine's own per-frame measurements (what the performance graphs above plot), so the change is the time logging adds to each frame's work. Times compare only on one machine and between runs of the same table. The peak memory is the replaying child's (n/a on Windows), and its output goes to a file, so a large difference there means the game keeps records in memory.

On one Mac (2026-10-28) info cost every recording within 1% of warning (0.08 to 0.33 records a frame), while debug doubled PaddleSlap's processing time per frame (about 10 records a frame) and added 15% to Brave Adventurer's papyrus golden (about 33).

At warning no recording should emit an INFO or DEBUG record (the startup options block is one CRITICAL record a run): a logger that does has a level set behind the command line's back (BUGS.md #236), which tests/replay/test_replays_log_quietly.py and tests/test_logger_levels_at_import.py fail on in the ordinary test run.

docs.title: Upstream Issues
docs.text:
Problems found in the tools this project depends on, worked around here, to be reported to their projects. Each entry holds the evidence an upstream report needs: the versions, the measurements, how the cause was found, a reproduction, and the issue text drafted for posting. None has been posted yet.

When a release fixes one, upgrade, check the reproduction no longer shows it, remove the workaround and move the entry to the Fixed section.

docs.title: mkdocs serve keeps every rebuild alive (griffe and mkdocstrings-python)
docs.text:
Found 2026-10-24, BUGS.md #213. A local mkdocs serve (nox -s docs-serve) was at 14.5 GB.

Versions: griffe (griffelib) 2.4.1, mkdocstrings 1.0.8, mkdocstrings-python 2.0.10, mkdocs 1.6.1, Python 3.14, macOS. Both griffe and mkdocstrings-python were the latest releases on PyPI when this was measured.

Measurements (resident memory after each build; the same inputs every time):

Build Four builds in one process, as serve builds With the workaround mkdocs serve, with the workaround start 674 MB 0 694 MB 688 MB 1 1016 MB 685 MB 913 MB 2 1375 MB 718 MB 936 MB 3 1532 MB 647 MB 920 MB 4 905 MB 5 928 MB

About 330 MB per rebuild was never freed, though gc.collect() ran after each build. In the live server (last column, rebuilds triggered by touching docs/index.md) the first rebuild raised it to about 920 MB, and it stayed there.

How the cause was found:

  1. Not the data: the graphs this project's hook generates are a few kilobytes, and its scripts load once (sys.modules stayed at 736 modules over the builds).
  2. Counting live objects by type across one build: the growth was griffe's models (ExprName +23,876, Alias +17,512, Parameter +9,304, Function +4,314, ...), mkdocstrings' InventoryItem and autorefs' BacklinkCrumb: a whole API tree and its handler per build. Weak references to each build's config and Python handler showed every one still alive.
  3. The old handler's referrers were all inside the build (the mkdocstrings plugin, its Markdown extension and AutoDocProcessor), so something outside reached that group. Clearing every populated functools cache in the process freed the first build's handler (958 -> 521 MB).
  4. Clearing the suspect caches one at a time: mkdocstrings-python's _test_existing_template freed the old handler (959 MB, its tree still held), then griffe's _dataclass_parameters freed the tree (530 MB). Clearing others after those changed nothing.

The two caches:

  • griffe, griffe/_internal/extensions/dataclasses.py:
@cache
def _dataclass_parameters(class_: Class) -> list[Parameter]:

An unbounded cache keyed by Class objects. Each Class references its module and the whole modules collection, so one entry keeps the build's entire API tree (about 430 MB here). - mkdocstrings-python, mkdocstrings_handlers/python/_internal/rendering.py:

@cache
@pass_environment
def _test_existing_template(env: Environment, path: str) -> bool:
    return path in env.list_templates()

Keyed by the Jinja Environment, which each build makes afresh; through it the cache keeps the build's PythonHandler.

Reproduction: run from a project whose mkdocs.yml uses mkdocstrings' Python handler on a package with dataclasses (uv run python repeat_builds.py 4):

"""Build the docs several times in one process, as mkdocs serve does, printing memory after each."""

import gc
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

from mkdocs.commands.build import build
from mkdocs.config import load_config


def resident_megabytes() -> int:
    output = subprocess.run(
        ['ps', '-o', 'rss=', '-p', str(os.getpid())], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True
    ).stdout
    return int(output) // 1024


site_directory = tempfile.mkdtemp()
for build_number in range(int(sys.argv[1])):
    # serve loads the config afresh for every rebuild (mkdocs/commands/serve.py builder())
    config = load_config(config_file='mkdocs.yml', site_dir=site_directory)
    config.plugins.on_startup(command='serve', dirty=False)
    build(config, serve_url='http://127.0.0.1:8002/')
    del config
    gc.collect()
    print(f'build {build_number}: resident {resident_megabytes()} MB', flush=True)

To name the caches, after two builds clear one at a time and watch the first build's handler (weakref.ref(config.plugins['mkdocstrings'].handlers.get_handler('python'))) and resident memory:

caches = {
    f'{item.__module__}.{item.__qualname__}': item
    for item in gc.get_objects()
    if isinstance(item, functools._lru_cache_wrapper) and item.cache_info().currsize
}
for name in [
    'mkdocstrings_handlers.python._internal.rendering._test_existing_template',
    'griffe._internal.extensions.dataclasses._dataclass_parameters',
]:
    caches[name].cache_clear()
    gc.collect()
    print(name, 'first handler alive:', first_handler() is not None, resident_megabytes(), 'MB')

Workaround here: on_post_build in scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py empties every module-level functools cache of the loaded griffe and mkdocstrings modules after each build (documentation_caches() finds them by scanning the modules, so a renamed cache is still found); tested in tests/test_generate_complexity_graphs.py. The caches only speed up work within one build, so emptying them between builds costs nothing. Remove both, and their tests, when both projects have fixed theirs.

Issue drafted for griffe (github.com/mkdocstrings/griffe):

_dataclass_parameters cache keeps every mkdocs serve rebuild's API tree alive

griffe/_internal/extensions/dataclasses.py decorates _dataclass_parameters(class_) with an unbounded functools.cache keyed by Class objects. Under mkdocs serve, each rebuild loads a new API tree, and the cache keeps the previous trees reachable (each Class references its module and the whole collection). With griffe 2.4.1 on a package of about 4,000 functions, memory grew by about 330 MB per rebuild (694 -> 1016 -> 1375 -> 1532 MB over four in-process builds, gc.collect() after each); calling _dataclass_parameters.cache_clear() after each build kept it flat (about 690 MB).

Suggestion: cache on the Class instance (e.g. a private attribute), or in a weakref.WeakKeyDictionary, so the cache dies with the tree.

Reproduction: load the config and call mkdocs.commands.build.build(config) several times in one process, gc.collect() between, tracking resident memory (script attached).

Issue drafted for mkdocstrings-python (github.com/mkdocstrings/python):

_test_existing_template cache keeps every rebuild's handler and Jinja environment alive

mkdocstrings_handlers/python/_internal/rendering.py decorates _test_existing_template(env, path) with functools.cache, keyed by the Jinja Environment. Each mkdocs serve rebuild makes a new environment, so the cache keeps every previous one and, through it, the previous PythonHandler (mkdocstrings-python 2.0.10). Clearing it after each build frees the old handler.

Suggestion: cache per environment (on env itself, or in a weakref.WeakKeyDictionary).

docs.title: sound_board_demo
docs.text:
Sound Board Demo: hear every built-in wave and noise, and compare notes, hertz and steps.

Run it with the sound-board-demo console script or python -m sound_board_demo.

One row per built-in wave and noise, each row showing the eight notes of C major. The keys:

  • 1-8 play the current row's notes.
  • Up and Down pick the row (the current row is lit).
  • L cycles the labels between note names, hertz and scale steps. Only the labels change: the same pitches play.
  • C plays a C major chord on the current row.

The Audio debug panel is on by default (--sound-diagnostics): it shows the voices playing and the compile log. Every sound is requested in setup(), so the log shows only setup compiles and playing a key never compiles anything.

docs.title: glitchy.games website on AWS — Design
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-10-27
  • Status: DRAFT, awaiting the owner's review. Nothing is built yet.
  • Repo: glitchygames (this repo). The site and its AWS setup live here; no separate repo.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
Put the GlitchyGames Arcade on the public web. A visitor opens play.glitchy.games and gets the arcade (the gallery in the owner's mockup: a featured demo with sound on top, a grid of live silent demo tiles below, arrows / d-pad to browse, Enter / A to play). Every game runs in the visitor's own browser (Pyodide/WebAssembly; plans/2026-10-23-game-host-and-browser-runner.md, scripts/build_browser_bundle.py), so the server only serves files.

Later, a GPU instance on AWS will run AI work (e.g. Bitmappy's AI sprite generation, AI players driven through the outer GameHost layer). It is out of scope to build now, but it is scoped into the cost estimate.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. https://play.glitchy.games serves the browser build, over HTTPS, fast worldwide.
  2. Every push to main on GitHub publishes the site automatically.
  3. The AWS setup is code in this repo, reproducible from scratch.
  4. Launch cost stays around $1.50–2.50 / month.
  5. The owner hears about it (email) before an AWS bill surprises them.

docs.title: Non-goals (for now)
docs.text:
• No servers at launch: no EC2, Lightsail, containers or databases.
  • No GPU instance yet (later phase, below).
  • No home page at glitchy.games yet — it redirects to play.glitchy.games.
  • No docs site yet (docs.glitchy.games is reserved for the MkDocs site, later).
  • The 24 other domains the owner holds at Namecheap (glitchygames.*, twitchplaysglitchy*) stay untouched.
  • Not transferring any domain registration away from Namecheap.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• Long-lived AWS access keys stored in GitHub.
  • A setup that only works because of hand-clicked console changes nobody can reproduce.
  • A bill that can grow silently (runaway GPU instance, traffic spike) without an alert.

docs.title: Constraints and facts
docs.text:
• AWS account: the owner's existing, long-standing account. It is past the old 12-month free tier and was created before the July 15, 2025 credit-based free plan, so only the "Always Free" allowances apply (CloudFront: 1 TB transfer and 10M requests / month; Lambda; DynamoDB).
  • Domains: registered at Namecheap (namecheap.com). Two are in scope: glitchy.games and glitchygames.ai.
  • Region: us-east-1 (CloudFront certificates must live there; cheapest GPU pricing later).
  • Browser build: scripts/build_browser_bundle.py (on main) writes build/browser/<game>: the page, the engine and our pygame-ce WebAssembly wheel. The wheel is built from the third_party/pygame-ce submodule and takes several minutes the first time.
  • The games already build as a site: python -m scripts.build_browser_bundle all writes build/browser/site (a directory per game plus an index.html linking them). nox -s docs-deploy runs it and publishes it with the docs as play/ on GitHub Pages (https://terrysimons.github.io/glitchygames/play/; scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py).
  • PyScript comes from a CDN: browser/index.html loads core.js / core.css from pyscript.net.
  • The Arcade app (plans/2026-10-23-arcade-showcase.md, feature #43) is a spec, not built. src/apps/ holds only Bitmappy today.
  • CI is CircleCI (.circleci/config.yml); there is no .github/. Its deploy-docs job runs after build-and-test-macos passes on main (macOS m4pro.medium, one at a time via serial-group), already caches the Pyodide toolchain (~2 GB) and the pygame-ce WebAssembly wheel keyed on the submodule commit, and runs nox -s docs-deploy -- --no-measure.
  • House style: uv, nox sessions, Python 3.14, explicit long names.

docs.title: Decided by the owner
docs.text: Decision Choice Hosting provider Amazon (AWS) Where the code lives this glitchygames repo Main address play.glitchy.games serves the Arcade glitchy.games (bare) redirects to play.glitchy.games for now; a home page may replace it later glitchygames.ai in scope (redirects; see below) Other 24 domains not now Publishing automatically on every push to main on GitHub (through the existing CircleCI pipeline) Spec location docs/specs/ Placeholder until the Arcade exists, the owner's mockup image is the placeholder GPU later, for AI work; include it in the cost picture only

docs.title: Address map
docs.text:
Address Behaviour play.glitchy.games the site (S3 via CloudFront) glitchy.games, www.glitchy.games 301 to https://play.glitchy.games (path kept) glitchygames.ai, www.glitchygames.ai 301 to https://play.glitchy.games (path kept) http:// anything upgraded to https:// docs.glitchy.games, ai.glitchy.games reserved, later phases

Redirect choices (301, path kept, www folded) are Claude's call. Keeping one canonical address matters beyond SEO: browser storage (the Arcade's saves, browser/browser_storage.py) is per-origin, so serving the site on two origins would split players' saves.

docs.title: Architecture (Claude's call unless noted)
docs.text:
Namecheap (registrar only)
                   | nameservers -> Route 53
                   v
 Route 53 zone: glitchy.games          Route 53 zone: glitchygames.ai
   play  -> ALIAS site distribution      @, www -> ALIAS redirect distribution
   @,www -> ALIAS redirect distribution
                   |                                   |
                   v                                   v
 CloudFront "site" distribution        CloudFront "redirect" distribution
   - origin: private S3 bucket (OAC)     - no real origin; a CloudFront Function
   - HTTPS cert (ACM, us-east-1)           answers every request with a 301 to
   - compression on                        https://play.glitchy.games<path>
   - response headers policy             - HTTPS cert (ACM) for the four names
                   |
                   v
 S3 bucket (private, versioned) holding build/browser/...
  • DNS: move the nameservers of both domains to Route 53 at Namecheap (one manual step per domain, done once). Route 53 then holds every record as code. $0.50 / zone / month.
  • Certificates: ACM in us-east-1, DNS-validated in Route 53 (automatic once the zones exist). Six names total, under ACM's default 10-name limit. Free.
  • S3: private bucket, CloudFront Origin Access Control, Block Public Access on. Versioning on so a bad deploy can be rolled back; a lifecycle rule expires old versions after 30 days.
  • CloudFront (site):
  • Serve .wasm as application/wasm (set at upload) and enable compression (gzip/brotli) for the large Pyodide / wheel / Python files.
  • Cache: index.html short (e.g. 60 s) so deploys show quickly; other assets long.
  • Response headers: HSTS and standard security headers. No COOP/COEP (cross-origin isolation): the build loads PyScript from pyscript.net, which COEP would block, and the runner uses JS Promise Integration rather than threads, so it doesn't need SharedArrayBuffer. If that ever changes, the bundle must self-host PyScript first. No strict Content-Security-Policy for the same reason (or one that allows pyscript.net and Pyodide's CDN — builder's call).
  • PriceClass_100 (North America + Europe edges) to keep costs down — Claude's call; widen later if needed.
  • CloudFront (redirect): separate distribution with a CloudFront Function (viewer request) returning the 301. Could instead be one distribution with a host-header check; two keeps the site's config simple. Builder may merge if it's cleaner.
  • Budget alarm: AWS Budgets, monthly, email the owner at $10 actual and at forecast > $10.

docs.title: Infrastructure as code (Claude's call)
docs.text:
• AWS CDK in Python, in infra/ as its own small uv project (own pyproject.toml), so the engine's dependencies don't change.
  • nox sessions in the existing style: nox -s infra-deploy, nox -s infra-diff, nox -s site-publish (build + sync + invalidate, also usable locally).
  • Stacks: DnsAndCertificates, Site, Redirects, GitHubDeployRole, Budget. Names are the builder's to settle.
  • First deploy (cdk bootstrap + deploy) runs from the owner's Mac with admin credentials.

docs.title: Publishing (owner: on every push to main)
docs.text:
The repo's CI is CircleCI, which already builds the browser games on every merge to main, so publishing to AWS joins that pipeline (Claude's call: no GitHub Actions, one CI system).

  • A new nox -s site-publish session: syncs a built site directory to the bucket (aws s3 sync --delete, .wasm as application/wasm, short cache on index.html files, long on the rest) and invalidates the CloudFront distribution. Also runnable from the owner's Mac.
  • CircleCI: after docs-deploy has built build/browser/site, run nox -s site-publish on that same directory — either as a final step of the deploy-docs job (no second ~2 GB toolchain restore) or a separate job that receives the directory through a workspace. The builder picks; Claude's lean is a step in deploy-docs, since it already holds the build. A failed AWS publish must not undo or block the GitHub Pages docs deploy that already pushed.
  • Credentials: CircleCI OIDC (no stored AWS keys). The AWS role trusts CircleCI's OIDC provider for this organization and project only, and may only write to the site bucket and create invalidations on the site distribution. The organization ID and project ID are values the owner reads from CircleCI's settings.
  • serial-group already keeps two merges from deploying at once.
  • Infra changes (infra/**): Claude's call is to keep these manual (nox -s infra-deploy) at first. Automating them is a later option.
  • GitHub Pages play/ keeps publishing as today; once play.glitchy.games is live, the docs' "Play in the Browser" link (mkdocs.yml) points to it. Whether to stop publishing play/ on GitHub Pages is a later cleanup.

docs.title: What gets published at launch
docs.text:
The Arcade does not exist yet. Until it does, play.glitchy.games serves a placeholder built around the owner's mockup image (the gallery screenshot), stored in the repo. When the Arcade app lands, the arcade bundle replaces it.

OPEN (owner): the games already build as a playable site (build/browser/site). The placeholder could link to them (each game at play.glitchy.games/<game>/), or the mockup could stand alone until the Arcade is ready.

docs.title: Launch (monthly, us-east-1)
docs.text:
Item Cost Route 53 hosted zones (2) $1.00 Route 53 queries ~$0 S3 storage (~100 MB incl. versions) + requests ~$0.05 CloudFront (within Always Free 1 TB / 10M req) $0 ACM certificates $0 CloudFront Functions (2M free invocations / month) $0 AWS Budgets (first 2 budgets free) $0 Total ~$1.50–2.50

Plus existing Namecheap renewals (unchanged). Pyodide-based pages are ~10–30 MB per first visit, so 1 TB covers roughly 35–100k first-time visitors / month before CloudFront charges (~$0.085/GB in NA/EU).

docs.title: Later: GPU for AI work (not built now)
docs.text:
Prices from third-party trackers (verify on AWS before buying):

Instance GPU On-demand 24/7 Start/stop on demand g4dn.xlarge NVIDIA T4, 16 GB ~$0.53/hr ~$384/mo ~$20–60/mo g6.xlarge NVIDIA L4, 24 GB ~$0.80/hr ~$588/mo ~$30–90/mo

Plus EBS storage (~$8/mo per 100 GB gp3) and ~$3.60/mo for a public IPv4 while running. Spot pricing is often 60–70% lower. New accounts usually have a GPU (G-family) vCPU quota of 0 — check and request an increase well before it's needed. "Dedicated Instances" (AWS's single-tenant option) cost extra and aren't needed; a normal on-demand instance is the owner's own machine.

docs.title: Manual steps for the owner
docs.text:
1. Run the first nox -s infra-deploy with admin AWS credentials.
  2. At Namecheap, set custom nameservers for glitchy.games and glitchygames.ai to the four Route 53 nameservers each zone reports.
  3. Confirm the AWS Budgets email subscription.

docs.title: Today's DNS (checked 2026-10-27 with dig)
docs.text: Both domains are identical: Namecheap BasicDNS (dns1/dns2.registrar-servers.com), a Namecheap parking page on @ and www, Namecheap email forwarding (MX eforward1-5.registrar-servers.com and TXT v=spf1 include:spf.efwd.registrar-servers.com ~all), no play record, and no DS record (DNSSEC off), so a nameserver move needs no DNSSEC step. Nothing but the parking page is served, so propagation time costs nothing.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• DNS cutover and email forwarding: see "Today's DNS". Namecheap's email forwarding is configured in Namecheap's panel and expects Namecheap DNS; whether it keeps working with the MX and SPF records copied into Route 53 must be verified (or the owner confirms the forwarding is unused).
  • .games / .ai nameserver changes can take up to 48 h to propagate; certificate validation waits on it.
  • CI build time: already handled; deploy-docs caches the toolchain and wheel.
  • Third-party CDN: the site depends on pyscript.net (and Pyodide's CDN) being up. Self- hosting them is a later option.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• Exact stack/construct names, bucket names, cache TTLs, CloudFront Function code.
  • Whether redirects share the site distribution or have their own.
