docs.title: Sprite QuickLook preview for macOS — Design
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-10-29
  • Status: BUILT on feat/sprite-quicklook (2026-10-29); the owner checked it in the real QuickLook panel and opened a PR. Plan: plans/2026-10-29-sprite-quicklook-implementation.md. How to build and install: src/quicklook/README.md.
  • Repo / location: glitchygames (this repo), under src/quicklook/ (the owner, 2026-10-29).

docs.title: Intent
docs.text: When the owner selects a GlitchyGames sprite .toml in Finder and presses space, QuickLook shows the sprite itself — rendered as the sprite, not the TOML text (the owner: "I want to see what the file contents are - rendered as the sprite"). Animated sprites play; static sprites show as one image.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Static sprites ([sprite] pixels = """…""", no [[animation]], e.g. src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/resources/sprites/small_heart.toml) render as a single image.
  2. Animated sprites ([[animation]] + [[animation.frame]], e.g. slime-jump.toml at the repo root) auto-play as soon as the preview opens (the owner, 2026-10-29), honoring each animation's frame_interval, each frame's own frame_interval override, and loop.
  3. Pixel art stays crisp: scaled up with nearest-neighbor to fill the preview, integer scale factors only, centered.
  4. Matches what the engine draws (rules below, taken from src/glitchygames/sprites/animated.py and pixel_utils.py). If the preview and the game disagree, the preview is wrong.
  5. Transparency is visible: transparent pixels show a checkerboard behind them; partial alpha blends over it.
  6. Every frame is visible: a film strip per animation (the owner, 2026-10-29: "we need to show all of the frames of the sprite"). Any sprite with more than one frame or more than one animation previews as one row per animation, in file order:
  7. the animation's name on the left; every frame left to right, each with its number above it and its duration below it ("0.50s"), wrapping onto more lines rather than scrolling sideways (the owner chose the annotated layout, number on top and timing on the bottom);
  8. the live animation playing at the right end of the row on a checkerboard, labeled "playing", "playing (once)" for a non-looping animation, or "still" for a one-frame one; the frame on screen is outlined in blue in its strip;
  9. every row plays at once from the moment the preview opens, which replaces the old picker. Claude's calls (the owner agreed 2026-10-29): strip frames fit a 64 pt cell and the live view a 192 pt box, both at a whole-number scale unless the sprite is bigger than that; the panel scrolls vertically when the rows don't fit; a static sprite (one animation, one frame) keeps the single large view, since a one-frame strip would only repeat it.
  10. Non-sprite .toml files (pyproject.toml, .taplo.toml, …) still preview as plain text. macOS gives every .toml the single type public.toml, so the extension is asked for all of them; it must fall back gracefully. An extension can't hand a file back to Apple's built-in text preview, so the fallback is the extension's own scrollable, monospaced, read-only text view with no highlighting. The owner accepted that it will look slightly different from Apple's (2026-10-29).
  11. No Python needed at preview time: parsing and rendering are native Swift.
  12. Finder thumbnails (the owner, 2026-10-29): icon view, column view, Get Info and the like show the sprite instead of a generic TOML icon. A QuickLook Thumbnail Extension sits in the same host app as the preview extension, and both use one shared parser/renderer.
  13. The thumbnail is the first frame of the first animation in file order (the frame that plays first in the preview). For a static sprite it is the single image.
  14. It is scaled nearest-neighbor to fit the requested size, centered, and transparent pixels stay transparent (no checkerboard), so it sits on Finder's own background.
  15. A sprite smaller than the requested size is scaled up by a whole-number factor. A sprite that doesn't divide evenly may be scaled down nearest-neighbor; it must never be smoothed.
  16. Non-sprite .toml files get no custom thumbnail. The extension fails the request, so Finder keeps the normal TOML icon. The builder must confirm that a failed thumbnail request really does fall back to the default icon (not a blank one) on this macOS.

docs.title: Non-goals (v1)
docs.text:
• No editing; preview only.
  • No hitbox / frame-anchor overlays, no [[transition]] state-machine playback.
  • No swatch (palette-swap) variants: the [colors] palette as written is what renders.
  • No distribution: no notarization, App Store, or Homebrew cask. It runs on the owner's Mac.

docs.title: Anti-goals (would make it a failure even if it works)
docs.text:
• Rendering that disagrees with the engine (wrong colors, transparency, frame order or timing).
  • Blurry / smoothed pixels.
  • Breaking QuickLook for ordinary .toml files.
  • Touching the engine or third_party/ (see the owner's "leave third_party alone" rule).

docs.title: The format, as the engine reads it
docs.text:
Source of truth: AnimatedSprite._load_toml and helpers in src/glitchygames/sprites/animated.py, plus src/glitchygames/sprites/pixel_utils.py.

Is it a sprite? It is if the parsed TOML has either a non-empty animation array of tables, or sprite.pixels. Anything else → plain-text fallback. A file that is a sprite but fails to render (bad TOML, no frames) shows a short error plus the text, never a blank pane.

Colors — [colors], keyed by a one-glyph string. Both forms appear in the repo: [colors."a"] sub-tables and inline tables ("█" = { red = 255, green = 0, blue = 255 }). Missing red/green/blue default to 0. alpha is optional: - absent → opaque RGB; - 0–254 → that alpha; - 255 → opaque.

Glyphs are Unicode code points, not bytes and not grapheme clusters. Python iterates a str by code point; Swift must iterate unicodeScalars to match (e.g. █ U+2588 is one pixel).

Transparency (is_color_transparent): a pixel is transparent when its color is magenta (255, 0, 255) with no alpha or alpha 255, or when its alpha is 0. Glyphs missing from [colors] render as magenta, i.e. transparent.

Pixel rows (static sprites and animation frames alike, normalize_pixel_rows): one rule since 2026-10-30, described in docs/specs/2026-10-30-unified-pixel-rows-design.md. Nothing is cut off; short rows are padded with transparent pixels to the longest. That design's "Before and after" table records the two rules this preview first copied (R4, animated: per-line strip, most common length, truncate, pad with the row's last glyph; R5, static: whole-string strip, longest row, pad with the most common glyph).

Animations: each [[animation]] has namespace (default "default"), frame_interval (seconds, default 0.5), loop (default true), and frame entries. Frames play in frame_index order, a frame without one at its file position, ties in file order (the engine's frame_tables_in_load_order; until 2026-10-31 the engine's sort was a no-op and frames played in file order, BUGS.md #232). Frames whose pixels are empty are skipped. A frame's own frame_interval overrides the animation's. A non-looping animation stops on its last frame.

Static sprite name: the single animation is named after sprite.name (default "idle").

docs.title: Decided "how" (the owner agreed in conversation; marked where it was Claude's call)
docs.text:
• A QuickLook Preview Extension inside a tiny host app — the only mechanism current macOS loads (the old .qlgenerator plugins are gone). Swift, AppKit/SwiftUI, Xcode 27.1 (installed). (Claude's call, agreed.)
  • Location: src/quicklook/ in this repo (the owner).
  • Auto-play on open (the owner).
  • Signing: this Mac has no code-signing identity, so the build uses ad-hoc "Sign to Run Locally". Install = copy the app to /Applications, open it once, enable the extension in System Settings if macOS asks. If macOS refuses an ad-hoc-signed extension, the fallback is the owner adding a free Apple ID team in Xcode — that is a step the owner does, not the builder.

docs.title: Claude's calls (from the builder check; the owner can override)
docs.text:
• Timing is wall-clock: each frame shows for exactly its frame_interval. The engine's per-tick rounding is not simulated.
  • Engine-exact for well-formed files. Malformed files may differ from the engine but must still render something sensible. Ragged rows are common in AI-generated sprites, so the preview copies both row-normalization rules. Duplicate namespace values show one label per distinct name, using the later table (which is where the engine reads its frames from).
  • No other .toml QuickLook extension is installed (checked with pluginkit, 2026-10-29), so there is nothing to compete with.

docs.title: Left to the builder
docs.text:
• TOML parsing: a vetted TOML 1.0 Swift package via SwiftPM (preferred, must handle inline tables, multi-line basic strings, quoted keys like ".") or a hand-written parser with tests. Results must match tomllib on every sprite in the repo.
  • How the Xcode project is generated/checked in (plain .xcodeproj, or XcodeGen if installed).
  • Preview UI details: label row styling, background, checkerboard size, maximum scale, dark mode.
  • A Makefile/script for build + install, and a short src/quicklook/README.md on installing, enabling, and resetting QuickLook (qlmanage -r, qlmanage -p <file> to test).
  • Animation timing mechanism (timer / display link), as long as per-frame durations are honored.

docs.title: How we know it works
docs.text:
• Swift unit tests for the parser + renderer: color forms, alpha rules, Unicode glyphs, both row normalization rules, frame sort order, per-frame intervals, static vs animated detection, non-sprite fallback.
  • A golden check: for a set of repo sprites (at least small_heart.toml, slime-jump.toml, slime-jump-alpha.toml, drawing_fire/sprites/soldier.toml, and one with [[transition]]), the frames the Swift renderer produces match RGBA frames dumped by the engine's own loader (a small Python script in src/quicklook/ that loads with AnimatedSprite and writes the frames out).
  • Manual: qlmanage -p on a static sprite, an animated one, and pyproject.toml; then space-bar in Finder.
  • Thumbnails: a unit test that the thumbnail image equals frame 0 scaled; then manually qlmanage -t -s 256 <file> on a static sprite, an animated one and pyproject.toml, and a look at a sprite folder in Finder icon view. Finder caches thumbnails, so reset first (qlmanage -r cache).

docs.title: Engine quirks noticed (reported, not fixed here)
docs.text:
• frame_index never orders frames: the engine's sort key reads an attribute no frame has, so frames play in file order. The preview copies that; tracked in plans/future-work.md. Fixed 2026-10-31 (BUGS.md #232): the engine and the preview both order frames by frame_index.

  • Static and animated sprites normalize ragged rows differently (longest row + most-common-glyph pad vs most-common length + last-glyph pad + truncation), and static rows are not stripped per line. The preview copies both behaviors so it matches the engine. The owner wants the engine unified later, on its own branch. Done 2026-10-30 (feat/unified-pixel-rows, docs/specs/2026-10-30-unified-pixel-rows-design.md); the preview follows the one rule. That is tracked in plans/future-work.md under "Bugs found and not fixed yet"; when it lands, the QuickLook parser and its golden frames change with it.

docs.title: Changed while building (2026-10-29)
docs.text:
• Frames play in file order, not frame_index order: the engine's sort is a no-op (see above).
  • CRLF files: tomllib turns CRLF into LF inside multi-line strings and TOMLDecoder doesn't, so SpriteCore turns every CRLF into LF before decoding.
  • The preview pre-scales each frame with nearest neighbor (offscreen renders blurred without it), capped at 512 px on the long side so a full-screen preview stays small; the layer's nearest-neighbor filter scales the rest. A sprite bigger than the preview shrinks to fit.
  • Thumbnails fit the pixels a Retina display really gives them (request.scale), and are drawn as a canvas of the whole requested size with the sprite centered on both axes (the owner, 2026-10-29: they were bottom-left anchored). QuickLook's thumbnail context is in pixels, so the image is drawn over the context's real bounds, not its point size.
  • Float color channels (red = 255.0) draw, truncated like pygame-ce does, instead of failing.
  • Film strip (goal 6, the owner, 2026-10-29) replaced the animation picker: every animation shows every frame at once. Layout is Sources/SpriteCore/FilmStripLayout.swift (unit-tested); the view is App/PreviewExtension/FilmStripView.swift. Checked offscreen with the render harness on player.toml (4 animations), slime-jump.toml (20 frames, wraps) and small_heart.toml (static, single view unchanged).
  • The app is named "GlitchyGames Sprite Preview" (the owner, 2026-10-29); the extensions are "GlitchyGames Sprite Preview" and "GlitchyGames Sprite Thumbnails". Bundle identifiers keep games.glitchy.SpritePreview. make install deletes the build copy after installing, because left on disk it registered again and showed in System Settings as a second app with no extensions.
  • App icon: shroom4.toml (the owner's pick), drawn by src/quicklook/tools/make_app_icon.py with the engine's loader, nearest neighbor on the preview's checkerboard in Apple's rounded square. macOS shows it as is (no gray backing plate).
  • qlmanage -t can't check thumbnail extensions on this macOS: it only uses old generators and hangs. Thumbnails are checked with src/quicklook/tools/make_thumbnails.swift, which uses Finder's API. Non-sprite .toml files keep the plain document icon they had before (checked with the extension switched off).

docs.title: One rule for sprite pixel rows — Design
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-10-30
  • Status: BUILT on feat/unified-pixel-rows (2026-10-30), from plans/2026-10-30-unified-pixel-rows-implementation.md. Was: DESIGN, approved (the owner, 2026-10-30: "Go for it"; the builder check's open questions were settled the same day, "You go ahead and patch it").
  • Branch: feat/unified-pixel-rows, on its own (the owner, 2026-10-29). Replaces the row in plans/future-work.md that tracks the two rules.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
A sprite's pixels = """…""" block is text, one glyph per pixel and one line per row. Whatever the text gets wrong (a short row, a stray space, a blank line), the engine has to turn it into a rectangle. Today it does that two different ways, and both of them can change the art without telling anyone:

  • Static sprites (AnimatedSprite._convert_static_sprite, src/glitchygames/sprites/animated.py) strip the whole block, widen every row to the longest one, and fill with the most common glyph in the sprite. That glyph is usually a color, so a short row gets solid pixels the author never drew.
  • Animated frames (parse_toml_pixel_lines and _validate_toml_frame_dimensions) strip every line, drop blank lines, take the most common row length as the width, cut longer rows off, and pad shorter ones with their own last glyph. Cutting deletes art: a sword drawn x / xxxx / x / x loads as four single x rows, and adding one more short row to abcd / ab cuts cd off the first row.

Bitmappy saves what it loaded, so whatever the repair did is written back into the file.

The goal is one rule, used everywhere, that never removes a pixel the author wrote, and that says so whenever it had to repair something.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. One function decides the rows of every pixel block: static sprites and animation frames, in the engine, Bitmappy, the AI path, the repo's sprite checks and scripts, and the QuickLook preview (which copies the engine).
  2. Nothing is ever cut off. A repair only adds transparent pixels.
  3. Repairs are reported. One log line per repaired block; a strict mode raises instead; the repo's sprite checks run strict.
  4. Bitmappy tells the person editing when a file it loaded had to be repaired, so that saving writes the repaired grid on purpose.
  5. The AI path rejects a generated sprite whose rows needed repair, the same way it rejects other invalid responses.
  6. Saving can't corrupt rows: glyphs that TOML treats specially are escaped.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Guessing where a short row's missing pixels belong (lining it up with its neighbors, or repeating a glyph). The adversarial review (below) measured this: it rescues some AI mistakes and invents pixels in others. The rule adds transparent pixels at the end of the row, nothing else.
  • Changing any art in the repo. Measured on the branch base (1e42b124): of 98 sprite files and 377 pixel blocks, the new rule draws exactly the same picture as today for all but the four hand-written ragged test fixtures under src/quicklook/ (repo sprites already pass check_rows_have_equal_lengths).
  • The Bitmappy \n corruption in _normalize_escaped_newlines (toml_processing.py): a \ glyph followed by an n glyph becomes a line break. Its own later branch (see "Bugs found").
  • The full sprite linter (plans/future-features.md #28). This branch provides its core check.

docs.title: Anti-goals
docs.text:
• Any repair that removes or recolors a pixel the author wrote.
  • Any repair nobody hears about.
  • QuickLook drawing something different from the game.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
Every pixel block, static or animated, goes through these steps. Lengths are counted in Unicode code points (what Python's str counts; Swift's unicodeScalars), never in grapheme clusters.

  1. Split the text on U+000A only.
  2. Trim the end of each line: remove trailing U+0020 (space), U+0009 (tab) and U+000D (carriage return, so Windows line endings work).
  3. Drop blank lines at the top and bottom. A blank line between rows stays.
  4. Remove shared indentation: the longest run of leading spaces and tabs that every non-blank line starts with, character for character. Indentation that only some lines have stays, and draws as transparent pixels (a space is never a palette glyph today). This keeps indented TOML working without moving art, and keeps a pyramid that uses leading spaces as its transparent pixels a pyramid.
  5. Make it a rectangle: the width is the longest row. Shorter rows are padded at the end with transparent pixels, and a blank line between rows becomes a row of transparent pixels.

Accepted costs (the owner agreed, 2026-10-30): one accidentally long row widens the whole frame by a pixel; a short row in a solid tile shows a see-through notch instead of a guessed fill. Both are reported, and neither destroys anything.

Transparent padding is the engine's transparency key, magenta (255, 0, 255), the color the engine already draws for a glyph that has no palette entry. On save, the writer finds the palette's magenta glyph, or adds one if there isn't one (checked on the branch base). My call, revised while planning: an earlier draft preferred the palette's own transparent glyph, but QuickLook reads the palette as an unordered dictionary, so it couldn't pick the same "first" glyph. Magenta is one answer that both sides give. A padded pixel is U+0000 in the returned rows (PADDING_GLYPH); a palette that defines U+0000 is reported as a bad palette key.

docs.title: What counts as a repair
docs.text:
Steps 2–4 tidy text; they never change the picture, so they are not reported. These change or might change the picture, and are reported (and raise in strict mode):

  • rows of different widths (step 5 padded something), naming each width found;
  • a blank line between rows;
  • a glyph that isn't in the palette (it draws transparent, which is probably not what the author meant; the report names the glyphs). My call: a space is the exception. It is the format's "no pixel here" glyph (step 4 relies on it), so it is never reported;
  • for the width report, a row counts as short only if it is still shorter than the width when its trimmed trailing spaces and tabs are counted back in. My call: a pyramid padded with spaces on both sides is not reported, but a row that really is missing pixels is.
  • a palette key that isn't exactly one code point (e.g. "❤️" is two: U+2764 and U+FE0F). It can never match a pixel, because pixels are single code points.

Animation frames of different sizes are logged at debug level only: they are legal.

docs.title: Strict mode
docs.text:
The function takes strict: bool. Strict raises one ValueError listing every repair in the block. Loading a sprite is not strict (old and AI-made files must still open). Strict is used by:

  • check_rows_have_equal_lengths in src/glitchygames/testing/sprite_files.py, which the workspace sprite test runs on every repo sprite. My call: it keeps running on every pixel block, now through the shared function in strict mode, so it also catches blank interior lines, missing glyphs and bad palette keys. Renaming it is the builder's call.
  • the AI path (Goal 5).

docs.title: Before and after: what each layer draws
docs.text:
The record for "what changed", so a later breakage can be traced to the rule. The two old columns were drawn by the engine itself on the branch base (1e42b124), loading each case as a static sprite and as a one-frame animation and reading the pixels back as glyphs. · is a transparent pixel. Rows are separated by /. The new column is the rule above, and Task 2 of the plan pins every row of it with a test (test_before_and_after_table).

Case (pixel text) Old static (_convert_static_sprite) Old animated (parse_toml_pixel_lines + _validate_toml_frame_dimensions) New (both) sword x / xxxx / x / x xxxx / xxxx / xxxx / xxxx (filled with the most common glyph) x / x / x / x (crossguard cut) x··· / xxxx / x··· / x··· one long row abcd / ab / ab abcd / abaa / abaa ab / ab / ab (cd cut) abcd / ab·· / ab·· short row in a tile xxxx / xxx / xxxx xxxx / xxxx / xxxx xxxx / xxxx / xxxx xxxx / xxx· / xxxx (notch, reported) blank line between rows ab / / ab ab / aa / ab ab / ab (row dropped) ab / ·· / ab one indented row ␣␣ab / ab / ab ab / ab / ab (whole-block strip) ab / ab / ab (per-line strip) ··ab / ab·· / ab·· (indent kept, reported) space pyramid ␣␣x / ␣xxx / xxxxx xxxxx / ·xxxx / xxxxx x / x / x ··x·· / ·xxx· / xxxxx tie in widths ab / abc aba / abc ab / ab (tie goes to the first width) ab· / abc

Read across a row to see which layer changed and how. Two of the old static results surprised the review: the whole-block strip also removes the first row's indentation, and filling with the most common glyph turns a short sword into a solid block.

Other records of the old behavior: the QuickLook golden frames at 1e42b124 (src/quicklook/Tests/SpriteCoreTests/Golden/ragged-*.json, and the R4 and R5 rules in docs/specs/2026-10-29-sprite-quicklook-design.md), and the old tests that the plan rewrites, in git history. Each plan task is its own commit, so git bisect across the branch names the task that broke something.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• Engine: one public function in src/glitchygames/sprites/pixel_utils.py, taking the pixel text, the palette and strict, returning the rows, their width and height, and the list of repairs. Builder's call on names and the result type, following the module's style. _convert_static_sprite and _create_toml_frame both use it. parse_toml_pixel_lines and _validate_toml_frame_dimensions go away; their other callers (sprite_files.py, scripts/audit_hitboxes.py) switch to it. colorize_pixels in src/glitchygames/tools/ascii_renderer.py (a third copy: whole-block strip, no repair) uses it for its rows. My call on two more copies the builder check found: BitmappySprite._parse_static_toml_data (src/glitchygames/sprites/bitmappy_sprite.py, the fallback loader that _inflate_toml also uses: it strips each line, drops blank lines, and takes the width from the first row) draws in the game, so it uses the function too. _extract_example_size (src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/ai_worker.py) sizes the AI prompt's examples, so it uses it too. Out of scope: the legacy ConfigParser loader scripts/sprite_loader.py.
  • Reporting: one warning per repaired block, naming the file, the animation and frame (or "sprite" for a static one) and each repair. The loaded sprite keeps the list of repairs so that Bitmappy (and tests) can read it. Builder's call on the attribute name.
  • Bitmappy: after a load that had repairs, the load message (_show_load_message in src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/animated_canvas.py, the editor's debug text box) says how many blocks were repaired, that the log has the details, and that saving writes the repaired grid. My call on that wording and place; the owner can change it.
  • AI path: a strict row check, worded so that build_retry_prompt (src/apps/bitmappy/src/bitmappy/ai_worker.py) can match it, plus a new correction text in build_retry_prompt telling the model every row must be the same width. There are two AI paths:
  • SpriteGenerationService._validate_and_build_result (no retries) calls validate_ai_response (src/glitchygames/ai/sprite_generator.py). That function gains the check on the cleaned response.
  • Bitmappy's ai_manager.py retries a failed check up to AI_VALIDATION_MAX_RETRIES (2) times. My call: there the check runs on the text Bitmappy actually loads, after its own clean-up (normalize_toml_data), so the rows checked are the rows drawn.

When Bitmappy's retries run out and the last response still needed repair, it is loaded repaired, with the Bitmappy repair notice, instead of being discarded (the owner, 2026-10-30: "2. Yes" to my recommendation). Every other validation failure still ends with "the sprite was not loaded".

My call: a response that doesn't parse as TOML skips the row check, so this check adds no new rejections. The existing checks and the loader handle it as they do today. - Writers: every place that writes pixel rows into TOML escapes each row the way toml_multiline_basic_string does (\, " and control characters). Today a row ending in a \ glyph joins the next row (TOML's line continuation), a\bc loads as a backspace, and a\a won't load. The writers are: - both writers in animated.py (the static writer and _write_toml_animations); - Bitmappy's AI rewrite (ai_manager._construct_toml_with_preserved_formatting and _format_animation_sections), which feeds the loader; - the prompt examples in sprite_generator.py (around lines 215 and 282);

ascii_renderer.py's output isn't on the list. It is a colorized terminal view with ANSI codes, and nothing reads it back as TOML (my call, while planning).

The PNG import (toml_processing.py) can't produce either glyph (SPRITE_GLYPHS), so it gets a test that pins that rather than a change. - QuickLook: src/quicklook/Sources/SpriteCore/PixelRows.swift's two functions become one that follows the rule, used for static and animated blocks alike. QuickLook doesn't report or go strict: it draws what the game draws. Its golden frames are regenerated from the engine with src/quicklook/tools/dump_engine_frames.py, and new golden fixtures cover: a long row, a short row, a blank interior line, shared and unshared indentation, CRLF, a \ and a " glyph, a combining mark, and a VS16 emoji (each code point its own pixel).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: TDD throughout. Every repair kind, and every step of the rule, gets an engine test, including the two examples above (the sword keeps its crossguard; abcd keeps cd). Existing tests that pin today's behavior (tests/sprites/test_animated_sprite.py, e.g. TestConvertStaticSpriteInconsistentWidths, and the Inconsistent line lengths log test) are rewritten for the new rule, not deleted. Round-trip tests save and reload sprites with \ and " glyphs. The Swift goldens prove engine and preview agree.

docs.title: Bugs found (to report in BUGS.md)
docs.text:
1. Writer doesn't escape pixel rows (fixed here, Goal 6).
  2. validate_ai_response never checks row widths (fixed here, Goal 5).
  3. _normalize_escaped_newlines turns a \ glyph followed by an n glyph into a newline (toml_processing.py; used by Bitmappy's AI manager and alpha path). Separate branch.
  4. cobra.toml (src/games/brave-adventurer/src/brave_adventurer_papyrus/sprites/) uses glyph e in 7 rows, but its palette has no e, so the cobra's second eye draws transparent. Strict mode fails on it. Fixed on this branch (the owner, 2026-10-30: "You go ahead and patch it"). My call: e = (180, 30, 30). It follows the palette's own convention, where a lowercase glyph is a darker shade of its capital (g is G minus 20 per channel), so e is E (200, 50, 50) minus 20.

  5. scripts/foo.toml has pixels and no palette at all; strict mode fails on it too. The owner decides whether it's kept.

  6. Bitmappy's AI rewrite (ai_manager._construct_toml_with_preserved_formatting) writes each color's red, green and blue but drops alpha, so a generated sprite with see-through colors loads opaque. It also writes name and description unescaped (description = """{…}"""), so a prompt containing \ or """ breaks the file. Found while planning; fixed on this branch with the writer escaping (fixups as we go), since it is the same function.
