Observations made while reading (reported per the owner's instructions; not bugs):

  • synth.oscillator's NOISE draws from the engine stream audio.synth, which is seeded from the run's master seed. The same recipe's noise therefore differs per run and depends on render order. That is harmless today, because nothing caches across runs, but it is incompatible with a content-keyed disk cache. §6.3 gives each sound its own seed, and v0 recipes keep today's behaviour (§10.4).
  • SoundBank.play renders on first use unless prerender() was called. Both users call prerender() at setup [Fact: mr_muncher/game.py:515, clockwork_keep/game.py:473]. That is the same "first request compiles" model the owner chose; the library generalizes it.

docs.title: 2.1 Layers
docs.text:
Game code ──► AudioEngine facade  (scene_manager.audio; one per engine context)
                 │
                 ├─ Asset layer      TOML → validated model → resolved SoundSpec (pure data)
                 ├─ Library          sound(...) → name/path resolution → compile once → cache
                 ├─ Renderer (DSP)   SoundSpec → float64 buffer   (pure numpy, no I/O)
                 ├─ Voices           channel table, priorities, stealing, handles, buses, live voices
                 └─ Output           pygame.mixer (SDL's C mixer thread)  |  OfflineMixer (files)
Layer Module [Proposal] Owns Thread Pitch and waves audio/pitch.py, audio/waves.py Note/Hz/Midi/Scale/PitchTable/Tuning; Wave, WaveTable, Harmonics, WavePoint, CYCLE, LEVEL, the wave registry main Asset audio/assets.py (pydantic v2 models [Fact: an engine dependency]) parsing, validation, migration, path resolution, the short-name index main Renderer audio/render.py (sources, envelopes, routes, filters, effects), built on synth.py pure functions of a SoundSpec, its seeds and the sample rate main Library audio/library.py SoundLibrary: sound(...), identity hashing, compiled sounds, memory and disk cache, compile accounting main Voices and buses audio/voices.py, audio/buses.py channel table, SoundHandle, generation counters, bus tree, stealing, pause bookkeeping main Live voices audio/live.py (extended) LiveVoice rendering chunks from a compiled live instrument main Facade audio/engine.py AudioEngine main Offline audio/offline.py OfflineMixer, render_to_file any (no device) Tool glitchygames sound subcommands (render, migrate, check) the CLI CLI

docs.title: 2.2 Data flow
docs.text:
1. Request: audio.sound(source, pitch=..., notes=..., chord=..., length=..., transpose=..., parameters=...).
  2. Strings are resolved per feature spec §3.2. A short name goes through the SOUND_DIRECTORY index, which is built on the first short-name lookup by reading only the table names of each .toml file. A path goes to that file's [sounds.<name>], or to the recorded file.
  3. Each sound file is parsed and validated once, when first touched, into frozen models.
  4. The source and identity arguments resolve to an immutable SoundSpec: the instrument, concrete Hz pitches, note events in seconds, fixed parameter values, seeds, tuning, and whether it is live.
  5. The identity key is the SHA-256 of the spec's canonical JSON (§6.2).
  6. Cache lookup: the key is looked up in the memory cache (then the disk cache, from M3). A hit returns the existing Sound object, so equal requests return the same object (AUD-FUNC-002).
  7. Compile (on a miss):
  8. Baked: render a float64 buffer and check it is finite. Report its peak; clip and warn if it is above full scale, or scale it to -1 dBFS if normalize. Convert to int16 at the mixer rate with synth.to_pcm16 [Fact], and make a pygame.mixer.Sound from it when a mixer exists.
  9. Live: build wave tables and filter coefficients; no audio.
  10. Recorded file: load it with pygame.mixer.Sound(path) (no mixer: decode it with the wave module for offline use, WAV only).
  11. In every case the time is recorded with clock.raw_counter_seconds [Fact], attributed to "setup" (before the scene's first logic frame) or to the current frame number.
  12. Play: sound.play(...) allocates a channel (§7.1), calls Channel.play(sound, loops) and then Channel.set_volume(left, right). The mixer (C, SDL's audio thread) does the rest.
  13. Live: sound.start(...) creates a LiveVoice on a reserved live channel. Each frame, AudioEngine.update renders the next chunk when the queue has room (today's mechanism [Fact]), reading the latest coalesced parameter values.
  14. Offline: OfflineMixer takes compiled float buffers (or steps live renderers with a parameter timeline) and sums them at exact sample offsets into a file.

There is no second clock and no second output device. The mixer is the only device owner [Proposal; decisions D3/D4].

docs.title: 3.1 Options considered
docs.text: Option Description Verdict A. pygame.mixer + compiled (baked) sounds + main-loop live chunks Extend what exists. Baked sounds mix in SDL's C mixer; live voices render on the main thread in chunks Recommended B. A Python render callback on a device thread (pygame._sdl2.audio.AudioDevice(callback=...) or miniaudio.PlaybackDevice with a generator) The classic "audio callback" architecture, with DSP in numpy on the audio thread Rejected: measured to miss deadlines under GIL contention (A.2) C. A Python render-ahead worker thread + copy-only device callback Render blocks on a worker thread into a ring buffer; the callback only copies Rejected for M1–M5: needs about 85 ms of lookahead to survive a busy game loop (A.3), no better than A's 100 ms chunks, while adding a second device and threads D. A native DSP core (C via cffi, or Rust) owning its own callback without the GIL The only route to low-latency, sample-accurate real-time mixing, real-time bus effects and a master limiter Deferred to an M6 gate [Open]: adds native builds for every platform plus a separate WebAssembly build, for features not yet asked for E. Free-threaded CPython (3.14t) running B or C without the GIL Removes the contention that sinks B and C Deferred [Open]: pygame-ce, numpy and the engine would all need free-threaded builds and audits

docs.title: 3.2 Why A
docs.text:
• [Owner] "the first time you call for a sound, it gets compiled ... the way you load it is the same as the way you'd use it in the game - one API." Option A compiles on request and plays compiled audio from memory, which is exactly that model.
  • A Python callback cannot reliably meet a 5.33 ms (256-frame) deadline while the game loop runs Python. [Measured A.2] With a pure-Python busy main thread, a numpy render in a miniaudio callback took 256 ms (p99) at the default 5 ms switch interval, 58 ms at 1 ms and 12.7 ms at 0.2 ms.
  • The same numpy render is cheap when uncontended [Measured A.1]: 64 voices of oscillator + envelope + pan take 0.40 ms (p99 0.47 ms) per 256 frames. On the main thread there is no contention.
  • Today's main-thread costs are small [Measured A.4]: a 100 ms live chunk with a low-pass takes 0.15 ms, and the worst existing recipe takes 9.7 ms, compiled once.
  • One device means no competing mixer, no second clock, and nothing new for the replay silencer, headless runs or the browser to learn.
  • There are no new dependencies (AUD-PORT-001).

docs.title: 3.3 What A gives up (recorded honestly)
docs.text:
• Trigger latency: play() starts at the next mixer buffer, about ≤ 11.6 ms after the frame that called it. It is not sample-accurate.
  • Live-parameter latency: up to one chunk (100 ms today; M3 evaluates 50 ms) plus one buffer.
  • Real-time bus effects and a master limiter are not possible, because SDL's mixer sums in C with saturation. Effects are compiled into sounds instead.
  • Sample-accurate transitions between music pieces are not possible. Inside a compiled sound, timing is sample-accurate.
  • Pitch at play time cannot change a compiled sound, because pygame plays at a fixed rate. Each pitch is its own sound, requested by identity.

docs.title: 3.4 The native-core gate (M6) [Open]
docs.text:
Option D is reopened only if the owner asks for one of:

  • real-time bus effects (a reverb send, a master limiter);
  • sample-accurate music transitions;
  • more than 8 simultaneous live voices;
  • trigger latency under 10 ms.

The experiment would be a C core built with cffi (the toolchain pyminiaudio already uses [Fact]) for macOS arm64/x86_64, Linux and Windows, plus an Emscripten build, measured with the Appendix A harness. If it fails, the fallback is A as specified. The Renderer layer is pure functions over SoundSpecs, so a native core would replace only the Output and Live layers.

docs.title: 4.1 Threads
docs.text:
Thread Runs Owner Main (game loop) all API calls, compiles, live chunk rendering, channel allocation, bus volume updates, diagnostics engine SDL audio thread pygame's C mixer: sums playing channels, and calls the channel-finished callback that queues a live voice's next chunk [Fact] SDL

No new thread is created [Proposal]. The brief's command-queue and memory-ordering requirements apply only to the deferred native core (§3.4). With one thread there is nothing to queue: an API call takes effect through pygame's own thread-safe mixer calls.

docs.title: 4.2 Bounded work per frame
docs.text:
AudioEngine.update(dt=...) runs once per frame, in the slot where LiveAudio.update runs today [Fact: scene.py:1227], with the same scene and pause arguments. It:

  1. advances scheduled plays whose frame has arrived (M2; feature spec §7.1, late rule);
  2. advances each unpaused voice's played time by dt and reaps voices whose sound has ended (§7.3);
  3. for each live voice whose queue has room, renders one chunk with the latest parameter values;
  4. applies bus fades and ducking (one gain step per bus per frame; M5);
  5. records diagnostics: counters and clock.raw_counter_seconds deltas, kept in fixed-size ring arrays.

The work is bounded: at most live_pool chunks, at most one reap per channel and one operation per bus. The only compiles in a frame are the ones the game requested in it. They are timed, counted and listed with their frame (AUD-FUNC-003).

docs.title: 4.3 Parameter updates (coalescing)
docs.text: LiveSoundHandle.set(name, value) writes latest[name] = clamp(value) into a small dict owned by the voice, and rendering reads the dict once per chunk. A thousand calls per frame cost a thousand dict writes and render nothing extra (AUD-GAME-003). Smoothing runs inside the chunk as a one-pole glide from the previous chunk's end value toward the new target, with time constant smoothing_ms, in closed form per sample: target + (start − target)·exp(−n/τ).

docs.title: 4.4 Handles and stale-handle protection
docs.text:
@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class SoundHandle:
    slot: int          # index into the voice table
    generation: int    # the slot's generation when this handle was issued

Each voice-table slot has a generation counter, incremented whenever the slot is reused. Every handle method first checks table[slot].generation == handle.generation. On a mismatch it does nothing and returns False. Handles hold no reference to the Sound, so a dropped handle releases nothing, and a kept one keeps nothing alive.

docs.title: 4.5 Resource release
docs.text: pygame.mixer.Sound objects are released when the library drops them. That happens only through LRU eviction (memory limit) or engine shutdown. Eviction never removes a sound that is playing, because the voice table holds a reference while the voice plays. Compiled sounds outlive scenes: a second scene requesting 'coin' gets the same compiled sound.

docs.title: 5. DSP decisions
docs.text:
All rendering is float64 numpy on whole buffers (baked) or chunks (live). Conversion to int16 happens once, at the end (synth.to_pcm16 [Fact]).

Stage Algorithm State Ranges Cost class Verification Phase Exclusive running sum of f/fs in cycles, wrapped % 1.0 (today's oscillator [Fact]); float64 keeps sub-cent accuracy for minutes phase float f ∈ [0, fs/2] O(n) AUD-PITCH-006 FFT measurement Phase reset phase_reset = "note" (restart at 0 for each note of notes/chord) or "free" (continue across notes) per source — — onset waveform check Saw, square, pulse Naive shape + PolyBLEP residual at each discontinuity (today's [Fact]); pulse is square with duty. Compiled, they render at 2× and are filtered down (a 101-tap Hamming-windowed sinc at 0.45 fs, applied centred): PolyBLEP alone measured aliases only 26.8 dB under a 3520 Hz fundamental, 2× gives 51 dB. Headroom (every periodic source): the output is divided by the wave's worst band-limited peak over the supported pitches (8 Hz–12 kHz), so a level-1 source never clips and the same shape is equally loud by either route. Table waves use the peak of the band tables those pitches read (Wave.band_limited_peak, computed once and cached). PolyBLEP shapes use measured values (the 2× output at level 1, 300 pitches, duties 0.01–0.99): saw 1.143; square and pulse max(|2d − 1| + (4/π)·sin(πd), 1.296), the first term being DC plus the lone fundamental of a high note and the second the Gibbs overshoot of narrow pulses; these are divided out with 1% to spare. Live voices (M2, draft tier) do not oversample — duty 0.01–0.99 2× O(n) + 101-tap convolution at 2× alias floor test (AUD-WAVE-006); no-clip test at level 1 Triangle Naive (harmonics fall at 12 dB/oct [Fact: comment in synth.py]); the Chip profile's 4-bit stepped triangle is quantized and intentionally unsmoothed — — O(n) shape + spectrum Custom waves and wavetables Band-limited mip tables. For each octave band, the wave's FFT is truncated to the harmonics below Nyquist at that band's highest frequency, then inverse-transformed into a 2048-sample table. Reading is linear interpolation within the table, with the band chosen per chunk from the highest frequency in it. Wavetable position crossfades two neighbouring waves' tables tables per wave, built at registration (≈ 11 bands × 2048 × 8 B ≈ 180 KB per wave) position ∈ [0, n−1] O(n) per source spectral alias test; morph discontinuity test Harmonics Direct additive synthesis into the 2048-sample table, then the mip tables above — up to 32 harmonics build time only harmonic level check (AUD-WAVE-004) WavePoint linear: piecewise linear. smooth: monotone cubic (Fritsch–Carlson), so it never overshoots between points — reference: F. N. Fritsch and R. E. Carlson, "Monotone Piecewise Cubic Interpolation", SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 17(2), 1980. steps: sample-and-hold. Then DC removal and normalization — — build time point reproduction White noise numpy.random.Generator(PCG64(seed)).uniform(-1, 1) per source; seed per §6.3 generator — O(n) identical recompile LFSR noise Galois LFSR stepped at rate; output ±1, held between steps. 15-bit taps (14, 13) and a 7-bit "short" mode with taps (6, 5); a table of maximal-length tap sets (Xilinx XAPP 052) is the only allowed input, and taps=None takes the width's entry register int rate up to fs (at most one step per sample; the public Noise(rate=...) is a pitch, so at most Nyquist) One full period (≤ 32,767 values) is precomputed once per tap set and bit width; output is an indexed gather at the step positions, O(n) period test Pink noise (M2) Paul Kellett's "refined" filter of white noise (seven one-pole sections) — reference: P. Kellett, "Filter to make pink noise from white", musicdsp.org (2000). Each section is a first-order IIR; it is computed per section with scipy-free numpy by chunked recursion. Cost measured in M2 against the live budget 7 floats — O(n) per section slope test Envelopes Piecewise segments in closed form per sample index: linear; exponential (a time constant that reaches 99% of the stage's target in its stated time); steps(n) quantized stage, level stage times ≥ 0.5 ms O(n) stage timing test Pitch curves synth.frequency_curve with the engine's easings [Fact: glitchygames.effects.easing] — — O(n) AUD-INST-008 Filters (M2) Trapezoidal-integrated state-variable filter, stable under fast modulation — reference: A. Simper, "Linear Trap SVF" (Cytomic technical paper, 2013). LP/HP/BP from one structure; resonance k = 2 − 2·res, with res clamped to [0, 0.95] 2 floats per filter cutoff 20 Hz–0.45 fs Per-sample recursion: a Python loop over samples with numpy across live voices (A.1 case B: 0.9 ms per 256 frames for 64 voices; live voices are ≤ 8). Compiled sounds run it once finite-output sweep at maximum resonance (AUD-INST-005) Existing FIR filters (M1) Hamming-windowed sinc, kept as the M1 filter [Fact] — — O(n·taps) via np.convolve existing tests FM (M4) Phase modulation, as in the DX-style chips the profile is inspired by: out = sin(2π(φc + I·m)), where m is the modulator's output and I (the index) is in cycles (public name index, 0–8). Feedback on one operator uses the average of its last two outputs × feedback (0–1) — reference: J. Chowning, "The Synthesis of Complex Audio Spectra by Means of Frequency Modulation", JAES 21(7), 1973. Operators evaluate in algorithm order, and feedback is the only allowed loop (one-sample delay). Algorithms are a fixed table of 2-op and 4-op graphs operator phases, 2 feedback samples index 0–8, ratio 0.5–16 per-sample loop only for the feedback operator; others vectorized sideband test vs Bessel predictions (AUD-INST-006) Ring modulation (M4) Sample-wise product of two sources — — O(n) spectrum Hard sync (M4) The slave's phase resets at each master wrap, with PolyBLEP on the reset step slave phase — O(n), vectorized via wrap indices spectrum + shape Samples (M4) Fractional read position; cubic Hermite interpolation (quality full, compiled) or linear (quality draft, live); loops get an equal-power crossfade of crossfade frames rendered at compile time read position rate 1/16–16 O(n) rate/duration test; loop boundary test Drive (exists) tanh waveshaper [Fact: synth.distort]; compiled at 2× oversampling when drive > 2: zero-stuffed, then the same 101-tap windowed-sinc kernel as the discontinuous waves, applied directly and centred (latency 0; a polyphase form would halve the work) — — 2× O(n·taps) finite, bounded, zero-latency test Bit / rate reduction (M2) Quantize to 2^bits levels; sample-and-hold at the reduced rate. These intentionally alias — bits 1–16; rate 500 Hz–fs O(n) level count Delay (M4) Circular buffer, feedback ≤ 0.9, optional one-pole damping buffer ≤ 2 s — O(n) tail bound Wow/flutter (M4) A delay-line read modulated by two LFOs (≈ 0.5 Hz, ≈ 7 Hz), with cubic read buffer ≤ 50 ms depth ≤ 30 cents O(n) modulation depth Reverb (M5) A small Schroeder-style comb + all-pass network, tail ≤ 3 s — reference: M. R. Schroeder, "Natural Sounding Artificial Reverberation", JAES 10(3), 1962 buffers — compile only tail bound, finite

Denormals and non-finite values: every stateful recursion flushes values with a magnitude below 1e-30 to zero at chunk boundaries. Every compiled buffer and live chunk is checked with np.isfinite. A compile that fails the check raises SoundRenderError naming the sound (a bug, surfaced at the request). A live chunk that fails it is replaced by silence, the voice is released, and the event is counted (AUD-RT-004).

Oversampling: only for compiled saw, square and pulse (PolyBLEP alone measured 26.8 dB at 3520 Hz, short of AUD-WAVE-006's 40), for drive above 2 and for FM with index > 4 (2×, compile-time only, so it is bounded by the sound's length). Live voices (M2, draft tier) never oversample. Quality tiers: full (compiled: cubic interpolation and oversampling where listed) and draft (live: linear interpolation, no oversampling). Neither tier is described as hardware emulation.

De-clicking without smoothing the waves [Call]: only boundaries get ramps, and only where needed:

  • A v1 sound whose first sample's magnitude is above 1/1024 gets a 1 ms fade-in. One whose last sample is above that gets a 2 ms fade-out. hard_edges = true turns both off, for intentional clicks.
  • Stops, steals and skips use Channel.fadeout (≥ 5 ms).
  • Live voices get rendered fades [Fact: today's _fade_gains].
  • Waveform edges inside a sound are never smoothed.
  • v0 recipes get none of this; they compile through today's renderer unchanged (§10.4).

Level [Call]: compiled sounds keep the author's levels; there is no automatic normalization (feature spec §6.5). normalize = true scales to -1 dBFS. A peak above full scale is clipped and logged once.

docs.title: 6.1 Schema (v1)
docs.text:
The models are pydantic v2 [Fact: an engine dependency] with extra='forbid'. Error messages render pydantic's loc tuple as a TOML path (instruments.vehicle.routes[1].output), with a "did you mean" from difflib.get_close_matches. A field that exists in the schema but belongs to a later milestone is rejected with "routes arrives in M2" until its milestone lands (AUD-ASSET-003). Defaults are listed; a field without one is required.

[glitchygames]: kind = "sounds" (required), version = 1 (required).

[waves.<name>] — exactly one of:

Field Type Default MS mix table of wave name → weight — M1 blend { from = name, to = name, amount = 0–1 } — M1 harmonics table: fundamental, octave, octave_and_fifth, two_octaves, harmonic_5…harmonic_32 (each 0–1, default 0), or drawbars = "888000000" — M1 points + shape array of { at, level } (numbers or CYCLE/LEVEL names in lower case); shape ∈ linear/smooth/steps shape = "linear" M1 samples + resolution_bits array of levels; 1–16 bits no quantization M4 sprite path to a sprite TOML — M4

Plus, for every kind: normalize (bool, default true).

[instruments.<name>]:

Field Type Default MS profile hybrid/chip/wavetable/fm/sampler hybrid M1 (field); M4 (constraints beyond hybrid) envelope preset name, or a table { attack, decay, sustain, release, curve } with curve ∈ linear/exponential/steps(n) "pluck" M1 live bool false M2 seed int derived (§6.3) M1 normalize bool false M1 hard_edges bool false M1 filter { type = low_pass/high_pass, cutoff } (FIR) none M1 filter with band_pass, resonance, envelope as above + resonance 0–0.95, envelope table with amount_octaves none M2 drive 0–20 0 M1 bits, sample_rate_reduction 1–16; Hz none M2 parameters.<name> { range = [lo, hi], default, smoothing_ms = 30, unit = "" } none M2 routes array of { from, to, curve = "linear", output = [a, b] } none M2 vibrato, lfos, glide, bend_range tables none M4 algorithm, operators, feedback FM none M4 delay, wow_flutter tables none M4 reverb table none M5

[instruments.<name>.sources.<source>] (1–4 sources; table order is the mix order):

Field Type Default MS exactly one of wave (name) / noise (white/lfsr/pink) / wavetable (array of names) / sample (path) — — wave, noise (white, lfsr) M1; pink M2; wavetable, sample M4 duty 0.01–0.99, for pulse 0.5 M1 lfsr { bits = 15 or 7, taps = [a, b], rate } { bits = 15, taps = [14, 13], rate = "pitch" } M1 level 0–1 1.0 M1 octave, semitones, detune_cents ints/floats 0 M1 pitch a pitch (fixed for this source, overriding the note) none M1 pitch_curve { to = pitch, seconds, easing = "linear" } none M1 envelope as the instrument's the instrument's M1 filter as the instrument's (FIR in M1) none M1 position { from = parameter } or a number 0 M4 root, loop sample root pitch; { start, end, crossfade } — M4

[sounds.<name>] — the short name <name>:

Field Type Default MS instrument an instrument name from any file in the sound directory, or "path#name" required unless file M1 file path to a WAV/OGG recorded sound — M1 pitch / notes / chord (at most one) pitch; "B5:0.06 E6:0.18" string or array of [pitch, seconds]; array of pitches none (unpitched instruments allowed) M1 length seconds per note or chord before release 0.25 M1 transpose semitones 0 M1 parameters table of fixed parameter values the instrument's defaults M2 bus, volume, pan, priority, loop playback defaults, overridable in .play() effects, 1.0, 0.0, 50, false M1

Bounds enforced when a file is read (AUD-RT, AUD-ASSET):

Item Limit Sources per instrument 4 Routes per instrument 8, with no cycles (FM feedback is not a route) LFOs 2 Wave table length 2048 internally; imported tables 8–65,536 samples Sample file 30 s and 32 MB decoded per file (longer → stream it with music.play_file) Delay / reverb tail 2 s / 3 s Compiled sound length 60 s Notes per notes 256 Pitches per chord 8 Live pool 4 by default, at most 8 in M2 (D2)

docs.title: 6.2 Identity and cache keys
docs.text:
The SoundSpec is serialized to canonical JSON: sorted keys, and floats written with repr, which round-trips exactly. The JSON also includes:

  • the mixer sample rate (44100 when no mixer is running);
  • the tuning;
  • AUDIO_RENDER_VERSION, an integer bumped whenever the renderer's output changes;
  • the numpy version;
  • the platform tag.

The key is the first 128 bits of the SHA-256 of that JSON. Any change to any of these is a miss (AUD-ASSET-006). A cheaper first-level lookup avoids re-resolving on every call: the library memoizes (source string or Instrument id, frozen identity arguments) → key. That makes a repeated audio.sound('coin') a dict hit.

docs.title: 6.3 Seeds
docs.text: Each source's seed is the instrument's seed if given; otherwise it is derived from the sound's name with int.from_bytes(sha256(sound name)[:8]). Either way it is combined with the source's index through numpy.random.SeedSequence. Compiles never touch glitchygames.randomness streams, which respects both the CRT power-on's "no randomness" rule and replays [Fact: the power-on rules in crt_power_on.py]. Version 0 recipes are the exception (§10.4).

docs.title: 6.4 The cache: None, 'ram' or 'disk' [Owner]
docs.text:
AudioEngine(cache=...) takes the --sound-cache option, which is replay-local (§10.2):

  • None: sound() resolves and validates, but keeps no audio. The returned Sound holds only its spec, and every play() compiles it in that frame. The compile is timed and accounted like any other (§11.0). This is the switch that forces mid-frame rendering.
  • 'ram' and 'disk': as below.

Today's code does not read the mode. It is migrated and removed first (M2, §10.4), and the benchmarks then run in the owner's order: None, then 'ram', then 'disk' (M3, §11.0) [Owner]. None and 'ram' exist from M1, so every test of the new engine can run under both.

  • Memory ('ram'): a dict[key, Sound] plus an LRU order on last play. Total int16 bytes are tracked. Above --sound-cache-memory (default 256 MB), the least recently played sounds that are not playing are dropped. They are recompiled on their next request, which is counted.
  • Disk ('disk', M3): memory first, then disk.
  • Layout: <cache>/sounds/<render_version>/<key[:2]>/<key>.wav (16-bit PCM WAV at the mixer rate), written with output_files.write_aside_then_replace [Fact].
  • The cache root is a new state/paths.get_cache_directory(app_name) beside get_save_directory [Fact]: macOS ~/Library/Caches/<app>/, Linux $XDG_CACHE_HOME/<app>/ (default ~/.cache/<app>/), Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\<app>\Cache\.
  • The size limit is 64 MB, and the oldest-accessed files are pruned at startup.
  • Reads verify the WAV header's rate and length. A bad file is deleted and recompiled.
  • In the browser and in tests, 'disk' falls back to 'ram' with one log line. Under --headless outside tests it is honoured, so the M2 startup benchmark can measure it.
  • [Call] The disk layer persists across runs and the engine prunes it, rather than using per-run temp files, because the identity hash makes re-use safe and that is what lets a second launch skip compiling.

docs.title: 6.5 Where compiles happen
docs.text:
There is one rule: the first request with a given identity compiles. The places it happens are conventions, not separate APIs.

  1. Setup (the convention): games call audio.sound(...) in setup(). Those compiles run before the scene's first logic frame and are attributed to setup. A setup whose compiles exceed 50 ms logs one INFO line naming the slowest sounds.
  2. Loading screens: audio.sounds.warm(requests, budget_ms=...) takes a list of sound(...) argument sets and compiles as many as fit in the budget each time it is called, returning progress from 0 to 1. It exists only so a loading scene can spread work across frames; it calls the same compile path.
  3. Gameplay: a first request inside a gameplay frame compiles there. It is timed, counted and listed with its frame (AUD-FUNC-003).
  4. The engine's own sounds (CRT) compile before the power-on, in GameEngine._power_on_sound_cues, which _run_game (the blocking start) and start_async (the browser's) call when the power-on plays (§10.1); only the process's first power-on compiles them, every later one reuses them (§10.1, compiled once per process).
  5. Recompiles: after eviction, a tuning change or (M4) a hot reload, the next request compiles again and is counted.

docs.title: 6.6 Hot reload (M4)
docs.text:
With --sound-hot-reload, the library records each sound file's mtime. At most once per second, measured with clock.elapsed_seconds [Fact], AudioEngine.update checks them. Hot reload is refused with --record-trace and --replay-trace (OPTIONS_REFUSED), so it never touches a replay. For each changed file:

  1. the file is re-parsed and the short-name index refreshed;
  2. memo entries that came from it are dropped, so the next request resolves again and compiles if its identity changed;
  3. playing voices finish the old audio.

docs.title: 7.1 Channel table and the legacy partition
docs.text:
At engine start, where the live pool is reserved today [Fact: game_engine.py:1817]:

set_num_channels(live_pool + library_channels + legacy_channels)   # default 4 + 32 + 8
set_reserved(live_pool + library_channels)                         # 0 .. 35 reserved
Channels Used by How chosen 0 .. live_pool-1 live voices (today's pool, unchanged [Fact]) LiveAudio live_pool .. live_pool+library-1 the sound library the library's own table (Channel(i).play) the rest (8, pygame's default count) legacy Sound.play() callers: SoundBank, load_sound, any game code SDL picks among unreserved channels

The library never calls Sound.play(), and legacy callers can never reach reserved channels, so neither cuts the other off (AUD-MIX-008). The one-time reservation keeps today's rule that the pool is never resized [Fact: BUGS.md #145; reserve_live_voice_pool already handles a second engine in one process].

Allocation for a library play on bus b with priority p:

  1. Take a channel that is free in the table. Whether a channel is free, and so whether a play steals, is decided by the table alone, so it is the same in a replay: a channel is free when its voice ended by played time (§7.3), or a stop's fade has run out in frame time. The device check (Channel.get_busy()) only chooses among the free channels: the lowest-numbered one not busy on the device, else the lowest-numbered free one anyway, accepting a cut tail of at most one device buffer. It never changes what the game sees (§7.3). A free channel counts against b's reservation if b is under its reservation. Otherwise only channels not needed by other buses' unmet reservations are eligible.
  2. Otherwise steal: among playing voices with priority ≤ p, choose by releasing first, then lowest priority, earliest start, lowest channel. Fade it with Channel.fadeout(10) and mark its channel fading. The new sound starts this frame on another free or fading-complete channel if one exists. Otherwise it starts on the stolen channel next frame, counted as a one-frame delayed play. [Measured] (M1, 2026-11-02, tests/benchmarks/test_channel_fade_relations.py, run under --benchmark-only because it depends on the mixer thread's timing, and tests/audio/test_channel_fades.py on SDL's disk driver; pygame-ce 2.5.8, SDL 2.32.10, SDL_mixer 2.8.2): Channel.play straight after Channel.fadeout(10) on the same channel replaces the fading sound at the next mixer chunk, so the fade is never heard (worst step 10.3 times a 440 Hz tone's own largest, over six steals), and the delay is kept. [Open] The delay does not make a steal smooth either: SDL_mixer sets a fading channel's volume once per chunk (512 frames, 11.6 ms), so a 10 ms fade is one plateau or an immediate halt (worst step 8.3 to 9.7 times the tone's own in two recordings of six steals). A smooth steal needs a fade of several chunks or an engine-rendered fade tail (risks R4 and R5); the owner decides.
  3. Otherwise drop and count.

Which voice is stolen is decided from the table alone, so it is deterministic (AUD-MIX-003). Which channel index a play lands on may vary with device timing; that is not visible to the game.

docs.title: 7.2 Volume and pan
docs.text:
Channel.set_volume(left, right) is called after Channel.play, because pygame resets channel volume on play [Fact: noted in replay/silence.py]. The gains are:

  • left = v·g_bus·g_master·cos(θ)
  • right = v·g_bus·g_master·sin(θ)
  • with θ = (pan + 1)·π/4, a constant-power law at -3 dB centre.

Bus changes re-apply to every playing channel of that bus. A bus fade is applied as one set_volume per frame (60 steps/s). [Measured] (M1, 2026-11-02, tests/audio/test_channel_fades.py on SDL's disk driver): each frame's gain reaches the channel whole at the next mixer chunk, so a 50 ms fade from full to silence is three steps of a third (levels 1, ⅔, ⅓, 0, each held for one or two chunks), with a worst step 5.2 to 5.3 times a 440 Hz tone's own largest. [Open] Whether those steps are heard as zipper noise for the gain ranges involved is the owner's listening check; the fallback is to render the fade into a short tail sound. Voice stops, steals and skips use Channel.fadeout, which SDL_mixer also steps once per chunk rather than ramping (§7.1, §10.1), so a fade shorter than a few chunks is a plateau or two and a halt.

docs.title: 7.3 Voice time without asking the device (fixes the builder check's first finding)
docs.text:
Each voice keeps played_seconds. AudioEngine.update(dt=...) adds the frame's served dt (the recorded dt in a replay [Fact]) only while the voice is not paused:

  • Ending: a baked voice ends when played_seconds ≥ length. A looping voice ends only when stopped (or released, at the end of its pass). A stopped, cancelled or stolen voice ends at once: its handle reports is_playing False immediately, while its channel stays fading for allocation until the fade has run out in frame time.
  • Pause: pausing (a pause screen over the owner scene, a playback scope [Fact: today's paused_owners]) calls Channel.pause() and stops advancing played_seconds. Resuming calls Channel.unpause(). A paused voice is never reaped, and its channel is never reused while it is held.
  • What the game sees: handle.is_playing and reaping use only played_seconds, never Channel.get_busy(). A game reading is_playing therefore gets the same answer in a replay (replay/silence.py warns that device-busy answers are not replay-safe [Fact]).
  • Silenced frames: FrameSilencer stops channels [Fact]. It also calls audio.silenced(channel) (one new call), which marks the channel's slot device-stopped and nothing more: the voice keeps its generation and its played_seconds, so is_playing, its end and later steal decisions follow frame time exactly as in the run that was not silenced. Only the channel is quiet; the table reuses it as usual. A rebuild's and a fast-forward's frames are compared with the recording, so a silenced frame must not change what the game sees.
  • Before frame 0: voices started by the engine itself (the CRT) belong to the engine's system owner, not a scene. During the power-on, the power-on's frame loop calls audio.update(dt=frame_seconds) with its own measured frame time. Those voices are never game-visible, so measured time is acceptable for them. After the power-on they persist into the first scene (§10.1).

docs.title: 7.4 Buses
docs.text:
The buses are a tree of Bus(name, parent, volume, mute, solo, reserved_channels, loudness_budget):

  • The effective gain is the product of the volumes along the path.
  • Solo mutes the subtrees of non-soloed siblings.
  • duck_under (M5) registers a rule. Each frame, if the trigger bus has a playing voice, the ducked bus's gain moves toward 10^(amount_db/20) at the attack rate. Otherwise it moves back at the release rate.
  • Loudness budget (M2): the sum over a bus's playing voices of peak × channel gain. When it is above the budget, the bus gain is multiplied by budget/sum, with a 30 ms recovery. This is an estimate from compiled peaks and never reads audio back.

docs.title: 7.5 Live voices (M2)
docs.text:
The existing LiveVoice/LiveAudio [Fact] is generalized. A LiveVoice renders chunks from a compiled live instrument (sources, routes, filter state, smoothed parameters) instead of a single waveform with a cutoff:

  • The chunk length is configurable with --live-chunk-ms (default 100). M3 measures 50 ms against the underrun probe (scripts/audio_glitch_probe.py [Fact]). The safety margin is the chunk minus the device buffer [Fact: module docstring], so 50 ms leaves about 38 ms.
  • The pool grows from 4 to 8 only if AUD-RT-002 holds on the CI Linux container profile (1 CPU [Fact: nox -s test-linux-ci]).
  • scene_manager.live_audio.create_voice(...) stays, implemented on the new voice table.

docs.title: 7.6 Streams (M5)
docs.text: audio.music.play_file wraps pygame.mixer.music: one stream, decoded by SDL_mixer. Its volume follows the music bus. FrameSilencer already follows mixer.music.pause/unpause [Fact].

docs.title: 8. API (settled signatures)
docs.text:
Units: seconds (float), hertz (Hz), linear gain 0–1, pan −1…1, frames (int). All arguments after the first are keyword-only. Thread affinity: the main thread only.

# --- pitch.py ---
PitchLike = Note | Hz | Midi | ScaleStep | str | float   # str → Note, float → Hz, int → ValueError

class Note:
    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None: ...      # 'C4', 'F#4', 'Bb3'; ValueError otherwise
    def up(self, *, semitones: float = 0.0, cents: float = 0.0) -> Note | Hz: ...
    def down(self, *, semitones: float = 0.0, cents: float = 0.0) -> Note | Hz: ...
    def detune(self, *, cents: float) -> Hz: ...
    def to_hz(self, *, tuning: Tuning | None = None) -> Hz: ...

class Hz(float):
    def times(self, ratio: float) -> Hz: ...
    def octave_up(self, octaves: int = 1) -> Hz: ...
    def octave_down(self, octaves: int = 1) -> Hz: ...

class Midi(int): ...                                 # 0-127

class Scale:
    def __init__(self, root: str, kind: str) -> None: ...
    def step(self, number: int) -> Note: ...

class PitchTable(Mapping[str, Hz]):
    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, table: Mapping[str, float]) -> PitchTable: ...

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Tuning:
    a4: float = 440.0

def resolve_pitch(pitch: PitchLike, *, tuning: Tuning,
                  sample_rate: int = 44100) -> Hz: ...   # the one conversion point

# --- waves.py ---
class CYCLE:
    START = 0.0; EIGHTH = 0.125; QUARTER = 0.25; THREE_EIGHTHS = 0.375; HALF = 0.5
    FIVE_EIGHTHS = 0.625; THREE_QUARTERS = 0.75; SEVEN_EIGHTHS = 0.875; END = 1.0

class LEVEL:
    TOP = 1.0; HIGH = 0.5; CENTER = 0.0; LOW = -0.5; BOTTOM = -1.0

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class WavePoint:
    at: float            # position in the cycle, 0-1
    level: float         # -1 to 1

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Harmonics:
    fundamental: float = 1.0
    octave: float = 0.0              # harmonic 2
    octave_and_fifth: float = 0.0    # harmonic 3
    two_octaves: float = 0.0         # harmonic 4
    # harmonic_5 ... harmonic_32: float = 0.0
    @classmethod
    def drawbars(cls, setting: str) -> Harmonics: ...   # nine digits 0-8

class Wave:
    def __init__(self, name: str, *, duty: float | None = None) -> None: ...
    @classmethod
    def mix(cls, **weights: float) -> Wave: ...
    def blend(self, other: str | Wave, *, amount: float) -> Wave: ...
    def detuned(self, *, cents: float) -> Source: ...           # a source, for layering
    @classmethod
    def from_harmonics(cls, harmonics: Harmonics) -> Wave: ...
    @classmethod
    def from_points(cls, points: Sequence[WavePoint], *, shape: str = 'linear',
                    normalize: bool = True) -> Wave: ...
    @classmethod
    def from_samples(cls, *, levels: Sequence[float], resolution_bits: int | None = None,
                     normalize: bool = True) -> Wave: ...       # M4
    @classmethod
    def from_sprite(cls, path: Path | str) -> Wave: ...         # M4

class Noise:
    def __init__(self, kind: str = 'white', *, level: float = 1.0, seed: int | None = None,
                 bits: int = 15, taps: tuple[int, int] | None = None,
                 rate: PitchLike | None = None) -> None: ...

class WaveTable:                                                 # M4
    def __init__(self, waves: Sequence[str | Wave]) -> None: ...

class WaveRegistry:
    def register(self, name: str, wave: Wave) -> None: ...   # ValueError on a built-in name

# --- instruments ---
class Instrument:                                            # immutable; hashable by content
    def __init__(self, *, wave: str | Wave | None = None, noise: str | Noise | None = None,
                 sources: Mapping[str, Wave | Noise | Source] | None = None,
                 envelope: Envelope | str = 'pluck', filter: Filter | None = None,
                 drive: float = 0.0, profile: str = 'hybrid', live: bool = False,
                 seed: int | None = None, normalize: bool = False,
                 hard_edges: bool = False) -> None: ...      # exactly one of wave/noise/sources
    @classmethod
    def load(cls, path: Path | str) -> Instrument: ...       # 'file.toml#name'

# --- engine.py ---
SoundSource = str | Instrument | Sequence_          # name, path, instrument, (M5) sequence

class AudioEngine:
    waves: WaveRegistry
    buses: BusTree
    music: MusicTransport            # M5
    tuning: Tuning
    sounds: SoundLibrary             # warm(), names(), cache statistics

    def sound(self, source: SoundSource, *, pitch: PitchLike | None = None,
              notes: str | Sequence[tuple[PitchLike, float]] | None = None,
              chord: Sequence[PitchLike] | None = None, length: float | None = None,
              transpose: float = 0.0,
              parameters: Mapping[str, float] | None = None) -> Sound: ...
    def play(self, source: SoundSource, *, pitch: PitchLike | None = None,
             notes: str | Sequence[tuple[PitchLike, float]] | None = None,
             chord: Sequence[PitchLike] | None = None, length: float | None = None,
             transpose: float = 0.0, parameters: Mapping[str, float] | None = None,
             volume: float | None = None, pan: float | None = None, bus: str | None = None,
             priority: int | None = None, loop: bool | None = None,
             at_frame: int | None = None, persist: bool = False,
             position: tuple[float, float] | None = None) -> SoundHandle: ...
             # = self.sound(identity...).play(playback...)
    def beep(self, *, pitch: PitchLike = 'A4', wave: str = 'square', length: float = 0.1,
             volume: float = 0.5, bus: str = 'effects') -> SoundHandle: ...
    def diagnostics(self) -> AudioDiagnostics: ...
    def stop_all(self, *, fade: float = 0.05, bus: str | None = None) -> None: ...

class Sound:                         # compiled, immutable, shared; returned by sound()
    name: str                        # the short name, the path, or a generated name
    length: float                    # seconds, including the release tail (baked)
    peak: float                      # length, peak and sample_rate are fixed at the first
                                     # request under any cache mode and survive eviction
    is_live: bool
    def play(self, *, volume: float | None = None, pan: float | None = None,
             bus: str | None = None, priority: int | None = None, loop: bool | None = None,
             at_frame: int | None = None, persist: bool = False,
             position: tuple[float, float] | None = None) -> SoundHandle: ...
             # None = the sound file's default, else the engine default
    def start(self, *, parameters: Mapping[str, float] | None = None,
              volume: float | None = None, pan: float | None = None, bus: str | None = None,
              priority: int | None = None, persist: bool = False) -> LiveSoundHandle: ...
              # live sounds only; TypeError on a baked sound

class SoundHandle:   # frozen (slot, generation); methods consult the engine's voice table
    def stop(self, *, fade: float = 0.05) -> bool: ...
    def cancel(self) -> bool: ...
    def release(self) -> bool: ...            # live: envelope release; looping baked: end loop
    def unschedule(self) -> bool: ...         # M2
    @property
    def is_playing(self) -> bool: ...
    def set_volume(self, volume: float, *, fade: float = 0.0) -> bool: ...
    def set_pan(self, pan: float) -> bool: ...

class LiveSoundHandle(SoundHandle):
    def set(self, parameter: str, value: float) -> bool: ...   # KeyError for an unknown name
    def note_on(self, pitch: PitchLike, *, velocity: float = 1.0) -> bool: ...
    def note_off(self) -> bool: ...

class SoundLibrary:
    def warm(self, requests: Sequence[Mapping[str, object]], *,
             budget_ms: float | None = None) -> float: ...       # progress 0-1
    def names(self) -> tuple[str, ...]: ...                      # the short names indexed
    def statistics(self) -> CacheStatistics: ...

def render_to_file(sound: Sound, path: Path | str, *, sample_rate: int | None = None,
                   sample_format: str = 'int16', loops: int = 1,
                   tail_seconds: float | None = None, stems: bool = False,
                   parameter_timeline: Mapping[str, Sequence[tuple[float, float]]] | None = None,
                   events: Sequence[OfflineEvent] = ()) -> RenderReport: ...

Rules:

  • Identity arguments: pitch, notes and chord are mutually exclusive (ValueError). transpose applies to notes and chord. parameters is a dict, so parameter names can never collide with keyword arguments.
  • Playback arguments left as None take the sound file's [sounds.*] defaults, then the engine's defaults.
  • Errors: SoundAssetError (file problems, duplicate names), SoundRenderError (a compile bug), KeyError (unknown short name or parameter) and ValueError (invalid argument). The new errors derive from the existing glitchygames.audio.exceptions hierarchy [Fact: AudioUnavailableError, SoundRecipeError].
  • No mixer: sound() compiles to float buffers (no pygame.mixer.Sound), so offline rendering and tests work. play() returns a handle whose methods return False, and a warning is logged once (AUD-FUNC-006).
  • Access point: SceneManager.audio, a property creating the AudioEngine on first use, as live_audio does today [Fact: scene.py:1262]. It is a ContextSlot value, so each engine context has its own library, voices and short-name index. [Call] M1 adds only the slot. Muting all but the audible context is Arcade work, done with the Arcade.
  • Scene.SOUND_DIRECTORY is a class attribute (default 'sounds'), resolved relative to the scene's package directory (identity.game_identity(...).package_directory [Fact]). The index is per directory, so scenes sharing a directory share it.
  • Compatibility: scene_manager.live_audio stays. In M2 it is implemented on the new voice table.

docs.title: 9. Determinism and offline rendering
docs.text:
• Scope (D8): bit-identical output for a fixed AUDIO_RENDER_VERSION, Python, numpy, platform tag, sample rate, configuration, asset set, seeds and parameter timeline. Across platforms, comparisons use a tolerance of max |Δ| ≤ 2⁻¹⁴ (about −84 dBFS) on float buffers before int16 conversion, because numpy's sin/exp may differ in the last ULPs.
  • Offline mixer:
  • It sums the float buffers of compiled sounds at round(event_seconds × rate), applying the same volume and pan law as §7.2, with bus stems if asked.
  • Live sounds are rendered offline by stepping their chunk renderer through a scripted parameter timeline. That is the same code as the device path, with the same chunking.
  • Parity: device-path parity is tested on the pre-device buffers. The buffer that feeds pygame.mixer.Sound must equal, bit for bit, the buffer OfflineMixer uses for a single event at offset 0. The device's own mixing (SDL, int16 saturation) is out of scope.
  • Tail termination: rendering stops when the output stays under −90 dBFS for 100 ms after the last event's nominal end, or at tail_seconds. The stop is reported in RenderReport with the peak and the clip count.
  • Recording soundtracks (M5, feature spec §13.3):
  • Each frame logs its plays (audio_events: sound identity, playback arguments) as a measurement field. It is never compared or served, like processing_seconds [Fact].
  • glitchygames sound render-recording run.jsonl.gz mixes them offline.

docs.title: 10.1 CRT power-on sound (M1)
docs.text:
• The sounds: a new leaf module, src/glitchygames/crt_power_on_sound.py, holds the CRT instruments and their tunable named constants (FLYBACK_WHINE_HZ, DEGAUSS_HUM_HZ = 60.0, BARS_TONE_HZ = 1000.0, STATIC_SEED). It requests them through audio.engine_sound(Instrument(...), pitch=..., length=...), the engine's own sounds' sound (SoundLibrary.engine_sound): the same identity, compile path and accounting as games' audio.sound, with one cache of its own.
  • Compiled once per process [Owner] (2026-11-02: "it'll be used at least once, but possibly multiple times, if we're playing in the arcade"): the CRT's compiled samples are kept in a process-wide cache owned by the engine (glitchygames.audio.library.ENGINE_SOUND_CACHE), keyed by each sound's identity key (§6.2: it holds the mixer's rate and the tuning, so a mixer restarted at another rate compiles anew and never reuses a wrong-rate sound). Every later power-on in the process reuses them: a second game run in one process (the Arcade, the test harness's repeated engines) and every engine context compiles nothing for the CRT.
  • Scope: only the engine's own CRT sounds. Game sounds stay per engine context in each context's SoundLibrary, and each context keeps its own AudioEngine, voices and accounting.
  • What is shared: the compiled samples (float64 and int16, made read-only) with their peak and rate, never a Sound: each library makes its own Sound over them, because a Sound carries its context's player (attach_player, the engine whose voices play it) and its own pygame sound, built from the samples on its first play. A pygame Sound could be played from several channels at once, but sharing one would tie every context to the mixer it was built on; building one per context is a copy of the samples, not a compile. The cache is a read-only cache in the engine context's sense (plans/2026-10-25-engine-context.md: values computed only from their keys, never written after they are made).
  • Cache mode and memory limit: the cache is exempt from both. Under --sound-cache none the CRT's sounds stay compiled and their plays compile nothing (none is a game's benchmark switch; the CRT is engine-owned); the memory limit never evicts them, and bytes_held leaves them out.
  • Accounting: the first compile is counted and attributed like any compile, in the context that triggered it (a miss, a setup compile, in its compile log); every reuse is a counted cache hit.
  • Lazy: they compile on the first power-on that plays its sound, so headless runs, tests that never power on and --crt-power-on-sound off pay nothing. Tests start with an empty cache (tests/harness.py empty_engine_sound_cache).
  • The cue hook: crt_power_on.play_power_on and play_power_on_async get one new keyword argument, sound_cues: PowerOnSoundCues | None = None. It is a small protocol:
  • at_progress(progress), called every power-on frame with the same progress value that drives the picture (§12.1 cues are progress fractions); each cue starts on the frame nearest its point, the next frame's progress predicted from the last step (ruling R42), so at a steady frame rate a sound is at most half a frame off;
  • skip(), which fades every CRT voice with Channel.fadeout(20). [Open] (AUD-CRT-003, ruling R41): SDL_mixer 2.8 recomputes a fading channel's volume once per mixing callback (mix_channels in src/mixer.c, from SDL_GetTicks) and applies it to the whole chunk (512 frames, about 11.6 ms), so the 20 ms fade is a plateau or two and then a halt, not a ramp. The voices end within 20 ms plus one chunk; the step on a pure tone is measured against the model in tests/test_crt_power_on_sound.py (a strict xfail holds the "no step above threshold" criterion). [Measured] (M1, 2026-11-02, tests/audio/test_channel_fades.py on SDL's disk driver): the model holds on the device: Channel.fadeout(20) on a 1 kHz tone is one or two plateaus then a halt, every level change on a chunk boundary, with a worst step 4.5 to 4.9 times the tone's own largest (from 1.0 to 4.9 across twelve skips; the model's worst over eight phases is 3.4). The criterion stays unmet (strict xfails in both test files). [Open] The owner's listening check decides whether the skip is heard as a click; the fallback, engine-rendered fade tails (risk R5), awaits the owner's decision;
  • frame(dt), which drives audio.update(dt=...) for the system owner (§7.3).

This keeps crt_power_on.py a leaf with no audio import [Fact: it is a leaf today], and tests pass a recording fake. - Wiring: GameEngine._power_on_sound_cues compiles the CRT sounds (a few ms, the first time in the process) and makes the cues when --crt-power-on-sound is not off; _run_game (the blocking start) and start_async (the browser's) call it, and pass the cues to the power-on, when _power_on_plays() (should_play) is true. The headless, replay, recording, audit and rebaseline rules are inherited from should_play [Fact]. - Carrying into the game: the bars tone (or channel 3 hiss) is a system-owned, persisting voice. AudioEngine holds a pending "fade the CRT tail" action, which the first AudioEngine.update of frame 0 performs (fadeout(500)). No scene owns the voice, so scene cleanup never stops it early. - Browser: boot.py waits for a click before the game starts [Fact], so the audio context is running when the power-on plays. [Open] This needs a real-browser listening check (AUD-PORT-003), the owner's: nox -s browser -- mr-muncher, then click the page in Chrome and in Safari. Not yet done (2026-11-02).

docs.title: 10.3 Replays, silence, scenes, shutdown
docs.text:
• Silence: FrameSilencer stops channels [Fact] and calls audio.silenced(...), which quiets the channels without ending their voices (§7.3).
  • Scenes: scene ownership and pausing behind a playback scope follow today's LiveAudio.update arguments [Fact]. AudioEngine.update takes the same ones.
  • Shutdown: GameEngine._shutdown calls audio.close() before pygame.quit(). That fades everything over 50 ms and waits at most 100 ms with clock.raw_sleep [Fact: the only allowed sleep].

docs.title: 10.4 Migration and clean-up (M2), and legacy parity (fixes the builder check's third finding)
docs.text:
Version 0 recipes compile through today's renderer. A [recipes.*] table (version 0) resolves to a LegacyRecipeSpec, and its compile calls SoundRecipe.render() unchanged [Fact: recipes.py]. That means no de-click ramps, no normalization changes and the same noise source as today, so the audio is bit-identical (AUD-FUNC-010). glitchygames sound migrate converts a file to version 1 when an author wants the new features; migrated sounds then follow the v1 rules and are checked by listening.

Today After SoundBank(ALL_RECIPES) + prerender() + play(name) audio.sound(name) in setup + .play(). SoundBank is removed Brave Adventurer's _generate_*_sound() functions Instrument(...) requests; GameSounds and its generator functions are removed scene_manager.live_audio.create_voice(waveform=..., frequency=..., low_pass_cutoff=...) audio.sound(Instrument(..., live=True)).start(parameters={'speed': ...}); live_audio and create_voice are removed game_objects.sounds.load_sound(file) audio.sound('sfx_slap') (a recorded file by short name); load_sound and the SFX constants are removed NOTE_FREQUENCIES tables unchanged, or PitchTable.from_dict(NOTE_FREQUENCIES)

Mr. Muncher and Clockwork Keep define their recipes in Python (ALL_RECIPES [Fact]), not TOML. audio.sounds.add_recipes(ALL_RECIPES) registers them as short names, a thin adapter that exists only for migration and compiles nothing. Brave Adventurer's re-authored sounds are compared within 1 LSB, or by RMS spectrum within 0.5 dB plus listening for noise.

Clean-up [Owner: "complete the API migration to clean everything up"; Call: removal, not deprecation]. Once all five games are migrated, the old paths are deleted from the engine in the same milestone: SoundBank, load_sound/SFX, the live_audio property and LiveAudio.create_voice (its chunk machinery lives on inside the new live voices), and each game's own generator code. The synth functions stay as the renderer's building blocks. add_recipes goes too, once the recipes are TOML (glitchygames sound migrate). Removal rather than a deprecation period is safe because neither the engine nor any game is published on PyPI yet [Fact: CLAUDE.md, Development Setup], so nothing outside this repository depends on them. Tests of removed code are removed with it; the 100% coverage gate holds.

docs.title: 10.5 The Audio debug panel (M1; live section M2; replay comparison M3)
docs.text:
The overlay's structure is kept [Fact: src/glitchygames/debug/overlay.py DebugPanel (F4 cycles in declaration order), panels.py with one draw_*_panel function per panel, DebugFrameInfo handed in each frame]:

  • DebugPanel.AUDIO = 'audio' is added after PERFORMANCE.
  • DebugFrameInfo gains audio: AudioDiagnosticsSnapshot | None. It replaces today's live_voice_count field, whose one line moves into the snapshot.
  • AudioEngine.update builds the snapshot once per frame. It is an immutable dataclass:
  • the cache mode, device format and voice counts;
  • the frame's accounting by kind;
  • the channel states (from the voice table, plus Channel.get_busy() for fading; display only);
  • bus levels;
  • the compile log ring (8 entries);
  • (M2) live voices' parameter values and queue state.
  • DebugOverlay keeps a rolling deque of per-frame audio work by kind, beside its frame-time history and over the same GRAPH_WINDOW_SECONDS [Fact]. The audio-time graph and the frame-time graph therefore share an x-axis.
  • draw_audio_panel(surface=..., overlay=..., font=..., frame_info=...) follows draw_performance_panel's conventions [Fact]: the cached translucent backings, the bundled font and HUD_* constants. Its new colour constants (compile red, decode orange, live blue, cache grey; channel idle, playing, fading, paused) sit beside the existing HUD colours.
  • The All panel draws only the header lines, through a draw_audio_header helper.
  • Watched replays (M3): the replay viewer already draws the overlay [Fact: rule list in replay/viewer.py]. When the recording's frames carry audio_seconds, the snapshot includes the recorded value for the frame being shown, drawn as a second, outlined bar per column.
  • Cost: overlay drawing is inside the measured frame time, as the Performance panel's footnote already says [Fact]. The benchmarks run with the overlay off, and the panel's own draw cost is measured once and noted on the Sound Performance page.
  • Tests: pixel assertions on the presented surface, per the repo's rule of asserting on drawn pixels rather than draw calls [Fact: CLAUDE.md, Testing Guidelines]:
  • a synthetic history with a gameplay compile at a known frame puts the compile colour in that frame's graph column;
  • each channel state's cell colour;
  • the compile log's red entry;
  • the panel's absence from Scene.screenshot.

docs.title: 11.0 Measurement design (M3; accounting from M1) [Owner]
docs.text:
Order. Migration and clean-up first (M2). Then the benchmarks run with the cache off (none), then ram, then disk (the disk layer is built at the start of M3, after the none and ram rows exist).

The "before" baseline is the replay ledger's rows at the commit before the migration [Fact: quality/replay-ledger/, one row per recording per commit and machine]. The Sound Performance page reads those rows for the games with sound and plots them beside the post-migration rows (AUD-MEAS-007). Nothing is added to code that M2 deletes.

Per-frame accounting (built in M1):

  • audio/accounting.py keeps a frame accumulator. A context manager, audio_work(kind, name), adds the elapsed clock.raw_counter_ns() to it. The kinds are compile, decode, live_chunk and cache_read.
  • At the end of each frame, SceneManager hands the accumulator to the doors with processing_seconds [Fact: end_frame(processing_seconds=...)] and resets it.
  • RecordingSources writes audio_seconds (float) and audio_work (a list of [kind, name, microseconds], at most 32 entries, the rest summed into one ["other", "", µs] entry). Both are added to MEASUREMENT_FRAME_FIELDS [Fact: recording_history.py], so they never enter a content hash and are never compared or served.
  • The cost of accounting itself (two counter reads per piece of work) is measured in the storm at k = 0 and reported.

Result rows.

  • A glitchygames sound-benchmark tool, registered in registry.TOOLS like measure [Fact], runs the three A/B tests under a chosen mode. It writes one JSON row per benchmark, mode and machine to quality/sound-ledger/, carrying the same provenance fields as LedgerRow (MeasurementRun: machine, versions, source revision, machine state [Fact]).
  • Rows are committed by hand after a run (nox -s sound-benchmark), not by the pre-commit hook: a full run takes minutes, not the hook's seconds.

The page. docs/quality/sound_performance.md is rendered by the docs hook through the same path as the replay performance page [Fact: scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py → performance_pages], with bokeh (an existing dependency [Fact: pyproject.toml]). Its charts:

Chart Data Reads Compile cost per sound the per-sound benchmark horizontal bars grouped by game, log ms axis, 1 ms and 16.7 ms lines The storm storm rows per mode p99 frame processing (and frames over budget) against k, one line per mode, in the order none → ram → disk; audio_seconds as a band under the none line Frame timelines real-game rebaselines per recording, none and ram frame processing overlaid, audio work shaded, a rug of frames that played a sound; zoomable Distributions real-game rebaselines ECDF of frame processing per mode Live chunks Clockwork Keep's elevator under each mode chunk cost histogram and its per-frame pattern Startup disk cold vs warm time from launch to the first frame Before and after the migration replay ledger rows p50/p99 per golden replay at the two commits By commit all rows each benchmark's p99 per mode by commit

The page opens with the findings in words, and each chart carries a one-line reading of it.

The A/B works without any sprite difference between the modes. --rebaseline records each run's processing_seconds whatever the frames compare, and --compare-processing reads only those [Fact: replay/processing.py]. Each record includes:

  • the reference hardware [Owner]:
Tier Machine Role Worst case Raspberry Pi 4 (RAM TBD), booting from an SD card, passively cooled, stock clocks every gate is set from this tier, from the slower of its two OSes Mid Raspberry Pi 5 (RAM TBD), booting from an SD card, the official case with its fan, stock clocks the typical Pi High Raspberry Pi 5 16 GB, booting from an NVMe SSD, in a Thrml Neo 5 NVMe PCIe case (direct-contact heatsink and fan), overclocked within the warranty the best a Pi does Desktop Apple M4 Max the high end (the Appendix A machine) Stand-in The CI Linux container (1 CPU, 2 GB [Fact: nox -s test-linux-ci]) automated, between Pi runs
  • Pi operating systems: each Pi tier runs on Ubuntu 26.04 and on the latest Raspberry Pi OS. The owner has two boards per tier, so one per OS. Python 3.14 comes from uv on both.
  • Pi provenance: each row records the board, RAM, OS and kernel, boot storage, cooling, overclock settings, temperatures and clocks, and whether the run throttled. Timed runs follow a thermal warm-up.
  • Runners: the Pis are measured by hand until self-hosted Pi runners exist (a separate branch, plans/future-work.md "Raspberry Pi hardware runners", which details the provenance and thermal protocol).
  • Each machine and OS is its own line on the charts;
  • the OS, driver, rate and buffer;
  • the workload;
  • percentiles, maximum, underruns and memory.

The thresholds above are proposals, to be fixed after the M1 measurements (the brief requires measured gates).

docs.title: 11.2 Deployment
docs.text: Nothing new to install: numpy and pygame-ce are already runtime dependencies [Fact]. The engine wheel gains only the CRT module. CI runs every sound test on the dummy driver. Browser bundles ship the same modules.

docs.title: M1 — One-call sound API + CRT (first implementable milestone)
docs.text:
1. pitch.py (types, scales, PitchTable, Tuning, resolve_pitch) + tests.
  2. waves.py (built-ins, mix/blend, registry, Harmonics, WavePoint/CYCLE/LEVEL, mip tables) + spectral tests.
  3. render.py for M1: oscillators, white and LFSR noise, ADSR curves and presets, pitch curves, up to 4 layered sources, FIR filter, drive, notes/chord/transpose/length, boundary de-click, peak report.
  4. assets.py: v1 models for the M1 fields (§6.1), "arrives in Mx" rejection, v0 recipes as LegacyRecipeSpec, error formatting, the malformed corpus (≥ 20 cases), the short-name index.
  5. library.py: sound() resolution, identity hashing and memoization, compile accounting (setup vs gameplay frames), the memory cache with its LRU limit, warm, add_recipes.
  6. voices.py/buses.py: the channel partition (§7.1), table allocation and stealing, handles with generations, played_seconds with pause, constant-power pan, bus volume/mute/solo.
  7. engine.py: the facade, the SceneManager.audio slot, update(dt) in the frame, the FrameSilencer hook, shutdown, beep, play shorthand.
  8. offline.py: render_to_file; the glitchygames sound render and migrate subcommands.
  9. Diagnostics, the M1 --sound-* options (§10.2) including --sound-cache none|ram, and the per-frame accounting fields (§11.0).
  10. The Audio debug panel (§10.5): header, audio-time graph, channel strip, bus meters and the compile log; --sound-diagnostics.
  11. CRT power-on sound (§10.1), with the owner's listening sign-off.
  12. Sound Board demo (src/demos/sound-board-demo/, console script sound-board-demo).
  13. Verify the open M1 items: fadeout then play on a channel (§7.1), frame-stepped bus fades (§7.2), and the CRT sound in a browser bundle (§10.1).
  14. Docs: docs/architecture/sound.md (with an mkdocs nav entry), the CLAUDE.md "Sound Synthesis" section, and plans/future-features.md #53 marked built for the sound.

docs.title: 13. Decision register
docs.text: # Decision Resolution D1 Voices vs sources/operators A voice is one playing instance. Baked voices cost a mixer channel and no Python time. Live voices cost render time by sources × stages. Diagnostics report voices, live sources and live render time separately D2 Default limits and quality tiers 32 library channels, 8 legacy channels, 4 live voices (8 if measured OK). Quality is full for compiled sounds and draft for live ones. The brief's 64-voice target applies to baked voices only (SDL's C mixer); 64 live voices in Python is rejected (A.2/A.3) D3 DSP and backend Option A (§3). The native core is gated in M6 [Open, with the experiment and fallback in §3.4] D4 Integration with pygame/SDL A shared device. The library is a layer over pygame.mixer, which stays the only owner. The channel partition keeps the library and legacy callers apart (§7.1) D5 Clock, queue, ordering, late events The frame clock and served dt for voice bookkeeping and scheduling; sample frames inside compiled sounds. No queue (single thread). Plays issue in call order within a frame. Late scheduled plays (M2) have a 2-frame tolerance, then drop, counted D6 Schema, versioning, extension TOML, .toml, [glitchygames] kind = "sounds", version = 1; v0 recipes compile through today's renderer. The owner was offered .sound.toml and has not asked for it; the default stands unless changed D6b The cache [Owner] A tri-state: None (nothing kept; every play compiles), 'ram', 'disk' (§6.4). The disk layer is persistent and pruned by the engine [Call], from M3 D12 Order of work [Owner] Build the API (M1), migrate every game and remove the old paths (M2), then benchmark: cache off, then ram, then disk (M3). The pre-migration replay-ledger rows are the baseline D7 Modulation and feedback limits, processing order ≤ 8 routes, acyclic. FM feedback 0–1 with a one-sample averaged delay. Order: sources → source envelopes → mix → filter (+env) → amp env → effects → gain/pan → bus → master D8 Determinism and parity §9: bit-identical within a fixed environment, a tolerance across platforms, parity on pre-device buffers D9 Platform, packaging, licensing No new dependencies. Native (including Linux ARM64 on Raspberry Pi ⅘, the low-end reference), headless and browser (compiled sounds) are supported; browser live sound is an open item; the Pi install path is risk R12 (Appendix B) D10 Milestones, gates, deferred scope §12, with the §11 gates set after the M1 measurements. Deferred: real-time bus effects, a master limiter, sample-accurate transitions, voice virtualization, hardware emulation D11 The one API [Owner] audio.sound(...) compiles on first request and returns the cached sound afterwards; getting never plays; setup is a convention. Short names and paths are both accepted (feature spec §3.2)

docs.title: Signal flow
docs.text:
per voice ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  per bus ────── master
 [src1]─env─┐
 [src2]─env─┼─ mix ─ filter(+env) ─ amp env ─ effects ─ gain ─ pan ─► channel ─► bus gain/duck ─► SDL mix ─► device
 [src3]─env─┤        ▲                ▲                    ▲
 [src4]─env─┘        └──── routes (envelopes, LFOs, velocity, game parameters, smoothed) ────┘
 (left of "channel": compiled once, or rendered in live chunks; right of it: SDL's C mixer)

docs.title: 15. Risk register (most severe first)
docs.text: # Risk Likelihood Impact Mitigation R1 Live voices underrun on slow machines (the Raspberry Pi 4 especially) or in the browser (main-thread chunks miss the margin) Medium–High Audible gaps in engines and ambience Keep the pool small; measure on the CI Linux profile and in the browser; restart-on-underrun exists [Fact]; prefer compiled loops where a sound need not follow a parameter R2 The owner later wants real-time bus effects or sample-accurate music, which option A cannot deliver Medium Rework of the output layer The renderer is pure and backend-agnostic; the native-core gate is defined (§3.4) R3 Games request sounds first in gameplay and hitch on big instruments Medium Frame spikes Diagnostics name every gameplay compile with its frame; the docs and the Sound Board model the setup convention; the A/B benchmark shows the cost R4 Channel.fadeout then play on the same channel cuts the steal fade Measured: it does (M1, §7.1) Clicks on stealing The §7.1 one-frame delay, kept. It is not enough: SDL_mixer steps the 10 ms fade per chunk, so a steal is a plateau or a halt (§7.1, measured); a longer steal fade or rendered fade tails, the owner's decision R5 Frame-rate volume steps cause zipper noise on bus fades and ducking Measured: steps of a third at chunk boundaries for a 50 ms fade (§7.2) Audible stepping Listening check; Channel.fadeout is stepped per chunk too (§10.1, measured); fallback of rendered fade tails R6 Variant counts (pitches × parameters) grow compile time and memory Medium Slow scene starts, memory pressure (44.1 kHz s16 stereo ≈ 10 MB/min) Diagnostics, warm with a budget, the disk cache (M2), mono compiles panned by channel volume (halves memory), the LRU limit R7 Browser audio differs (ScriptProcessorNode deprecation, autoplay, queue/end callbacks) Medium The browser is silent or glitchy The compiled path is verified for basic play [Fact]; explicit browser checks per milestone R8 Floating-point differences make cross-platform golden audio flaky Medium Flaky tests Tolerances (§9); golden comparisons per platform tag only R9 Scope creep (FM, music, editor) delays the visible win Medium The owner sees nothing for weeks M1 is small and ends with the CRT sound and the Sound Board R10 Short-name ambiguity across files surprises authors Low Confusing errors Duplicates raise naming both files; paths are always available R12 The Pi install path: numpy resolves to 1.26.4, which has no Python 3.14 wheel on any platform, and miniaudio 1.71 has no Linux ARM64 wheel, so both build from source on a Pi [Fact: uv.lock] High (for the Pi) No Pi measurements until it installs Settle on the Pi runners branch (plans/future-work.md) before M3's Pi runs R11 Copyright or likeness concerns with "inspired by" presets Low Legal or reputational Original presets only; a review checklist item (AUD-RETRO-004)

docs.title: 16. Summary
docs.text:
Recommended architecture:

  • pygame.mixer stays the only device owner.
  • One call, audio.sound(...), takes a short name, a path or an Instrument. The first request compiles the sound into memory, later requests return it from the engine-owned cache, and .play() plays it.
  • The surrounding API covers pitch types (notes, hertz, MIDI and scale steps side by side), named and blendable waves whose numbers are named, and TOML instruments.
  • Continuously controlled sounds render in live chunks on the main thread, extending today's LiveVoice.
  • There are no new dependencies and no new threads, and nothing new for replays, headless runs or the browser's compiled-sound path to learn.

Demonstrated by experiment (Appendix A, throwaway):

  • a numpy renderer is fast when uncontended (64 voices at about 9% of a 256-frame budget);
  • the same renderer on an audio thread misses deadlines badly under GIL contention;
  • render-ahead on a worker needs about 85 ms of lookahead under a busy loop;
  • today's recipe and live-chunk costs are small.

Still proposals:

  • every API shape and default, and the schema;
  • the cache and disk layout;
  • the DSP algorithm choices (from cited literature);
  • the stealing, fading and bus behaviours on pygame's channels (R4 and R5 need M1 checks);
  • all performance gates.

Main risks: live-voice underruns on slow targets (R1), a future need for real-time effects that option A cannot meet (R2), and gameplay-time compiles (R3, made visible by diagnostics).

Order of work [Owner]: API (M1), then migration and clean-up (M2), then measurement with the cache off, ram, then disk (M3), then the deeper features.

First implementable milestone (M1): the pitch, wave and instrument API; audio.sound(...) with compile-on-first-request, short names and paths; notes and chords; buses and voice management with the legacy channel partition; offline render to WAV; the CRT power-on sound; the Sound Board demo; and the A/B benchmark that measures the smoothness claim.

docs.title: Appendix A — Feasibility measurements (throwaway; not in the repository)
docs.text: Machine: Apple M4 Max, macOS (Darwin 27.0), Python 3.14.8, numpy 1.26.4, pygame-ce 2.5.8 (SDL 2.32.10), miniaudio 1.71, on 2026-11-02. The scripts were kept in the session scratchpad and are disposable. The method is described here so it can be repeated.

docs.title: A.1 Uncontended block render (64 voices, 48 kHz, numpy vectorized across voices)
docs.text:
• Workload A: phase accumulation + PolyBLEP square + linear envelope + constant-power pan to stereo.
  • Workload B: A + a state-variable filter as a Python loop over samples (numpy across voices).
  • Workload C: A + a scipy lfilter biquad. scipy is present only transitively, through aisuite, and is not a proposed dependency.
Block Budget A p50 / p99 / max B p50 / p99 C p50 / p99 128 2.67 ms 0.23 / 0.28 / 0.41 ms 0.46 / 0.53 ms 0.27 / 0.64 ms 256 5.33 ms 0.40 / 0.47 / 0.50 ms 0.88 / 0.94 ms 0.48 / 0.56 ms 512 10.67 ms 0.78 / 0.94 / 1.96 ms 1.77 / 1.88 ms 0.92 / 1.03 ms

docs.title: A.2 Python render in a device callback under GIL contention
docs.text:
A miniaudio.PlaybackDevice (float32, stereo, 48 kHz) rendered workload A in its generator on each callback. Meanwhile another thread ran pure-Python arithmetic continuously, a worst-case busy game loop.

Switch interval Render time in callback, p99 Callback period p50 5 ms (Python default) 256.6 ms 230 ms 1 ms 58.4 ms 50 ms 0.2 ms 12.7 ms 15 ms

Each numpy call releases and reacquires the GIL, and every reacquisition waits behind the busy thread. Even at 0.2 ms the render takes more than twice the 5.33 ms budget. Conclusion: option B is rejected.

docs.title: A.3 Render-ahead worker + copy-only callback under the same contention
docs.text:
A worker thread rendered 256-frame blocks into a ring, and the miniaudio callback only copied bytes. The switch interval was 0.5 ms, the engine's own [Fact]. Each run lasted 5 seconds.

Ring (lookahead) Workload Underrun blocks / callbacks Callback copy p99 Render p50 / p99 4 (21 ms) C 145 / 980 0.017 ms 3.10 / 18.4 ms 8 (43 ms) A 68 / 973 0.018 ms 1.89 / 19.7 ms 8 (43 ms) B 156 / 995 0.016 ms 4.10 / 18.2 ms 16 (85 ms) B 18 / 991 0.015 ms 3.87 / 15.7 ms 16 (85 ms) C 0 / 967 0.015 ms 2.30 / 20.2 ms 8 × 512 (85 ms) C 291 / 450 0.025 ms 5.56 / 28.1 ms

The copy-only callback is cheap, but the worker inherits the contention: render p99 is 15–28 ms. Underruns stop only at about 85 ms of lookahead, which is today's live-chunk margin [Fact: ≈ 88 ms]. Conclusion: option C buys nothing over A, so it is rejected for M1–M5. A real game loop sleeps for part of each frame, so these numbers are pessimistic. A is still preferred because it has no contention at all.

The pygame._sdl2.audio.AudioDevice variant of this test hung on start in this environment and was abandoned without investigation, since the miniaudio variant answered the question.
